en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nuns in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
1. Ekakanipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of a Certain Elder Nun (Aññatarātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā).
Now, the opportunity has arrived for the commentary on the meaning of the verses of the elder nuns (therīgāthā). In this regard, since [the verses] of the bhikkhunīs...

Having first explained how his going-forth and full ordination were obtained, it will be easy and clear to elucidate the origin of the verses (*aṭṭhuppatti*) as they are presented in the commentary on the meaning; therefore, to explain that, here is this brief sequential narrative starting from the beginning: The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying at Madhurā in the Ghaṭā Monastery. Then, while the Venerable Mahākaccāna was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in his mind: “It is a gain for me, it is a great fortune for me, that I have obtained the going-forth under the Blessed One and the full ordination. It would be well if I were to go and visit the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then the Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed a certain bhikkhu: “Come, friend, go to the Blessed One and, having approached him, pay homage in my name with your head at his feet, and say: ‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet. Then say: ‘Venerable sir, it would be well if the Blessed One were to grant the Venerable Mahākaccāna permission to visit him. “Yes, friend,” that bhikkhu replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna. He went to the Blessed One, and after approaching and paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and says: ‘Venerable sir, it would be well if the Blessed One were to grant the Venerable Mahākaccāna permission to visit him. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been free from illness, free from affliction, and living in comfort? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been free from illness, free from affliction, and living in comfort. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been diligent in his practice? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been diligent in his practice. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to meditation? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to meditation. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to wakefulness? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to wakefulness. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to solitude? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to solitude. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of concentration? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of concentration. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of insight? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of insight. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the path? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the path. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the fruits? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the fruits. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of Nibbāna? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of Nibbāna. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the Dhamma? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the Dhamma. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the Saṅgha? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the Saṅgha. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the self? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the self. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of mindfulness? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of mindfulness. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of wisdom? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of wisdom. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of virtue? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of virtue. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of concentration? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of concentration. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of energy? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of energy. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of joy? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of joy. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of equanimity? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of equanimity. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of loving-kindness? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of loving-kindness. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of compassion? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of compassion. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of sympathetic joy? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of sympathetic joy. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of equanimity? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of equanimity. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the foundations of mindfulness? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the foundations of mindfulness. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the right efforts? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the right efforts. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the bases of psychic power? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the bases of psychic power. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the faculties? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the faculties. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the powers? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the powers. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the factors of enlightenment. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the Noble Eightfold Path? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the Noble Eightfold Path. “Friend, has the Venerable Mahākaccāna been devoted to the development of the Dhamma-eye? “Yes, venerable sir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna has been devoted to the development of the Dhamma-eye. “Friend,
For this Lord of the World, having combined the eight factors stated as "human birth, perfection of gender," and so forth,
and having made his great resolve at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, fulfilled the thirty pāramīs, received the prophecy from twenty-four Buddhas,
and gradually completed the pāramīs through the conduct for one's own benefit and the conduct for the benefit of the world—

Having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven; remaining there for the full duration of his lifespan, he was exhorted by the devas of ten thousand world-systems to attain Buddhahood:
"It is now the time for you, O Great Hero, to descend into a mother’s womb."
"Delivering the world together with its gods, awaken to the deathless state!
Having thus been entreated by those deities who desired his rebirth among humans, he gave them his promise;

then, having performed the five great observations, he entered the womb of his mother, mindful and clearly comprehending, while remaining in the house of King Mahāsuddhodana of the Śākya clan, mindful and clearly comprehending for ten months.
Having stayed there, mindful and clearly comprehending, he emerged from it; then, having attained his noble birth in the Lumbinī grove,
being properly cared for with great honor— beginning with various nurses— and gradually reaching maturity,
experiencing prosperity like a god surrounded by diverse theatrical troupes in three palaces, [he was moved] by the sight of an old man, a sick man, and a dead man.

Having become filled with spiritual urgency due to the ripening of his wisdom, and having seen the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, on the very day Prince Rāhula was born, accompanied by Channa, he mounted the noble horse Kaṇḍaka.
At the hour of midnight, through a gate opened by deities, he made the Great Renunciation; and during the remainder of that same night, [he traversed] three...
Having crossed the rivers and reached the bank of the Anoma River, he took up the banner of Arahatship brought by the Great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra and went forth.

At that very moment, becoming endowed with the proper deportment like a sixty-year veteran elder, he gradually reached Rājagaha with his graceful manner of movement; there, having wandered for alms, he [sat] on the slopes of Mount Paṇḍava.
Having partaken of alms-food, and having declined the invitation from the King of Māgadha to accept his kingdom,
he went to the Bhaggava hermitage. Having observed the proper time for that, and then having observed the proper time for the Āḷāra Kālāmas,
and finding all of that unsatisfactory, he gradually proceeded to Uruvelā, where he practiced austerities for six years.
Having done so and realizing that there was no penetration of the noble Dhamma through that [asceticism], he thought, "This is not the path to enlightenment.
Then, taking solid food, he regained his strength within a few days;
on the full moon day of Visākha, having eaten the excellent meal given by Sujātā, he cast the golden bowl upstream against the river, and made the firm resolve: "Today I shall become a Buddha."

At the time of evening, his virtues praised by the Naga King Kāla, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and sat upon the invincible throne (aparājitapallaṅka) in the immovable position, facing the eastern world-system.
Resolving upon energy endowed with four factors, even before the sun had set, he shattered the army of Māra;
in the first watch of the night, he recollected his former births (pubbenivāsa), and in the middle watch, [he attained] the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

Having purified [his mind], and having applied his knowledge to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) during the last watch of the night, he increased his insight by contemplating the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) in both forward and reverse order;
then, having attained the supreme enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)— which is unique and not shared by any other Buddhas—
he spent seven days right there in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) which has Nibbāna as its object, and by that very means...

Following this method, having spent the other seven days likewise at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and having partaken of the meal of honey-clots at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, he sat again at the foot of the Ajapāla-nyagrodha tree.
There, reflecting upon the profundity of the Dhamma according to its natural law, his mind inclined toward inaction; then, being entreated by Mahābrahmā, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye.

Having seen beings distinguished by sharp faculties, dull faculties, and so forth, and having been requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma, he reflected, "To whom indeed should I first teach the Dhamma?
Realizing that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away, he thought, "The group-of-five monks were very helpful to me; they attended upon me when I was intent on striving."

Thinking, "What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the group of five monks," he set out from the Great Bodhi tree toward Bārāṇasī on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, traveling the eighteen-yojana road.
On the way, after conversing with the Ājīvaka Upaka, he arrived in due course at Isipatana; there, he made himself known to the group of five monks.
“Bhikkhus, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth,” and so on;

with these words from the teaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he caused eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, headed by Aññā Koṇḍañña, to drink the nectar of the Dhamma. Then, on the first day of the fortnight (the *pāṭipada*), he ordained the Elder Bhaddiya;
on the second day of the fortnight, the Elder Vappa; on the third day of the fortnight, the Elder Mahānāma; and on the fourth day—
Having established the Elder Assaji in the fruit of stream-entry, and on the fifth day of the fortnight having established everyone in Arahatship through the teaching of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta,
thereafter [he established] fifty-five men headed by the youth Yasa,
about thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group in the Kappāsika grove, and one thousand former matted-hair ascetics on the Piṭṭhipāsāṇa rock at Gayāsīsa.
Having thus led the great multitude to the plane of the Noble Ones, having established eleven million people headed by Bimbisāra in the fruit of stream-entry and in the three refuges,
and having accepted the Veḷuvana grove, while dwelling there, he requested Sañjaya—
who had attained the first path through the assistance of the Elder Assaji— to come together with his retinue into his presence.
Having established Sāriputta and Moggallāna— who had attained the fruit of the highest attainment (*aggaphala*) and reached the pinnacle of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramī*)—
in the position of chief disciples, he went to Kapilavatthu at the request of the elder Kāḷudāyin. There,

having subdued his haughty kinsmen through the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), he established his father in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*).
Having established [the community], and having ordained Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula, the Teacher returned once again to Rājagaha.

Then, at a later time, while the Teacher was dwelling in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī, the Great King Suddhodana realized Arahantship beneath the white parasol and passed away into Parinibbāna. Thereafter, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...
The thought of going forth arose in her; then, at the conclusion of the teaching on the *Kalahavivāda Sutta* on the banks of the Rohiṇī River, she went forth.

Having become of one mind with the five hundred maidens who were the attendants of the princes who had gone forth, they all approached Mahāpajāpatī, saying, "We shall go forth in the presence of the Teacher," and [addressed] Mahāpajāpatī.

Making Jeṭṭhikā their leader, they desired to go into the presence of the Teacher. Now, Mahāpajāpatī had previously requested admission to the order from the Teacher on one occasion, but she did not receive it;

therefore, having summoned a barber to have her hair cut, and having dressed herself in saffron robes, she took all those Sākiyan women and went to Vesālī, where she approached the Ten-Powered One through the Elder Ānanda.
Having made her request, she received both the going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā) by means of the acceptance of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma).

As for the others, they all likewise received full ordination together as one group. This is the summary here; however, this account in its detailed form has already been recorded in various places in the Canon (Pāḷi).
Having been thus ordained, Mahāpajāpatī approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood to one side.
Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, she attained arahantship.
And the remaining five hundred bhikkhunīs attained arahantship at the conclusion of Nanda’s exhortation. Thus...
When the community of bhikkhunīs was well-established and had become widespread throughout various villages,

market towns, districts, and royal capitals, noble women, daughters-in-law, and young maidens— having heard of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, the Dhamma’s sublime nature, and the Saṅgha’s excellent practice—
became deeply devoted to the Teaching and felt a sense of spiritual urgency regarding saṃsāra; [they then approached] their husbands, parents, and relatives...

Having obtained permission and committed their hearts to the Teaching, they went forth. Having gone forth, endowed with virtue and proper conduct, and having received instruction from the Teacher and those elders, they applied themselves with diligence and effort, and before long they realized arhatship.
The verses spoken by them here and there, such as the Udānas and others, were later compiled by the reciters of the Council.
Having brought them together, they included them in the formal recitation (*saṅgīti*) by way of single-groupings (*ekakanipāta*) and so forth, [deciding] that "these are called the Therīgāthā.
The classification of these into groupings and so forth has already been stated above. Among those groupings, the Single-Verse Grouping (*ekakanipāta*) is the first.
Within that as well: "Sleep happily, young nun (*therikā*), having covered yourself with a cloth;..."
"Truly, your passion has been stilled, like the dried meat in a pot"—this is the opening verse.

What is its origin? It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, a certain daughter of noble family, having developed deep faith in the Teaching, invited the Teacher and, on the following day, had a pavilion of branches constructed.
Having spread out sand, tied up a canopy above, and performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, she announced that it was time for the Teacher.
The Teacher went there and sat down on the prepared seat.

She paid homage to the Blessed One, served him with excellent hard and soft foods, and when the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, she [offered] the three robes.

He covered it for her. After the Blessed One had offered words of appreciation, he departed. Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as her life lasted, at the end of her lifespan she was reborn in the world of the devas.
Wandering through happy destinies alone for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, she was reborn into a household of lay devotees during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa.
Upon reaching maturity, having become spiritually stirred by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), she went forth into homelessness within the Teaching.
Having received full ordination and fulfilled the bhikkhunī precepts for twenty thousand years, she passed away as an ordinary person (puthujjana) and was reborn in the heavenly realms.

After experiencing celestial prosperity for the duration of one Buddha-interval, she was reborn in Vesālī during this current dispensation of the Buddha into a prominent khattiya family of great wealth. Because her physical body remained firm and unchanging, they called her Therikā. When she reached maturity...
Given by her parents to a noble youth of the same caste as herself from a distinguished family, she lived as a devoted wife to her husband.
Later, having gained faith in the Teaching during the Teacher’s visit to Vesālī, she became a lay follower (*upāsikā*).

Subsequently, after hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, she conceived a desire for the going forth; resolving, "I shall go forth," she announced her intention to her husband.

Her husband did not give his permission. However, because she had already performed her duties, she dwelt devoted to insight meditation, reviewing the Dhamma as she had heard it and discerning both material and immaterial phenomena.
Then one day, while a curry was being cooked in the kitchen, a great flame of fire arose. That flame of fire [reached] the entire vessel...
It was crackling with a *taṭataṭa* sound as it burned. Seeing this, she took that very sight as her object;

perceiving impermanence (*aniccatā*) appearing even more clearly, she then applied the characteristics of suffering (*dukkha*), impermanence, and non-self (*anattatā*) to it, and by developing insight (*vipassanā*) and gradually intensifying it, she established herself in the fruit of Non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) according to the sequence of the paths. From that time forth, she [discarded] her ornaments...
She did not wear ornaments or finery. When her husband asked her, "My dear lady, why do you no longer wear jewelry or ornaments as you did before?
she informed him of her own incapacity for the life of a householder and obtained his permission for her to go forth.
Just as the lay follower Visākha [acted] for Dhammadinnā, he [acted] with great ceremony for Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
Having led her into his presence, he said, "Noble lady, please grant her the going-forth.
Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, having granted her the going-forth and the full ordination, led her to the monastery and presented her to the Teacher.
The Teacher, revealing to her only those objects of perception that were natural to her, spoke this verse: "Sleep in happiness."
In this context, "sukham" (pleasure) is a neuter noun used in the abstract sense. "Supāhi" (abandon it) is a word of command. "Therike" (O Elder Nun) is a form of address.
"Having covered yourself with a rag" is an exhortation toward fewness of desires. "For your passion has been stilled" is a praise of her practice.
"Like a dried-up scrap of food" is a demonstration of the insubstantiality of the defilement that is to be stilled. "In the pot" refers to its container.
This is a demonstration of the nature of impermanence, emptiness, and so forth.
"Sukha" (bliss) is a designation for what is desirable; the meaning is: "having become free from suffering by means of bliss.
"Supāhi" is a demonstration of reclining among the four postures; therefore, maintain the four postures in bliss alone and dwell in bliss.
The meaning is as follows: "Therikā" (the Elder Nun)—although this is her name, because she possesses a designation that corresponds to her actual state, the meaning is:
"one who has become firm in the firm Teaching," or "one endowed with firm qualities such as virtue.
"Having made a robe from cloth and wrapped herself" means: having fashioned a robe from rags (*paṃsukūla*) and covered her body, she was both clad and wrapped in it.

"Upasanto hi te rāgo": here the word *hi* has the sense of a reason (*hetvattha*). Since the sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) arising in your continuum has been stilled—burnt away by the fire of the knowledge of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*)—the intention is:
"Now, having burnt the remaining lust with the fire of the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamagga*), sleep in peace.
"Like a pot of dried rice" means as in the case of that [rice] in a baked vessel.
A small amount of curry sauce being cooked over a great mass of flames burns and dries up before it subsides;
or, just as when curry sauce mixed with water is placed on a stove and cooked while water is still present,
it makes the sound "cicciṭā" and "ciṭiciṭā," but once the water is exhausted, it becomes completely quiet— so too within your mental continuum.
“Sensual lust has been stilled; having calmed the rest as well, sleep in happiness.

Because her faculties had reached maturity and due to the Teacher’s skillful teaching, at the conclusion of the verse the Elder Nun attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“A pavilion was built by me for the Buddha Koṇāgamana;”
“I certainly gave the triple robe to the Buddha, the Kinsman of the World.
To whichever country, town, or capital city I go, everywhere I am honored;
this is the fruit of that meritorious deed.”
“The defilements have been incinerated by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a female elephant that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
How wonderful it was for me to come into the presence of the Supreme Buddha!”
The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
“The four analytical insights and these eight liberations;
the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained arahantship, the Therī uttered that same verse as an inspired utterance (udāna); therefore, this verse became the Therī’s own verse.
In that regard, within the verse spoken by the Therī, lust is encompassed in its entirety because the intended meaning is the subsiding of that [lust] by means of the supreme path.
And it is by the very subsiding of lust that the subsiding of all defilements is stated here.
It should be regarded as such because it is one with all defilements, since it is established through the subsiding of them all. For it is said:
“The delusion that is considered innate to restlessness and doubt Is associated with greed by virtue of being one with what is to be abandoned.”
And just as the subsiding of all defilements is stated here, it should be understood that their subsiding is likewise stated everywhere else:
by way of partial removal (*tadaṅga*) in the preliminary stage; by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) at the moments of serenity and insight;
by way of eradication (*samuccheda*) at the moment of the Path; and by way of tranquillization (*paṭippassaddhi*) at the moment of the Fruit, because of the accomplishment of subsiding.

By this, the accomplishment of all four kinds of abandoning should be understood. Therein, the accomplishment of perfection in virtue (*sīlasampadā*) is shown by abandoning through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅgappahāna*);

the accomplishment of perfection in concentration (*samādhisampadā*) by abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhanappahāna*); and the accomplishment of perfection in wisdom (*paññāsampadā*) by the other two, because they bring about the clear realization of abandoning (*pahānābhisamaya*).
Just as one effects the clear realization of development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*), for in its absence, that [realization] would not exist.

Likewise, it should be understood that by this verse, the fulfillment of the four realizations (*abhisamaya*), the three trainings (*sikkhā*) through the accomplishment of those four realizations, the threefold excellence of practice (*paṭipatti*), and the seven purifications (*visuddhi*) are all made manifest.
[She was] "a certain elder nun" (*aññatarā therī*), unknown—that is, not public—by way of name, clan, and so forth; she was one.
The intention is that the Elder Nun Lakkhaṇasampannā spoke this verse. The commentary on the verses of a certain Elder Nun is finished.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Muttā.
“Muttā, be released from the bonds, like the moon from the grasp of Rāhu;
with a mind completely liberated, eat your almsfood free from debt.
This is the verse for the female trainee named Muttā. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas in various places.
Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as a support for turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), she was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher walking along the road, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration with a mind full of faith;
through the force of her joy, she fell prostrate at the feet of the Teacher. By virtue of that meritorious deed, she [was reborn] in the world of the devas.
Having been reborn and wandering from one happy destination to another, she was born during this current dispensation of a Buddha into a prominent brahmin family in Sāvatthī;
her name was Mutta-Tissā. Because she was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), at the age of twenty she went forth under Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
While still a trainee (*sikkhamānā*), she requested a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and applied herself to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*).

She did so. One day, having finished her meal and returned from her alms round, she performed the duties toward the elder bhikkhunīs, went to her daytime resting place, and sat in seclusion, beginning to apply her mind to insight meditation (*vipassanā*).
While seated within the Fragrant Chamber (*surabhigandhakuṭi*), the Teacher emitted a radiance and manifested himself as if sitting right before her.
Having shown this, he spoke this verse: “O Muttā, be released from the bonds.
In this context, “Muttā” is an address to her. “Be released from the bonds” means: through the sequence of the Path, be released from the four bonds, beginning with the bond of sensual desire;
let your mind be liberated from them. How is this so? “Like the moon from the grasp of Rāhu”—that is, from what is designated as Rāhu.

Be freed from defilements as the moon is freed from clouds. "With a mind well-liberated" means with a mind that is thoroughly liberated by the noble path through the liberation of total eradication (*samucchedavimutti*); this is an instrumental case used in the sense of a state of being.

"Eat alms-food free from debt" means that having abandoned the debt of the defilements (*kilesa*), you should eat the alms-food of the kingdom without debt. For he who, without abandoning the defilements...
When one makes use of requisites permitted by the Teacher, he is said to "make use [of them] debt-free. As the Venerable Bākula said:
"For seven days only, friends, did I eat the country alms-food debt-free.
Therefore, one who has gone forth in the Dispensation should make use of what is given in faith, having become debt-free through the abandoning of the debts of sensual desire and the rest.

"Alms-food" (*piṇḍaka*) is merely a synonym for "teaching"; the meaning is "the four requisites. "He exhorted her frequently" means that, purifying the defilements obstructing the attainment of the Noble Path, he gave her exhortation many times.
By abiding in that exhortation, she attained *arahantship* before long. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“When the Blessed One Vipassī, the World’s Elder, the Neutral One,
had set out upon the highway, ferrying living beings across,
I went forth from my home and lay down face-downward.”
The compassionate Lord of the World stepped upon my head.
Having stepped upon my head, the Leader of the World departed;
through that clarity of mind, I went to the Tusita heaven.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she uttered that very verse. Having completed her training and received full ordination, she later repeated that same verse at the time of her final nibbāna.
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of the Bhikkhunī Thera Muttā.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Puṇṇā "O Puṇṇā, may you be filled with the Dhammas"—this is the verse of the female trainee (sikkhamānā) named Puṇṇā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, [was reborn] in a world empty of a Buddha in the time of Candabhāgā.

She was reborn on the bank of a river in the womb of a *kinnarī*. One day, having seen a certain *paccekabuddha* there, her heart filled with serene faith, she honored him with a garland of reeds and stood with palms joined in reverence.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering only through happy realms, she was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in the family of a wealthy householder in Sāvatthī.

Her name was Puṇṇā Tissa. Because she was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), while living there for twenty years, she heard the Dhamma in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
Having gained faith, she went forth; and even while still a trainee (*sikkhamānā*), she began the practice of insight (*vipassanā*).
While the Teacher was seated within his fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*), he emitted a radiance and said:
“Be filled with the qualities of the Dhamma, like the moon on the fifteenth day;
with perfected wisdom, shatter the mass of darkness.”—he spoke this verse.
Therein, “Puṇṇe” is an address to her. “Pūrassu dhammehīti” means by means of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*).
"Be fulfilled. In the phrase "like the moon on the fifteenth," the letter *ra* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*).

Just as the moon on the fifteenth—the full-moon day—is complete with all its digits, [so be you]. "With wisdom fulfilled" means with the wisdom of the path of Arahantship fulfilled through the completion of the sixteen tasks.
"Shatter the mass of darkness" means [shatter] the mass of delusion without remainder.
“Break it! Cut it off! With the very shattering of the mass of delusion, all defilements were shattered as well.
Having heard that verse, she developed insight and attained arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“At that time, I was a kinnarī on the banks of the Candabhāgā River.”
I saw the stainless Buddha, the self-arisen, the unconquered.
With a clear mind, joyful and filled with rapture, I joined my palms in reverence;
taking a garland of reeds, I paid homage to the self-arisen one.
“By that well-performed karma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the body of a kinnarī, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, I exercised the supreme sovereignty over thirty-six divine kings.”
I served as the chief queen to ten universal monarchs;
then, having stirred my heart with a sense of spiritual urgency, I went forth into the homeless life.
"The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been utterly uprooted."
"All taints are utterly destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
Ninety-four aeons ago, because I offered that flower in worship, I have not known a miserable rebirth—this is the fruit of that flower-offering."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, that elder nun uttered this very verse. This indeed was her verse of declaration of final knowledge (*aññābyākaraṇagāthā*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Puṇṇā is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Tissā "Train in the training, O Tissā"—this is the verse of the trainee (sikkhamānā) Tissā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, through the conditions of that accumulated merit, in this [life]...
Having been born into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu at the time of a Buddha’s appearance, she grew up and became part of the Bodhisatta’s harem.
Later, having gone forth together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, she applied herself to the practice of insight (vipassanā).
Then, the Teacher, emitting a radiance in the same manner as described below, said:
“Train yourself in the training; let not the bonds overcome you.
Free from all bonds, wander through the world without taints”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, *tisse* is an address to her. *Sikkhassu sikkhāya* means [train] in the threefold training, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
"Train in the training"—the meaning is: "Accomplish the three trainings associated with the Path. Now, he states the reason for accomplishing them:

"May the bonds not overtake you. This means: may these bonds and opportunities—which are difficult to find—namely, human birth, the integrity of the faculties, the arising of a Buddha, and the attainment of faith—not pass you by.
Or else, it refers to the four bonds themselves, such as the bond of sensual desire and so forth.
"May they not approach me; may they not overcome me. "Freed from all bonds" means liberated from all bonds such as the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*);
thus, having become free from taints (*anāsava*), wander in the world and dwell in the blissful state of the seen—this is the meaning.
Having heard that verse, she developed insight and attained *arahantship*; the sequence of events should be understood in the same manner as described below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Tissā is finished.
5–10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nuns beginning with Tissā:
"Tissa, apply yourself to the teachings"—this is the verse of the Elder Nun Tissā. The story concerning her is similar to the story concerning the probationer (sikkhamānā) Tissā.
Having become a senior elder (therī), she attained arahantship.
Just as with her, the accounts of the five elders—Dhīrā, Vīrā, Mittā, Bhadrā, and Upasamā—are identical from this point forward.
All of these women were residents of Kapilavatthu who, having been members of the Bodhisatta’s harem, went forth together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, accompanied by the Radiant Verses (obhāsagāthā).

Except for the seventh, they all attained arahantship. However, she—without the verse of illumination and even before [the others]—relying on the exhortation received in the presence of the Teacher, further intensified her insight (vipassanā) and, having reached arahantship, uttered the verse "The heroes by the heroes" as an inspired utterance (udāna). The other one also, having attained arahantship—
“Yoke yourself to the teachings; let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have let the moment pass grieve when cast into hell.
O wise one, touch cessation—the blissful stilling of perception.”
Strive for Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
“A heroine by means of heroic qualities, a bhikkhunī with developed faculties,
she bears her final body, having conquered Māra along with his mount.”
“Having gone forth out of faith, be one who delights in friends;
develop wholesome qualities for the sake of attaining security from bondage.
Having gone forth out of faith, O noble lady, be one who delights in what is noble.”
“Cultivate wholesome states, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Through tranquility, cross over the flood, the realm of death so difficult to cross;
bear your final body, having conquered Māra and his mount. Thus they spoke these verses.

In this regard, "apply yourself to the teachings" means: apply yourself, practice the yoga, with the teachings of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), and with the noble teachings conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).

"Let not the opportune moment pass you by" means: for that person who does not thus practice the cultivation of yoga, the moment of rebirth in a suitable place, the moment when the six sense bases are complete, and the moment of the appearance of a Buddha—[let not these pass you by].
The opportunity obtained through faith—indeed, this very opportunity passes away. May that opportunity not pass you by.
For those who have let the opportunity pass, and for those persons to whom that opportunity has not come, they grieve, being consigned to hell;
the meaning is that having been reborn there, they experience great suffering.

"May you touch cessation" means: having touched and attained the cessation of defilements (*kilesa-nirodha*). "Attain the bliss that is the stilling of perceptions, Nibbāna": attain Nibbāna, the ultimate bliss which is the cause for the subsiding of evil perceptions such as the perception of sensual desire (*kāma-saññā*).

"The heroes by means of heroic qualities": through the noble path-qualities (*ariya-magga-dhamma*)—which are heroic because they are characterized by the exertion of vigor and are synonymous with splendor—the heroic bhikkhunī, having developed her faculties and increased her faculties such as faith, has conquered Māra along with his mount by means of the objects of sense-desire (*vatthu-kāma*).
Because there will be no further renewed existence in the future, she shows herself as one who has attained final Nibbāna in this very body;

thus the Elder Nun presents herself as if she were someone else. She addresses her as "Friend. "Delighting in good friends" means being devoted to virtuous companions. In that regard, "be one who offers honor and respect.
"Cultivate wholesome states" means increase the states of the Noble Path. "Of security from bondage" refers to Arahantship.
"And for the sake of attaining and reaching Nibbāna.

He addresses her as "Bhadrā" (the auspicious one). "Be delighted in the auspicious things" means be devoted to and take pleasure in the virtuous qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*) and so forth.

"The unsurpassed security from bondage": this refers to Nibbāna, which is secure and free from calamity because it is beyond the four bonds (*yoga*); the meaning is that you should cultivate the wholesome states conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*) for the sake of its attainment.
He approaches and addresses him: "Cross the flood, the realm of death, so difficult to cross. Here, the "realm of death" (*maccudheyya*) is so called because death is deposited therein;
it is "difficult to cross" (*suduttara*) because it is very hard to cross for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit.

"Cross the great flood of saṃsāra"—you should cross by means of the ship of the Noble Path. "Bear your final body"—the meaning is that by means of that very crossing, you shall become one who bears his final physical form.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Tissā is finished.
The commentary on the first chapter is finished.
11. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Muttā.
The verses beginning with “I am well-liberated, truly liberated” are the stanzas of the Therī Muttā.

She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated wholesome karma in various states of existence, was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha as the daughter of a poor Brahmin named Oghātaka in the Kosala country. When she reached maturity, her parents [gave her] to a certain...

They gave her to the hunchbacked brahmin. Disliking the household life, she obtained his permission, went forth, and applied herself to the practice of insight (vipassanā). Her mind wandered among external objects;

restraining it, she uttered the verse, "I am well-freed, truly freed," and while speaking thus, she intensified her insight and attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) together with [the fruits of] enlightenment.
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye of all phenomena, entered the city for alms, showing compassion to all living beings.”
As the Teacher approached, all the city-dwellers gathered together in joy and delight, and they scattered sand over him.
Having swept the streets, they raised banners of plantain trees and full water-jars.
Incense, powder, meat, and hospitality were offered to the Teacher.
Having prepared a pavilion and invited the Guide,
and having given a great gift, he aspired for supreme enlightenment.
“Padumuttara, the Great Hero, the bringer of joy to all living beings,
having offered his appreciation, the Supreme Person made this prophecy:
‘When a hundred thousand aeons have passed, there will be a fortunate aeon.’”
Having attained happiness in various states of existence, you will reach enlightenment.
"And whatever men and women have performed manual labor,
all of them shall stand face-to-face with you in the future."
“By the ripening of that karma, and by your intentions and aspirations,
those women became your attendants when you were born in the celestial realm.
You experienced divine happiness beyond measure, and human happiness likewise incalculable.”
We have experienced [the results] for a long time, wandering through various states of existence.
A hundred thousand aeons ago, whatever karma I performed then,
I was delicately nurtured among humans as well as in the cities of the gods.
“I constantly obtain beauty, wealth, fame, long life, as well as reputation, happiness, and what is dear—
all this through the excellence of well-performed karma.
When my final existence was reached, I was born into a brahmin family.”
With delicate hands and feet, in a delightful dwelling:
“At all times, I have never seen the earth unadorned;
nor have I ever seen it as muddy ground or impure.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“I am well-liberated, truly liberated, through liberation from the three hunchbacks.”
With the mortar, the pestle, and with my husband the hunchback, I have been well released from birth and death;
the conduit to existence has been uprooted—thus she spoke this verse.
Therein, "well released" (*sumuttā*) means thoroughly released. "I am well released" (*sādhumuttāmhī*) means I am properly and completely released. But from what?
She said, "Well released, truly well released," meaning "released from three hunchbacks," that is, completely freed from three crooked things.
Now, showing those very things by their specific nature, she said: "By the mortar, by the pestle, and by the hunchbacked husband.
For when one throws grain into the mortar, turns it over, and pounds it with the pestle, her back [is strained].
"It must be bent" means that because those two [shoulders] are the cause for making one hunchbacked, they are called "hunchback. Her husband, however, was indeed hunchbacked.

Now, in order to illustrate the liberation by means of three types of hunchbacks, she says, "I am liberated from birth and death," and states the reason for this: "The conduit to existence has been uprooted."
The meaning of this is as follows: "I am not only released from the three types of hunchbacks;
rather, I am released even from all birth and death, because craving—the leader and guide of all existence—has been eradicated by me through the supreme path.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Mutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā.
"Born of desire, she was overcome"—this is the verse of the elder nun Dhammadinnā.

It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, while living in the city of Haṃsavatī under the dependence of others, she made offerings and paid homage to the Chief Disciple who had emerged from the attainment of cessation.

Having given gifts, she was reborn in the world of the gods. Passing away from there, as she transmigrated among gods and humans, during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, while living in the house of a servant of the Teacher’s maternal uncles’ brothers, she gave two portions of food when her husband said, "Give one," because of her previous generosity.
Having performed much merit, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, [she was born] in the household of King Kiki of Kāsī...
Having taken rebirth in that household and become one of seven sisters, she practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years; then,
wandering through the realms of gods and humans for the duration of one interval between Buddhas,
she was reborn in this present dispensation of the Buddha in a noble family in Rājagaha, and upon reaching maturity, she went to the house of the merchant Visākha.
Then one day, after hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, the merchant Visākha became a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
Upon returning home and ascending the palace, he did not take hold of the hand extended by Dhammadinnā as she stood at the foot of the stairs;
instead, having ascended the palace, he ate in silence. Observing him, Dhammadinnā reflected:
“Noble son, why did you not take my hand today? Even while eating, you said nothing.
Is there perhaps some fault on my part? Visākha replied, “Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you.
However, from this day forward, I am unworthy to touch a woman’s body or to feel greed for food; such a person as I—”
“I have realized the Dhamma. But if you so desire, stay in this very house.
If you do not desire it, take as much wealth as you need and go to your family home,” he said.
“I will not, noble son, sip back the vomit that you have spat out; grant me permission to go forth,” she replied. Visākha said, “Very well.”
“Dhammadinnā,” he said, and sent her to the nuns’ quarters in a golden palanquin. Having gone forth and received a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), she stayed there for a few days;
then, desiring to live in seclusion, she went to her preceptor and teacher and said, “Venerable ladies, my mind does not delight in this crowded place; I am going to a village residence.”

The bhikkhunīs led her to that village monastery. Dwelling there, because she had mastered the crushing of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*) in the past, she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long. Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena...”
One hundred thousand aeons ago, the Leader appeared in this world.
At that time, I was born in a certain family in Haṃsavatī as a laborer for others,
being prudent and restrained by virtue.
“Under the Buddha Padumuttara, the Well-Born One was the foremost disciple.
Having gone forth from the monastery, he was walking for alms.
At that time, a water-carrier was going along carrying a water-pot.”
Seeing him, with a clear heart, I gave him a cake with my own hands.
Having accepted it, he sat right there and consumed it;
then, having led him to my home, I gave him food.
“Then my grandfather, being pleased, made his daughter-in-law his own;
having gone together with my mother-in-law, I paid homage to the Sambuddha.
At that time, he was praising a bhikkhunī who was a preacher of the Dhamma.”
He placed me at the very forefront; hearing this, I was filled with joy.
Having invited the Sugata, the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha, and having offered a great gift, I aspired for that state.
Then the Sugata, whose voice was like the deep resonance of a thundercloud,
spoke to me as I was intent on attending upon him, providing a meal for him and his Saṅgha.
“You are devoted to hearing the True Dhamma, with a mind increased by virtue.”
“Be joyful, Bhaddā; you shall obtain the fruit of your aspiration.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan, named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world.”
“She shall be an heir to his teachings, a true-born daughter fashioned by the Dhamma;
by the name Dhammadinnā, she will become a female disciple of the Teacher.
Having heard this, being filled with joy, [she served] the Great Sage for as long as life lasted.
With a mind of loving-kindness, I served the Guide with the necessary requisites.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great fame, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan— the best among those who speak—
appeared. At that time, the lord of men was the attendant of the Great Sage.”
In the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king of Kāsi named Kikī.
I was his sixth daughter, well-known as Sudhammā;
having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror’s son, I resolved upon the going-forth.
“Father did not grant us permission;
we then lived as householders for twenty thousand years, wandering about without weariness.
We were daughters of royalty, raised in comfort, yet we practiced the celibate life of a maiden.”
Delighting in waiting upon the Buddha, there were seven joyful daughters:
Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā,
Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāyikā.
“Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā and Kuṇḍalā;
Gotamī and I myself—Visākhā is the seventh.
By those well-performed deeds and by our intentions and aspirations,”
Having cast off the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
And now, in my final existence, in the supreme city of Giribbaja,
I was born into a prosperous family of merchants, abundant in all desirable things.
“When I was endowed with the beauty of form and established in the first stage of youth,
I went to another family and lived there, fully possessed of happiness.
Having approached the Refuge of the World and heard his teaching of the Dhamma...”
“My wise husband attained the fruit of non-returning.
Having then given his permission, I went forth into the homeless life;
before long, I reached the state of an arahant.”
“Then that lay follower approached me and asked questions profound and subtle; I answered them all.
The Victor, pleased with that virtue, placed me in the foremost position.”
“I see no other bhikkhunī who is such a preacher of the Dhamma as this.
‘O bhikkhus, remember the wise Dhammadinnā just as she is;
for thus am I a learned one, favored by the Leader.’”
“I have served the Teacher; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—”
Thus has my goal been attained: the destruction of all fetters.
I am a master of the supernormal powers, possessed of the divine ear-element, and I know the minds of others, fulfilling the Teacher’s instruction.
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
Having exhausted all taints, I am pure and stainless.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained arahantship, she thought, "My mind has reached its culmination; what more shall I do by staying here?
I will go to Rājagaha itself, pay homage to the Teacher, and many of my kinsmen will perform meritorious deeds.
Thus, together with the bhikkhunīs, she returned to Rājagaha. When Visākha heard that she had arrived, he...
Investigating his realization, he asked questions concerning the five aggregates and so forth.
Dhammadinnā answered each question as it was asked, just as one might cut a lotus stalk with a very sharp knife.
Visāka reported the entire sequence of questions and answers to the Teacher. The Teacher said, "Visāka, Dhammadinnā is wise."
Praising her with the words beginning "the bhikkhunī," and having declared her state of being one who has attained the answer by correlating it with the knowledge of omniscience,
[the Buddha]— taking that very *Cūḷavedalla-sutta* as the occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*)— placed her in the foremost position among the bhikkhunīs who are expounders of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, while she was dwelling in that village residence, she attained the lower paths.
He established insight for the sake of the supreme path. At that time, it was said:
"One who has conceived desire, who is resolute, and who is suffused with the mind;
whose heart is unattached to sensual pleasures—such a person is called 'one who flows upwards'."
He spoke this verse.
In this context, "having conceived desire" means having conceived a desire for the sake of the supreme fruit. "Resolute" (*avasāyī*): *avasāya* is said to mean the end or conclusion;
and because his mind is unattached to sensual pleasures, he will later be called an "upstream-goer" (*uddhaṃsota*) due to his fulfillment of the duties of a recluse.
The culmination is to be understood as belonging to no one else;
therefore, by means of these two phrases, the meaning expressed is: "those who have not yet reached their goal and who aspire to the unsurpassed security from bondage.

And "one should be touched by the mind" means that one should be touched—that is, contacted—by Nibbāna through the three lower path-consciousnesses. "With a mind unattached to sense pleasures" refers to the stage of the non-returner path.
Their minds are not bound to sensual pleasures. "Upstream-bound" (uddhaṃsota) means that her stream of the path and her stream of saṃsāra flow only upwards;

thus she is "upstream-bound. For just as for a non-returner (anāgāmin) no other path arises than the highest path, so too for one born in the Aviha heaven and the others, there is rebirth only upwards as far as the Akaniṭṭha heaven.
The commentary on the *Therīgāthā* of Dhammadinnā is finished.
13. Commentary on the *Therīgāthā* of Visākhā:

"Follow the Teaching of the Buddha" is the verse of the elder nun Visākhā. Her story is identical to that of the elder nun Dhīrā. Having attained *arahantship*, she spent her time in the bliss of liberation—
“Follow the teaching of the Buddha, having done which one does not regret;
quickly wash your feet and sit down to one side.
With this verse, he declared his final knowledge (arahantship).
In this context, "fulfill the Buddha’s teaching" means: fulfill the Buddha’s instruction and guidance; the sense is that you should practice according to what has been taught.

"Having done which one does not regret" means that having followed the instruction, one does not regret it because of having performed it, since for the doer, their intentions have been successfully fulfilled.
Having quickly washed one's feet, [one sits] to one side...
"Sit down"— she said this because she herself, having returned from her alms round after the meal, had performed the duties toward her teachers and preceptors,
washed her feet in her own daytime resting place, and sat in private until she had brought her own goal to its ultimate perfection;
therefore, she spoke thus while enjoining others to do the same.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Visākhā is finished.
14. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sumanā:

“Having seen the elements as suffering” refers to the verse of the Elder Nun Sumanā. The background story for her is similar to that of the Elder Nun Tissā. For her, too, the Teacher, having emitted a radiance, revealed himself standing before her as if present in person—
“Having seen the elements as suffering, do not come to birth again;
having dispelled desire for existence, you shall wander at peace.
He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of that verse, she attained arahantship.

In this context, "having seen the elements as suffering" means having seen with the eye of knowledge that the elements such as the eye, which are included within one's own continuity, as well as others, are "suffering" due to being oppressed by arising and passing away, and so forth.
"May I not come to birth again" means may I not undergo birth again in the future, [that is,] renewed existence.
"Having dispelled desire for existence" means having abandoned craving and desire for all forms of existence, beginning with the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*).
"Having abandoned [them] by means of the path known as dispassion. "You will wander at peace" means that you will dwell extinguished (nibbūta) through the total abandonment of the defilements.
And here, by the phrase "having seen the elements as suffering," insight (vipassanā) is shown by way of the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā).
It should be understood that by the phrase “having abandoned desire for existence,” the Path is shown;

by the phrase “you shall live in peace,” the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining is shown; and by the phrase “may you not come again to birth,” the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining is shown.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumanā is finished.
15. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Uttarā:
“Restrained in body, she was... These are the verses of the elder nun Uttarā. Her story is similar to that of the elder nun Tissā.
For she too was born into the Sakyan clan, served as a member of the Bodhisatta’s harem, and went forth together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
But having attained arahantship while reciting the *Obhāsa-gāthā*, he declared:
“I was restrained in body, and likewise in speech and mind;
having uprooted craving with its very root, I have become cooled and extinguished.”
Out of inspiration, he recited that very verse.
Therein, "we were restrained in body" means we were restrained by bodily restraint. "In speech" is to be construed as "we were restrained by verbal restraint";
thus, with these two phrases, he speaks of the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*). "Udā" means "then. "In mind" (*cetasā*)...

"By a mind of concentration": by this he refers to the cultivation of insight (*vipassanā-bhāvanā*). "He has plucked out craving with its root": that is, together with its underlying tendency (*sānusaya*), or having uprooted craving along with ignorance (*avijjā*).
For it is when the dangers of the three realms of existence are concealed by ignorance that craving arises.
Another interpretation: "Restrained in body" means that through right action (*sammā-kammanta*) and the very restraint of the Path, wrong action is entirely abandoned.
"I was restrained in body. Regarding "speech": by right speech, through the total abandonment of wrong speech, the meaning is that I was restrained in speech precisely by the restraint of the Path.
"By mind" means by concentration (*samādhi*). Here, right concentration is expressed by the term "mind";
and by the inclusion of right concentration, the factors of the Path—right view and so forth—which share the same characteristic as the Path, are also included.
"They have been grasped" means that the abandonment of non-restraint, such as covetousness and so forth, has been shown to be complete through the restraint of the Path.
For this very reason it was said: "Having uprooted craving with its root.

"I am become cool and extinguished" means that, by the total absence of the fever of the defilements, I have attained a state of coolness and am extinguished in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Uttarā is finished.
16. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumanā, who went forth in old age:
"May you live happily, O elder woman," these are the verses of Sumanā, who had gone forth in old age. She too, among previous Buddhas...
Having performed meritorious deeds and accumulated wholesome karma throughout various existences,
she was reborn in this current age of a Buddha in Sāvatthī as the sister of King Mahākosala. Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher to King Pasenadi of Kosala—
beginning with the words, "Great King, these four should not be despised because they are young"— she conceived a deep sense of faith.
Having established herself in the refuges and the precepts, she who desired to go forth delayed for a long time, thinking, "I will look after my grandmother.
Later, when her grandmother had passed away, she had costly rugs and coverlets prepared with the king;
she went to the monastery, had them offered to the Saṅgha, heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, and [attained] the fruit of non-returning.
Having established herself [in virtue], she requested the going-forth. Seeing her maturity of knowledge, the Teacher said:
"May you live happily, O elder woman, having clothed yourself in a hempen robe;
for your passion has been stilled, you have become cool, and you are extinguished."

She spoke this verse. At the conclusion of that verse, having attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), she spoke that very same verse as an utterance of exultation (udāna).
This itself was her declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa), and she went forth into homelessness at that very moment.

Regarding the phrase "in the growth of the verse," it means "grown old" (*vuḍḍhe*), which signifies "advanced in age. Furthermore, she was also "grown" (*vuḍḍhā*) by virtue of her qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*); thus she was an Elder Nun (*therī*).
In the fourth line of the verse cited, it should be construed as: "you have become cool and attained Nibbāna. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumana, who went forth in old age, is finished.
17. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Dhammā.
"Having wandered for alms," etc., are the verses of the Elder Nun Dhammā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated the equipment of merit by gathering wholesome roots conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the arising of this Buddha.
Upon reaching maturity, she entered the household of a suitable husband.
Having gained faith in the Teaching and desiring to go forth, she was not permitted by her husband;
later, after her husband had passed away, she went forth and applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*). One day, while returning to the monastery after wandering for alms, she fell down.
Taking that very incident as her object of meditation, she developed insight and attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).—
“Having wandered for alms, leaning on my staff,
weak and with limbs trembling, I fell right there upon the ground.
Having seen the peril in the body, my mind was then liberated.”
He spoke this verse by way of an udāna.
Therein, "having wandered for alms" (*piṇḍapātaṃ caritvāna*) means having wandered through the city for the sake of alms, leaning upon a staff (*daṇḍamolubbha*);
"on the ground" (*chamā*) means on the bare earth (*chamāyaṃ bhūmiyaṃ*), by way of the feet.

The meaning is that they fall upon the ground. "Having seen the danger in the body" means having perceived with the eye of wisdom the defects in the physical frame through various modes such as its impurity, impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

"Then my mind was liberated" means that, by means of the contemplation of danger, and subsequently through the contemplations of disenchantment and so forth, my mind was liberated from the defilements by way of suppression.
Furthermore, by means of the paths and fruits in their respective order, she was completely liberated through both total eradication and subsidence;
there was nothing further for her to be liberated from. This itself constituted her declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verse of the Elder Nun Dhammā is concluded.
18. Commentary on the Verses of Saṅghā Therī "Having left home and gone forth...
These are the verses of the Elder Nun Saṅghā. The background story for her is similar to that of the Elder Nun Dhīrā. The verses, however, are as follows:
"Having left home and gone forth, having abandoned son, cattle, and what is dear; ... [the rest of the verse follows]"
"Having abandoned both lust and hatred, having dispelled ignorance, and having uprooted craving, I am at peace and extinguished"—thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, "having abandoned" means having cast away. "Ghare" means a house. For the word *ghara*, even when referring to a single object, sometimes...
It is expressed by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhivasena*) as "seed" even when referring to many things.

"Having abandoned their children and cattle"—that is, having abandoned both the children who ought to be loved and the cattle such as cows and buffaloes, by means of abandoning the desire and lust (*chandarāga*) bound to them.

"Having abandoned passion and hatred"—that is, having completely eradicated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) passion, which has the nature of being impassioned, and hatred, which has the nature of being hostile.
"And having dispelled ignorance" means that, having dispelled delusion—which is the precursor among all unwholesome states—and having eradicated it by means of the Path;
such is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Saṅghā is finished.
The commentary on the Ekaka-nipāta is finished.
2. The Duka-nipāta: 1.
The commentary on the verses of the Bhikkhunī Thera Abhirūpanandā.
In the Second Book (Dukanipāta), there are the verses beginning with “The sick, the impure, the putrid,” spoken by the female trainee Abhirūpanandā.
It is said that she was born during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī as the daughter of a wealthy householder in the city of Bandhumatī;
having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher, she became established in the refuges and the precepts. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, at the relic-shrine...
Having made an offering with a golden parasol adorned with jewels, she passed away and was reborn in the heavenly realms.
Passing from one happy destination to another, she was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance in the city of Kapilavatthu, in the womb of Khema, the chief queen of the Sakyan Khema.
Her name was Nandā-tissā. She was exceedingly beautiful in her physical form.
Having attained the pinnacle of physical beauty, she was handsome, lovely to behold, and inspiring; thus she became known as Abhirūpanandā.
When she reached maturity, on the very day of her marriage, the Sakyan prince chosen as her husband passed away. Then her parents, against her will, ordained her.
Even after she had gone forth, she gave rise to pride based on her beauty, thinking: "The Teacher disparages and censures beauty in many ways."
She did not go to attend upon the Buddha, thinking, “He shows the danger in form.
When the Blessed One knew that her knowledge had reached maturity, he commanded Mahāpajāpatī, “Let all the bhikkhunīs come for exhortation in order of seniority.
When her own turn arrived, she sent another in her place. The Blessed One said, “When one’s turn arrives, one must come oneself.”
"No other [messenger] should be sent," he said. Being unable to transgress the Teacher's command, she went with the bhikkhunīs to attend upon the Buddha.
The Blessed One, having by means of his psychic power conjured up the form of a beautiful woman and then again shown her as aged and decrepit, stirred a sense of spiritual urgency in her and said:
“Behold, Nanda, this body: afflicted, impure, and putrid.
Develop a mind focused on the foul, one-pointed and well-concentrated.
Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit.”
“Then, through the realization of pride, you shall live in peace.
He spoke these two verses. Their meaning is exactly as explained in the method below. At the conclusion of the verses, Abhirūpanandā attained *arahantship*. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a kshatriya named Bandhuma;”
I was the queen of that king, and we lived together as one.
Seated in seclusion, I then thought thus:
"Having taken this life away, there is no wholesome deed performed by me that I may take with me."
“I shall surely go to the hell of Great Torment—bitter, terrible in form, and most dreadful; of this there is no doubt for me.
Having thought thus, and having gladdened my mind, I said:
Having approached the king, I spoke these words:
"O King, we women are always followed by men;
give me one ascetic, O Kshatriya, and I shall feed him."
“The Great King gave me a monk whose faculties were well-developed;
taking his bowl, I filled it with excellent rice.
Having filled it with that excellent rice, [I did so] with what was worth a thousand pieces.”
Having covered her with a pair of garments, I gave them to her with a joyful mind.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned this human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
“I exercised the sovereignty of a chief queen over a thousand kings of the gods;
I exercised the sovereignty of a chief queen over a thousand wheel-turning monarchs.
I held extensive regional kingdoms, beyond counting.”
From the fruit of that manifold and abundant merit,
my complexion became like that of a blue lotus— excellent, beautiful, and lovely.
I am a woman endowed with every limb, well-born, and radiant.
“In my final birth, I was born into the Sakyan clan as the foremost among a thousand women, the wife of Suddhodana’s son.
Having become disenchanted with the household life, I went forth into homelessness.”
Having reached the seventh night, I attained the Four Noble Truths:
“I am unable to measure the robes, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings; this is the fruit of almsfood.”
“O Sage, that wholesome karma which I previously generated—
O Great Hero, much was performed by me for your sake.
Thirty-one aeons ago, whatever gift I gave at that time,”
“I do not recognize a state of woe; this is the fruit of almsfood.
‘I know two destinations: that of the gods and that of humans;
I know no other destination—this is the fruit of almsfood.’”
“I know myself as having been born into high families, three times into wealthy *sāla* clans;
I know no other family—this is the fruit of almsfood.
Having wandered through various existences, I was impelled by the root of my wholesome merit.”
“I see nothing unpleasant as the fruit of my joy.
O Great Sage, I am a master of the supernormal powers, of the divine ear-element,
and I am a master of the knowledge of others' minds.”
“I know my former births; the divine eye is purified;
all taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
In the meanings, the teachings, the definitions, and likewise in inspired eloquence—”
“Knowledge has arisen in me, O Great Hero, in your presence:
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she herself also spoke this very verse as an inspired utterance (udāna), and this was her declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Abhirūpanandā is finished. 2.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Jentā begins with the words "These seven factors of enlightenment," etc. Regarding her past and present...
The setting is similar to that of the story of Abhirūpanandā; however, the distinction here is that she was reborn in the Licchavi royal family in Vesālī.
Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher and having attained Arahatship at the conclusion of the teaching, she reflected upon the excellence she had realized and, out of joy, [spoke as follows]:
“These seven factors of enlightenment, the paths for attaining Nibbāna—
all of these have been developed by me just as they were taught by the Buddha.
For I have seen that Blessed One, and this is my final physical body.”
“The wandering in birth is exhausted; now there is no further existence”—he spoke these two verses.
Therein, “these seven factors of enlightenment” refers to those known as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

There are seven states that have acquired the name "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) because they are factors of the aforementioned enlightenment (*bodhi*), or because they are factors of the person who possesses that enlightenment and awakens to it. They are called "the path for the attainment of Nibbāna" because they serve as the means for reaching Nibbāna.
All these thirty-seven states conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) have been developed by me just as they were taught by the Buddha.
All these have been generated and increased by me exactly as they were taught by the Blessed One, the Buddha.

The word *hi* in the phrase "for that Blessed One has been seen by me" (*diṭṭho hi me so bhagavā*) expresses a reason; because that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One whose body is the Dhamma (*dhammakāya*), has been seen by me through the vision of the Noble Dhamma attained within myself, therefore the construction is: "this is my final physical frame. [This is] by means of the vision of the Noble Dhamma.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and other Noble Ones are said to be "seen" by virtue of having seen the Dhamma, not merely by the sight of the physical body (rūpakāya).
As it is said: "Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me," and "Bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple is one who has seen the Noble Ones," and so forth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Jentā is finished.

3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumaṅgalamātā: The verses beginning with "Sumuttikā" belong to the Elder Nun Sumaṅgalamātā. She, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.
Having accumulated wholesome merit in various states of existence, she was reborn in this present era of a Buddha’s appearance into a poor family in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, she was given in marriage to a certain reed-worker, and in her very first pregnancy, she gave birth to a son who was to be her final existence.
His name was Sumaṅgala; from that time on, she became known as Sumaṅgala’s mother.
However, because her name and clan were not well-known, she is described in the Pāḷi as "a certain elder nun, unknown.
Her son, having reached maturity, went forth into homelessness and, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), attained Arahantship;
he became famous as the Elder Sumaṅgala. His mother, having gone forth among the nuns, [applied herself] to insight meditation (*vipassanā*)...
While performing her work, one day she reflected on the suffering she had experienced during her time as a householder;
filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, she developed insight, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), and uttered this exclamation:
“Truly released, truly released! I am well-released from the pestle!”
“My lizard is my sunshade, my tortoise is my mortar,” he said.
“Passion and hatred, I strike them down with the sound ‘cicciṭi cicciṭī’;
having gone to the foot of a tree, I meditate on happiness, thinking, ‘Oh, what bliss!’”
He spoke these two verses.
Therein, *sumuttikā* means "well-liberated. The syllable *ka* is merely for the purpose of completing the meter; the meaning is "she is indeed well liberated.
Having seen the excellence she herself had attained within the Teaching, he addressed her out of faith or, alternatively, by way of praising her.
It was said, “Well freed! Well freed! But showing her liberation from that which she especially loathed during her time as a householder, she said, “I am well freed,” and so forth.
In that context, “I am well freed” means: “Truly, I am rightly liberated. “From the pestle” means from the pestle.
It is said that because of her poverty during her time as a householder, she herself used to perform the work of pounding with the pestle.
