He says this because he does so. "My husband is shameless" means: my husband is shameless and devoid of modesty; the ellipsis is that "he is not pleasing to me.
She speaks thus, loathing the conduct of those intent on sensual pleasures, due to her natural detachment from such desires.
"Even a sunshade" means: even a sunshade made for the sake of sustaining life is not pleasing to me.
The word *vā* has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, she includes items such as baskets and boxes.
She speaks out of loathing for a life of suffering, which consists of taking up bamboo poles and other materials to fashion parasols and the like day after day.
Regarding the phrase “*ahitako me vāto vātī*,” some say the meaning is: “In my body during my time as a householder, an unwholesome wind—one that brings about old age—was blowing.”
They say this. Others, however, explain the meaning as: "A wind more foul-smelling than my own body blows, bringing harm to others.
Regarding the phrase "my mortar blows the scent of a water-snake," it means that my vessel for cooking rice, due to its long-term storage and lack of cleanliness, blows the odor of a water-snake;
from that, the construction is: "I am one who possesses excellent fragrance."
"I shall strike away passion and hatred with the sound 'cicciṭi cicciṭī,'" she said;
that is to say, I shall strike away, dispel, and abandon passion and hatred—the foremost of the defilements—along with this sound "cicciṭi cicciṭī.
It is said that, loathing her own husband, she would on those days [use] dried bamboo stalks and the like that were being split.
Criticizing sound, she spoke by equating its abandonment with the abandonment of lust and hatred.
"Having approached the foot of a tree" means that I, Sumaṅgalamātā, having approached a secluded spot at the foot of a tree. "I meditate for the sake of happiness" means I meditate on happiness;
entering attainment from time to time, I experience the bliss of the fruit and the bliss of Nibbāna.
The meaning is: "I meditate with the fruition-jhāna. As for the words "Oh, what happiness!", this is stated by way of the attention occurring after the attainment;
it is also quite appropriate as being by way of prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumaṅgalamātā is finished.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Aḍḍhakāsī.
The verses beginning with “As far as the Kāsi country” belong to the elder nun Aḍḍhakāsī. It is said that she was born into a noble family during the time of Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers;
having reached maturity, she went into the presence of the bhikkhunīs and heard the Dhamma.

Having gained faith and gone forth into homelessness, she insulted a certain elder nun—an arahant who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and was established in the virtue of a bhikkhunī—by calling her a "prostitute.
After dying from there and being cooked in hell, she was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha in a merchant family of great wealth in the kingdom of Kāsī.
Upon reaching maturity, as a result of the outflow of that past verbal misconduct, she...
Having fallen from her status, she became a courtesan. By name she was called Aḍḍhakāsī.
Her going forth and her higher ordination by messenger are recorded in the Khandhaka itself. For it is said:
"Now at that time, the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī had gone forth among the bhikkhunīs. She [went] to Sāvatthī..."
She desired to go, thinking, "I shall receive full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.
The scoundrels heard that the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī intended to go to Sāvatthī, so they ambushed her on the road.
When the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī heard that the scoundrels had indeed ambushed the road, she sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying: "As for me..."
“Desiring full ordination, how indeed should we proceed?

Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma on this occasion and in this context, addressed the bhikkhus: “I allow you, bhikkhus, to grant full ordination even by means of a messenger.”

Having thus attained full ordination, she applied herself to the practice of insight (vipassanā) and before long reached Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“In this auspicious eon, a glorious kinsman of Brahmā, Known by the clan-name Kassapa, arose as the best among those who speak.”
“Then, having gone forth in the teaching of that Buddha,
I was restrained by the Pātimokkha and in the five sense faculties.
I was moderate in eating and devoted to wakefulness.”
“Vasanti, I was joined with improper conduct; I reviled a nun who was free from taints.
With a wicked mind, I then called her a ‘prostitute.
Because of that evil deed, I burned in hell.”
“By the remainder of that karma, I was born into a family of courtesans;
for much of my final birth, I was dependent on others.
Through the power of my practice of celibacy, I was born into a merchant family in Kāsī.”
Like a celestial nymph among the gods was my perfection of form.
Having seen me, so beautiful to behold, in that most excellent city of Giribbaja,
they established me in the profession of a courtesan by means of their power of abuse.
“Having heard the true Dhamma taught by the Best of Buddhas,
and being endowed with the latent tendencies of my past lives, I went forth into the homeless state.
While traveling to the presence of the Victor for the purpose of receiving full ordination, I said:”
Having heard that the bandits were stationed on the road, I received the higher ordination as a messenger.
"All karma is utterly exhausted—both merit and likewise evil;
I have crossed over the entire saṃsāra, and my life as a courtesan is cast away."
“I am a master of the supernormal powers, of the divine ear-element,
and I am a master of the knowledge of others’ minds, O Great Sage.
I know my past lives, and the divine eye has been purified.”
"All taints are utterly destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
Regarding the meanings, the phenomena, the definitions, and likewise the inspired eloquence—O Great Hero, knowledge has arisen in me in your presence."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, however, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“As far as the Kāsi country, my toll was just that much;”
Having done that, the merchant guild set my price at half the value.
Then, becoming disenchanted with form, and being disenchanted, I became dispassionate:
"May I never again run on through the cycle of birth, time and again."
"The three knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished"—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, "the toll was as much as that of the Kāsi country" means the toll existing in the Kāsi countries is "the Kāsi-country toll."
Whatever it was, that much became my toll. But how much was it? It amounted to a thousand.
It is said that at that time, the revenue arising for the king in the kingdom of Kāsi on a single day by way of toll was a thousand;
the wealth obtained from these men’s hands on a single day was exactly that much. Therefore it is said: “As much as…”
“The country of Kāsi; such was my toll. Because it was measured by that amount of Kāsi-toll, it received the designation “Kāsi.
There, most people being unable to pay a thousand [pieces], would go away after enjoying themselves for only half a day by paying half of that;
on account of them, this place became known as “Aḍḍhakāsī” (Half-Kāsi). Therefore it was said: “Having done that...”
"The merchant guild has set my price at half [of what it should be].

Having fixed the value of that wealth at about five hundred [pieces], the merchant guild—the people living in the town—though she was priceless due to her being a jewel among women, established me under the designation "Half-Kāsī" by taking half as the indicative price;
the meaning is that they addressed me in such a manner.
“Then, ‘I became disenchanted with form’—thus I remained subsisting upon form. Afterwards, however, relying on the Teaching, I became disenchanted with form;
seeing that ‘in this way form is impermanent, in this way this form is suffering, and it is unattractive,’ I grew weary of it.
And while becoming disenchanted, I became dispassionate—thus, becoming disenchanted, I subsequently attained dispassion.”
And here, by the mention of "disenchantment" (*nibbinda*), he shows nascent insight (*taruṇa-vipassanā*); by the mention of "fading away" (*virāga*), he shows powerful insight (*balava-vipassanā*).

For it is said: "Becoming disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. By the phrase "May I not run on again and again through the cycle of births," he demonstrates the modes of disenchantment and dispassion.
By the words "The three true knowledges" (*tisso vijjā*) and so forth, he shows their reaching the ultimate point, which is in the manner already described.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Aḍḍhakāsī is finished. 5.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Cittā begins with the words "Though I am indeed emaciated. This [nun] also had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome merit that serves as a necessary condition for liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, she was reborn ninety-four aeons ago on the bank of the river Candabhāgā in the womb of a *kinnarī*.
One day, seeing a Paccekabuddha sitting at the foot of a tree, her mind became serene;
she made an offering with reed flowers, paid homage, and raised her hands in reverential salutation (*añjali*).

Having performed a circumambulation, she departed. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, she was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha in a wealthy merchant family of great standing in Rājagaha.
Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith at the time of the Teacher’s entry into Rājagaha, she later went forth under Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. In her old age, [she went] to Gijjhakūṭa Mountain.
Having ascended [the vehicle], while practicing the duties of a recluse and increasing her insight (vipassanā), she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a kinnarī;”
I saw the stainless Buddha, the self-become, the unconquered.
With a clear mind, joyful and filled with rapture, I joined my palms in reverence;
taking a garland of reeds, I worshipped the self-become one.
“By that well-performed karma and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned my body as a kinnarī, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, I exercised the supreme sovereignty over thirty-six kings of the gods.”
I served as the chief queen for ten wheel-turning monarchs;
then, having stirred my heart with spiritual urgency, I went forth into the homeless life.
"The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been utterly uprooted."
"All taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
Because I offered that flower ninety-four eons ago, I have never known a state of misery; this is the fruit of that flower-offering."
“The defilements have been incinerated by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she reflected upon her own practice:
“Although I am emaciated, ill, and exceedingly weak;”
“Clinging to my staff, I went forth, having ascended the mountain.
Having laid aside my outer robe and turned my bowl upside down,
I fixed myself upon the rock, shattering the mass of darkness.”
She spoke these two verses.
Regarding them: "Even though I am emaciated" means that although I am worn out by old age and my body is emaciated due to the lack of flesh and blood;
"sick and very weak" means sick through the transformation of the bodily elements and so forth, and very weak because of that very illness.
"Taking up my staff, I go"—meaning that wherever I go, I go only by leaning upon a walking stick.
"Having ascended the mountain"—even while in such a state, out of a desire for seclusion, having climbed Mount Vulture Peak.
"Having laid aside the outer robe"—meaning, being clad only in the inner and upper robes, [I take] the outer robe which was placed on my shoulder as it had been folded.
"Having placed [the bowl] within arm's reach. "And having turned the bowl upside down" means having set aside my personal use-bowl with its opening facing downwards in a secluded spot.

"I established myself upon the rock, shattering the mass of darkness" means that while seated on the mountain, having shattered the mass of delusion—which had never before been shattered throughout this long period—it was by that very [means].

By crushing the mass of delusion, I have suppressed my self and my personal existence; the meaning is that I have suppressed it by bringing about the state of non-arising for my mental continuum in the future.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Cittā is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Mettikā The verses beginning with "Though I am indeed afflicted" are the verses of the elder nun Mettikā.
She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; accumulating merit conducive to liberation throughout various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha—
Having been reborn in a household of lay devotees and having reached maturity, she made an offering of a jeweled belt adorned with gems at a shrine of the Teacher.
By that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in this current dispensation of the Buddha into a prominent brahmin family in Rājagaha.
The rest is as described in the preceding account. However, this one [offered] a replica-stupa.
Having ascended [the path], while practicing the duties of a recluse and increasing her insight (vipassanā), she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“I was the one who had a stupa built for the Blessed One Siddhattha.”
"A girdle was given by me for the construction work of the Teacher.
When the Great Thūpa was completed, with a mind full of faith, I gave that girdle once more to the Sage, the Lord of the World, with my own hands."
“Ninety-four eons ago, when I gave that girdle, I do not recall ever being born in an unhappy state; this is the fruit of one who built a stupa.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained arahantship and reflected upon her own practice,
she uttered this inspired verse: “Though I am afflicted, weak, and past my youth,
I climb the mountain, leaning on my staff.”
“Having laid aside my outer robe and turned my bowl upside down, I sat upon the rock; then my mind was liberated.
The three knowledges were attained, and the Buddha’s teaching was accomplished.”
He spoke these two verses.

Therein, "afflicted" (*dukkhitā*) means afflicted by the onset of disease, having experienced suffering, having reached a state of pain. "Weak" (*dubbalā*) means deprived of strength both by that experience of suffering and by the decrepitude of old age. Therefore he said, "whose youth has passed"; the meaning is "advanced in years.
Then my mind was liberated—while I was seated upon a rock (*selamhi*), immediately thereafter, through the balance of energy (*vīriyasamatāya*).
Because it was rightly applied according to the sequence of the paths, my mind was liberated from all taints (*āsava*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the elder nun Mettikā is finished.
7. Commentary on the verses of the elder nun Mittā.
The verses beginning with “On the fourteenth, on the fifteenth,” and so forth, belong to another elder nun named Mittā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was reborn in a noble warrior family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having attained maturity, she became a member of King Bandhuma’s harem and [attended upon] Vipassī.
Having seen a certain elder nun, a disciple of the Blessed One whose taints were exhausted, she became filled with serene faith;
taking the bowl from her hand, she filled it with choice hard and soft foods and gave it to her along with a pair of costly robes.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, she was born here in Kapilavatthu during this appearance of a Buddha.
Having been born into the Sakyan royal family and reaching the age of discretion, she heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher;

having gained faith, she became a lay follower (*upāsikā*). Later, having gone forth under Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and performed the preliminary duties, she applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a kshatriya named Bandhuma;
I was the queen of that king, and we lived together as one.
Seated in seclusion, I then reflected thus:”
For I have done no wholesome deed that might be taken with me when I go.
"I shall surely go to hell—greatly burning, bitter, terrible in form, and most dreadful; of this there is no doubt for me."
“Approaching the king, I spoke these words:
‘O Kṣatriya, give me one ascetic; I shall feed him.
The great king gave me an ascetic whose faculties were well-developed.”
Having taken his bowl, I filled it with excellent rice.
Having filled it with the excellent rice, I applied a coating of perfume;
having covered it with a net, I shielded it with a pair of cloths.
“This was my object of focus; I remember it for as long as I have lived.
Having gladdened my mind therein, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, I served as the chief queen to thirty kings of the gods.”
Whatever I desired in my mind was produced exactly as wished.
Having served as the chief queen to twenty universal monarchs,
and having been one who was worthy of such status, I have wandered through various states of existence.
“I am released from all bonds; my substrate of rebirth has departed.
All taints are utterly exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
That gift which I gave ninety-one eons ago—”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of alms-food.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [etc. ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he was filled with rapture and joy and uttered this inspired verse:
“On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as during the fortnight of miracles, I observed the Uposatha fully endowed with its eight factors, delighting in the hosts of devas.”
"Today, with but a single meal, shaven-headed and clad in the saṅghāṭī robe, I shall not long for the host of devas, having removed the fear from my heart"—with these two verses he spoke.
Therein, "on the fourteenth or the fifteenth" means: that which completes fourteen days is the fourteenth; that which completes fifteen days is the fifteenth.

The fifteenth day—meaning both the fourteenth and the fifteenth; this is connected with the word "of the fortnight" (*pakkhassa*), and this is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
The construction is: "and that which is the eighth day of the fortnight. And "the fortnight of miracles" (*pāṭihāriyapakkha*) refers to the protective fortnight (*pariharaṇakapakkha*);
for the Uposatha precept, these [days] are respectively at the beginning and the end of the fortnight, by way of entering and departing.
The meaning is: "and on the sides to be avoided," namely on the thirteenth, first, seventh, and ninth days.
"Well-endowed with the eight factors" means well-equipped with the eight factors beginning with abstention from taking life.
"I approached the Uposatha" means I undertook the fast; the sense is that I observed it. With reference to this, it was said:
“One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given; one should not speak falsehood, nor be a drinker of intoxicants;
one should abstain from unchaste conduct, that is, sexual intercourse; and one should not eat at night, which is eating at the improper time.
One should not wear garlands, nor use perfumes; one should lie on a mat upon the ground rather than on a bed.”
"For this is what is called the Eightfold Uposatha, proclaimed by the Buddha who has reached the end of suffering.

Regarding the phrase "delighting in the hosts of gods": the construction is that she approached the Uposatha desiring rebirth there, specifically longing for the host of gods beginning with the Cātumahārājika realm.
"She today with one meal" means: I, today, on this very day...

"At a single moment of eating a meal. "Shaven-headed and clad in the saṅghāṭī" means that having become one whose hair is shorn and whose body is covered by the saṅghāṭī robe, they have gone forth—that is the meaning.
"They do not long for a host of devas": because the supreme path has been attained, [one thinks] "I do not long for any class of devas.
For this very reason it was said: "Having removed distress from the heart," referring to the distress of the defilements residing in the mind.
The meaning is: "having guided her by means of complete eradication. And this very thing was her declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Mittā is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Abhayamātā.
The verses beginning with "Above the soles of the feet" are those of the Elder Nun Abhayamātā.
She too, having performed meritorious deeds in previous Buddhas' eras and accumulating merit in various existences, was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa.
Having reached maturity, one day, seeing the Teacher wandering for alms, she took his bowl with a mind full of faith.

She gave a portion of almsfood the size of a ladle. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, she was born during this appearance of a Buddha with the natural result of that karma as Padumavatī, the beauty of the city, in Ujjenī.
King Bimbisāra, having heard of her excellence such as her perfection of form and other qualities, informed his domestic priest: "In Ujjenī..."
“It is said there was a courtesan named Padumavatī; I am desirous of seeing her.

The chaplain replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and by the power of mantras summoned a yakkha named Kumbhīra. Through the supernatural power of the yakkha, he transported the king to the city of Ujjenī at that very moment.
The king spent one night in union with her, and she conceived a child from him. To the king—
She announced: "A fetus has taken root in my womb. Upon hearing this, the king said to her, "If it should be a son, raise him and show him to me," and having given her his signet ring, he departed.
When ten months had passed, she gave birth to a son; on the day of the naming ceremony, she gave him the name Abhaya. And when the son was seven years old—
“Your father is the great king Bimbisāra,” he sent word to the king. When the king saw his son and regained his affection for him, he raised him with the care appropriate for a prince.
His acquisition of faith, his going forth, and his attainment of distinction have already been related above.
Later on, his mother [listened to] the Dhamma from her son, the Elder Abhaya.

Having heard this, she gained faith and went forth among the bhikkhunīs. Performing the work of insight (vipassanā), she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“While the Teacher named Tissa was wandering for alms, ... [text continues] ...”
Taking up almsfood with a ladle, I gave it to the Buddha,
the Best of Men. Having accepted it, the Fully Enlightened One, Tissa, the Leader Supreme in the World,
the Teacher standing in the street, offered me a blessing of thanksgiving.
“Having given this spoonful of alms-food, you will go to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
there you will exercise the supreme sovereignty over thirty-six divine kings.
You will exercise the supreme sovereignty over fifty wheel-turning monarchs.”
"Everything you desire in your mind, you shall obtain at all times.
Having experienced prosperity, you will go forth as one free from worldly attachments;
having fully understood all taints, you will attain Nibbāna, free from taints."
Having said this, the Sambuddha, Tissa, the leader of the world, the Hero, rose up into the sky like a king of swans in the air:
“My supreme gift has been well given; my perfection of sacrifice has been well offered.”
Having given alms with a ladle, I attained the unshakable state.
"In the ninety-two aeons since then, because of that gift I gave, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of giving alms."
“The defilements have been consumed by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained Arahantship, she herself repeated those very verses that had been spoken as an exhortation by her son, the Elder Abhaya, while he was preaching the Dhamma:
“From the soles of my feet upward, O mother, And from the hair on my head downward, [there is nothing left].”
“Reflect upon this body, impure and foul-smelling.
‘While dwelling thus, all passion has been uprooted;
the fever has been cut off; I have become cool and attained Nibbāna,’ she said.”
Regarding this, the summary meaning of the first verse is as follows: "Mother Padumavatī, with the eye of wisdom, contemplate this body— the physical frame—
which from the soles of the feet upwards and from the crown of the head downwards, is filled with various kinds of impurities, is foul-smelling at all times due to its emission of stench,
and is called 'kāya' (body) because it is a locus (*āyatana*) for things that are contemptible."
This verse was indeed spoken by her son in the form of an exhortation.

Having heard it, she attained *arahantship* and, expressing her joy (*udāna*), spoke that very same verse first as an act of honoring her teacher. Then, describing her own practice, she spoke the second verse beginning with "Living thus" (*evaṃ viharamānāya*).
In this context, "living thus" means living in the manner described by my son, the Elder Abhaya, starting with the words "From the soles of the feet upward... and so forth.
Having stood by the instruction given, seeing the entire body as foul, and with a one-pointed mind,

having discerned therein the material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) consisting of the primary elements and the derived elements, as well as the immaterial phenomena (arūpa-dhamma) such as feeling which are bound up with them, and having applied the three characteristics to them,
she dwells by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth. Thus, "all lust is eradicated" refers to insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*).
"By means of the path, through the sequence of the path, all lust has been eradicated and uprooted by me with the supreme path.
'The fever has been cut off' means that for that very reason, the entire fever of the defilements has been completely severed;
and because it has been severed, we have become cooled and extinguished in the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining."
The commentary on the *Therīgāthā* of Abhayamātā is finished.
9. The commentary on the *Therīgāthā* of Abhayā:
The verses beginning with "Abhayā, the body is fragile" belong to the Elder Nun Abhayā. She, too, had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating merit that serves as the necessary condition for the turning away from existence in various states of being, she was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi in a great khattiya family of high standing.
Having reached maturity, she became the chief queen of King Aruṇa. One day, the king gave her seven lotuses endowed with exquisite fragrance.
Taking them, she thought: "What is the use of my wearing these? What if I were now..."
Having thought, “I shall worship the Blessed One,” she sat down. At the time for the alms-round, the Blessed One entered the royal palace.
Seeing the Blessed One, her mind filled with serene faith, she went out to meet him, worshipped him with those flowers, and paid homage by prostrating herself at his feet in the fivefold manner.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, as she transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, she was born in Ujjain during this current dispensation of a Buddha.
Having been reborn in a noble family and reached maturity, she became a companion to Abhayamātā.

When Abhayamātā had gone forth, out of affection for her, she herself also went forth. While living together with her in Rājagaha, one day she went to the Sītavana forest to contemplate the foulness [of the body].
Even while seated in the Gandhakuṭī, the Teacher [perceived] the object that she had previously experienced.
Placing it before her, he revealed its state as a bloated corpse and so forth. Seeing this, she stood there with a mind filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
The Teacher, having radiated light, manifested himself as if sitting right before her and said:
"O Abhayā, the body is fragile, wherein ordinary beings [cling]."
“I shall cast off this body, fully aware and mindful.
Through my delight in heedfulness amidst many painful conditions, the destruction of craving has been attained;
the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.”
She spoke these verses. At the conclusion of those verses, she attained Arahatship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Aruṇavatī, there was a kṣatriya named Aruṇa;
I was the queen of that king, and I would prevent what was forbidden.”
“Taking a garland of seven lotuses, divine and fragrant,
she sat in that excellent palace and at that moment thought thus:
‘What use have I for these garlands, even though they are placed upon my head?’”
I offered a boon to the Best of Buddhas regarding my knowledge:
"While waiting for the Fully Enlightened One, I shall sit near the gate;
when the Fully Enlightened One arrives, I will pay homage to the Great Sage."
“Like a lion, the king of beasts,
Kakudha was radiant as he went along the street with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, the Conqueror.
Seeing the radiance of the Buddha, they were joyful and their minds were moved with awe.”
Having opened the gate, I made an offering to the Buddha, the Most Excellent.
Seven lotus flowers were scattered in the sky;
they formed a canopy and held it over the head of the Buddha.
“With uplifted hearts, joyful and filled with rapture, I paid homage with palms joined;
having inspired confidence in my heart, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
A great sunshade was held over my head.”
“I waft a divine fragrance; this is the fruit of a single lotus.
Once, when I was being led away by my circle of kinsmen, as long as my assembly remained, a great stench was borne [by me].”
“I exercised the role of chief queen among seventy kings of the gods;
having been sovereign in every state, I wandered through various existences.
I exercised the role of chief queen among sixty-three universal monarchs.”
Everyone followed my lead, and my words were accepted.
"My complexion is like that of a blue lotus, and a fragrance wafts from me;
I do not even know what it is to be ill-favored—this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“Skilled in the bases of psychic power, delighting in the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment,
and having reached perfection in the direct knowledges— this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha.
Skilled in the foundations of mindfulness, with concentration and jhāna as their domain...”
Dedicated to right effort—this is the fruit of worshiping the Buddha:
"My energy is the beast of burden that bears the yoke, carrying me toward security from bondage.
All taints are utterly exhausted; now there is no further becoming."
“In the thirty-first aeon from now, because I offered that flower in worship, I have not known a state of misery.
This is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.’”
Having attained arahantship, she repeated those same verses in altered form and spoke them.
Therein, "O fearless one" (*abhaye*) is how she addresses herself. "Frail" (*bhiduro*) means having the nature of breaking up; the meaning is "impermanent.
"Wherein beings are worldlings" (*yattha sattā puthujjanā*) refers to that which, by its very moment of arising, has the nature of breaking up, being impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
These blind worldlings are attached and clinging to this body;
but as for me, thinking "I shall cast off this body," I shall—without further grasping and without regard for it—throw away and discard this putrid body. He states the reason for this:
"Clearly comprehending and mindful."
"By many states of suffering" means the intention is that they are touched by numerous states of suffering such as birth, aging, and so forth.

"Delighting in heedfulness" means delighting in heedfulness, which consists in the non-abandonment of mindfulness, because of the sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) obtained through that very state of being overwhelmed by suffering.
The rest is exactly as explained above. And here, according to the method taught by the Teacher—
“Cast off this body, for you who delight in heedfulness;
attain the destruction of craving and fulfill the teaching of the Buddha.

This is the reading, for it was included in the Council exactly according to the sequence spoken by the Elder Nun. Regarding the phrase “appamādaratāya te,” the meaning is: “By you, there must be delight in heedfulness.”
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Abhayā is finished. 10.

Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sāmā: The verses beginning with "Four times, five times," etc., belong to the Elder Nun Sāmā. She, too, had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various births, and wandering only among happy destinies, she was reborn during this appearance of a Buddha in a great merchant family in Kosambī, where she was named Sāmātissā.
Upon reaching maturity, she became a dear companion to the female lay follower Sāmāvatī; when Sāmāvatī passed away, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*sañjātasaṃvega*).
She went forth. Having gone forth, however, she was unable to dispel the grief arising from Sāmāvatī and thus failed to attain the Noble Path.

Later on, having heard the exhortation of the Elder Ānanda while he was seated in the assembly hall, she established insight meditation and, on the seventh day thereafter, attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
But having attained arahantship and reflecting upon her own practice, she explained it thus:
“Four times and five times I went out from my dwelling;
Failing to find peace of mind, I lacked mastery over my own heart.”
This is my eighth night since craving was uprooted.
Through delighting in heedfulness amidst many states of suffering, the destruction of craving has been attained;
the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished.
Out of inspiration, he uttered these two verses.
Therein, regarding the phrase "four times, five times, they went out from the monastery":

"In the monastery where I dwell, those who sit engaged in the mental application of insight (*vipassanā-manasikāra*) are unable to bring their ascetic task to completion due to the lack of favorable weather conditions; is it not indeed for my sake..."
Thinking, "Vipassanā must be joined with the path," she went out from her residence outside the monastery nine times—four or five times each.
Therefore he said: "Not having attained peace of mind, lacking mastery over the mind. Therein, "peace of mind" (cetaso santiṃ) is said with reference to the concentration of the Noble Path.
"Lacking mastery over the mind" (citte avasavattinī) is due to the absence of balance in effort.
My mind was not under my control during meditation; it is said that she possessed exceedingly exerted energy.

"For me, this is the eighth night"—from the time I received instruction from the Elder Ānanda, from that point on, practicing the work of insight without weariness day and night, four or five times during the night...
The meaning is that, having emerged from her dwelling and applied her attention, she attained a state of evenness in energy without yet reaching a further distinction;
then, on the eighth night, she exhausted the defilements according to the sequence of the paths. Therefore it was said:
“On that eighth night of mine, craving was uprooted. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Sāmā is finished.
The commentary on the Second Book (Dukanipāta) is finished.
3. The Third Book (Tikanipāta).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Aparā Sāmā. The verses beginning with “Twenty-five years” belong to the elder nun Aparā Sāmā in the *Tikanipāta*.

She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, and in various existences she accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*). Under the Blessed One Vipassī...
In due time, she was reborn in the womb of a *kinnarī* on the bank of the river Candabhāgā.

There she wandered about, intent on sporting with the *kinnaras*. Then one day, for the purpose of planting the seeds of merit within her, the Teacher went there and walked back and forth along the riverbank.
Upon seeing the Blessed One, she was filled with joy and delight; taking *saḷala* flowers, she approached the presence of the Teacher.
Having gone there and paid homage, she honored the Blessed One with those flowers.

By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a noble family in Kosambī. Upon reaching maturity, she became a companion to Sāmāvatī;
when Sāmāvatī passed away, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went forth into homelessness, and for twenty-five years maintained concentration of mind.

Having failed to obtain the Sugata’s instruction while she was old, she later obtained it, increased her insight (vipassanā), and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a kinnarī;”
I saw the God of Gods, the bull among men, walking in meditation.
Having plucked a *saḷala* flower, I gave it to the Best of Buddhas;
the Great Hero inhaled the *saḷala* flower, which was fragrant as the scent of the gods.
“Having accepted it, the Fully Awakened One, Vipassī, the Leader of the World,
the Great Hero, then smelled it while I was looking on.
Having raised my hands in añjali and paid homage to the Supreme among Bipeds,”
Having gladdened my own mind, I then ascended the mountain.
"In the ninety-first aeon, because I gave that flower at that time, I have not known an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“For twenty-five years, since I went forth...”
“I do not recall ever having attained even a moment’s tranquility of mind.
Having failed to gain peace of mind and being unable to exercise mastery over my own thoughts,
I was moved to a sense of spiritual urgency upon recollecting the teaching of the Conqueror.”
“Through delighting in heedfulness amidst many states of suffering, the destruction of craving has been attained by me; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Today is my seventh night since craving was dried up.”
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "calming of the mind" (*cittassa sama*) means the pacification of the mind; the meaning is the concentration of the path and the fruit, which is mental tranquility (*cetosaṃatha*).
"Therefore" (*tato*) means because of the state of being unable to bring the mind under control. "Attained a sense of spiritual urgency" (*saṃvegamāpādi*) [even] while the Teacher was still living.

Unable to bring the duties of one gone forth to their ultimate fulfillment, I fell into a state of spiritual urgency and the terror of knowledge, thinking, "How shall I bring them to completion later?
"Recalling the teaching of the Conqueror" means recollecting the Teacher’s exhortation, such as the Simile of the Blind Turtle and others.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the elder nun Aparā has been concluded. 2.
The commentary on the verses of the elder nun Uttamā begins with the words "Four times, five times," and so forth. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as the necessary condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of being, she was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Vipassi in the city of Bandhumatī as a domestic slave in the household of a certain householder.
Having reached maturity, she lived performing services for her mistresses. At that time, on the full-moon day, King Bandhuma...
Having observed the Uposatha, he gave gifts before the meal and went afterwards to listen to the Dhamma.
Then the great multitude, following the example of the king, conducted themselves by undertaking the Uposatha precepts on the full-moon day.
Thereupon, this thought occurred to that maidservant: "Nowadays, indeed, both the Great King and the great multitude undertake the Uposatha precepts."
“People are living this way; what if I were to undertake the Uposatha precepts on Uposatha days and live accordingly?
Acting thus, she protected the perfectly pure Uposatha precepts and was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas.
Passing from one happy destination to another, during the arising of this Buddha, she was reborn in a merchant’s family in Sāvatthī, and having reached maturity, she—
Having heard the Dhamma from the Elder Nun Paṭācārā, she went forth and applied herself to insight (vipassanā), yet she was unable to bring it to its ultimate consummation.
The Elder Nun Paṭācārā, perceiving her state of mind, gave her instruction.
Abiding by that instruction, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a kshatriya named Bandhuma;
on the day of the full moon, he observed the Uposatha fast.
At that time, I was a water-carrier slave-girl there.”
Seeing the army together with the king, I then thought thus:
"The king too, having abandoned his kingdom, observed the Uposatha;
surely that deed was fruitful, for the multitude of people is filled with joy."
“Having reflected thoroughly upon rebirth in the lower realms and poverty,
and having gladdened my mind, I observed the Uposatha.
Having performed the Uposatha in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, I— ”
By that well-performed kamma, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, I had a well-constructed mansion built,
rising two yojanas high, adorned with excellent gabled chambers and furnished with a magnificent throne.
“Hundred thousand celestial nymphs always attend upon me;
surpassing all other gods, I shine forth forever.
I exercised the role of chief queen over sixty-four divine kings.”
I served as the chief queen to sixty-three universal monarchs.
Having become golden-hued, I transmigrated through various states of existence;
in every place I was preeminent—this is the fruit of the Uposatha vow.
“Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and palanquins—I obtain all of these;
this is the fruit of the Uposatha.
Golden, silver, and even crystal [palaces].”
I obtain everything made of red gold.
I obtain silken garments, woolen blankets, and clothes made of linen and cotton—all garments of great value. I obtain it all.
“Food, drink, and solid food, as well as clothing and lodgings—I obtain all this;
this is the fruit of the Uposatha.
Exquisite perfumes, garlands, scented powders, and ointments—”
One obtains all this: this is the fruit of the Uposatha.
A gabled house, a palace, a pavilion, a turret, and a cave—one obtains all this:
this is the fruit of the Uposatha.
“At seven years of age, I went forth into homelessness;
before half a month had passed, I attained arahantship.
My defilements have been incinerated; all states of existence have been uprooted.”
All taints are utterly destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
"In the ninety-first aeon, whatever deed I performed then, I have not known a miserable rebirth—this is the fruit of the Uposatha."
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he uttered this inspired verse:
“Four times and five times I went forth from my dwelling;”
Having failed to attain peace of mind and being unable to master her own heart,
she approached a bhikkhunī who had been a source of faith for her;
that bhikkhunī taught her the Dhamma concerning the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements.
“Having heard the Dhamma from her, just as she instructed me,
I sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, endowed with rapture and bliss.
On the eighth day, I stretched out my feet, having shattered the mass of darkness.”
She spoke these verses.

Regarding them: "I approached that bhikkhunī who was trustworthy to me" means that she approached and went to that bhikkhunī who was one whose word could be relied upon and was worthy of faith; she speaks thus of the Elder Paṭācārā out of faith.
“*Sā bhikkhunī upagacchi, yā me sādhayikā*”—this is also a reading. The meaning is: that Bhikkhunī Paṭācārā approached me out of compassion, she who is the accomplisher of my own goal.
She taught me the Dhamma: the aggregates, the bases, and the elements. That elder nun Paṭācārā said: “These are the five aggregates; these are the twelve bases; these are the eighteen elements.”
Having analyzed and shown the aggregates and so forth, she taught the Dhamma to me.

"Having heard her Dhamma" means: having heard the Dhamma of subtle and refined insight—which was taught by that Elder Nun who had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)—and which led to the attainment of the Noble Path preceded by the analysis of the aggregates and so forth. "Just as she instructed me."
Acting according to how that elder nun instructed and exhorted me, and having brought my practice to its ultimate perfection, I sat for seven days on a single seat.
How so? "Endowed with rapture and bliss" means being possessed of the rapture and bliss born of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
On the eighth day, I stretched out my feet; thus, I shattered the mass of darkness—that is, the entire aggregate of delusion (*moha*)—without remainder.
Having shattered [the defilements] with the supreme path, on the eighth day, as she was breaking her cross-legged posture, she stretched out her feet.
This itself was her declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Uttamā is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of Another Supreme Therī.
These verses beginning with "These seven factors of enlightenment" belong to another supreme therī.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, [served] the Blessed One Vipassī.
In her time, she was reborn in the city of Bandhumatī as a slave girl belonging to a noble family.
One day, having seen a disciple of the Teacher—a certain elder whose taints were destroyed—wandering for alms, she gave him three sweetmeats with a devout heart.
By virtue of that meritorious deed, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was born here, during the arising of this Buddha, in a certain part of the Kosala country.
Having been reborn in a great brahmin family and reached maturity, she heard the Dhamma from the Teacher while he was wandering on a journey through the countryside.
Having gained faith, she went forth and, before long, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a water-carrier slave-girl;
having taken my share, I was going to fetch water.
On the road, I saw a monk whose mind was peaceful and composed.”
With a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave three sweetmeats.
By that well-performed deed and by my intention and aspiration,
for ninety-one eons I did not go to a state of ruin.
“Having performed that act of merit, I experienced all its fruits;
by giving three sweetmeats, I attained the unshakable state.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as above]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained arahantship and reviewing his own practice, he uttered this inspired utterance:
"These seven factors of enlightenment, The paths for the attainment of Nibbāna,
All have been developed by me Just as they were taught by the Buddha."
“I am one who attains emptiness and the signless at will;
I am the Buddha’s own daughter, always delighting in Nibbāna.
All sensual pleasures have been utterly cut off—both those of the devas and those of humans.”
“The wandering in birth is exhausted; now there is no further existence”—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, “I am one who attains at will the void and the signless” refers to the attainment of emptiness (*suññata-samāpatti*) and the attainment of the signless (*animitta-samāpatti*).

And the meaning is: "I am one who obtains whatever I desire; whatever attainment I wish to enter into, wherever and whenever I wish, I enter into that very attainment there and then, and dwell therein.

For although any given path—whether named emptiness (*suññatā*), the wishless (*appaṇihita*), or otherwise—can have a threefold fruit consisting of the distinctions of emptiness and so forth, this [attainment] however...
The elder nun enters only into the attainments of emptiness (*suññatā*) and the signless (*animitta*). Therefore it is said:
"I am an obtainer of the empty and the signless at will. Alternatively, this was said by way of the majority; others say that this is merely an illustration.
"Those divine and those human" refers to the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāmā*) included within the world of the gods and those included within the world of humans.
All of these have been rightly cut off by me through the abandoning of the desire and lust bound to them, and rendered unfit for enjoyment.
For it is said: "Friend, a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures in the same way as he did formerly when he was a householder.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the elder nun Aparā Uttamā is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the elder nun Dantikā:
"Having emerged from her daytime retreat," and so forth, are the verses of the elder nun Dantikā. She too had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as a support for the turning away from existence in various states of being, she was reborn in the womb of a *kinnarī* on the bank of the Candabhāgā River during a time when there was no Buddha.
One day, while wandering about sporting with the *kinnaras*, she saw a certain *paccekabuddha* sitting at the foot of a tree for his midday rest. Having seen him, she...
With a mind full of serene faith, she approached, made an offering of *sāla* flowers, paid homage, and departed.
Through that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, she was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in the household of a brahmin chaplain to the King of Kosala in Sāvatthī.
Having reached maturity, she gained faith upon the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery and became a lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Later, having gone forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and residing in Rājagaha,
one day after her meal she ascended Gijjhakūṭa mountain and sat for her midday rest. There, seeing an elephant extending its leg in order for a mahout to mount it,
she took that very sight as her object, developed insight, and [attained the fruits] together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
He attained arahantship. Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“On the banks of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a kinnarī;
I saw the stainless Buddha, the self-enlightened one, the unconquered.”
“With a clear mind, joyful and filled with rapture, I joined my palms in reverence;
taking sal and māla flowers, I worshipped the Self-Existent One.
By that well-performed deed, and by my volition and aspiration...”
Having cast off my kinnarī body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
There, I exercised the supreme sovereignty over thirty-six divine kings;
whatever was desired by my mind arose for me exactly as I wished.
“I served as the chief queen to ten universal monarchs;
having been worthy of such status, I wandered through various states of existence.
Yet, wholesome merit remains within me, for I have gone forth into the homeless life.”
Today I am worthy of worship in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyas.
With a purified mind today, free from mental evil,
and with all taints utterly destroyed, there is now no further becoming.
“For ninety-four eons, since I worshipped the Buddha, I have not known a bad rebirth.
This is the fruit of that *sāla* garland.
The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest as usual]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
But having attained arahantship and reflecting upon his own practice, filled with joy and gladness, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having come out from my midday rest on Mount Vulture Peak,
I saw an elephant emerging from the water at the river’s edge.”
“A man, taking up a goad, requested, ‘Give me your foot!
The elephant extended his foot, and the man mounted the elephant.
Having seen him—once untamed but now tamed, brought under the control of men—the people were amazed.”
“Then I composed my mind, having indeed gone to that forest”—thus he spoke these verses.
Regarding them: *nāgaṃ ogāhamuttiṇṇaṃ* means a noble elephant who, having entered the river, has plunged in and emerged from it.
Alternatively, the reading is *ogayha muttiṇṇaṃ*; the letter *m* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*). They saw him on the bank of the river Candabhāgā.
"I saw [him] on the bank of the river.

To show what he was doing, it is said, "A man," and so forth. Therein, "he begs, 'Give me a foot'" means he gives a signal to extend his foot for the purpose of climbing onto his back; for, as is well known...
"He asks here for one who gives consent" means he requests it here.

"Having seen one untamed, tamed" means that which was previously untamed by nature has now been brought to the state of being tamed through the training of an elephant trainer (*hatthācariya*) in the art of elephants.
What kind of taming? It is having come under the control of humans; whatever humans—

The construction is: "Having seen this and that, they commanded. Then, "I concentrated my mind, for indeed she had gone to the forest"—here, *khalu* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇatthe*).

Thus, after seeing the elephant, because of her action regarding the elephant which served as the cause, I concentrated my mind precisely upon her having gone to the forest, to the wilderness. How so? "Even this one, it seems, is a beast..."

“Since even an elephant has attained taming through the power of an elephant-tamer, why should the mind of one who has become human not attain taming through the power of the Teacher, the Tamer of Men?

Having thus become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she developed insight (*vipassanā*) and concentrated her mind upon me by means of the supreme path-concentration (*aggamagga-samādhi*).
The meaning is that, through this ultimate concentration, she completely exhausted all defilements (*kilesa*).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Dantikā is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Ubbirī: "Mother, live," etc., are the verses of the Elder Nun Ubbirī. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. There...

There, having accumulated wholesome kamma as a support for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*), she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
Having reached maturity, one day, while her parents had gone elsewhere to observe an auspicious festival, she remained alone at home.
As the time drew near, she [beheld] a certain Elder who was an Arahant and disciple of the Blessed One.
Seeing him walking near the door of her house, she, wishing to give alms, said, "Venerable sir, please enter here.
When the Elder had entered the house, she paid homage to him with the fivefold prostration, prepared a seat with woolen rugs and other coverings, and offered it to him.
The Elder sat down on the prepared seat. She took his bowl, filled it with alms-food, and [presented it] to the Elder.
He placed it in her hand. Having offered words of thanksgiving, the Elder departed. By virtue of that meritorious deed, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas;

there, having enjoyed magnificent divine prosperity for the full span of her life, and passing away from there, she wandered through happy destinies alone until, during the present arising of a Buddha, she was reborn in the family of a wealthy householder in Sāvatthī as Ubbarī.
She was well-named, beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring. When she reached maturity, she was taken to the home of the King of Kosala.
After several years had passed, she gave birth to a daughter. They gave her the name Jīvantī.
When the king saw his granddaughter, his heart was filled with joy, and he bestowed upon her the consecration of Ubbarī. As for his own daughter...
Having run about and wandered hither and thither during her time of wandering, she passed away.
Her mother went to the cemetery where her body had been laid and lamented day after day.
One day, having gone into the presence of the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down for a short while, she then stood on the bank of the river Aciravatī and lamented concerning her daughter.
Seeing him, the Teacher, remaining seated right where he was in the Fragrant Chamber, manifested himself and asked, "Why do you lament?

"I am lamenting for my daughter, Blessed One," he replied. "In this very charnel ground, eighty-four thousand of your daughters have been cremated; which of them are you lamenting for? [He spoke] of each one of them.
Having shown her the place of cremation, he said:
"Mother, you cry out 'Jīvā' in the forest; O Ubbirī, regain composure for yourself!
Eighty-four thousand women, all bearing the name Jīvā,"
"Those who have been burnt in this funeral pyre—why do you grieve for them?"—with these words he spoke the half-stanza.
Therein, "O Mother," is an address to his daughter using a term of endearment for a mother; this shows the manner of her lamentation.
"You wail in the forest" means you lament in the midst of the woods. "Attain yourself, O Ubbirī" means, O Ubbirī, [recover] yourself.
First, awaken yourself; know yourself as it truly is. "Eighty-four thousand" means eighty-four thousand.
"All bearing the name Jīvā" means that all those who bear that same name are living.
"Burnt in this cremation ground" means consumed in this charnel ground. "Whom among them do you grieve for? refers to those eighty-four thousand who are currently living and bearing that name.

"Whom do you grieve for, that you fall into such grief? When the Teacher had thus taught the Dhamma, [the bhikkhu] directed his knowledge according to the teaching, began insight meditation, and—by means of the Teacher’s skillful exposition and his own perfection of causes—intensified his insight exactly as it stood.
He then became established in the fruit of Arahantship, the highest fruit, following the sequence of the paths.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was a young girl at that time;
both my mother and my father had gone away on business.”
“At midday, when the sun was high, I saw a recluse walking along the street; I prepared a seat for him.
Having prepared my seat with woolen rugs and antelope skins, I said:”
With a serene mind and joyful heart, I spoke these words:
“The earth is parched and steaming, the sun stands at midday;
the breezes do not blow, and it will surely rain here today.”
“This seat has been prepared for you, O Great Sage;
out of compassion, please sit upon my seat.
There the ascetic sat, well-tamed and pure in mind.
Having taken his bowl, I gave it back to him according to its condition.
By that well-performed deed and by my volition and aspiration,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
“Therein I have constructed a celestial palace, well-fashioned and beautifully furnished with seats;
sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width.
It is made of gold, made of jewels, and likewise made of crystal.”
My couches were of various kinds, made of red sandalwood.
They were furnished with cotton mattresses, woolen rugs, and embroidered coverlets;
my well-constructed couches were also covered with long-haired blankets spread out on one side.
“When I desired to go, while engaged in laughter and play,
I would go wherever I wished along with my most excellent couch.
I exercised the supreme sovereignty over eighty kings of the gods.”
I exercised the sovereignty of a Great Queen over seventy universal monarchs.
"As I wandered through various existences, I obtained great wealth;
there was no deficiency in my riches—this is the fruit of that single seat."
“I have transmigrated through two states of existence—among the gods and among humans;
I know no other state of existence. This is the fruit of the single-seat meal.
I am reborn into two kinds of families: among the Khattiyas and the Brāhmaṇas.”
I am of high birth everywhere; this is the fruit of eating at a single sitting.
I know no mental distress that scorches the heart;
I know no change in my complexion; this is the fruit of eating at a single sitting.
“Nurses attend upon me—many hunchbacked female slaves;
I go from lap to lap; this is the fruit of a single seat.
Others bathe me, others feed me, and others always delight me.”
Others anoint me with perfumes; this is the fruit of using a single seat.
Whether dwelling in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, knowing my intention, a couch appears before me.
“This is my final one; my last existence is now unfolding.
Even today, having renounced my kingdom, I went forth into the homeless life.
That gift which I gave back in a hundred thousand aeons—”
“I do not know a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of the single seat.

Having thus established herself in Arahantship, she proclaimed the distinction she had attained: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Then, manifesting the excellence she had personally realized—
“Pull out the arrow from my heart, so difficult to see, which has struck me down with grief;
dispel the sorrow for my daughter that has overwhelmed me.
Now that the arrow has been pulled out, I am free from craving and have attained final peace.”
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, O Sage”—
these two verses he spoke. Therein,

“The arrow has indeed been pulled out from my heart, so difficult to see,” refers to [the state] of those who have not accumulated the equipment of wholesome merit, regarding things as they truly are.
"Difficult to see" refers to sorrow and craving, which have acquired the name "dart" because they produce affliction, are difficult to extract, and pierce within;
he has indeed pulled them out, he has indeed removed them. Regarding the phrase "which [was] for me overcome by sorrow":

since he completely dispelled my daughter's grief—that is, removed it without remainder—for me who was overwhelmed by sorrow, therefore the construction is: "He has indeed pulled out the dart from me."
"Today, with the arrow extracted": today I have completely uprooted the arrow of craving;

therefore, I am free from hunger and have attained final Nibbāna. "The Sage" refers to the Omniscient Buddha, as well as the ninefold supramundane Dhamma consisting of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna taught by him, and the Saṅgha, which is the assembly of the eight types of noble persons established therein.
[I pay homage] because of my union with those unsurpassed qualities.

Because it destroys all the suffering of saṃsāra, it is a refuge, a protection, a shelter, and a final resort; thus, "I go for refuge" means that I approach, I draw near, I awaken to, and I serve [it].
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Ubbirī is finished.
6. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sukkā. The verses beginning with "What have I done in Rājagaha? are the verses of the elder nun Sukkā.
She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī—
Having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Bandhumatī and having reached maturity, she went to the monastery with female lay devotees (*upāsikā*).
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she acquired faith, went forth (*pabbajita*), and became one who was learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and possessed of ready eloquence.
Having practiced the holy life (*brahmacariya*) there for many thousands of years, she passed away as a worldling (*puthujjana*).

Having done so, she was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Likewise, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi and the Blessed One Vessabhu—thus, having guarded her virtue under the dispensations of three Sammasambuddhas—she became one who was very learned and a bearer of the Dhamma.
Similarly, having gone forth under the dispensations of the Blessed Ones Kakusandha, Konagamana, and Kassapa, she was pure in virtue.
She became one who was very learned and a preacher of the Dhamma.

Thus, having accumulated much merit here and there and wandering only among the happy destinies, she was reborn in this present arising of a Buddha in the city of Rājagaha into a family of great householders as a daughter named Sukkā. When she reached maturity...
Having attained faith upon the Teacher’s entry into Rājagaha, she became a lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Later, having heard the Dhamma from the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Having gone forth in her very presence, she applied herself to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and before long attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Ninety-one eons ago, a leader named Vipassī arose,
beautiful to behold and possessing insight into all phenomena.
At that time, I was born in a certain family in Bandhumatī.”
Having heard the Dhamma from the Sage, I went forth into the homeless life.
"I was one who had heard much, a bearer of the Dhamma, likewise possessed of inspired eloquence,
a speaker of diverse discourses, and a fulfiller of the Victor’s teaching."
“Then, having delivered a discourse on the Dhamma for the benefit of many people,
I passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven, possessed of great glory.
Thirty-one eons ago, like the Conqueror Sikhī, I was Sikhī.”
Shining with glory throughout the world, the best among those who speak arose.
"At that time also, having gone forth and becoming experts in the Buddha's teaching,
they illuminated the words of the Victor and likewise went to the triple heaven."
“In the thirty-first aeon, a leader named Vessabhū, a possessor of great wisdom, appeared; and at that time, I was likewise.
Having gone forth as a bearer of the Dhamma, I illumined the teaching of the Conqueror.”
Having gone to the delightful city of the gods, I experienced great bliss.
In this auspicious eon, Kakusandha, the supreme Victor, arose as a refuge for humanity;
and at that time, too, I was exactly like this.
“Having gone forth and illuminated the Sage’s teaching for the duration of my life,
I passed away from there and went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
as if to my own abode. In this very eon, the Leader named Koṇāgamana— ”
The refuge of the world arose, free from defilement, having reached the deathless state.
Then too, having gone forth in the teaching of that Tathāgata,
those who were learned and upholders of the Dhamma illuminated the Conqueror’s dispensation.
“In this very eon, Kassapa, the supreme sage,
arose as a refuge for the world— one free from defilement, who has reached the end of death.
Having gone forth under the teaching of that hero among men, too— ”
Having mastered the true Dhamma, confident in their inquiries,
virtuous and modest, and skilled in the three trainings—
having delivered many discourses on the Dhamma throughout her life, O Great Sage.
“By the ripening of that karma, and through my volition and aspiration,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
And now, in this final existence, in the most excellent city of Giribbaja...”
She was born into a prosperous merchant family, amidst a great accumulation of precious jewels.
"When the Leader of the World, surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus and praised by the Thousand-Eyed One, arrived at Rājagaha..."
“The Tamed One, together with the tamed, the ancient matted-hair ascetics;
the Liberated One, together with the liberated—[he who is] the color of molten gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.
Having seen that majesty of the Buddha, and having heard of the accumulation of his virtues,”
Having inspired confidence in my mind toward the Buddha, I honored him according to my ability.
And at a later time, having gone forth from the home into homelessness, I went into the presence of Dhammadinnā and took up the life of a wanderer.
"While my hair was being cut off, I extinguished the defilements;
having gone forth, I mastered the entire teaching after a long time.
Thereafter, I taught the Dhamma in a great assembly of people."
While the Dhamma was being taught, there was a penetration of the Dhamma.
Having seen that for many thousands of beings, the Yakkha, who had wandered through Giribbaja, became deeply moved and full of faith in me.
“What have the people of Rājagaha done to me, that they act like nymphs who have drunk honey—
those who do not wait upon the One who teaches the deathless state?
And that [teaching] is irresistible, refreshing, and full of vigor.”
"The wise, I think, drink [me] as travelers drink from a cloud. O Great Sage,
I am a master of the supernormal powers, a master of the divine ear-element,
and a master of the knowledge of others' minds."
“I know my former births; the divine eye is purified;
all taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
In the meanings, the phenomena, the definitions, and likewise in inspired eloquence,”
“Knowledge has arisen in me, O Great Hero, in your presence:
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she became a great preacher of the Dhamma with a retinue of five hundred bhikkhunīs. One day, she—
Having walked for alms in Rājagaha and finished his meal, he entered the nuns’ quarters and taught the Dhamma to a large assembly that had sat down;
he taught as if squeezing out honey-essence and pouring it out most sweetly, or as if sprinkling them with the Deathless.
And the assembly listened to his discourse on the Dhamma with attentive ears and undistracted minds, paying full respect.
He heard it. At that moment, a deity dwelling in a tree at the end of the elder nun’s walking path, having become inspired by her teaching of the Dhamma,
entered Rājagaha and wandered from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads,
proclaiming her virtues:
“What have the people of Rājagaha done to me? They are like nymphs who have drunk honey!
For they do not approach the pure one as he teaches the Buddha’s dispensation.
And that [dispensation] is irresistible, its vital energy is unquenchable.”
"The wise ones drink me in, like travelers drinking from a cloud"—these two verses he spoke.
Therein, "What have these people done in Rājagaha? means: what have these people in Rājagaha done; in what matter indeed?

"Busy. "They have drunk the honey, O Apsarases"—just as those who have taken fermented honey and drunk it become unconscious and are unable to lift their heads, so too these people, having become unconscious through the perception of phenomena (*dhamma-saññā*), seem unable to lift their heads;
the meaning is that they merely remain still. "Those who do not wait upon the bright [light]."

"Those who do not wait upon or attend to the Elder Sukkā, who teaches and proclaims the Buddha’s dispensation (sāsana) exactly as it is"—this is the construction: "What have these people in Rājagaha done?
And that [dispensation] is "unopposable," meaning it brings about a state from which there is no turning back, it is leading to liberation, and because of its excellence.
Or, because it is enchanting to the ears of those who hear it, it is "unremovable" (*anapanīya*), "unquenchable" (*asecanaka*), and "unsurpassed" (*anāsittaka*);
by its very nature it possesses great flavor, and for that very reason it is "nutritious" (*ojavanta*). There is also a textual variant reading *osadha*.

It is like a medicine for curing the disease of the suffering of saṃsāra. "The wise drink it, as travelers [drink] from a cloud"—this refers to water issuing forth from within a cloud in a waterless wilderness.
Wise and learned men, it seems, drink in that Dhamma like wayfarers; they listen as if they were drinking.
Having heard it, people with serene minds approached the Elder Nun and listened to the Dhamma with great respect.
Later, at the end of her life, when the time for her Parinibbāna arrived, she uttered a declaration of attainment (*aññā*) in order to demonstrate the liberating nature of the Dispensation:
“Pure by means of pure qualities, free from passion, and composed, she bears her final body, having conquered Māra and his mount”—thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “pure” (sukkā) refers to the Elder Nun Sukkā, who describes herself as another. “By means of pure qualities” (sukkehi dhammehi) means by means of those that are perfectly purified.

"By means of supramundane states. "Free from passion and concentrated" means completely free from passion by means of the supreme path and concentrated by means of the concentration of the fruit of arahantship. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Bhikkhunī Sukkā is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Selā.
The verses beginning with "There is no escape from the world" belong to the elder nun Selā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having been reborn and reached the age of discretion, she was given by her parents to a young man of the same caste.
After living with him for many hundreds of years in happy companionship, when he had passed away, she herself had also advanced in years and reached old age.
Having become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and seeking what is wholesome, she would from time to time wander from monastery to monastery and from vihāra to vihāra.
“I shall hear the Dhamma in the presence of ascetics and brahmins.

One day, she approached the Bodhi tree of the Teacher and sat down, saying, “If the Blessed Buddha is peerless, equal to the unequaled, and without a rival, let this Bodhi tree display a miracle for me! At the very moment that thought arose in her, the Bodhi tree burst into flames.
All its branches became made of pure gold and shone in every direction.

Having seen that miracle, her mind filled with serene confidence, she established a sense of profound reverence and, raising her joined palms to her head, remained seated right there for seven days and nights.
On the seventh day, she performed a magnificent offering and honor. By virtue of that meritorious deed, she [was reborn] among gods and humans.
Wandering through the cycle of existence, she was reborn during this current dispensation of a Buddha as the daughter of King Āḷavika in the kingdom of Āḷavi.
Her name was Selā, but because she was the daughter of King Āḷavika, she was also commonly addressed as Āḷavikā.
When she reached maturity, the Teacher subdued the yakkha Āḷavaka and placed his bowl and robe in his hand; by him—
Having arrived at the city of Āḷavī together with the King, she became a young girl;

having approached the Teacher along with the King and heard the Dhamma, she attained faith and became a lay follower (*upāsikā*). Later, having become spiritually stirred, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs.

Having performed the preliminary duties and established insight (*vipassanā*), she contemplated conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*); and because she was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), [she attained realization].
When her knowledge was fully ripened, she attained arahantship before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was then a wandering nun;
seeking what is wholesome, I went from monastery to monastery.”
On the day of the dark fortnight, I beheld the supreme Bodhi tree;
having inspired confidence in my heart there, I sat down at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Establishing a mind of reverence and placing my joined palms upon my head, I paid homage.
Having proclaimed his joy, he then thought thus:
"If the Buddha, who possesses immeasurable qualities and is a peerless person, is indeed so,
let him show a miracle to me and let this Bodhi tree radiate light."
“As soon as I directed my attention, the Bodhi tree burst into flame;
all directions became entirely golden and shone forth brilliantly.
For seven days and nights, I sat there at the foot of the Bodhi tree.”
When the seventh day had arrived, I performed an offering of lamps.
Surrounding the seat, I lit five lamps;
as long as the sun did not rise, my lamps continued to burn.
“By that well-performed kamma, and through my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm. There,
a well-constructed palace was mine, which is called ‘The Five Continents.’”
Sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width,
countless islands surrounded me and blazed with light,
