so that the entire realm of the gods was illuminated by the radiance of those lamps.
“Even sitting with my back turned, if I wish to see,
I see everything— above, below, and across— with my eye.
To whatever extent I desire to see the well-fared and the ill-fared, [I see it].”
Therein there was no obstruction, whether from trees or mountains:
“I exercised the role of chief queen among eighty kings of the gods;
I exercised the role of chief queen among hundreds of wheel-turning monarchs.”
“Whichever womb I am reborn into, whether among the gods or among humans,
a hundred thousand lamps surround and illuminate me.
Having passed away from the world of the gods, I was conceived in a mother’s womb.”
While remaining in my mother’s womb, my eyes did not close.
Because of my possession of meritorious deeds, hundreds of thousands of lamps burn in the birth-chamber;
this is the fruit of the five lamps.
“When my final existence was reached, I turned back the mind;
I touched Nibbāna, the cool state, free from aging and death.
At seven years of age, I attained Arahatship.”
The Buddha Gotama, recognizing her virtues, granted her full ordination.
"While dwelling in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut,
may a lamp then blaze forth for me"— this is the fruit of the five lamps.
“My divine eye is purified; I am skilled in concentration.
Having reached the perfection of direct knowledge, this is the fruit of the five lamps.
With all duties completed, my task done, I am free from taints.”
“O Great Hero, O Eyeful One, I pay homage at your feet.
Because I gave a lamp five hundred thousand eons ago, I have not known a miserable rebirth;
this is the fruit of those five lamps.”
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, the Therī was dwelling at Sāvatthī;
one day, after her meal, she departed from Sāvatthī and, entering the Andhavana forest for the sake of her midday rest, sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Then Māra, desiring to sever her from solitude, approached her in the guise of a stranger and spoke this verse:
“There is no escape in the world; what will you achieve through solitude?
Enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure, lest you be filled with regret later.”

The meaning of this is as follows: even when all systems in this world are investigated, there is no such thing as Nibbāna as an escape for those various recluses and brahmins; what they profess is merely a matter of verbal convention based on their own desires.
Therefore, what will you achieve by seclusion? Being established in such a prime of youth, what is the use of this physical seclusion?
Will you do so? Rather, enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure based on both material objects and mental defilements;
experience the delights of play. Why? Lest you later feel remorse, thinking: "For the sake of which I practiced the holy life—that very Nirvana does not exist;
for that reason it was not attained, and yet I have fallen away from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. Alas, this has been to my loss!"
The intention is: "Do not be one who later feels regret.
Having heard that, the Elder Nun thought: "This Māra is truly a fool, he who denies Nibbāna which is manifest before my very eyes.
He invites me to sensual pleasures and does not know my state of having exhausted the taints. Come now, let me inform him of this and reprimand him. Having reflected thus—
“Sensual pleasures are like spears and pikes, a violent hacking at the aggregates.
That which you call delight in sensual pleasures is now, for me, no longer delight.
Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.”
"Know this, O Evil One: you are slain, O Ender!"—with these words he spoke this pair of verses.
Therein, "desires are like spears and stakes" means that desires should be regarded as being like a sharpened spear or a stake, because they pierce through the being who is intent upon them.
"The aggregates" refers to the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). "They sit" means they dwell within those [aggregates].
*Adhikuṭṭanā* means the state of cutting or the basis of cutting; the meaning is the state of excessive grasping (*accādāna*).

For by excessively grasping at the aggregates, beings undergo being cut and torn apart by sensual pleasures. "That which you call delight in sensual pleasures, that is now a source of aversion for me," [said the Buddha].
O Evil One, that which you speak of as delight in sensual pleasures—something to be enjoyed and cultivated—is now, for me, of the nature of aversion because I am free from such passion.
“Like excrement, I have no need for her. Regarding this, he states the reason with the words, “In every way, delight has been destroyed,” and so forth. In that context, “Know me thus” means:

“Know me as one who has utterly abandoned craving and ignorance. For that very reason, O Antaka, you of base conduct, [you are surpassed] by my power, my destruction [of defilements], and my transcendence of your domain.
"Māra, you have been defeated and oppressed by me; it is not I who am to be oppressed by you"—this is the meaning.

Thus, having been rebuked by the elder nun, Māra vanished right there. The elder nun, too, having spent part of the day in the Andhavana grove in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), went back to her dwelling place in the evening.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Selā is finished.
8. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Somā. The verses beginning with “That which is to be attained by the seers” belong to the elder nun Somā.
She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation throughout various existences, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhi...
Having been reborn in a great khattiya family and having reached maturity, she became the chief queen of King Aruṇa;
thus, the entire past account is similar to that of the Elder Nun Abhayā. As for the present account:
wandering through various realms among gods and humans, this elder nun was, during the arising of this Buddha, the chaplain to King Bimbisāra in Rājagaha.
Having been offered as an oblation, she was reborn. Her name was Soma.

When she reached maturity, she gained faith upon the Teacher’s entry into Rājagaha and became a lay follower (*upāsikā*). Later, having developed a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she went forth among the bhikkhunīs.

Having performed the preliminary duties and applied herself to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*), she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“In the city of Aruṇavatī, there was a kṣatriya named Aruṇa;
I was the queen of that king, and I prevented what should be prevented. ‘As far as...
[the verse continues] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.’”
Everything is identical to the Apadāna of the Elder Nun Sabba.
Having attained Arahantship, she dwelt in Sāvatthī enjoying the bliss of liberation.
One day, having entered the Andhavana forest for her midday rest, she sat down at the foot of a certain tree. Then Māra, desiring to sever her from her seclusion, approached her.
Approaching while remaining invisible and standing in the air,
he recited this verse: “That state which is to be attained by seers, so difficult to achieve—
That cannot be reached by a woman with her two-fingered wisdom.”

The meaning of this is as follows: That which is to be attained by the Buddhas and others of great wisdom—who are called "seers" (*isi*) in the sense of seeking the aggregate of virtue and so forth—is difficult for others to approach and difficult to accomplish.
That state of supreme consolation known as Arahantship cannot be reached by a woman of two-fingered wisdom or inferior intelligence.
For women, from the age of seven or eight years onward, they cook rice at all times;
yet, having thrown the rice grains into boiling water, they do not know, "The rice is cooked to this extent.
Rather, while the rice is boiling, they take a grain with a ladle, press it between two fingers, and thereby know. Therefore, she is said to possess "the wisdom of the two fingers."
Having heard this, the Elder Nun, warding off Māra, said:
“What could our female state matter, when the mind is well-concentrated,
while knowledge is active and one is correctly discerning the Dhamma?”
“Delight has been destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness has been shattered;
know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!”—with these words she spoke the other two verses.
In that regard, "what would womanhood do? means: what would the state of being a woman do for us; what kind of obstacle would it create for the attainment of Arahatship?
"When the mind is well-composed" means: when the mind is thoroughly concentrated by means of the concentration of the supreme path.
"While knowledge is proceeding" means: while the knowledge of the path to Arahatship is thus occurring. "The Dhamma correctly..."
"Vipassati" means seeing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths correctly by way of full understanding and so forth. This is the summary here:
"O Evil One, whether it be a woman or a man, once the supreme path has been attained, Arahatship is as good as held in one's own hand.
Now, showing directly his own state of attainment, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sabbattha vihatā nandī. Its meaning is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Somā is finished.
The commentary on the Tika-nipāta (The Book of Threes) is finished.
4. Catukka-nipāta (The Book of Fours).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kāpilānī.
The verses beginning with “The son of the Buddha is an heir” belong to the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kāpilānī.
It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and, having reached maturity...
Having reached the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī as the foremost among those who recollect their past lives (*pubbenivāsa*).
Having performed an act of service and herself aspiring for that very position, she practiced meritorious deeds throughout her life.
Passing away from there, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans until, during the time before a Buddha had appeared, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī.
Having been reborn in a noble family and having gone to her husband’s home, one day while quarreling with her sister-in-law,
she said, "This woman, having given this gift to the Paccekabuddha, will obtain magnificent prosperity. Having spoken thus,
she took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha’s hand, threw away the food, and [filled it] with mud.
Having filled it, she gave it to him. The great multitude reviled her, saying, "Foolish woman! What offense has the Paccekabuddha committed against you?
Ashamed by their words, she took the bowl again, removed the mud, washed it, rubbed it with fragrant powder, and filled it with the four sweets.
She then offered it to the Paccekabuddha, shining with the ghee poured over it, which was the color of the interior of a lotus.
Placing her hand upon it, she made this aspiration: "Just as this alms-food has become radiant, so may my body become radiant.
Having passed away from there, she wandered through the happy realms of existence alone. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the daughter of a very wealthy merchant.
Due to the fruit of her previous karma, her body was foul-smelling, and she was [shunned] by people.

Having become disgusted and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she had a golden crest made from her own ornaments and established it at the shrine of the Blessed One, and she also made an offering with a handful of blue lotuses.
Consequently, in that very same existence, her body became fragrant and enchanting. Being beloved and pleasing to her husband, she performed wholesome deeds throughout her life, and from there—
Having passed away from there, she was reborn in heaven. There too, having experienced divine bliss for as long as life lasted, she passed away and became the daughter of the King of Bārāṇasī.
There, experiencing a prosperity equal to that of the gods, she attended upon the Paccekabuddhas for a long time.
When they had attained final Nibbāna, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; she went forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller and lived in a park.

Having developed the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), she was reborn in the Brahma-world. Passing away from there, she was reborn in the city of Sāgala in the home of a Brahmin family of the Kosiya clan.
Having grown up with great luxury and having reached maturity, she was led to the house of Pipphali-kumāra in Mahātittha village.
When he had gone forth [into homelessness], she left behind a vast mass of wealth and a large circle of kinsmen.
Having renounced the world and gone forth for the sake of the religious life, he entered the monasteries of the non-Buddhist sects for five years.

Later, having received the going-forth and full ordination in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, he established insight meditation and before long attained Arahantship. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had reached the further shore of all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now. At that time,
in Haṃsavatī, there was a man known by the name Videha.”
I was the wife of a wealthy merchant who possessed abundant jewels.
Once, having approached the Sun among Men together with his retinue,
he heard the Dhamma of the Buddha, which dispels all suffering and fear.
“The Leader proclaimed me the foremost of his disciples who preach the ascetic practices (dhuta),
having heard me praise the seven-day gift given to the Tathāgata Buddha.
Prostrating with my head at his feet, I aspired for that very state.”
Then that bull among men, causing the assembly to laugh, spoke these verses out of compassion for the merchant:
"You shall attain the state you have desired; be extinguished, my son."
“In a hundred thousand aeons from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world.
His heir in the Dhammas, his own legitimate son, fashioned from the Dhamma— ”
"One named Kassapa by clan will become a disciple of the Teacher.
Hearing this, he became joyful and served the Jina,
the Guide, with a mind of loving-kindness and with the four requisites for as long as he lived.
“Having illuminated the Dispensation and crushed the false teachers,
and having disciplined those who were to be disciplined, he has attained Nibbāna together with his disciples.
When that Foremost One in the World had passed away, for the sake of honoring the Teacher— ”
Having gathered his kinsmen and friends,
he had them construct together with them a stupa seven yojanas in height, made of jewels,
blazing like the sun with its rays, like a king of sal trees in full bloom.
“Seven hundred thousand bowls he had made there,
shining like flames of reed-fire with the seven kinds of jewels.
Filling them with fragrant oil, he lit lamps there.”
For the purpose of worshipping the Great Sage, who is compassionate toward all beings,
he had seven hundred thousand water-pots made;
they were filled with jewels for the sake of worshipping the Great Seer.
“In the midst of the eight sets of eight jars, golden arches were raised up;
they outshone everything in color, like the sun in autumn.
At the four gates, the jeweled gateways shone brilliantly.”
The delightful, elevated planks made of jewels shine brilliantly.
Encircled by well-fashioned earrings that gleam,
the raised banners and jewels radiate light.
“The well-painted, well-fashioned mind, this shrine made of jewels,
outshines in its radiance the sun at dawn.
He filled the three tiers of the stupa’s pedestal with yellow orpiment.”
One [image] was made of emerald, one of sapphire,
and one of collyrium. Having commissioned such a beautiful worship,
that speaker of excellent words gave gifts to the Saṅgha for as long as he lived, according to his ability.
“Together with that merchant Seṭṭhi, having performed all those meritorious deeds throughout their lives,
they both went to a happy destination.
Having enjoyed prosperity in the states of gods and then humans,”
Like a shadow with the body, I transmigrated along with him.
Ninety-one eons ago, a leader named Vipassī arose,
beautiful to behold and possessing insight into all phenomena.
“At that time, this brahmin was a highly esteemed lord of prisoners;
though he was wealthy in virtue, he was very poor in riches.
Even then, I was his wife, a brahmin woman of even mind.”
Once that noble brahmin encountered the Great Sage,
who was seated amidst a multitude of people teaching the deathless state.
Having heard the Dhamma, he was filled with joy and offered him a single robe.
“Having gone home with only a single garment, he returned and said this to me:
‘Rejoice in this great merit: a cloth has been given to the Buddha.
Then, having made the añjali gesture, I rejoiced with great joy.”
“Sudinna, my lord, was the robe for the Best of Buddhas, the Tathāgata.
Having been happy and well-prepared as I transmigrated through various states of existence,
I became a king, a lord of the earth, in the delightful city of Vārāṇasī.”
“At that time, among the harem of queens, I was the most excellent;
through former affection for my husband, I was his beloved.
While those eight individual leaders were wandering for alms, [I saw them].”
Having seen him, he became joyful and gave a most precious alms-offering.
Having invited him again and having constructed a jeweled pavilion,
[he offered] a golden bowl of that very size, fashioned by smiths.
“Having gathered them all together,
he gave that gift to them as they sat upon golden seats, with his own hands full of faith.
At that time, I too, along with my wife, gave that same gift to the King of Kāsi.”
Again, I was born in Bārāṇasī, in a village of Kāsika.
In a prosperous family of householders, I lived happily together with my brothers;
I was the devoted wife of my eldest brother.
“Having seen the Paccekabuddha, I gave a portion of food to my younger husband; when he had returned, I spoke to him:
‘He did not rejoice in the gift,’ and then I gave it to him.”
Having brought that food in a pot, he gave it back to him again.
"Having discarded that food, I was then angry with the Buddha;
I gave that bowl full of mud to that Tathāgata."
“Regarding giving and receiving, as well as the unworthy and the impure—
having seen his face with an even mind, I was then deeply moved.
Again, having taken up his bowl and cleansed it with fragrance,”
With a clear and confident mind, having filled [the vessel], I gave it along with ghee and sugar.
"Wherever I am reborn, may I be beautiful as a result of this gift;
yet through my offense against the Buddha and my foul-smelling mouth, [may I suffer]."
“Furthermore, when the stupa of Kassapa the Hero was being built,
I joyfully gave an excellent golden brick.
Having plastered that brick with a fourfold mixture of fragrances,”
Free from the defect of foul odor, her every limb perfectly proportioned.
Having had seven thousand lamps made with the seven precious gems, along with thousands of wicks.
“Having placed them inside and lit them, I set up seven rows for the sake of worshipping the Lord of the World with a serene mind.
Even then, she was especially a partaker in that merit.”
Again, I was born in Kāsī, known by the name Sumittā.
I was her wife— happy, adorned, and beloved—
and at that time, I gave a thick turban to a paccekabuddha.
“I was also her sister, having rejoiced in that supreme gift.
Once more, in the kingdom of Kāsi, I was born into the Koliya clan.
At that time, together with five hundred sons of the Koliyas,”
She attended upon five hundred paccekabuddhas.
Having served them for three months, she gave them the triple robe;
at that time, I was her wife, following after her path of meritorious deeds.
“Falling from there, I became a king named Nanda of great renown;
I was also his chief queen, one who had all her desires fulfilled.
Then, having been King Brahmadatta, the lord of the earth,”
At that time, I attended upon five hundred Paccekabuddhas, the sons of Padumavatī, for as long as they lived;
having settled them in the royal park, I honored them when they had attained final Nibbāna.
“Having both caused cetiyas to be built and gone forth into homelessness,
we developed the immeasurables and went to the Brahma-world.
Passing away from there, I was reborn at Mahātittha as Sujāta Pipphalāyana.”
My mother was Queen Sumanā, and my father was a brahmin of the Kosika clan.
"In the Madra country, in the most excellent city of Sākala,
I was the daughter of the brahmin Kappila and the wife of Sucimati."
“Having fashioned me in the likeness of household gold,
my father gave me to the steadfast Kassapa, who is devoid of sensual desires.
Once, that compassionate one, having gone to inspect his work, [said:]”
Seeing living beings being devoured by crows and other scavengers, I was filled with spiritual urgency.
"While I was still at home, having seen sesame seeds growing and scorched by the heat of the sun,
and seeing worms being devoured by crows, I then attained a sense of spiritual urgency."
“Then that steadfast one went forth, and I followed him in going forth;
for five years I lived according to the rules of the wandering life.
When Gotamī, the nourisher of the Conqueror, had gone forth,”
Then, having approached him, I was instructed by the Buddha:
"In no long time at all, I attained Arhatship.
Oh, the excellence of the spiritual friendship of the glorious Kassapa!"
“Kassapa, the well-composed son and heir of the Buddha,
who knows his former abodes and beholds both heavenly realms and states of woe;
moreover, the sage who has reached the destruction of birth and perfected direct knowledge.”
“By means of these three knowledges, a brahmin becomes one possessed of the threefold knowledge.
In the same way, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, possessing the threefold knowledge and having abandoned death,
bears her final body, having conquered Māra along with his mount.”
“Having seen the peril in the world, we both have gone forth;
we are now those whose taints are destroyed, tamed, become cool, and attained to nibbāna.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.’”
Having attained arahantship, she became one who had mastered the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*).

Because she had performed her duties with exceptional excellence therein, at a later time, while the Teacher was seated in Jeta’s Grove in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, he—while assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions—placed her in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives. One day, she [attended] upon the Elder Mahākassapa.
Praising his virtues first, she uttered an inspired utterance (*udāna*) by way of manifesting her own fulfillment of duty and so forth:
“The son of the Buddha, the heir, Kassapa, well-composed;
he knows his former births and beholds both heaven and the states of woe.”
“Then, having reached the destruction of birth, the sage who has perfected direct knowledge—
by means of these three knowledges, he is a brahmin possessing the threefold knowledge. Likewise,
Bhaddā Kāpilānī was a possessor of the threefold knowledge, one who had overcome death.”
He bears his final body, having conquered Māra together with his mount.
“Having seen the danger in the world, we both have gone forth;
we are now those whose taints are exhausted, self-controlled, become cool, and attained to Nibbāna.”
He spoke these verses.
Therein, "The son is the heir of the Buddha" means that because he is one who has awakened following the Buddha (*buddhānubuddha*), he is the son born after the Perfectly Enlightened One;
for that very reason, by taking up the nine supramundane states which constitute his inheritance, Kassapa is his heir through both mundane and supramundane [attainments].
"Perfectly concentrated" means having a mind well-composed through the various meditative absorptions (*samādhis*).

"He who knew his former existences" refers to the Elder Mahākassapa, who—having made his own and others' past lives, that is, the continuity of aggregates (*khandha-santāna*) in which they dwelt, manifest through the knowledge of recollecting past existences (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*)—knew, understood, and realized them.
"And he saw the heavenly realms and states of woe" refers to the heavens, comprising the twenty-sixfold division of celestial worlds.
With the divine eye, he sees the fourfold plane of misery as clearly as an amalaka fruit on the palm of his hand.
Furthermore, "having attained the destruction of birth" means that thereafter he has attained the state of Arahantship, which is characterized by the destruction of birth.

Having understood with direct knowledge—that is, with preeminent wisdom—the phenomena to be directly known, and having fully understood those phenomena to be fully understood, [and] having abandoned those to be abandoned...
Having abandoned [what is to be abandoned], having realized what is to be realized, he is one who has reached fulfillment, attained the goal, and finished his task.

He is a sage (*muni*) because he has attained the silence (*mona*) known as the wisdom of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). Likewise, Bhaddā Kāpilānī is called "one possessed of the three knowledges" (*tevijjā*) by virtue of these three knowledges just as Mahākassapa was.
“Maccuhāyī” (the slayer of death), and likewise “Bhaddākāpilānī, the possessor of the threefold knowledge, the slayer of death.
Thus, by saying “she bears her final body, having conquered Māra and his mount,” she shows herself as if she were another person.
Now, showing that just as the Elder’s practice was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, so too is mine:
“Having seen the danger,” he spoke this final verse. Therein, “we are tamed, with taints destroyed” means:
we—both the Elder Mahākassapa and myself—are tamed by the supreme taming and have entirely destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).

“We are become cool and extinguished” means: because of the very absence of the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*), we have become cool and are extinguished in the element of Nirvana with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
The commentary on the Bhaddākāpilānī Therīgāthā is finished.
The commentary on the Catukkanipāta is finished.
5. Pañcakanipāta (The Chapter of Five).
1. Commentary on the Verses of a Certain Elder Nun (*Aññatarātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā*). The verses beginning with "Twenty-five years" belong to a certain elder nun.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation in various states of existence, [was born] during this appearance of a Buddha.
In the city of Devadaha, she raised Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī as her nurse; however, she remained unknown by name or clan.
When Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī went forth into homelessness, she herself also went forth.
For twenty-five years, being afflicted by sensual lust, she could not attain one-pointedness of mind even for the duration of a finger-snap, and so she threw up her arms.
Having heard the Dhamma from the presence of the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā while weeping, her mind turned away from sensual pleasures.
Taking up a meditation subject and applying herself to its cultivation, she soon attained the six supernormal powers. Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“For twenty-five years, since I went forth, I have been devoted to the holy life.”
“I did not attain even a moment’s tranquility of mind for as long as it takes to snap one’s fingers.
Failing to find peace of mind, drenched by sensual lust,
I entered the monastery wailing with my arms outstretched.”
“I approached that bhikkhunī who had been my source of faith;
she taught me the Dhamma concerning the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements.
Having heard her Dhamma, I withdrew to a secluded place.”
I know my former births, and the divine eye is purified.
I possess the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, and the faculty of the divine ear is purified.
My supernormal powers have been realized, and the destruction of the taints has been attained by me.
"The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished."—These verses he spoke.
Therein, "not even for the duration of a finger-snap" means not even for a moment as brief as the clapping of hands, or merely the snapping of a finger.
The meaning is "at the [wrong] time. The construction is: "They did not attain tranquility of mind" means they did not attain one-pointedness of mind; the meaning is that they did not obtain it.
"Drenched with sensual lust" means their minds were soaked by a thick craving and passion due to their intense fixation upon the objects of desire known as the strands of sensuality (*kāmaguṇa*).
"Bhikkhunī" refers to the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā.
"And the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others" (cetopariccañāṇa) is connected with "purified" (visodhita); the meaning is that it was attained. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Aññatarā is finished.
2. The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Vimalā. The verses beginning with “Mattā vaṇṇena rūpena” belong to the elder nun Vimalā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various states of being, was born in this current dispensation of a Buddha in Vesālī.
She was reborn as the daughter of a certain woman who lived by means of her beauty. Her name was Vimalātissā.
When she reached maturity, while maintaining that same livelihood, she one day saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna walking for alms in Vesālī;
her heart became bound to him, and she went to the Elder’s dwelling place and [approached] the Elder.
She began to engage in acts of seduction directed toward him. Some say she did so because she had been incited by the heretics.
The Elder, having rebuked her by means of the contemplation of the foul (asubha), gave her an exhortation. This has already appeared below in the Therīgāthā;
however, when the Elder had thus given his exhortation, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and established herself in moral shame (hiri) and dread of blame (ottappa).
Having gained faith in the Teaching and become a laywoman, she later went forth among the bhikkhunīs.
Striving and exerting herself, because she was endowed with the necessary causes, she attained arahatship before long. Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Intoxicated by my complexion, my beauty, My good fortune, and my fame;”
Arrogant because of my youth, I held others in contempt.
Having adorned this body— so beautifully decorated, yet a deceiver of fools—
I stood at the door of a brothel like a hunter who has set a snare.
“Displaying my ornaments, revealing many secrets that should have been hidden,
I practiced various deceptions while laughing loudly at the many people.
But today, having gone for alms with shaven head and clad in the saṅghāṭi robe— ”
Seated at the foot of a tree, she was one who had attained the state beyond thought:
“All bonds have been severed—those divine and those human;
having exhausted all taints, I have become cooled and extinguished.”
He spoke these verses.

In this context: "Intoxicated by color and form" means by virtue of the praise of one's qualities and by the perfection of physical beauty. "By good fortune" means by way of being fortunate. "By fame" means by the excellence of one's retinue.
Thus, it is by way of intoxication with color, intoxication with form, intoxication with good fortune, intoxication with fame, and intoxication with retinue.
The meaning is "having fallen into intoxication. "Arrogant because of youth" means being increasingly stiffened by the intoxication of youth;
with minds stiffened by the conceit (*ahaṅkāra*) caused by youth, their minds are unpacified.

"She would despise other women" means she thinks, "I surpass all other women in every way through my own qualities such as beauty," or [she thinks] regarding the qualities of beauty and so forth of other women.
I despised it; having transgressed, I overestimated it and treated it with contempt.

"Having adorned this body, which is a deception for fools"—this refers to my body, which is filled with various kinds of impurities and is loathsome, yet which deceives (lāpana) fools by making them say "This is mine" and "This is I," through such acts as applying skin-coloring cosmetics and arranging the hair.
Having adorned my body with well-colored garments and ornaments, making it beautifully decorated and pleasing, I stood at the door of the brothel.
Just as a deer-hunter sets a snare— such as a staff, a net, or other snares for the purpose of binding deer— I stood having set my aforementioned body,
which had become a snare for Māra, at the door of the brothel, at the entrance of the courtesan’s house.
Displaying her ornaments— both those that were concealed and those that were manifest—
she showed many various kinds of jewelry and adornments, such as the secret parts of her thighs and hips, as well as the manifest parts of her feet,
knees, and head. Intoxicated by the pride of youth, she performed manifold deceits while laughing loudly before the great multitude.
In order to deceive foolish people, I laughed and used perfumes, garlands, clothing, ornaments, and the like to conceal the true nature of my body;
through laughter, flirtatious gestures, and such means, I practiced various forms of deception in many ways.

Yet now, having wandered for alms... [and so on] ...I am one who attains the state free from applied thought (*avitakka*). Thus, while living in such negligence, I—[am now...]—one who attains the state free from applied thought.

The construction is as follows: "Today, having now stood by the instruction of the Venerable Elder Mahāmoggallāna, having gone forth in the Dispensation, being shaven-headed and clad in the saṅghāṭi robe,
having wandered for alms and eaten the food obtained as alms, sitting at the foot of a tree— at a secluded seat at the foot of a tree—
I have become an attainer of the fruit supreme [the Arahant-fruit] which is without applied thought (avitakka), by means of the second jhāna as its basis."

"All fetters" refers to all four fetters, beginning with the fetter of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*). "Completely severed" means they have been rightly cut off and abandoned, as appropriate, by the first path and so forth. The remainder is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Vimalā is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Therī Sīhā.
The verses beginning with "Inappropriate attention" (*ayoniso manasikāra*) are those of the Elder Nun Sīhā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha as the daughter of the General Sīha in Vesālī. Thinking, "Let us give her a name," they named her Sīhā.
They gave her a name. When she reached the age of discretion, one day, while the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma to the general Sīha, she heard that teaching.
Having gained faith, she asked her parents for permission to go forth, and having received it, she was ordained.
Even after going forth and beginning the practice of insight (vipassanā), she was unable to turn back her mind, which continued to wander toward external, manifold objects.
For seven years, being oppressed by wrong thoughts and finding no delight in her mind, she thought, "What is the use of this wretched life?

I shall hang myself and die. Taking a noose and fastening it to a tree branch, as she was about to place it around her neck, she directed her mind toward insight (vipassanā) through the force of her former practice, owing to her being in her final existence.

The snare was around her neck; because her knowledge had reached maturity, she immediately increased her insight (vipassanā) and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). At the very moment she attained arahantship, the bond of the snare was released from her neck and fell away.
Established in arahantship, she uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
“Through improper attention, tormented by sensual lust,
I was formerly restless, lacking mastery over my own mind.
Overwhelmed by defilements, I followed after the perception of beauty.”
I found no composure of mind, being under the sway of a lustful heart.
For seven years I wandered about, emaciated, pale, and discolored;
neither by day nor by night did I find happiness, being deeply afflicted by suffering.
“Then, taking a rope, I entered the depths of the forest:
‘Better for me to hang myself here than to live on again in such degradation.
Having fashioned a strong noose and fastened it to a tree branch,”
“I cast a noose around his neck, and then my mind was liberated.”—
He spoke these verses.
Therein, “unwise attention” means by way of unskillful attention, through the distorted perception that grasps the beautiful in the ugly.
"Afflicted by sensual lust" means oppressed by desire and passion for the strands of sensuality (*kāmaguṇa*).

"I was restless in the past, lacking mastery over my mind" means that formerly, when my mind did not remain under my control, I was restless—my mind scattered among various objects and lacking concentration.
"Overwhelmed by defilements, following after the perception of beauty" means [overcome] by defilements such as sensual lust that have reached the state of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
They were overwhelmed by the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) which proceeds by taking beauty in forms and so forth as its object;

they were of a nature to follow after it. "I did not attain even a moment’s composure of mind" means that, following the power of a mind associated with sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), I did not attain even the slightest composure of mind—that is, mental tranquility (*cetosamatha*) or one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*).

“Emaciated, pale, and discolored”—thus, through a state of longing, she became emaciated with limbs covered in visible veins, turned yellowish-pale, and consequently discolored, with her natural skin complexion vanished. “For seven years” means for seven full years.
“I wandered” means I wandered. “Neither by day nor by night did I find happiness, being so deeply afflicted”—thus I [spoke].
For seven years, afflicted by the suffering of the defilements, I did not obtain the happiness of a recluse even once, whether by day or by night.

"Because of that"—meaning because of the failure to obtain the happiness of a recluse due to the obsession of the defilements—"I entered the midst of the forest having taken a rope," means that I took a noose-rope and entered the interior of the forest.
If it is asked for what purpose I entered, he said: "Better for me to hang myself here."

"And should I practice what is base": the meaning is that if I, being unable to perform the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*), were to practice again—that is, were to resort to or abide in—the base state of a householder, then a death by hanging in this forest retreat would be for me a hundredfold, a thousandfold better.
"Then my mind was liberated" means when [she hung] from a tree branch...

She cast the binding noose around her neck; then, immediately thereafter, because it was joined by the path of insight leading to emergence, my mind was liberated from all taints through the sequence of the paths—it became liberated.
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sīhā.
4. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sundarīnandā The verses beginning with “Āturaṃ asuci... are the verses of the elder nun Sundarīnandā.
It is said that she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, she heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Hearing the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhunī as the foremost among those who practice jhāna, she performed acts of service, made an aspiration for that position, and accumulated merit.

For a hundred thousand aeons, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and during this current dispensation of a Buddha, she was reborn into the Sakyan royal family. They gave her the name Nandātissā. Later on—
By virtue of her physical perfection, she was known as Sundarīnandā and Janapadakalyāṇī.
After our Blessed One had attained omniscience, she gradually went to Kapilavatthu, ordained Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula,
and after the Great King Suddhodana had passed away and Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the mother of Rāhula, had also passed away...

And having gone forth, she thought: "My elder brother, having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, went forth and became a Buddha, the supreme person in the world; his son, Prince Rāhula, has also gone forth;
my husband King Nanda, my mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, and my sister Rāhulamātā have also gone forth; what shall I do now at home?"
Thinking, “I shall go forth,” she went to the nuns’ quarters and went forth out of affection for her relatives, not out of faith.
Therefore, even after going forth, she became intoxicated by the pride arising from her physical beauty. Thinking, “The Teacher disparages and censures form;
in many ways he shows the danger in form,” she did not go to attend upon the Buddha, and so on—all of this is as described below in the case of Abhirūpanandā.
This should be understood according to the method already stated in the account of the Vessantara Jātaka. However, this is the distinction:

having seen a female form created by the Teacher gradually overcome by old age, the mind of the Elder Nun became directed toward her meditation subject as she reflected upon it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Seeing her, the Teacher taught the Dhamma to her in accordance with what was suitable for her:
“Behold, Nandā, this body: afflicted, impure, and putrid.
Develop a mind focused on the foul, one-pointed and well-concentrated. As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this.”
"It smells foul and putrid, yet it is what fools delight in.
Examining this thus, untiring by day and night,
one sees through it with one's own wisdom and breaks out in revulsion."
She spoke these three verses.
By directing her knowledge according to that teaching, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*).

As he was explaining a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for her to attain the higher paths, he said: "Nandā, in this body there is not even the slightest essence; it is merely a coating of flesh and blood."
To show that this [body] is merely a heap of bones, serving as the dwelling place for old age and the rest,
it is said: "A city has been built of bones, plastered with flesh and blood,
In which old age and death, pride and hypocrisy are stationed."
The Buddha spoke this verse in the *Dhammapada*.
At the conclusion of that teaching, she attained *arahantship*. Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena...”
In this hundred thousandth aeon, the Leader appeared.
An instructor, an inspirer, a deliverer of all living beings;
a Buddha skilled in teaching, he ferried across a vast multitude of people.
“Compassionate and merciful, seeking the welfare of all living beings,
he established all the heretics who arrived there in the five precepts.
Thus it became free from turmoil and empty of heretics.”
Adorned by Arahants, those who have attained mastery and are poised in equanimity:
"The Great Sage stands tall like a mountain peak, possessing eighty-four thousand jewels;
resembling a golden statue, he is endowed with the thirty-two supreme marks."
“A lifespan of one hundred thousand years existed at that time;
remaining for that long, he delivered many people.
At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī in the family of a merchant.”
Amidst the radiance of various jewels, we were endowed with great bliss.
Having approached that Great Hero, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma—
the nectar, the supreme delight, which reveals the ultimate truth.
“Then, having invited the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha,
and having given him a great gift with my own hands in faith,
I aspired to the foremost place among the meditating bhikkhunīs.”
Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Wise One, the Leader of the World, together with the Saṅgha, the Lord,
the Tamer of the Untamed, the Refuge of the Three Worlds,
the Charioteer of Men, then declared: "You shall obtain that which you have so well aspired for."
“In a hundred thousand aeons from now,
one born of the Okkāka clan, named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world.
His heirs in the Dhamma, his own legitimate sons fashioned from the Dhamma, [will follow him].”
“By the name of Nandā, she will become a female disciple of the Teacher.
Having heard this, she became joyful and for as long as she lived,
she served the Jina, the Guide, with a mind of loving-kindness and with the four requisites.
“By that well-performed karma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Passing away from there, I went to Yāma, and from there I went to Tusita.”
And from there, to Nimmānarati, and from there to Vasavatti’s city.
"By the power of that karma, wherever I was reborn,
right there I served as the chief queen to kings."
“Having passed away from that human state,
I became the queen-consort of a universal monarch (cakkavattin), as well as of regional kings (maṇḍalī).
Having experienced such prosperity among both gods and humans, [I attained this state].”
Having been happy everywhere, I wandered through many eons.
When my final existence was reached in the delightful city of Kapilavatthu,
I was the blameless daughter of King Suddhodana.
“Seeing her, beautiful with splendor, that family was filled with joy;
because of that, my name ‘Nandā’ became lovely and excellent.
And among all the young women, I was renowned as ‘Kalyāṇī.’”
In that delightful city, having left behind that Yasodharā:
“My eldest brother is the foremost in the three worlds, and likewise my youngest is an Arahant;
I alone am a householder, urged on by my mother.”
“Born into the Sākiya clan, you are the daughter of the Buddha’s younger brother;
even separated from Nanda, why do you remain in the household?
Youth ends in old age, and beauty is considered impure.”
Even health ends in disease, and life ends in death.
"This beautiful form of yours, so lovely and enchanting,
adorned with ornaments like a cluster of *śirīṣa* flowers."
“Like a heap of the world’s essence, an elixir for the eyes,
a generator of merit and fame, a delight to the clan of the Kukkutas—
before long, old age will surely overcome him.”
“Leaving home out of compassion, practice the blameless Dhamma.
Having heard my mother’s words, I went forth into homelessness;
yet it was not with my body, but because of my mind, that I was captivated by beauty, youth, and charm.
“With great effort, my mother spoke to me, saying, ‘You must practice the supreme absorption (jhāna) in meditation,’ yet I had no zeal for that.
Then the Greatly Compassionate One, seeing me longing for sensual pleasures,”
For the purpose of dispelling my attachment to form, while I was within the range of his vision,
the Victor, by his own supernatural power, conjured up a beautiful woman—
one lovely to behold, radiant, and more fair even than I.
“Seeing him, I was struck with wonder, my body filled with great amazement;
I thought, ‘May my human gain of eyesight have borne fruit.
Then I said to him: ‘Come, O blessed one, tell me what you require.’”
“Tell me your family, your name, and your clan, if it is dear to you.
“This is no time for deception, O blessed one; let me rest upon your lap.
My limbs are as if sinking; let me have but a moment’s respite.”
Then that beautiful-eyed woman, having placed my head upon her lap, lay down;
and the fierce, most dreadful hunter fell upon her forehead.
With his falling, pustules broke out upon her.
And they flowed forth, bursting open—corpses of pus and blood.
“The face, too, was burst open—a corpse with a putrid stench;
swollen, discolored, and oozing pus from the body.”
With all her limbs trembling, sighing again and again,
and experiencing her own suffering, she lamented piteously:
“I am tormented by pain, and these sensations strike me.”
“I am submerged in great suffering; be my refuge, O friend!
Where is the stream of your face? Where is your lofty nose?
Where has your face gone—those lips as excellent as copper-red bimba fruit?”
“Where has the complexion like the moon gone? Where has the shell-like neck disappeared?
Your ears, once swaying like a swing, have now reached a state of discoloration.
Your breasts, shaped like budding *khāraka* flowers, are like flower buds.”
"Burst open and putrid, they have come to a state of foul stench.
Like a sacrificial altar with beautiful hips, yet like a slaughterhouse from which the sin has been removed;
filled with no marrow, alas! the impermanence of this form."
“Everything produced from the body is foul-smelling and terrifying;
it is as loathsome as a charnel ground, yet fools find delight therein.
At that time, my brother, the Great Compassionate One, the Leader of the World—”
Seeing me with a heart filled with spiritual urgency, he spoke these verses:
“Behold, Nandā, this body: afflicted, putrid, and foul.
Develop a mind of foulness, one-pointed and well-composed.”
“As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this:
it smells foul and putrid, yet it is what fools delight in.
Contemplating this thus, unwearied by day and night,”
Then, through my own wisdom, I saw clearly after having gained insight.
"Thereupon, being deeply moved upon hearing those well-spoken verses,
I remained steadfast there and attained arahantship."
“Wherever I sat down, always devoted to meditation, the Victor, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship and reviewing her own practice, she uttered, by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*), together with the three verses taught by the Teacher beginning with “The sick,
the impure,” the following: “For me, being heedful and investigating thoroughly,
This body, both inside and out, has been seen as it really is.”
“Then, becoming disenchanted with the body and becoming detached within,
heedful and disjoined from fetters, I am calmed and extinguished.”—
He spoke these two verses.

Therein, those who thus contemplate this... [as follows]... will see this body, which has the nature of being afflicted and so forth, in the manner described by the phrase "as this is, so is that," and so on.
Having become untiring throughout the day and night at all times, they let go of the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), which is caused by the voice of another;
thereafter, because it has arisen within themselves based on that very object, they [proceed] by means of the cultivation consisting of their own bodily experience (*sakāyabhāvanāmaya*).
Having become disillusioned by means of wisdom through the thorough analysis of the solid mass [of aggregates] as it truly is, [she asks:
"How indeed shall I see?"—the meaning is that she is looking and investigating with the eye of preliminary knowledge preceded by mental application (*ābhoga*).
Therefore he said, "Of me, who was heedful," and so forth. The meaning of this is: "Of me, who was heedful due to the non-departure of mindfulness."
By means of wise method— that is, by investigating and examining with the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) through the aspects of impermanence and so forth—
one sees this body, comprised of the five aggregates, as it truly is, both internally and externally, distinguished according to one's own continuum and the continua of others.
Then, subsequent to such seeing, one becomes disenchanted with the body by means of path-wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight-wisdom.
"I became disenchanted with the self-body; specifically, I grew detached from and attained dispassion toward my own internal continuum.
Through the practice of heedfulness reaching its culmination, I have become heedful; because all fetters have been utterly severed, I am now dissociated, calmed, and extinguished."
The commentary on the *Sundarīnandā Therīgāthā* is finished.
5. The commentary on the *Nanduttarā Therīgāthā*:
the verses beginning with "The fire and the moon" belong to the elder nun Nanduttarā. She too had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) throughout various existences, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a brahmin family in the town of Kammāsadhamma in the kingdom of Kuru.
Having mastered certain branches of knowledge and fields of craft, she entered the ascetic order of the Nigaṇṭhas;
being renowned for her debating skill, she took hold of a branch of the rose-apple tree (jambusākha) and became Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā.
Wandering about as if on the surface of Jambudīpa, she approached the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, asked him a question, and having been defeated, she followed the Elder’s advice.

Having gone forth in the Dispensation and practiced the duty of a recluse, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
“I worshipped the fire, the moon, and the sun, and the deities;
having gone to river fords, I bathed here in the water.
Having undertaken many vows, I shaved half of my head.”
I spread my bed upon the ground; I did not eat food at night.
Yet, delighting in adornment and decoration, and through bathing and clothing, I embellished this body, tormented by sensual lust.
“Then, having gained faith, I went forth into the homeless life;
seeing the body as it truly is, sensual lust was uprooted.
All states of existence were cut off, as were desire and aspiration.”
“Freed from all bonds, he has attained peace of mind”—
these five verses he spoke. Therein,
“They shall worship the fire, the moon, and the sun, and the deities”— that is, the deities headed by Agni, and the Indras.
Having prepared an oblation for the sake of propitiating the deities, I worshipped Agni month by month on the second day of the bright fortnight;
I worshipped Canda (the Moon) every day at dawn and dusk;
and I worshipped the Sun and other external deities such as Hiraññagabba while seeking the Path of Purification—I paid homage and performed acts of veneration. Having gone to the river fords...
"I descend into water" means that having approached the bathing-places (*tittha*) of rivers such as the Gaṅgā for worship, I enter the water morning and evening;
having submerged in the water, I perform the sprinkling of my limbs.

"Many undertakings of vows" refers to the undertaking of various kinds of vows, such as the fivefold practice of self-mortification by heat (*pañcātapatappanā*). The word "many" is used for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse.
"Making [the hair] long. "They shave half the head" means: "I shave only half of my head. Some explain the meaning as:
"Having bound half of the mass of hair by way of tying it in a matted braid (jaṭā), they release the other half.
"I make my bed on the ground" means: having become one who sleeps on a bare spot (thaṇḍila), [on] the earth that is not covered [by grass or leaves].
I say: having become one who abstains from food at night (*rattūparata*), I did not eat a meal during the night.

As for those who delight in adornment and decoration, their bodies are exhausted by long-term devotion to self-mortification; [I thought]: "In this way, there is no purification of wisdom through the exhaustion of the body.
However, if, by means of satisfying the sense faculties, the body is refreshed..."
Thinking, “There might be purity,” she did not attend to this body, but was devoted to adornment and decoration— delighting in adorning herself with clothes and ornaments,
and in beautifying herself with perfumes, garlands, and the like. And by means of bathing and anointing— that is, by having massages and so forth performed,
as well as by bathing and anointing herself— she thought, “I have benefited this body,” meaning she attended to this body of mine.

They were satisfied. "Afflicted by sensual lust" means that, having thus become preoccupied with physical strength, they were afflicted and frequently oppressed by sensual lust—which was overcome by the condition of improper attention.
"Then, having gained faith" means that, having thus broken the vows they had undertaken, they became preoccupied with physical strength and devoted to debate.
Having sacrificed there and wandered from place to place, she later, at a subsequent time,
received instruction and counsel from the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and attained faith. Having seen this body as it truly is— meaning, together with insight,
having seen this body of mine as it truly is through the wisdom of the path— she completely eradicated sensual lust by means of the non-returning path (*anāgāmimagga*).
Thereafter, by means of the supreme path (aggamagga), all states of existence (bhava) were utterly cut off; the construction is as follows:

both "desire" (icchā)—defined as the longing for present objects—and "aspiration" (patthanā)—defined as the longing for future existence—as well as all states of existence, were completely eradicated.
"He attained peace of mind" (santiṃ pāpuṇi cetaso) means that he reached and realized the ultimate peace, the fruit of Arhatship (arahattaphala).
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Nanduttarā is finished.

6. The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Mittākāḷī, beginning with "Having gone forth out of faith," etc., refers to the Elder Nun Mittākāḷī. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as the necessary condition for the turning away from existence in various future births, she was reborn in this current appearance of a Buddha in a brahmin family in the town of Kammāsadhamma in the kingdom of Kuru.

Upon reaching maturity, having gained faith through the teaching on the Great Foundations of Mindfulness, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs; however, for seven years she remained greedy for gain and honor.
Having offered herself, practicing the duties of a recluse, and wandering here and there, she later emerged with wise discernment;
having become filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, she established insight and, before long, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.
Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith,
I wandered here and there, longing for gain and honor.
Having neglected the supreme goal, I pursued a lowly goal.”
Having fallen under the power of the defilements, I did not realize the goal of the ascetic life.
As I sat in my dwelling, a sense of urgency arose within me:
"I have entered upon a wrong path, having come under the sway of craving."
“Short is my life, and old age and sickness crush it;
before this body breaks apart, there is no time for me to be negligent.
Observing the arising and passing away of the aggregates as they truly are,”
"With a liberated mind I arose, the Buddha’s teaching was accomplished"—thus she spoke these verses.

Therein, "I wandered here and there, eager for gain and honor" means that being intent and preoccupied with gain and honor, I wandered about for various reasons for generating profit, such as great learning and preaching the Dhamma.
"Neglecting the supreme goal" means having abandoned and discarded the highest goal, namely the meditations, insight, the path, the fruit, and so forth.
"I pursued a base object"— because it consists of material things defined as the four requisites, I pursued a base and contemptible object through improper search.
"Falling under the sway of the defilements"— having come under the control of the defilements such as conceit,
pride, and craving, I did not awaken to, nor did I know, the goal of asceticism, which is the duty of a recluse.
While sitting in the dwelling, as I sat in my own room, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in me. If you ask how, she said:

"We have set out upon a wrong path. In this context, "we have set out upon a wrong path" means that while this teaching is intended solely for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging, having gone forth in that teaching, we do not attend to our meditation subject; thus, we have set out upon a wrong path.
“We are. “Falling under the sway of craving” means having come under the power of the craving that produces conditions.
“My life is short” means my life is limited, meager, and fragile, because its duration is restricted and it is beset by many calamities.
“Old age and disease crush it” means they fall upon it from all sides and pound it to pieces.
Old age and disease crush and grind one down like mountains. There is also a reading, "maddare.
"Before this body breaks" means that this body will break up before long. Since its breaking is certain, therefore there is no time for me to be negligent;

this is the ninth occasion, excluded from the eight inopportune moments, and it is not right to be negligent—such was his sense of urgency (*saṃvega*). This is how the construction should be understood.

“Contemplating things as they really are” means that, having thus aroused a sense of spiritual urgency, they establish insight and contemplate things as they really are through attention directed toward impermanence and so forth.
To the question “What do they contemplate? it is said: “The arising and passing away of the aggregates.

This refers to the arising and cessation of the five aggregates of clinging, which are divided into fifty-five types according to such passages as “With the arising of ignorance comes the arising of form,” and so on.

Contemplating by means of the observation of rise and fall, I intensified my insight and emerged with a mind entirely liberated from all defilements and from existence through the sequence of the paths;
having emerged from both sides, I had emerged from the three realms of existence by means of the path.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Mittākāḷī is finished. 7.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sakulā begins with the verse starting "While living in the home... It is said that she [was a follower] of the Blessed One Padumuttara.
In the city of Haṃsavatī, at that time, she was reborn as the daughter of King Ānanda, named Nandā, the half-sister of the Teacher.

Having reached the age of discretion, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhunī as the foremost among those possessing the divine eye. Inspired with zeal, she performed acts of service.
Having done so, she herself also made an aspiration, longing for that same state.
Having performed much sublime wholesome karma there throughout her life, she was reborn in the world of the devas;

passing from one happy destination to another, she was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, and having gone forth as a wandering ascetic, she entered the religious life.
Wandering alone, one day she went about for alms of oil; having obtained some oil, she performed a lamp-offering throughout the entire night at the stupa of the Teacher.
Passing away from there, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and, possessing perfectly purified divine vision, wandered among the devas for an entire interval between Buddhas.
Then, during this current appearance of a Buddha, she was born into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī.
She was born and named Sakulātissā. When she reached maturity, she gained faith upon the Teacher’s acceptance of the Jetavana monastery and became a lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Later, having heard the Dhamma from a certain elder whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and went forth.
Applying herself with diligence and exertion, she established insight meditation and before long attained *arahantship*.
Therefore it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.”
“For the welfare of all beings, for their happiness, the Best of Speakers;
for the benefit of the world with its devas, the Noble Steed among Men has set out on the path.
Having attained the pinnacle of glory, majestic, and possessed of fame and renown, the Victor—”
Honored by the entire world, renowned in all directions:
“He has crossed over doubt, transcended all perplexity;
with his mental aspirations fulfilled, he has attained supreme enlightenment.”
“The Supreme among Men is the arouser of the path not yet arisen;
he has proclaimed what was unproclaimed and generated what was ungenerated.
The Knower of the Path, the Discerner of the Path, the Proclaimer of the Path, the Bull among Men.”
The Teacher is skilled in the path, the most excellent of charioteers.
"The Teacher of great compassion, the Leader, teaches the Dhamma;
he lifts up living beings who are submerged in the mire of sensual desire."
“At that time, born in Haṃsavatī, I was a delight to the kshatriyas;
beautiful, possessed of wealth, beloved, and illustrious.
I was the most radiant daughter of the great king Ānanda.”
My half-sister and I, Padumuttara by name,
accompanied by royal maidens and adorned with every ornament,
approached the Great Hero and heard his teaching of the Dhamma.
“At that time, the One Honored by the World, praising that bhikkhunī who possessed the divine eye in the midst of the assembly, established her in the position of foremost rank.
Having heard this, I was delighted; and having given a gift to the Teacher,”
Having worshipped the Fully Awakened One, I aspired for the divine eye.
Then the Teacher said to me: "Nandā, you shall obtain what you have aspired for;
this is the well-determined fruit of offerings of lamps and the Dhamma."
“In a hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan,
known by the family name Gotama, will appear as a Teacher in the world.
His legitimate heirs in the Dhamma, fashioned from the Dhamma, shall be his spiritual sons.”
“By name she will be known as Sakulā, a female disciple of the Teacher.
By that well-performed deed and by her intentions and aspirations,
having cast off the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.”
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great renown, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan, arose as the best among those who speak.
At that time, I was a wandering female ascetic, living alone.”
Having wandered for alms, I obtained only a small amount of oil.
With that, I lit a lamp and attended upon the shrine of the Best of Bipeds with a mind full of serene confidence, observing every form of restraint.
“By that well-performed karma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Wherever I was reborn, it was by the power of that karma.”
"Great lamps blaze for me wherever I go.
Piercing through walls, through rocks, and over mountains, I see whatever I wish;
this is the fruit of the gift of lamps."
“I have come to possess pure eyes and am ablaze with glory;
I am endowed with faith and wisdom—this is the fruit of giving a lamp.
And now, in my final existence, I have been born into a brahmin family.”
When he was possessed of abundant wealth and grain, joyful, and honored by kings—
“I, endowed with every limb and adorned with all ornaments,
stood at a window in the city as the Sugata entered.”
“Having seen him blazing with glory, honored by gods and humans,
endowed with the secondary marks and adorned with the primary characteristics,
my heart was uplifted and joyful, and I resolved upon the life of renunciation.”
In no long time at all, I attained arahantship.
I have mastery over the supernormal powers, the divine ear-element, and I know the minds of others;
I am a fulfiller of the Teacher’s instruction.
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
Having exhausted all taints, I am pure and stainless.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.”
Heavy is the burden left behind, the uprooting of the guide to existence.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home to the homeless life—that purpose has been attained by me: the destruction of all fetters.
“Then the Greatly Compassionate One, the Supreme among Men, placed me at the very head of those with divine vision, saying, ‘Among the Sakulas, [she] is the foremost.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”
Having attained arahantship, however, because of her prior performance of meritorious deeds, she had mastered the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
For that reason, the Teacher placed her in the foremost position among the bhikkhunīs possessing the divine eye.
Reflecting upon her own practice, she was filled with joy and gladness, and as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), she said:
“While living here in the home, having heard the Dhamma from a bhikkhu,
I saw the stainless Dhamma, Nibbāna, the deathless state. So,
casting aside my son and daughter, as well as my wealth and grain, I went forth.”
Having had my hair shorn, I went forth into the homeless life.
Being a trainee, I cultivated the straight path;
I abandoned lust and hatred, as well as the taints associated with them.
“Having attained full ordination as a bhikkhunī, I recollected my former births;
the divine eye was purified, stainless and well-developed.
Having seen conditioned phenomena as alien, born of causes, and subject to dissolution;”
“I have abandoned all taints; I am cooled and extinguished.”—These verses she spoke.
Therein, “While dwelling in the home, having heard the Dhamma, I am a bhikkhunī”—this means that formerly, while living in the midst of the household life...
Having heard a discourse on the Dhamma containing the essence of the Four Noble Truths from a certain bhikkhu whose defilements were destroyed, [he said]:
"I have seen the stainless Dhamma, Nibbāna, the deathless state. It is "stainless" (*viraja*) because of the absence of the dust of passion and other such stains;

it is "Nibbāna" because it has emerged from craving (*vāna*); and it is "Nibbāna" because, due to the absence of falling away (*cavana*), it is the cause of non-decline for those who have attained it.

I saw—that is, I perceived—with the Dhamma-eye known as "vision," which is adorned with a thousand methods, that unconditioned phenomenon (asaṅkhata-dhamma) which has obtained the name "the deathless" (accuta). "Sāhaṃ" means:
thus, by the manner described, I am a stream-enterer (sotāpanna).
"A *sikkhamānā* (probationary nun)" means while she is still a *sikkhamānā*, having gone forth [into homelessness] even before her rains-residence (*vassa*) was completed.
"Developing the straight path" means producing the higher path—the straight way—by virtue of cultivating the middle practice (*majjhimapaṭipatti*).

"And the taints associated with that" refers to the taints to be abandoned by the third path, which are associated with passion and hatred (*rāga-dosa*) both as co-existent associates (*sahajekaṭṭha*) and as those to be abandoned together (*pahānekaṭṭha*).
I abandoned and utterly severed [them].
"A bhikkhunī who has attained" means having attained full ordination when the rains-residence was complete, and thus being a bhikkhunī.
"Vimala" (Stainless) means free from stains due to liberation from defilements such as ignorance; it has been well, respectfully, and correctly developed.
The connection is as follows: "purified" means the divine eye was cultivated and produced by the virtuous ones, such as the Buddhas and others.

"Formations" refers to the formations belonging to the three planes of existence. "From the other side" means from the perspective of non-self. "In that which is born of causes" means in that which has arisen through conditions.

"Having seen with the eye of wisdom" means having seen with the eye of wisdom those things whose nature is to disintegrate and which are subject to dissolution. "I abandoned all taints" means by means of the supreme path.
"In what remained," they abandoned all taints (*āsava*); the meaning is that they exhausted them. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sakulā is finished.
8. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Soṇā.
“Having given birth to ten sons,” and so forth, are the verses of the Elder Nun Soṇā. She too,

having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, and having attained maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher,
heard the Teacher [prophesy] a certain bhikkhunī as being foremost among the bhikkhunīs who are energetic in their striving.
Seeing him being appointed [to that position], she performed acts of service and herself aspired to that same office.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she passed away from there and, after wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons, was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a noble family in Sāvatthī.
Upon reaching maturity, she went to her husband’s home and obtained ten sons and daughters.

She became known as Bahuputtikā (The One with Many Children). When her husband had gone forth and reached old age, she established her sons and daughters in the household life, divided all the wealth among her children, and set nothing aside for herself.
After attending to her for only a few days, her sons and daughters treated her with contempt. She thought, "What use have I for these?"
“...so that I may live in my home without being treated with contempt,” she said, and having approached the bhikkhunīs, she requested the going forth. The bhikkhunīs granted her the going forth.
Having received full ordination, she thought, “I have gone forth at an advanced age; I must be diligent.
Thus, while performing the duties and services for the bhikkhunīs, she thought, “I shall practice the ascetic’s duty throughout the entire night,” and went to the lower terrace of the palace.

Holding a single pillar with her hand and not letting go of it while performing the duties of a recluse, even as she walked back and forth, she thought, "In this dark place, my head might strike against a tree or something else";
thus, holding a tree with her hand and not letting go of it, she performed the duties of a recluse. From that time on, through her application of energy, she—

She became clearly manifest. Seeing her maturity of wisdom, the Teacher, while remaining seated within the fragrant chamber, emitted a radiance and manifested himself as if sitting directly before her, saying:
"Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma..."
"One single day of life is better for one who sees the supreme Dhamma"—thus he spoke this verse.
At the conclusion of that verse, he attained *arahantship*. Therefore it is said in the *Apadāna*:
"The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena..."
One hundred thousand aeons ago, a Leader appeared in this world.
At that time, born into a guild-president’s family, happy, honored, and beloved,
I approached that best of sages and heard his sweet speech.
The Conqueror praised the nun Āraddhavīriyā as foremost.
Having heard this, she became joyful and performed an act of service for the Teacher.
After paying homage to the Fully Awakened One, she then made a resolve for that state.
The Great Hero rejoiced: "May your aspiration be fulfilled!
One hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan, known by the family name Gotama, shall become a Teacher in the world."
“She shall be an heir to his teachings, a true-born daughter fashioned by the Dhamma;
she will be a female disciple of the Teacher, known by the name Soṇā.
Having heard this, she became joyful and served the Conqueror for as long as she lived.
With a mind of loving-kindness, I served the Guide with the necessary requisites.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“In my final existence now, I was born into a family of merchants in Sāvatthī,
the preeminent city, which was prosperous, flourishing, and possessed of great wealth.
And when I had reached the prime of youth, I went to my husband’s home.”
I gave birth to ten sons, especially handsome in appearance.
"They were all well-nourished and captivating to the eyes of their mother;
they would have been pleasing even to enemies, let alone to me."
“Then, against my will, while surrounded by ten sons, my husband went forth into homelessness in the teaching of the God of Gods.
Thereupon, all alone, I reflected: ‘Enough of this life for me!’”
Because of my four sons and because of that wretched old woman, I thought:
"I too shall go there, to where my husband has gone.
Having reflected thus, I went forth into the homeless life.
“Then the bhikkhunīs, leaving me alone in the bhikkhunī quarters, went away saying, ‘Heat the water.
Having then poured water into the pot and having sprinkled it, [I thought:]”
Sitting down after setting aside my bowl, I then concentrated my mind.
Having seen the aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self,
and having destroyed all taints, I attained arahantship.
“Then the bhikkhunīs, having come there, asked for hot water;
resolving upon the fire element, I quickly heated the water.
Astonished, they reported this matter to the Supreme Victor.”
Having heard that, the Lord, being gladdened, spoke this verse:
“Though one should live for a hundred years, lazy and lacking in vigor,
Better is a single day’s life of one who exerts firm energy.”
“The Great Hero was propitiated by me through my excellent practice;
that Great Sage declared me to be the foremost among those who have aroused energy:
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

Then the Blessed One, while establishing the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks, placed her in the foremost position among those who have aroused energy. One day, reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Having given birth to ten sons within this heap of form, I was then weak and aged, and I approached a bhikkhunī.”
