“She taught me the Dhamma—the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements.
Having heard her Dhamma, I cut off my hair and went forth.
While I was still a trainee under her, the divine eye was purified.”
I know my former abodes, where I dwelt in the past.
I cultivate the signless, one-pointed and well-composed;
I attained the immediate liberation, extinguished through non-clinging.
“The five aggregates have been fully understood;
they stand with their roots cut off. Enough of you, O old age, O birth! There is now no further becoming.”—he spoke these verses.
Therein, “in the mass of form” means in the mass designated as form. For this word “form” (rūpa) [is used] in dependence on the eye... [and so forth].

In such passages as “And eye-consciousness arises in relation to visible form,” it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). In such passages as “Whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present,” it refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).

In such passages as “One is lustful for pleasant and agreeable forms,” it refers to intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). In such passages as “He sees external forms,” it refers to the sense-sphere of the kasiṇas (*kasiṇāyatana*).
In such passages as “Possessing form, he sees forms,” it refers to the form jhāna (*rūpajhāna*). [And] “Dependent upon bone and sinew...”
In such passages as, "Dependent upon flesh, dependent upon skin, and enclosed by space, it is reckoned simply as 'form' (rūpa)," [the term refers to] the material body (*rūpakāya*).
Here too, it should be understood as the material body alone. Furthermore, the word *samussaya* is a synonym for the physical frame of bones;
in such passages as, "The hundred skeletons," it is used as a synonym for the skeletal body. And: "Behold, Nanda, the sick, impure, and putrid... [etc.]
In passages such as "samussaya," it refers to the body. Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to the body. Therefore it is said: "in the massing of form" (*rūpasamussaye*);
the meaning is "in the massing known as form, that is, in the body. The word "standing" (*ṭhatvā*) is an elliptical expression. For the construction is:
"having stood in this massing of form—meaning, having relied upon this physical body—one gives birth to ten sons."
“*Tato*”: therefore, because of the birth of ten sons. For she, having passed her prime and giving birth to children, gradually became weak of body and worn out by old age.
Thus it is said: “Then I was weak and worn out. “*Tassa*”: from that;

or alternatively, *tassa* means “in her presence. Again, the genitive case (*tassā*) is used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is “by her. “*Sikkhamānāya*”: one who trains in the three trainings is a *sikkhamānā*.

"Immediately preceding liberations" means that the liberations arisen immediately after the supreme path were [my] experience. For even though the eight liberations beginning with "one possessing form sees forms" are not called "immediately preceding liberations," the fruition-liberations— which do not arise until after the path— nevertheless, because they arise for the very first time immediately after the first path,
they are designated as such in reference to that [path], even when they occur at the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"Immediate liberations" (anantaravimokkhā) means that just as the concentration of the path (maggasamādhi) is called "uninterrupted concentration" (ānantarikasamādhi).

"Extinguished without clinging" (anupādāya nibbutā) means that she was extinguished by the final extinction of defilements (kilesaparinibbāna), having grasped nothing whatsoever among form and the other aggregates.

Having thus clarified the threefold true knowledge (vijjāttaya) and uttered an inspired utterance (udāna) while reaching the pinnacle through the fruit of Arhatship, [she now spoke] regarding old age...

Reproaching her body, which had been afflicted for a long time, he spoke this final verse—“The five aggregates have been fully understood”—to clarify his state of transcendence along with the underlying reason. Therein, *dhi tavatthu jare jamme* means: *dhi* (shame!
be upon you, O *jarā* (old age), O *jamme* (wretched one)—upon you, the contemptible and base old age that causes the limbs to become flaccid and so forth; let there be a cry of reproach against you.
"There is now no further becoming"—the intention is that "therefore you have been surpassed and overcome by me.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Soṇā is finished.
9. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā.
The verses beginning with "Lūnakesī" are the stanzas of the elder nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā.
She, too, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, attained maturity;
one day, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those of quick higher knowledge.

Having performed the formal act of dedication (*adhikārakamma*), having aspired for that particular state, and having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she wandered among gods and humans for a hundred thousand eons.
Then, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she became one of the seven sisters in the household of King Kiki of Kāsī;
there, for twenty thousand years, she undertook the ten precepts and lived the celibate life of a maiden.

Having lived out one interval between Buddhas while wandering through happy destinies after having had a dwelling-monastery built for the Saṅgha, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha into a merchant family in Rājagaha. Her name was Bhaddā Tissa.
As she grew up with a great retinue and reached maturity, [she married] the son of the chaplain in that very city, named Sattuka.
Having caught a thief with his stolen goods, as he was being led by the city guard to the execution ground to be put to death by the king’s command, she looked out from the lion-window and saw him.
Her heart became bound to him, and thinking, "If I obtain him, I shall live;
if not, I shall die," she lay down upon her bed with her face turned downward.
Then her father, having heard this news and feeling a powerful affection for his only daughter, gave a ransom of a thousand pieces of gold.
By this means, he had the thief released, bathed him with scented water, adorned him with all kinds of ornaments, and sent him back to the palace.
Bhaddā, her wishes fulfilled, adorned herself with even more lavish ornaments and attended upon him.

After Sattuka had spent a few days there, greed arose in him for her ornaments, and he said, "My dear, as soon as I was seized by the city guard, I made a vow to the deity dwelling in the thieves' pit, saying: 'If I regain my life, I shall present you with an offering.
Therefore, prepare the offering. She [said], "To satisfy his mind..."
Thinking, "I shall fulfill [the vow]," she prepared an offering and, adorned with all her ornaments, mounted a single carriage together with her husband.
Intending to perform an offering to the deity, she began to ascend the Corapapāta precipice.
Sattuka thought, "If everyone mounts [the carriage], it will not be possible to seize her ornaments," and so he [dismissed] the retinue.
Leaving her right there and having her take that very offering bowl, he climbed the mountain without engaging in pleasant conversation with her.
She understood his intention through a mere gesture. Sattuka said, "My dear, remove your upper garment and make a bundle of the ornaments worn on your body. She replied, "Master, for me..."
“What is the offense? “Foolish girl, why do you think I have come for the sake of a ritual offering (*balikamma*)?
I have come under the pretext of a ritual offering to take your ornaments. “But whose ornaments are these, noble sir, and whose am I?
“I do not know this distinction. “Very well, noble sir; but fulfill one of my requests according to the manner of being adorned.”
“Please let me embrace you. He consented, saying, “Very well.
Knowing that he had agreed, she embraced him from the front and, as if embracing him from behind, threw him over a mountain precipice. Having fallen, he was reduced to a mass of shattered fragments.
Seeing the marvel she had wrought, the deity dwelling on the mountain, manifesting her skill, spoke these verses:
“For it is not the case that in all circumstances a man is wise;
even a woman may be wise and discerning in various matters.
For it is not the case that in all circumstances a man is wise.”
“A woman, too, can be wise, quickly discerning the meaning.
Then Bhaddā thought: “It is not possible for me to go home in this manner;
rather, having gone from here, I shall go forth into homelessness. She went to the Nigaṇṭha monastery and requested ordination from the Nigaṇṭhas. Then they—
They asked, "By what rule shall our going forth take place? He replied, "Do exactly that which is the most excellent for your going forth.
Saying, "Very well," they plucked out her hair with a palm-leaf fan and ordained her. As her hair grew again, it grew back in curls and ringlets.
From that time on, she became known by the name Kuṇḍalakesā. There she—
Having mastered the conventions and the paths of debate, and having realized, "These people know only this much;
there is nothing superior beyond this," he departed from there. Going wherever there were wise men, he mastered their arts of knowledge;
yet, finding no one capable of conversing with him on equal terms, [he went to] where...
Whatever village or town he enters, he makes a heap of sand at its gate, places a branch of a rose-apple tree (*jambu*) there, and gives notice to the children standing nearby:
"Whoever is able to refute my argument, let him crush this branch.
Having said this, he goes to his dwelling place. Even after seven days have passed while the rose-apple branch remains exactly as it was, he takes it and departs.
And at that time, our Blessed One, having arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, was dwelling in gradual stages near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove.
Kuṇḍalakesā also, wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals in the manner described, reached Sāvatthī;
there, at the city gate, she placed a branch of a rose-apple tree upon a heap of sand for the children.
Having given his instructions, he entered Sāvatthī.
Then, as the Venerable Dhammasenāpati was entering the city alone, he saw that branch;
desiring to tame it, he asked the boys, "Why has this branch been placed in such a manner? The boys explained the matter to the Elder. The Elder—

"If it is so, then crush this branch," she said. The children crushed it. Kuṇḍalakesā, having finished her meal and departing from the city, saw that branch being crushed; having asked, "By whom was this crushed?
and learning that it had been caused to be crushed by the Elder, she thought, "A one-sided argument does not look well. Thus, entering Sāvatthī, she went from street to street.
While wandering about, she proclaimed, “May you see my debate with the recluses, the sons of the Sakyans!
Surrounded by a great crowd, she approached the General of the Dhamma, who was seated at the foot of a certain tree;
after exchanging greetings, she stood to one side and asked, “Did you cause my *jambu* branch to be crushed? “Yes, it was by me.”
“[It was] caused to be made by me. “If that is so, let there be a debate between you and me. “Let it be, lady.
“Who shall ask the questions, and who shall provide the answers? “The right to ask the questions has fallen to us; you ask whatever you know.
She asked every question concerning what she knew. The Elder answered them all.
Not knowing what to ask in reply, she remained silent. Then the Elder said to her, “You have asked many questions;
let us also ask you a single question. “Ask, venerable sir,” she replied. The Elder asked this question: “What is called ‘one’?
Kuṇḍalakesā, unable to see either the end or the limit, entered into darkness.
Acting as if she were so, she said, "I do not know, Bhante. He said, "If you do not know even this much, what else will you know?
Having said this, he taught her the Dhamma. She fell at the Elder's feet and said, "Bhante, I go for refuge to you.
He replied, "Do not go for refuge to me, lady; go for refuge only to the Blessed One, the Supreme Person in the world with its devas."
“I shall go for refuge. “I will do so, Bhante,” she replied.
Then, at the time of the evening Dharma teaching, she went into the presence of the Teacher, prostrated herself with the five-pointed salutation, and stood to one side.
Knowing that her wisdom had reached maturity, the Teacher—
“Even a thousand verses, if they are composed of meaningless words, are not worth a single verse-quarter which, having been heard, brings about perfect peace.
Having spoken this verse, at its conclusion, she attained Arhatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) while remaining exactly as she was. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had reached the further shore of all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from here.
At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī in the family of a merchant.”
In that place radiant with various jewels, I was endowed with great bliss.
Having approached that Great Hero, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma;
then, having conceived faith, I went for refuge to the Conqueror.
“Then the Greatly Compassionate One, named Padumuttara,
established the nun Subhā on the path of swift direct knowledge.
Having heard this, she became joyful and gave a gift to the Great Sage.”
Bowing my head at his feet, I aspired for that very place.
The Great Hero rejoiced in what you had aspired for, Bhaddā:
"All that shall be fulfilled; may you be happy and at peace."
“In a hundred thousand aeons from now, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will appear as a Teacher in the world.
His legitimate heirs in the Dhammas, fashioned by the Dhamma, shall be his true sons.”
"Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā shall become a female disciple of the Teacher.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
“Then, passing away from there, I went to Yāma; from there, I went to Tusita;
and from there, to Nimmānaratī, and then to Vasavatti’s city.
Wherever I was reborn, it was by the power of that karma.”
In those very places, I served as the chief queen to kings.
Then, passing away from there, among humans I served as the chief queen to universal monarchs (cakkavattins), regional kings, and other rulers.
“Having experienced prosperity among both gods and humans,
having been happy everywhere, I wandered through many eons.
In this auspicious eon, I was a man of great fame, a kinsman of Brahmā.”
One named Kassapa by clan, the best among those who speak,
appeared. At that time, the lord of men, the king of Kāsi named Kikī, was the attendant of the Great Sage in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī.
“I was his fourth daughter, known as Bhikkhudāyī;
having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror’s chief, I resolved to go forth.
My father did not grant us permission, so at that time we remained in the household.”
For twenty thousand years, we wandered about untiringly.
Seven daughters, daughters of royal lineage raised in luxury, were devoted to serving the Buddha and were full of joy, having lived the celibate life of a maiden.
“Samaṇī and Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī and Bhikkhudāyikā;
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and Saṅghadāyikā as the seventh.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, and I myself at that time.”
Kisāgotamī and Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā was the seventh.
“By those well-performed deeds and by my intentions and aspirations,
having left the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.”
“In my final existence now, in the supreme city of Giribbaja,
I was born into a prosperous family of merchants when I had reached the prime of youth.
Seeing a thief being led away for execution, I fell in love with him there.”
“Having ransomed him from execution for a thousand pieces of gold,
my father then gave me to him, knowing my heart’s desire.
I was devoted to him, exceedingly beloved and dear.”
“Thus, out of greed for ornaments, Sattuka, with his mind set on plunder,
led me to the Corappapāta mountain and intended my execution. Then,
having bowed down to Sattuka with palms joined in reverence,”
Protecting my own life, I spoke these words:
“This golden bracelet, many pearls and beryl gems—
take all of this, O fortunate one, and declare me to be your slave.”
“Take it off, O beautiful one; do not lament so bitterly.
I do not recall ever having brought wealth here by killing anyone.
As far as I can remember myself, from the time I reached the age of discretion...”
"And I do not recall anyone dearer to me than you.
Come, I shall embrace you after circumambulating you;
for now there shall be no further meeting between me and you."
“For it is not the case that in all circumstances a man is wise;
even a woman may be wise, discerning in each and every situation.
For it is not the case that in all circumstances a man is wise.”
Even a woman can be wise, quickly discerning the meaning:
"Truly, with speed and swiftness, I aimed right at his vital spot;
just as one might strike a deer on its neck-hair, so did I then slay Sattuka."
“He who does not quickly comprehend a matter that has arisen is destroyed,
dull-witted as he is, like a thief in a mountain cave.
But he who quickly understands a matter that has arisen— ”
“I was liberated from the oppression of enemies,
just as Sattuka was. Having thrown Sattuka down into a mountain ravine,
I then approached those clad in white robes and went forth.”
“Then, having plucked out all my hair with a pair of tongs,
they explained the rules of conduct for one who has gone forth without interruption.
Having mastered that, I sat down all alone.”
I reflected upon that moment, as the dog was making for the human hand:
"Having seized it near me, he dropped it and departed;
seeing the sign, I obtained that hand, which was infested with maggots."
“Then, rising up with a sense of urgency, I questioned my fellow practitioners of the Dhamma.
Those Sakyan bhikkhus, who understand that matter, spoke to me.
Therefore, having approached the disciples of the Buddha, I asked about that matter.”
Taking me with them, they went into the presence of the Best of Buddhas.
He taught me the Dhamma— the aggregates, the bases,
and the elements— as well as foulness, impermanence, suffering, and non-self, O Leader.
“Having heard his Dhamma, I purified the eye of Dhamma;
then, having understood the true Dhamma, I received the going-forth and the full ordination.
Then, being requested, the Leader said: ‘Come, Bhadda!’”
Then, having been ordained, I saw a small amount of water.
Having understood rise and fall through the washing of my feet,
I then reflected that all conditioned phenomena are likewise such.
“Then my mind was liberated, entirely without clinging;
the Victor then pointed out to me the path of swift direct knowledge.
I became a master of the supernormal powers and of the divine ear-element.”
I know the minds of others, fulfilling the Teacher’s instruction.
I know my former births, and my divine eye has been purified;
having exhausted all taints, I am pure and stainless.
“The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That goal for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—”
Thus has my goal been attained: the destruction of all fetters.
Regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the linguistic analysis, and likewise inspired eloquence—my knowledge is stainless and pure within the teaching of the Best of Buddhas.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she immediately requested ordination. The Teacher granted her permission to go forth.
She went to the nuns’ quarters, received ordination, and spent her time in the bliss of the fruits of the path and the bliss of Nibbāna.
Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
"With matted hair and covered in mud, wearing but a single cloth, I wandered in the past;
regarding what was blameless as blameworthy, and seeing blame in what was blameless."
“Having emerged from my midday rest on Vulture Peak Mountain,
I saw the stainless Buddha, honored by the community of monks.
Kneeling with my knees upon the ground, I paid homage and placed my joined palms before him.”
“Come, blessed one,” she said to me; that was my full ordination.
I have traversed Aṅga and Magadha, Vajjī, Kāsī, and Kosala;
for fifty years I have lived on alms from the kingdoms.
“Truly he has produced much merit; truly this lay follower is wise,
who gave a robe to Bhaddā, who is completely liberated from all fetters.”—
These verses he spoke.

In this context, "lūnakesī" means one whose hair has been shorn or plucked out; she is one who has plucked out her hair with a palm-stick during her renunciation among the Nigaṇṭhas—it is with reference to her that he speaks thus.
"Paṅkadharī" means a wearer of mud, so called because she wears the grime and dirt on her teeth due to not chewing tooth-sticks.
"Ekasāṭī" means one wearing a single garment, according to the practice of the Nigaṇṭhas. "She wanders about in the town."

Having previously been a Nigaṇṭhī, I wandered thus: perceiving what is blameless as blameworthy, I was one whose mind regarded as blameworthy such blameless things as bathing, clothing, and chewing tooth-sticks;
and seeing blameworthy things as blameless, I held the view that such blameworthy things as pride, malice, spite, and perversion were blameless.
Having emerged from my own place for the midday rest—this too occurred at the time when the midday hour had arrived.
Having met with the Elder, their pride and arrogance were subdued by his answers to the question and his teaching of the Dhamma;

with minds full of faith, they desired to approach the presence of the Teacher. Having returned to their own dwelling place and sat in their daytime quarters, they approached the presence of the Teacher in the evening.

"Having lowered my knees and paid homage" means: having lowered both knees to the ground and established them there, I paid homage by prostrating myself with the five points of the body touching the earth.
"Face to face I joined my palms in reverence" means: in the presence of the Teacher, I made a gesture of reverence with my ten fingernails joined together in brilliance.
"'Come, blessed one,' he said to me; that was my full ordination"—this refers to when the Blessed One, having attained arahantship, spoke those words to me.

To her who stood there having requested both the going-forth and the full ordination, he said, "Come, Bhaddā; go to the nuns' quarters and receive the going-forth and the full ordination from the bhikkhunīs," and he gave the command.
Because that command of the Teacher was the cause for her full ordination, it became her full ordination.
The two verses beginning with "Ciṇṇā" are verses of the declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*). Therein, "Ciṇṇā aṅgā ca māgadha" means:
those countries—Aṅga, Magadha, Vajjī, Kāsī, and Kosala—which were formerly frequented and traversed by me while I was eating country alms-food in coarse hempen cloth;
from the moment I met the Teacher in those very places, I have been free from debt, faultless, and cleansed of defilements.
Having offered it, for fifty years I consumed the alms-food of the kingdom.

By way of praising the specific merit of that lay follower who, with a mind of deep faith, gave his own robe, she declared her attainment of final knowledge (aññā) and spoke the concluding verse: "Truly, he has produced much merit! This [verse] is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is finished.
10. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā.
The verses beginning with "Plowing the field with plows" are the verses of the elder nun Paṭācārā.
She, too, having been born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, and having attained maturity, one day [came] into the presence of the Teacher.
While listening to the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.

Having performed a meritorious deed, she aspired to that very office. Having practiced wholesome deeds throughout her life, she passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans until, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the household of King Kiki of Kāsi, where she [became] one of the seven...
Having lived as one of her sisters and practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years, she built a dwelling for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Passing away from there, she was reborn in the world of the devas;

after enjoying celestial splendor for the duration of an interval between Buddhas, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha in the house of a merchant in Sāvatthī, and upon reaching maturity, she—
In her home, she formed an intimate attachment through defilement with a certain laborer.
Her parents set a day to give her in marriage to a youth of the same caste.
Knowing this, she took her personal belongings and, having departed through the main gate with the man with whom she had formed that intimacy, lived in a certain village and became pregnant. She...
When the fetus had matured, she said, "What is the use of living here as a dependent? Husband, let us go to our family home.
While he delayed, saying, "Let us go today," or "Let us go tomorrow," she thought, "This fool will not take me away.
When he had gone outside, she put the household in order and said, "Tell my husband that I have gone to my family home."
Having informed her neighbors and relatives, she set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go to my family home alone.
He returned and, not seeing her at home, questioned the neighbors;

hearing that she had gone to her family home, he thought, "Because of me, this daughter of good family has become destitute," and following her step by step, he caught up with her along the way. While she was on the road—
Thus her delivery took place. From the time of giving birth onwards, having ceased her efforts to go on, she returned with her husband.
She became pregnant for a second time, and so forth—all of this is to be detailed in the same manner as before.
However, this is the distinction: when the karma-born winds began to stir within her while she was on the road, then a great unseasonal cloud arose.
It arose. The sky became as if ablaze with lightning on all sides, as if being torn apart by thunderclaps, and was filled without interval by the falling of torrents of water.
Seeing this, she said, "Master, find for me a place sheltered from the rain.
Looking here and there, he saw a thicket covered with grass; having gone there, with the axe in his hand, upon that—
Desiring to cut down a bamboo pole, he felled a tree-stump that had grown up at the mouth of an anthill covered with grass.
At that very moment, a venomous snake emerged from that anthill and bit him;
he fell right there and died. Experiencing great agony and watching for his arrival, she [the mother] [tended to] her two children.
Unable to endure the wind and rain, she cried out; then, placing her son between her breasts, pressing her two knees and two hands against the ground, she spent the night exactly where she stood.
When the night had dawned, she laid one son, who was the color of a piece of raw flesh, upon a pillow of cloth, and embracing him with her hands and chest, [she looked at] the other.
Saying, "Come, dear one, your father has gone from here," she followed the path her husband had taken;
seeing him sitting near an anthill, having passed away, she wept and lamented, crying out, "Because of me, my husband has died.
Because it had rained throughout the entire night, the river along the way was flowing knee-deep and breast-high.
Having reached the other side, she— unable to descend into the water due to her own dull-wittedness and weakness—
left her eldest son on this shore, took the other child, went to the opposite bank, spread out a bundle of broken branches,
laid him down there upon a pillow made of rags, and thought, "I shall go to the other one."
Unable to leave her young child behind, she repeatedly turned back and looked at him as she entered the river.
Then, when she had reached the middle of the river, a hawk saw the boy and, perceiving him to be a "piece of meat," swooped down from the sky.
Seeing this, she raised both hands and let out three loud cries of "Sūsū! (Eat! Eat! at the top of her voice.
Not perceiving him due to his distance, the hawk seized the boy and flew up into the air.
Standing on the near bank, the mother saw her son raising both hands and letting out a great cry; thinking, "He is speaking of me," she plunged into the water with speed.
Thus the foolish son was killed by the hawk, and the eldest son by the water. She thought, "One of my..."
"My son was seized by an army, one was carried away by water, and my husband died on the road.
Weeping and lamenting as she went along, she saw a man coming from Sāvatthī and asked him, "Where do you live, dear sir?
"I live in Sāvatthī, mother," he replied. "In Sāvatthī, there is a certain family in such-and-such a street; that—
“Do you know, dear? “I know, mother, but do not ask that; ask something else. “I have no need for anything else;
I ask only that, dear. “Mother, you will not let me tell you yourself:
today I saw it raining all night long. “I saw it, dear; it rained for me alone all night long.”
“I will tell you that reason later; for now, tell me what has happened at the merchant’s house.
“Mother, tonight the merchant, his wife, and the merchant’s son—these three people—fell into the house while it was on fire;
they are burning on a single funeral pyre, and this smoke is visible, mother. At that moment, she...
Even though she was wearing her clothes, she did not perceive them falling away. Having fallen into a state of madness through grief, as if possessed by a spirit, she cried out:
“Both my sons have died; my husband has perished on the road;
my mother, father, and brother—all are burning together in a single funeral pyre.”
Lamenting, she wandered about.
From that time on, because she had fallen from proper conduct and did not even wear a single cloth for a lower garment, she became known by the name Paṭācārā (She Who Wanders in Rags).
Seeing her, some people would say, "Go away, you madwoman! and throw rubbish upon her head.
Others threw dust at her, while others hurled clods of earth.
The Teacher, seated in the midst of a great assembly in Jeta’s Grove and teaching the Dhamma, saw her wandering about in that manner;
and perceiving the ripeness of her wisdom, he acted so as to cause her to come toward the monastery. When the assembly saw her, they said, "Do not let this madwoman come here!"
He said, "Blessed One, do not stop her. When she had reached a spot not far away, he said, "Regain your mindfulness, sister!
At that very moment, through the power of the Buddha, she regained her mindfulness;
perceiving that the garment she was wearing had fallen off, she established a sense of shame and modesty and sat down in a crouching posture.
A certain man threw his upper robe to her. She put it on, approached the Teacher, and after paying homage with the fivefold prostration, said:
"Venerable sir, be my refuge! A hawk has seized one son of mine;
another was swept away by water; a third fell dead on the road; and my mother, father, and brother have died at home and are burning on a single funeral pyre."
She explained the cause of her grief. The Teacher said, “Paṭācārā, do not grieve; you have come into the presence of one who is capable of being your refuge.

For just as you are now shedding tears because of the death of your children and others, so too, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*anamatagga-saṃsāra*), the tears shed due to the death of children and others would equal the waters of the four great oceans.”
Showing that [the tears] are more than the water [of the oceans], he said: “The water in the four oceans is but a trifle;
the flood of tears shed by a man afflicted by suffering is far greater and not small. For what reason, mother, do you neglect this?”
He spoke this verse.
As the Teacher was thus delivering a discourse on the beginningless cycle of existence, her grief became diminished.
Then, perceiving that her grief had been attenuated, he said: "Paṭācārā, sons and the like are no refuge for one who goes to the world beyond."

"Neither sons, nor father, nor kinsmen can become a shelter or a refuge"—since even those who exist are not truly present [as such], the wise person, having purified their own virtue (*sīla*), should accomplish only the path leading to Nibbāna; showing this, he says:
"Sons are no protection, nor is a father, nor even kinsmen."
For one seized by the End-maker, there is no protection among kinsmen.
"Knowing this fact, the wise person, restrained by virtue,
should quickly purify the path leading to Nibbāna."
He taught the Dhamma with these verses. At the conclusion of the teaching, Paṭācārā was established in the fruit of stream-entry and requested ordination from the Teacher.
The Teacher led her into the presence of the bhikkhunīs and granted her the going-forth.
Having received full admission, she applied herself to insight meditation for the sake of the higher paths. One day, while carrying water in a jar, she [was washing] her feet...
While washing, she poured out water. Having gone a short distance, that [stream] was cut off; when poured out a second time, it went further than that;
when poured out a third time, it went even further still.
Taking that very object as her theme, she delimited the three stages of life and reflected: "Just like this water I first poured out, these beings, even in their first stage of life..."
“They die; they die even in middle age, like water poured for the second time that has traveled far;
and they die even in old age, like water poured for the third time that has traveled even further,” he thought.
While sitting in the Gandhakuṭī, the Teacher emitted a radiance and, as if standing before her and speaking, said: “It is even so.”

"Paṭācārā, all these beings are subject to death; therefore, for one who lives for a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, it is better to live for even a single day or a single moment seeing them. Showing this meaning, he said:
"And he who might live for a hundred years, Not seeing the arising and passing away..."
"One single day of life is better for one who sees its arising and passing away"—thus he spoke this verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, Paṭācārā attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
"The Conqueror named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena..."
One hundred thousand aeons ago, the Leader appeared in this world.
At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī into a family of merchants,
illumined by various jewels and endowed with great happiness.
“Having approached that Great Hero, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma;
then, with faith born within me, I went for refuge to the Conqueror.
Thereafter, the Leader praised the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.”
To that modest and upright bhikkhunī, who was skilled in what is proper and improper,
I then, with a joyful heart and longing for that state,
invited the Ten-Powered One, the Leader of the World, together with the Saṅgha.
“Having fed him for seven days and having given him the three robes,
I bowed my head at his feet and spoke these words:
‘O Hero, that which was described by you, O Sage, on the eighth day from now— ’”
“May I become such as that, O Leader, if it is to be accomplished.
Then the Teacher said to me: “Bhadde, do not fear;
take heart! In a future time, you shall obtain that heart’s desire.”
“In a hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world.
His legitimate heirs in the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, shall be his true sons.”
“By the name of Paṭācārā, she will become a female disciple of the Teacher.
“At that time, having become joyful, I served the Jina together with the Saṅgha, the Leader of the World, for as long as I lived, with a mind of loving-kindness.”
“By that well-performed karma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
In this auspicious aeon, I was a highly renowned companion of Brahmā.”
One named Kassapa by clan, the best among those who speak,
appeared. At that time, the lord of men, the king of Kāsi named Kikī, was the attendant of the Great Sage in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī.
“I was his third daughter, well-known as a bhikkhunī;
having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror’s foremost disciple, I resolved to go forth.
My father did not grant us permission, so at that time we remained in the home.”
For twenty thousand years we wandered about untiringly.
The seven daughters, daughters of kings, raised in luxury,
delighted in attending upon the Buddha and lived the celibate life of a maiden.
“Samaṇī and Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī and Bhikkhudāyikā;
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and Saṅghadāyikā as the seventh.
I, Uppalavaṇṇā, and the bhikkhunīs Khemā and Bhaddā;”
Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā was the seventh.
“By those well-performed deeds and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.”
“In this my final existence, I was born into a family of merchants in Sāvatthī,
the preeminent city— prosperous, flourishing, and possessed of great wealth.
And when I had reached the prime of youth, I fell under the sway of discursive thoughts.”
Seeing a man who was a paramour, I went with him.
"I have given birth to an only son, and this second one is in my womb;
therefore, I am firmly resolved that I shall leave my parents behind."
“I did not inform my husband when he had gone away on his journey;
alone, I left the house to go to the supreme Sāvatthī.
Then, O Lord, having arrived, you encountered me on the road.”
Then, winds born of my karma arose, most terrible.
And at the time of my delivery, a great cloud rose up;
having gone then for fodder, my husband was killed by a snake.
“Then, destitute and miserable with the pain of childbirth,
seeing the small river filled [with water], I was going toward my own home.
Taking the child, I crossed over, leaving him alone on the far bank.”
Having laid my young son down, I crossed over to the other side.
The water buffalo turned back, bellowing for its calf that was crying out;
the river carried the other one away, and so I was overwhelmed with grief.
“Having gone to the city of Sāvatthī, I heard that my kinsmen had died.
Then, overcome by grief and overwhelmed by great sorrow, I spoke:
‘Both my sons have passed away, and on the road my husband has died.’”
“Mother, father, and brother dwell together in a single body.
At that time, emaciated, pale, helpless, and dejected in mind,
as I was wandering here and there, I saw the Charioteer of Men.”
Then the Teacher said to me: “Do not grieve for your sons;
take heart. Seek out your own self; why do you distress yourself in vain?
Sons are no refuge, nor are kinsmen or relatives.”
"For one seized by the Ender, there is no refuge among kinsmen.
Having heard those words of the Sage, I attained the first fruit;
not long after going forth, I reached arahantship.
“I have mastery over the supernormal powers, and with the divine ear-element I know the minds of others,
carrying out the Teacher’s instruction.
I know my former births, and the divine eye has been purified.”
Having dispelled all taints, I became purified and stainless.
Then, in the presence of the All-Seeing One,
I mastered the entire Vinaya in its full detail and explained it exactly as it is.
“The Jina, pleased with that quality, placed me in this foremost position:
‘Paṭācārā alone is the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s dispensation has been fulfilled.”
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.

Having attained Arahantship, while still in the stage of a trainee (*sekha*), she reflected upon her own practice and, manifesting the manner in which she had brought about further distinction, uttered this inspired verse (*udāna*):
“With ploughs they till the field, sowing seeds upon the ground;”
“While supporting their wives and children, young men acquire wealth. But why is it that I—
who am endowed with virtue, who carry out the Teacher’s instruction,
and who am neither indolent nor restless— do not attain Nibbāna?”
“Having washed my feet in the waters,
and having seen the water for washing my feet flowing down from the high ground to the low,
I then concentrated my mind like a well-trained, noble steed.”
Then, taking the lamp, I entered the monastery;
having looked about for a bed, I sat down upon a couch.
Then, taking a needle, I drew back the wick.
“Like the extinguishing of a lamp, there was liberation of the mind”—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, *kasanti* means “plowing,” performing the work of plowing. This singular form is used in the sense of a plural.
*Pavapanti* means “sowing,” planting seeds. *Chamā* means “on the ground. This nominative form is used in the sense of a locative. This is the meaning here.

The summary of the meaning: These young men, plowing the field with plows and shares, sowing seeds consisting of various grains such as rice and barley in the field according to their intention, and thereby supporting themselves, their wives, children, and so forth, acquire wealth for that cause and for that purpose.
Thus, in this world, there is purposeful application.
Personal exertion indeed bears fruit and brings success. In this regard, one reflects:
"Though I am endowed with virtue and am a follower of the Teacher’s instruction, why is it that I do not attain Nibbāna? Am I not untiring and free from agitation?
Thus, being of perfectly purified virtue, she is untiring due to her application of energy (*āraddhavīriyatā*), and because her mind is well-composed within, she is free from agitation.
"Being undisturbed and practicing the Teacher’s instruction known as the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, why should I not attain Nibbāna? I shall surely attain it.
Having thought thus, she performed the work of insight (vipassanā), and one day, a sign appeared in the water used for washing her feet.
He grasped it. Therefore he said, “Having washed my feet,” and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
while washing my feet, for the purpose of washing my feet, I saw the foot-wash water that had flowed down from the high ground into the water poured three times; seeing that, I made a mental sign:
“Just as this water is subject to exhaustion and subject to decay, so too are the life-formations of sentient beings. Thus, [I took] the characteristic of impermanence.
Following that, having contemplated the characteristic of suffering and the characteristic of non-self,
I developed insight and concentrated my mind. Just as a skilled charioteer easily guides a noble, well-bred horse,
so did I easily concentrate my mind through the concentration of insight (vipassanā-samādhi).
I brought it to a state of concentration. Thus, while increasing my insight, desiring what was conducive to my physical well-being, I entered a small room;

taking a lamp for the purpose of dispelling the darkness, I entered the chamber, placed the lamp, and as soon as I sat down upon the couch, I pulled the wick toward the door-bolt so that the lamp would go out. At that very moment, by obtaining what was conducive to her physical well-being, she—
The mind became concentrated, it entered the path of insight, and it was struck by the Path.
Thereupon, through the sequence of the Path, there was the total destruction of all taints (āsava). Therefore it is said: "Then, having taken a lamp... [etc.
...there was liberation of the mind. In that context, "having looked at the bed" means having seen the bed by the light of the lamp.
“Sūci” means a needle; “aggaḷasūciṃ” means a door-pin. “Vaṭṭiṃ okassayāmi” means I pull the wick toward the oil in order to extinguish the lamp.
“Vimokkho” means liberation from the defilements (kilesa). Since that liberation, in the ultimate sense, is the continuity of the mind (citta), it is therefore said to be “of the mind” (cetaso).
Just as a lamp is fit to arise when conditions such as a wick and oil are present—

Because it does not arise in their absence, it is called "extinguished" (*nibbūta*); likewise, because the mind—which is prone to arising when conditions such as the defilements are present—does not arise in their absence, it is called "liberated" (*vimutta*). Thus he said:
"As the extinguishing of a lamp, there was liberation of the mind."
The commentary on the *Therīgāthā* of Paṭācārā is finished.
11. The commentary on the verses of the thirty therīs beginning with "Having taken up the pestles" (*musalāni gahetvāna*). They too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.
Accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of being, they gradually amassed the requisites for liberation.
Impelled by their own past actions, they were reborn in various noble families during this current appearance of a Buddha;
having reached maturity and heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā, they gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and became pure in virtue.
They lived fulfilling their duties and obligations. Then one day, while the Elder Paṭācārā was giving them instruction, she said:
“Taking up their pestles, the young men pound the grain;
supporting wives and children, the young men acquire wealth.”
“Fulfill the teaching of the Buddha, having done which one does not regret;
quickly wash your feet and sit to one side;
devoted to the tranquility of mind, fulfill the teaching of the Buddha.”—he spoke these two verses.
Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: These beings, for the sake of livelihood, take pestles and pound the grain of others;
they perform the work of the mortar. Having performed other such lowly work as well, while supporting their wives and children, they accumulate wealth as appropriate.
Yet that work of theirs is low, vulgar, worldly, painful, and conducive to harm.
Therefore, having abandoned such defiled proliferation (*saṃkilesika-papañca*), you should perform the teaching of the Buddha;
perform and accomplish the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, known as the Three Trainings, and bring it forth within your own continuum. Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Having done which, one does not regret. That is, because of performing that, one does not fall into regret both now and in the future.
Now, in order to show the preliminary duties and the method of practice for that [meditation], it is said: "Having quickly washed his feet," and so forth.

In this regard, because one who has not washed his feet and has not rinsed his mouth finds neither comfort in sitting nor the attainment of a favorable climate, whereas for one who has washed his feet, rinsed his mouth, and sat down in a secluded place, both of these are obtained.
Therefore, not missing this opportunity as it has been obtained,
wash your feet with your own hands and sit down, settle yourselves, in a secluded place apart from others.
Having bound your minds to whichever among the thirty-eight objects of meditation you prefer, being devoted to mental serenity (*cetosamatha*), remain concentrated.
"By means of the mind, through the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths, carry out and accomplish the instruction, the exhortation, and the guidance of the Buddha,
the Blessed One. Then those bhikkhunīs, abiding by that elder nun's exhortation, established insight and applied themselves to the work of cultivation.
Having reached the full maturity of knowledge and being endowed with the necessary causes, they attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
Reflecting upon their own practice, they spoke these verses of instruction along with [the following]:
“Having heard those words of hers, the instruction of Paṭācārā;”
Having washed their feet, they sat down to one side;
devoted to mental tranquility, they carried out the Buddha’s teaching.
During the first watch of the night, they recollected their former births.
During the middle watch of the night, they purified their divine eye;
during the final watch of the night, they shattered the mass of darkness.
Rising up, they paid homage at his feet, saying: "Your instruction has been fulfilled."
“Just as the thirty-three gods place Indra at their head when he is undefeated in battle,
so shall we dwell, having placed him at our head— we who possess the threefold knowledge and are free from taints.
Thus they spoke these verses.
Therein, having heard her words— that instruction of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā which constitutes an instruction in the sense of being a message to the enemy that is defilement—
those thirty bhikkhunīs, having heard it, having agreed to it, and having accepted it with their heads,
rose and paid homage at her feet, saying, "Your instruction has been carried out," thus taking to heart the message she had delivered exactly as it was accepted.
Having applied their minds and sat down in a comfortable place, they developed meditation until it reached its culmination.
Then, rising from their seats to announce the distinction they had attained, they went into her presence and said, "Great Elder,
we have carried out your instructions exactly as you directed," and they paid homage at her feet by prostrating themselves with the five points of the body touching the ground.
"Just as the thirty-three gods [stand] before Indra, who is unconquered in battle with the Asuras,
so too, O Great Elder, we shall dwell placing you at our head, since there is nothing else remaining for us to do.
Therefore, proclaiming their own gratitude by saying, "We are possessors of the three knowledges and free from taints," this very [statement] was theirs.
The declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*) took place. Furthermore, whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is exactly according to the method already stated below.
The commentary on the thirty verses of the Elder Nun Tiṃsa is finished.
12. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Candā.
“‘I was poor in former times,’ etc., are the verses of the Elder Nun Candā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation in various states of existence, gradually gathered the requisites for emancipation;
with her wisdom fully matured, during this current appearance of a Buddha, she [was born] in a certain brahmin village to an unknown brahmin.
She took rebirth in that household. From the moment she was born, that family’s wealth went to ruin.
Having gradually reached the age of discretion, she lived in misery. Then, a snake-epidemic broke out in that house;
because of it, all her relatives met with the calamity of death. When her kin had perished, she [went] elsewhere.
Unable to survive, she wandered from house to house with an alms-bowl in hand, sustaining herself on whatever food she obtained through begging.
One day, she went to the place where the Elder Nun Paṭācārā was taking her meal.
Seeing her distressed and overcome by hunger, the nuns were moved by compassion; they welcomed her with kind treatment and, using what was available there—
They satisfied her with food that was pleasing by way of its preparation.
She, having gained confidence in their conduct and virtue, approached the Elder Nun, paid homage, and sat down to one side. The Elder Nun preached the Dhamma to her.

Having heard that Dhamma, she became deeply inspired toward the Teaching, developed a sense of spiritual urgency regarding *saṃsāra*, and went forth. Having gone forth, [she remained] under the Elder Nun...
Abiding by that instruction and establishing insight, she devoted herself to meditation.

Because she had performed her duties and because her knowledge had reached maturity, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Reflecting upon her own practice, she said:
“I was once in a miserable state, a widow without a son;”
“Without friends or relatives, I obtained no food or clothing.
Taking my bowl and staff, I wandered from family to family for seven years, scorched by cold and heat.”
“Seeing again a bhikkhunī who had obtained food and drink,
I approached her and spoke of going forth into the homeless life.
Out of compassion for me, Paṭācārā ordained me.”
Then, having exhorted me, she directed me toward the ultimate goal:
“Having heard her words, I carried out her instruction;
the noble lady’s advice was not in vain, for I have attained the three knowledges and am free from the taints.”
He spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Herein, "miserable" (*duggata*) means poor. "Formerly" (*pure*) means before going forth.
For from the time of going forth onwards, a person here cannot be described as either wealthy or poor in terms of material possessions. However, in terms of virtues, this elder was indeed wealthy.
Therefore he said, "In the past, I was ill-fated. "A widow" (*vidhavā*): a husband (*dhava*) is called a master;
due to the absence of that, she is a widow, meaning one whose husband has died. "Childless" (*aputtikā*): devoid of sons. "Without friends" (*vinā mittehi*):
deprived and separated from both friends and kinsmen. "I did not obtain food and clothing": I did not attain the full measure of food and clothing.
The intended meaning is that they obtained nothing more than mere food and clothing, consisting solely of alms-food and scraps of cloth.
Therefore he said, “Having taken a bowl and a staff,” and so forth. In this context, “bowl” (patta) refers to an earthenware vessel.

“Staff” (daṇḍa) refers to a stick for warding off cattle, dogs, and the like. “From family to family” (kulā kulaṃ) means from one household to another. “Burning with cold and heat” means being oppressed by cold and heat due to the absence of a dwelling house.
"Bhikkhunī" refers to the Elder Nun Paṭācārā. "Later" means after seven years had passed.

"In the ultimate sense" (*paramatthe*) means in the supreme, highest goal: both in the practice leading to Nibbāna and in Nibbāna itself. "She enjoined her" means that while explaining the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), she directed her toward it. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Candā is finished.
The commentary on the Pañcakanipāta is finished.
6. Chakkanipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Five Hundred Therīs.
In the *Chakkanipāta* (The Chapter of Sixes), there are approximately five hundred stanzas by elder nuns beginning with "He whose path you do not know.

These [nuns] had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, and having gradually gathered the requisites for liberation, they were born into various noble families at the time of this Buddha's appearance.
Having been born and reached maturity, they were brought by their parents to the families of their husbands; there, having obtained sons in various places, they lived the life of householders.
Because they had performed similar deeds of that same nature, all of them became mothers whose children had died.
Overwhelmed by grief for their sons, they approached the Elder Nun Paṭācārā, paid homage, and sat down, [explaining] the cause of their own sorrow.
They reported this. The Elder Nun, dispelling their grief, said:
“Of one whose path you do not know—whether he has come or gone— why do you weep, crying ‘my son,’ for that being from whom he came?”
“You know his path, whether he has come or gone;
do not grieve for him, for such is the nature of living beings.
He came here unasked, and he has departed from here unbidden.”
“Having surely come from somewhere, and having lived for a few days;
he has gone from here by one way, and will go from there by another.
Passing through the cycle of existence in human form, the deceased one will continue on.”
“As he came, so he went; what lamentation can there be in that?”—with these four verses she taught the Dhamma.
Having heard her Dhamma, they were moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and went forth in the presence of the Elder Nun. Having gone forth, through insight (*vipassanā*)...
As they performed their duties, because the qualities that ripen liberation had reached maturity,
they soon established themselves in Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Then, having attained Arahantship and reflected upon their own practice,
they uttered, by way of inspired exclamation (udāna), the verses of instruction beginning with "He whose path you do not know," along with—
“Truly, the arrow has been pulled out from my heart, that arrow so difficult to see,
which had driven away the grief for my son from me who was overcome by sorrow.
Now, with the arrow extracted, I am free from craving and have attained final peace.”
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, O Sage”—
thus they each spoke these verses.
In this regard, “of whom you do not know the path, whether coming or going” refers to whichever being has come here.
"You do not know the path by which [the being] has come, nor the path by which one who has gone from here has gone.

He says this with reference to the immediately preceding past and future existences and rebirths. "From where has that being come?"—referring to one who has come from some place of departure along a path whose route is thus unknown, and who, like a man encountered on the way with whom there has been no prior acquaintance whatsoever, is entirely unfamiliar.
Having merely produced the sense of "mine" toward this being, for what reason and by what cause do you weep, thinking, "He is my son"?
The intention is that there is no reason here for weeping, because there is no way to repay him and because nothing can be done for one's son.
And you know his path: you know the path by which this being, whom you consider your son, has come.
"And you should know the path taken by one who has gone; do not mourn for him. Thus you should not mourn for him.

Why? Because such is the nature of living beings; even in this very life, all beings are subject to change and separation from those who are dear and pleasing, due to the absence of mastery over them, let alone in the life to come.
“Uninvited he came from there”: from the other world, he came here uninvited by anyone.
There is also a reading “he arrived,” which has the same meaning. “Without permission he went from here”: from this world, he went to the other world without being permitted by anyone.
“From somewhere”: from wherever he went, such as from hell and so forth. “Nūna” (surely) is used in the sense of suspicion. “Having dwelt for a few days”: for the duration of just a few days.
"Having dwelt here": "gone from here by another [existence]" means gone from this state of existence to another by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*);
he has approached yet another state of existence. "Going from there by another" means he will go from that state of existence to another; he will approach yet another state of existence.
"A ghost" (*peta*) means one who, having been born into various states of existence, has departed from them. "In human form" is merely an illustration.

The meaning is: by way of human existence and by way of animal existence, etc. "Wandering" means wandering from one birth to another by way of rebirth. "As he came, so he went": just as he came from an unknown destination without informing anyone, so he went to an unknown destination without being permitted.
What lamentation is there in that? In such a case, where one has no mastery over oneself...
"What lamentation indeed can there be for one in the desire realm? What is the purpose of lamenting?"—this is the meaning. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
And herein, the first four verses were spoken individually by the Elder Nun Paṭācārā for the sake of dispelling the sorrow of those approximately five hundred women.
[They were spoken] by those who, having stood by her instruction and gone forth, attained specific spiritual distinctions.
It should be understood that each of those five hundred bhikkhunīs recited one of the six verses.

Regarding the phrase "the five hundred Paṭācārās": because they had received instruction in the presence of the elder nun Paṭācārā and reported what she had said, these five hundred bhikkhunīs acquired the name "Paṭācārās.
The commentary on the Therīgāthā of the five hundred [nuns] is finished.

2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Vāseṭṭhī. The verses beginning with “I am tormented by grief for my son” belong to the elder nun Vāseṭṭhī. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;
having accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, she gradually gathered the requisites for liberation.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in this current age of a Buddha’s appearance in a noble family in Vesālī.
Upon reaching maturity, she was given in marriage by her parents to a young man of equal caste; having gone to her husband’s home, she lived happily with him.
After obtaining a son, when that boy was running about and playing, she passed away.

Afflicted by grief for her son, she became insane. While her kinsmen and husband were providing medical treatment for her, she fled without their knowledge and, wandering here and there, arrived at the city of Mithilā.
There she saw the Blessed One walking along the middle of the street—a tamed, guarded, and self-controlled elephant. Having seen him, she...
Upon seeing him, through the power of the Buddha, she was freed from her madness and regained her natural state of mind.
Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma in brief. Having heard that Dhamma, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency;
she requested the Teacher for the going-forth, and by the Teacher’s command, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs. Having performed the preliminary duties and established insight meditation, she—
Striving and exerting herself, through the ripening of her knowledge, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long.
Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Distressed by grief for my son, my mind was distracted and I lost consciousness;”
Naked and with disheveled hair, I wandered here and there.
For three years I lived among heaps of refuse in the streets, in cemeteries, and by the roadsides, overcome by hunger and thirst.
“Then I beheld the Sugata as he was approaching the city of Mithilā—
the Tamer of the untamed, the Fully Awakened One, free from fear from any quarter.
Having regained my own mind and paid homage to him, I entered [the city].”
Thus Gotama, out of compassion, taught me the Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness;
applying myself to the Teacher’s word, I realized the auspicious state.
“All sorrows are utterly cut off; they are abandoned, and this is their end.
For the bases from which sorrows arise have been fully understood by me.
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, *aṭṭā* means distressed (*aṭṭitā*). Or rather, this is the reading: *aṭṭitā*, meaning oppressed (*pīḷitā*). *Khittacittā* means her heart is distracted by the madness of grief.

For that very reason, due to the disappearance of her natural consciousness, she is unconscious (*visaññinī*). Because of the absence of shame and dread of blame, and because she is stripped of her clothes, she is naked (*naggā*).
Because her hair is disheveled, she has disordered hair (*pakiṇṇakesī*). "Hither and thither" means from village to village, from city to city, along the streets.
I wandered through the streets.
"Then" (*atha*) means subsequently, upon the exhaustion of the karma conducive to madness.

"Sugata" refers to the Blessed One because of his beautiful gait (*sobhanagamana*), because he has gone to a beautiful place (*sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gata*), because he has gone rightly (*sammā gata*), and because he has gone completely (*sammā ca gata*). [He went to] Mithilā.
"Patīti" means toward Mithilā; the meaning is that they are going toward the city of Mithilā.
"Sacittaṃ paṭiladdhānā" means having regained their own natural state of mind by abandoning their madness through the power of the Buddha.

"Yuñjanti satthuvacane" means applying themselves to the word of the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One—that is, practicing the application of effort (*yoga*) and devoting themselves to meditation within the Dispensation.
"I have realized the auspicious state"—I have realized Nibbāna, the auspicious, secure state that is unassailed by the four *yogas*.
"This is the end": these sorrows have this as their limit, namely the Arahantship now attained by me; thus they are "ending here.
The meaning is that there is no further arising of them now. "From which the arising of sorrows [comes]" refers to that from which [sorrows] characterized by inward brooding arise.

The origin of sorrows: the bases and foundations for those sorrows, which consist of the five aggregates of clinging, have been fully understood through the full understandings of knowing, scrutinizing, and abandoning.
Therefore, the construction is: "Sorrows end here.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Vāseṭṭhī is finished.
3. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Khemā.
The verses beginning with "You are young and beautiful" belong to the elder nun Khemā.

It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she lived in the city of Haṃsavatī as a slave dependent on others, performing services for others. By performing these services for others...

While making their livelihood, one day, upon seeing the Elder Sujāta—the foremost disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One Padumuttara—walking for alms, they gave him three sweetmeats. On that very same day, they offered their own hair as a gift to the Elder and made a resolution:
"In the future, may we become female disciples of a Buddha possessed of great wisdom. Thus they lived out their lives.
Having been diligent in wholesome deeds, they wandered through the realms of gods and humans,
eventually being reborn in succession among the six celestial heavens as the chief consorts of various divine kings. In the human world as well,
having many times attained the status of chief consort to universal monarchs and regional kings, they experienced great prosperity until [the time of] the Blessed One Vipassī.
Having been reborn in the human world at a favorable time and attained maturity, she heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher;
moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she went forth into homelessness. Having practiced the holy life for ten thousand years, she became deeply learned and a preacher of the Dhamma.
By performing deeds conducive to wisdom through preaching the Dhamma to many people and other such acts, she passed away from there and was reborn only in the happy destinies.
Wandering through this eon, during the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha and the Blessed One Koṇāgamana,
she was reborn into a family endowed with great wealth; having reached maturity, she had a large monastery constructed and dedicated it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.
In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Great Seer, she was the eldest daughter of King Kiki of Kāsī, named Samaṇī.
Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and remained in the life of a householder;
yet, practicing the celibacy of a maiden for twenty thousand years, she lived together with her sisters, Samaṇaguttā and the others.
Having had a beautiful pariveṇa constructed, he dedicated it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.

In this very way, having performed sublime meritorious deeds pertaining to the sense bases in various successive existences and wandering only through happy destinies, he was reborn into a royal family in the city of Sākala in the kingdom of Madda during the arising of this Buddha. His name was Khemātissa.
She was golden-hued, with skin resembling refined gold. Having reached maturity, she went to the house of King Bimbisāra.
While the Teacher was dwelling in the Veḷuvana Grove, she remained merely concerned with physical beauty and did not go to see the Teacher, thinking, "He points out the defects in form.
The king, having had the praises of the Veḷuvana proclaimed by his men, conceived the desire to show the monastery to the queen.

Then the queen asked the king, "I wish to see the monastery. The king said, "You shall not be permitted to return unless you have seen the Teacher after going to the monastery," and he gave orders to his men:
"By force, even if necessary, show the Ten-Powered One to the queen. The queen went to the monastery, spent a portion of the day there, and as she was returning, she [saw] the Teacher.
Having seen him, she began to depart. Then the king’s men led her into the presence of the Teacher, even though she was unwilling.
When the Teacher saw her approaching, he manifested through his psychic power a woman resembling a celestial nymph (*devaccharā*), who took a palm leaf and stood fanning him.
Queen Khemā, seeing this, thought: “Such as this is a woman who resembles a celestial nymph.”
"The women are standing not far from the Blessed One; I am not even capable of serving them, for my mind has been ruined by the power of evil thoughts without cause.
Having grasped this sign, she stood there gazing at that very woman.
Then, while she was looking on, by the power of the Teacher’s resolve, that woman passed beyond her first stage of life.
Having passed beyond middle age and reached old age, with broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin, she lay there turning over like a palm leaf.
Then Khemā, because of her previous spiritual accomplishments, thought:
"Even a body such as this has met with such a calamity; my own body, too, will surely follow this same course. Then to her...
Having understood their mental conduct, the Teacher said:
“Those who are dyed by passion follow the stream, like a spider following the web it has itself made;
having cut even this as well, they go forth as wanderers, indifferent, having abandoned sensual pleasure.”

He spoke a verse. According to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is recorded that at the conclusion of that verse, she attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
However, in the *Apadāna*, it is recorded: "Having heard this verse, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*);
having obtained the king's permission, she went forth and attained *arahantship*. Herein, this is the text of the *Apadāna*:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye-seer regarding all phenomena,
arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.
At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī in the family of a treasurer.”
In that city, radiant with various jewels, I was endowed with great bliss.
Having approached that Great Hero, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma;
thereafter, having conceived faith, I went for refuge to the Victor.
“Having requested my mother and father,
I invited the Guide together with his disciples for seven days and provided them with food.
When those seven days had passed, [I honored] the one supreme among those of great wisdom.”
The Charioteer of Men placed her as the foremost among the bhikkhunīs.
Having heard this, I became joyful;
having performed an act of service for that Great Seer and prostrated myself at that spot, I made a solemn aspiration.
Then the Conqueror said to me: "Your aspiration shall be fulfilled;
for the service you have performed for me and the Saṅgha will yield immeasurable fruit.
One hundred thousand aeons hence, you shall be born into the lineage of Okkāka."
"One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
Among his teachings, there will be a legitimate daughter, fashioned from the Dhamma, who has attained the foremost state;
she shall be known as Khemā."
“By that well-performed kamma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Passing away from there, I went to the Yāma world, and from there I went to Tusita.”
And from there to Nimmānarati, and from there to Vasavatti’s city.
"Wherever I was reborn, by the power of that karma,
right there I served as the chief queen to kings."
“Falling away from that human state, I served as the chief queen of universal monarchs,
of regional kings, and of local rulers.
Having enjoyed such prosperity among both gods and humans,”
Having been happy in every state, I wandered through many eons.
Ninety-one eons ago, the World-Leader Vipassī arose,
beautiful to behold and possessing insight into all phenomena.
“Having approached that Leader of the World, the Charioteer of Men,
and having heard the Dhamma he spoke, I went forth into the homeless life.
For ten thousand years, under the teaching of that Hero...”
Having practiced the holy life, disciplined in yoga, and deeply learned;
skilled in the analysis of conditions, confident in the Four Noble Truths;
subtle in their mental discourse, they carry out the Teacher’s instruction.
“Having passed away from there, I was reborn in the Tusita heaven, illustrious and renowned.
There, I surpass others by the fruit of my holy life (*brahmacariya*).
Wherever I am reborn, I possess great wealth and vast riches.”
“I am wise and virtuous, and my assembly is well-disciplined.
By that karma and by my application to the teaching of the Conqueror,
all prosperities— dear to my heart— are easily obtained by me.”
“Whosoever has been my husband, wherever I have gone,
no one has ever treated me with contempt, owing to the power of my practice.
In this auspicious eon, there was a man of great renown who was a kinsman of Brahmā.”
By name Koṇāgamana, the best among those who speak, appeared.
At that time, in Bārāṇasī, there were three people: Dhanañjānī, Sumedhā, and myself, from a family of great prosperity.
“In the past, we were donors who assisted in giving at the monasteries,
and we even had a monastery built specifically for the Saṅgha.
Having passed away from there, we have all gone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.”
They attained preeminence in fame among human beings as well.
In this very eon, a highly renowned kinsman of Brahmā arose,
named Kassapa by clan, the best among those who speak.
“At that time, the lord of men, the King of Kāsi named Kikī, was the attendant of the Great Sage in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī.
I was his eldest daughter, renowned as Samaṇī.”
Having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror’s son, I resolved upon the going-forth.
My father did not grant us permission, so we remained in the household life;
for twenty thousand years, we wandered about without weariness.
“Seven daughters, raised in happiness as princesses, were devoted to the celibate life of a maiden (komāribrahmacariya) and delighted in attending upon the Buddha:
Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, [and others].”
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and the seventh was Saṅghadāyikā.
“I, Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, and Kuṇḍalā;
Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.”
“At one time that Sun among Men taught the wonderful Dhamma;
having heard the Mahānidāna Sutta, I mastered it.
By those well-performed deeds and by my intentions and aspirations,”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
And now, in this final existence, in the supreme city of Sākala,
I am the daughter of King Madda— charming, beloved, and dear.
“As soon as I was born, there was safety in that city;
therefore, the name ‘Khemā’ arose for me on account of my virtue.
When I reached youth, adorned with beauty and grace,”
Then my father gave me to King Bimbisāra.
I was his beloved Suppiyā, delighting in the play of beauty;
yet, because he spoke of the faults of beauty, I did not approach that most compassionate one.
“At that time, King Bimbisāra, with the intention of favoring me,
praised Veḷuvana and had singers sing of me:
‘By whomsoever the delightful Veḷuvana, the abode of the Sugata, has not been seen— ’”
"We consider that Nandana has not been seen by him.
But by whoever Veḷuvana— the delighter of the delighters of men— has been seen, by him Nandana,
the great joy of the Lord of the Immortals, has been truly seen."
“Leaving the Nandana grove and descending to the surface of the earth,
the gods beheld the delightful Veḷuvana and were not satiated, being utterly amazed.
It was produced by the merit of the king and adorned by the merit of the Buddha.”
Who could describe that forest’s entire abundance of accumulated virtues?
Having heard of that flourishing grove, which was so enchanting to my ears,
I then informed the king of my desire to see that garden.
“Then that lord of the earth, with a great retinue,
sent me to that garden, eager for a sight of it.
‘Go and see the forest of great splendor, a balm for the eyes.’”
That which always shines with splendor, colored by the radiance of the Sugata.
And when the Sage entered Giribbaja, the most excellent of cities, for alms,
at that very moment I approached the forest to see him.
“Then that flowering forest, resounding with the warbling of various bees,
accompanied by the songs of cuckoos, and graced by the dancing of flocks of peacocks—
tranquil, uncrowded, and adorned with various walkways.”
Filled with small pavilions and graced by the most excellent of yogis, I wandered about and thought: "My eyes have truly borne fruit.
There, seeing a young bhikkhu engaged in his practice, I reflected:
“In such a delightful forest, this youth stands in the prime of his life,
endowed with beauty like that of the spring season.
Seated at the foot of a tree, shaven-headed and clad in a saṅghāṭī robe,”
“Truly, this bhikkhu meditates, having abandoned the delight born of sense-objects.
Is it not the case that a householder, having enjoyed sensual pleasures as he wishes,
may later, when aged, practice this sublime Dhamma?”
“Knowing it to be empty, I approached the Perfumed Chamber, the abode of the Conqueror;
there I beheld the Conqueror, like the rising sun.
He was sitting alone in happiness, being fanned by a choice woman.”
Having seen him, I thought thus: "This bull among men is not coarse.
