That maiden, with a golden radiance, lotus-face and eyes, bimba-red lips, and jasmine-like teeth, is a true elixir for the eyes of the mind."
“Her breasts were like golden swings, her waist was shaped like a *kalikā* bud;
her hips were like the middle of a sacrificial altar, and her thighs were like plantain trunks, adorned with lovely ornaments.
She was draped in a red silk upper garment and wore a smooth blue lower robe.”
With a form beyond reproach and endowed with a state of joy, upon seeing her I thought: "Oh, how beautiful she is!
Never before have I seen anyone such as this with my own eyes."
“Then, overcome by old age, she was discolored and her face was distorted;
her teeth were broken, her hair white, with saliva flowing and her mouth impure.
Her ears were shriveled, her eyes white, and her breasts were pendulous and unsightly.”
Her entire body was covered with wrinkles, and her frame was spread with veins.
With trembling limbs, leaning on a staff as her only companion,
emaciated and wasted away, she fell down shuddering, gasping for breath again and again.
“Then a sense of urgency arose within me, extraordinary and hair-raising:
‘Fie on this impure form, in which fools take delight!
Then the Greatly Compassionate One, seeing my mind filled with such urgency,”
With a joyful heart, the Sugata spoke these verses:
“Behold, Khema, this heap of bones—sick, impure, and putrid;
oozing and trickling, it is what fools delight in.”
“Develop the mind on the foul, one-pointed and well-concentrated;
let mindfulness directed to the body be present, and be full of disenchantment. As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this.”
“Both internally and externally, cause desire for the body to fade away.
Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full comprehension of conceit, you shall wander at peace.”
“Those who are stained by passion follow the stream, like a spider following the web it has woven itself.
Having cut even this asunder, they wander forth, free from longing, having abandoned sensual pleasure.
Then, the Charioteer of Men, knowing my mind to be ready, [spoke].”
He taught me the Mahānidāna Sutta for the sake of discipline.
Having heard that supreme discourse, I recollected my former perceptions;
standing there in peace, I purified the eye of Dhamma.
“Having prostrated at the feet of the Great Seer, I spoke these words for the purpose of confessing my transgression:
‘Homage to you, O All-Seeing One! Homage to you, O Compassionate One!’”
Homage to you who have crossed over saṃsāra; homage to you who bestow the deathless.
Those who had plunged into the thicket of views and were deluded by sensual lust have been disciplined by you through the right means, O you who delight in discipline.
“Because they do not see such great seers,
beings experience great suffering in the ocean of saṃsāra.
When I am the refuge of the world— the one free from conflict who has reached the end of conflict— ”
“I did not see you standing nearby; I confess that transgression.
Fearing what was harmful while you were a great benefactor and giver of boons, and being infatuated with form, I did not approach you; I confess that transgression.”
Then the Conqueror, the Greatly Compassionate One,
with a sweet voice, said to me, "Stay, O you who seek safety," as if sprinkling me with the Deathless.
Then, bowing my head and circumambulating him three times, I departed.
Having gone and seen the lord of men, I spoke these words:
"O Subduer of Enemies, how excellent is this means devised by you!
For one desiring to see the forest, the Sage has been seen as the very Nirvana."
“If it pleases you, O King, in the teaching of that Tathāgata,
I shall go forth in this very form, weary of the world as taught by the Sage. Then,
raising his hands in reverent salutation, the lord of the earth said:
“I grant you permission, Bhaddā; may your going forth be accomplished.
Then, having gone forth, when half a month had passed, I saw the rising and the setting of the island, and my mind was filled with spiritual urgency.
“Disenchanted with all conditioned things, skilled in the nature of conditions,
having transcended the four floods, I attained arahantship.
I was masterful in the supernormal powers and possessed the divine ear-element.”
I have attained mastery over the knowledge of the minds of others.
I know my former births, and the divine eye has been purified.
All taints are utterly destroyed; now there is no further becoming.
“Regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the terminology, and likewise regarding inspired eloquence—
my knowledge has become completely pure, having arisen within the Buddha’s teaching.
I am skilled in purifications and proficient in the topics of discourse.”
“Knowing the method of the Abhidhamma, I have attained mastery in the Teaching.
Then, at Toraṇavatthu, when questioned on subtle points by the King, the Lord of Kosala, I answered them exactly as they were.”
“Then that king approached the Sugata and questioned him;
the Buddha explained it to him exactly as it was explained by me.
Pleased with that quality, the Victor placed me in this foremost position.”
“The Supreme among Men [said], ‘The path for those of great wisdom’;
‘My defilements have been burnt away... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Now, although this Elder Nun was dwelling in the bliss of the fruit and the bliss of Nibbāna after having attained Arahantship,”
However, among the other elder nuns who had destroyed the taints, her status as one of great wisdom became manifest due to the excellence she had achieved there.
For it was while seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Great Monastery in Jetavana that the Blessed One, assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks, declared:
"This, monks, is the foremost among my female disciples, the bhikkhunīs..."
“Among those of great wisdom, she is Khemā,” he said, thus placing her in the foremost position for great wisdom.
One day, while she was sitting at the foot of a tree for her midday rest, Māra the Evil One approached her in the form of a youth and, seeking to entice her with sensual pleasures, said:
“You are young and beautiful, and I too am a youth;”
He spoke this verse: “Come, Khemā, let us delight in the fivefold musical ensemble.
Its meaning is as follows: “Khemā, you are young, established in youth, and endowed with beauty; I too am young and a youth.
Therefore, without wasting our youth, come and delight in the pleasure of sensual play and sport while the fivefold musical ensemble is being played.”

Having heard this, she—manifesting her own state of detachment from sensual pleasures and all phenomena, his nature as Māra, her deep-seated lack of confidence in beings who cling to a self-identity, and the fact that her task was accomplished—spoke thus:
“With this putrid body, diseased and fragile, I am repelled and ashamed;
craving for sense-pleasures has been uprooted.”
“Sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes, a violent hacking at the aggregates.
That which you call delight in sensual pleasures is now, for me, no delight at all.
Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.”
"Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!
Worshipping the constellations and tending the fire in the forest, fools—failing to understand things as they truly are—imagined that purity lay therein."
“And I, indeed, while paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme among Men, am liberated from all sufferings, carrying out the Teacher’s instruction”—thus she spoke these verses.

Therein, “worshipping the fire in the forest” means performing the fire-sacrifice (*aggihutta*) in the ascetic grove. “Not knowing according to reality” means not fully understanding the occurrences as they truly are. The rest here is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Khemā is finished.
4. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sujātā:
The verses beginning with "Adorned, well-dressed... belong to the Elder Nun Sujātā. She too had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, and having gradually gathered the requisites for liberation, she was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in a merchant family in the city of Sāketa.
Upon reaching maturity, she was given in marriage by her parents to a merchant’s son of equal caste; she went to her husband’s home and lived there in happy harmony with him.
One day, while returning to the city with her retinue after going to a park and enjoying a festival of constellations, Vāsantī saw the Teacher in Añjana Forest;
with a mind full of faith, she approached, paid homage, and sat down to one side.
The Teacher, having delivered a progressive discourse to her and knowing her mind was ready, [proceeded] to the higher, most excellent teaching.

He proclaimed a teaching on the Dhamma. At the conclusion of that teaching, because her own past merits had reached maturity through the completion of her service, and by the excellence of the Teacher’s instruction, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) while still seated as she was.
She then paid homage to the Teacher, went home, and having obtained the permission of both her husband and her parents, [she set out] by the Teacher’s command.
Having gone to the nuns' quarters, she went forth in the presence of the bhikkhunīs. And having gone forth, reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“Adorned, well-dressed, garlanded, and anointed with sandalwood;”
Adorned with all my ornaments and surrounded by a host of female servants,
taking food and drink, as well as no small amount of hard and soft delicacies,
I departed from my home and proceeded toward the pleasure garden.
“Having enjoyed myself and played there, I was returning to my own home when I entered the Añjana Grove at Sāketa to see the monastery.
Having seen the Light of the World, I paid homage and entered.”
Thus the One with Vision taught me the Dhamma out of compassion.
And having heard it from the Great Seer, I penetrated the Truth;
right there I touched the stainless Dhamma, the deathless state.
“Then, having understood the true Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness;
the three knowledges were attained, and the Buddha’s dispensation has borne fruit.”—
Thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "adorned" means decorated. To show that manner of adornment, it is said: "well-dressed, garlanded, and anointed with sandalwood.
Therein, "garlanded" means wearing a garland; "anointed with sandalwood" means smeared with sandalwood paste.
"Covered with all ornaments" means her body was completely covered by way of decoration with all types of ornaments, such as bracelets and so forth.

"Taking food and drink, and no small amount of solid and soft food"—that is, taking a great quantity of rice-gruel and other foods such as *sāli* rice, drinks such as mango juice, snacks such as flour-based sweets, and whatever else is reckoned as food;
"I brought them to the pleasure garden"—I led them to the garden for the sake of a festival celebration. Having brought the food, drink, and so forth there, I sported together with my attendants.
The intended meaning is that they delight in attending upon [him].
At Sāketa, "they seek ointment" (añjanaṃ vananti) means that he entered the monastery in Añjanavana near Sāketa.
"The Lamp of the World" means one who has become a lamp for the world by means of the lamp of knowledge.
"Phusayiṃti phusiṃ" means "I have touched; I have attained. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Sujātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the Verses of the Therī Anopamā.
"Born into a high family," and so forth, are the verses of the Elder Nun Anopamā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, gradually cultivated the qualities that ripen for liberation;
and now, during the arising of this Buddha, she was born as the daughter of a merchant named Majjha in the city of Sāketa.
Having made the offering, she was reborn. Because of her peerless physical beauty, she was named Anopamā.
When she reached maturity, many sons of wealthy merchants, royal ministers, and kings sent messengers to her father, saying:

"Give us your daughter Anopamā; we shall give you this and that. Upon hearing this, because of her possession of the necessary spiritual predispositions (upanissaya), she thought: "With regard to household life..."

"I have no need [for it]," she said. Then, having gone into the presence of the Teacher and heard the Dhamma, because her knowledge had reached maturity, she began insight meditation (vipassanā) following the course of the teaching.
Striving with diligence, she established herself in the third fruit of the path according to the sequence of the paths.
Having requested the Teacher for admission to the order, and by the Teacher's command, she entered the nunnery.
Having gone forth in the presence of the bhikkhunīs, on the seventh day she realized arhatship.
Reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:
“I was born into a noble family, possessing great wealth and vast riches;”
Endowed with beauty and form, my own daughter, born of Majjha, was sought after by princes and coveted by the sons of wealthy merchants.
She sent a messenger to my father, saying: "Give me the peerless one."
“However much this peerless daughter of yours was weighed,
I shall give eight times that amount in gold and precious gems.
Having seen the Fully Awakened One, the Supreme One, the Foremost in the World;”
Having bowed at his feet, I sat down to one side.
Out of compassion for me, Gotama taught me the Dhamma;
while seated on that very seat, I realized the third fruit.
“Then, having cut off my hair, I went forth into homelessness;
today is the seventh night since craving was severed.”—
he spoke these verses.
In that context, "in a high family" means in a most exalted Vessa family. "Possessing much wealth" means having abundant wealth and requisites such as ornaments.
"Possessing great riches" refers to the fact that there was a great amount of wealth, measured at forty crores, existing in the form of hidden hoards;
thus the construction is: "I was born in one possessing great riches. "Endowed with beauty and form" means both endowed with beauty (*vaṇṇa*) and endowed with physical form (*rūpa*).
The meaning is that she was endowed with a beautiful, radiant complexion and with the perfection of her bodily limbs, such as her garments and ornaments.
"Daughter of Majjha" means the legitimate daughter of the merchant named Majjha.
"Sought after by princes" means she was longed for by royal princes, [thinking], "How indeed might we obtain her?"
“Coveted by the sons of the merchants” means that she was likewise coveted and longed for by the merchant princes.
The princes and others sent a messenger to her father, saying, “Give Anopamā to me! Give her to me!
As for the phrase “as much as she was weighed”: the experts in marks weighed her, determining how much wealth her daughter Anopamā was worth.
The construction is: “Having been informed [of this], [she thought], ‘I shall give eight times that amount,’ and she sent a messenger to my father. The remainder is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Anopamā is finished.
6. Commentary on the Verses of the Therī Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
The verses beginning with "Buddha vīra namo tyatthu" were spoken by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
It is said that she was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara.

Having reached maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of foremost among those of long-standing seniority.

Having performed the formal act of dedication (*adhikārakamma*), having aspired for that particular status, and having practiced meritorious deeds such as giving throughout her life, she wandered among gods and humans for one hundred thousand eons.

Then, during the interval between the Blessed One Kassapa and our own Blessed One, when the world was devoid of a Buddha, she was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the eldest of five hundred female slaves. Then, at the time of the entry into the rains retreat (*vassūpanāyika*),...
The five paccekabuddhas descended from the Nandamūlaka mountain cave to Isipatana;
having wandered for alms in the city and returned to Isipatana itself, they were seen during the time of the rains-retreat seeking manual labor for the construction of huts.
Those female slaves, having encouraged both their own husbands and those of the paccekabuddhas, [provided] five [huts] complete with walkways and other requisites.

Having had huts built and having provided beds, stools, water vessels, drinking bowls, and other requisites, they obtained a promise from the Paccekabuddhas to dwell right there for three months and established a system of rotating alms-giving.
Whoever was unable to provide alms on her own turn would herself take food from her own house and give it to him. Thus...
Having looked after them for three months, when the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) arrived, he had each maidservant distribute one garment each.
There were five hundred coarse garments (*sāṭaka*). Having exchanged them, he made three robes (*ticīvara*) for the five paccekabuddhas and gave them to them.
While they were looking on, the paccekabuddhas departed through the air for Mount Gandhamādana.
Having all performed wholesome deeds for as long as they lived, they were reborn in the world of the devas.
The eldest among them, passing away from there, was reborn in the house of the chief weaver in a weavers’ village not far from Bārāṇasī.
Upon reaching maturity, she saw the five hundred Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Padumavatī; feeling great affection for them, she paid homage to them all and offered alms-food.

She gave it to them. Having finished their meal, they went back to Gandhamādana. She too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as she lived, passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans, and even before our Teacher was born, took rebirth in the city of Devadaha in the house of Mahāsuppabuddha.
Gotamī was her name, derived from her clan; she was the younger sister of Mahāmāyā.
The readers of signs also prophesied, "The children dwelling in the wombs of these two shall both become universal monarchs (cakkavatti).
When they had reached maturity, King Suddhodana performed auspicious ceremonies for both and brought them to his own home.
Later on, after our Teacher had appeared in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, he eventually arrived there.
While the Teacher was staying in the Gabled Hall near Vesālī, providing assistance to those capable of being trained,
King Suddhodana attained Arahantship beneath the white parasol and passed away into Parinibbāna.
Thereafter, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, desiring to go forth, requested the Teacher for ordination on one occasion but did not receive it.
Having had her hair cut for a second time and donned the saffron robes,
she went to Vesālī together with the female attendants of the five hundred Sakyan princes who had gone forth at the conclusion of the Teacher’s discourse on the *Kalahavivāda-sutta*. There,

having requested the Elder Ānanda to petition the Teacher on her behalf, she received both the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*) by means of the eight weighty rules (*garudhamma*).
She received it. But all the others were ordained on one side only. This is the summary here; however, this story is recorded in detail in the Pāḷi itself.
Having been thus ordained, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Teacher, paid homage to him, and stood to one side.

She stood there. Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. Having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, she devoted herself to its cultivation and before long attained Arahantship, accompanied by the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).

As for the other five hundred bhikkhunīs, at the conclusion of Nanda’s discourse, they all became possessors of the six higher knowledges. Then one day, while the Teacher was at the Great Monastery of Jetavana—
Seated in the midst of the noble assembly, he established the bhikkhunīs in their respective ranks,
placing Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī at the foremost position among the bhikkhunīs of long standing. Spending her time in the bliss of the fruits [of the path] and the bliss of Nibbāna,
she stood in gratitude and one day, after first extolling the virtues of the Teacher, declared her realization by way of manifesting the benefits of his past favors:
“Homage be to you, Hero Buddha, supreme among all beings;
you who have liberated me from suffering, as well as many other people.
All suffering has been fully understood, and its cause, craving, has been dried up.”
The Eightfold Path has been cultivated; cessation has been touched by me.
"In the past, I was mother, son, father, brother, and grandfather;
not knowing things as they truly are, I wandered through saṃsāra without finding satisfaction."
“I have indeed seen that Blessed One; this is my final physical aggregation.
The wandering in birth is exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
To one who has aroused energy, who is resolute, and who is constantly firm in effort...”
“May he see his disciples united—this is the homage to the Buddhas.
He spoke these verses: “Truly, for the welfare of many did Māyā give birth to Gotama;
he has dispelled the mass of suffering for those tormented by disease and death.”

In this context, "Buddha-hero" refers to the hero among those who have awakened to the Four Truths. For all Buddhas are called "heroes" because they have achieved victory over what was to be conquered through supreme vigor, or by virtue of accomplishing the fourfold right effort (*sammappadhāna*).

The Blessed One, however, is distinguished by his fulfillment of the perfection of vigor (*vīriya-pāramī*) and by his accomplishment of the functions of the fourfold right effort with extraordinary excellence, through his resolve upon vigor endowed with the four factors.

And because he has been perfectly established within the mental continuum of those to be trained (*vineyya*), he especially deserves to be called a "Hero" (*vīra*) due to his possession of heroic energy (*vīriya*).
"Namo tyatthu" means: let there be homage (*namakkāra*) to you.

"The supreme among all beings" means that the Blessed One is the most excellent among all beings—whether footless or otherwise—by virtue of qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*). [I shall describe] one part of that: the quality of his benefit to the Teacher.
In order to demonstrate this, she said, "He who has liberated me from suffering, and many other people as well," and while clarifying her own state of being freed from suffering,
she spoke the verse beginning with "all suffering. Then,
pointing out in part that very suffering of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) from which he had liberated her, she spoke the verse beginning with "mother, son."
In that context, "not knowing things as they truly are" means not understanding, as they really are, the causes for the process of existence and so forth.

"Wandering through saṃsāra without finding rest" means wandering through the ocean of saṃsāra—speaking thus because one wanders from existence to existence by way of successive rebirths, failing to find or obtain a footing—saying, "mother, son," and so on. From whichever existence he was the mother of this person...
The meaning is that in one existence he was his son, and in another existence he was his father or brother.
In the verse beginning with “For I have seen him,” he likewise clarifies his own state of being liberated from suffering.
Therein, “For I have seen that Blessed One” means that the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was seen by him through the vision of the supramundane Dhamma realized within himself.
I have seen this directly with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*). For he who sees the Dhamma is said to see the Blessed One. As it is said:
"Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, he sees me," and so forth. "One of aroused energy" means one whose energy is exerted.
"One of resolute mind" means one whose consciousness is directed toward Nibbāna. "Always firm in effort."
For one who has not yet attained, for the sake of attainment; for one who has attained, for the sake of its increase; at all times, with firm perseverance.
"In harmony" means those who are united by the commonality of virtue and view, and by being bound together. "Disciples" refers to those born from hearing the Teacher’s instruction;

he sees them as they truly are, thinking, "These are established on the path, these are established in the fruit. "This is the homage to the Buddhas" refers to that [homage] paid to the Teacher, who is the embodiment of the Dhamma-body.
This is the act of making the supramundane Dhamma—which constitutes the noble state of the noble disciples—evident to oneself;
it is the homage to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas and the Disciple-Buddhas, characterized by an inclination toward their qualities as they truly are.

Even in the concluding verse, “For the benefit of many indeed,” the Teacher reveals precisely his great service to the world. As for whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning, that is easily understood.
Then, on one occasion, while the Teacher was dwelling at Vesālī in the Gabled Hall of the Great Forest,
Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was dwelling in her own quarters for bhikkhunīs in Vesālī. Having walked for alms in Vesālī during the morning and finished her meal,
she spent her time in her daytime resting place enjoying the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) according to her scheduled time.
Having emerged from the attainment of fruition and reflected upon her own practice, she became joyful.
Attending to the formations of her own life-span and knowing that they were exhausted, she thought:
"What if I were now to go to the monastery, obtain the Blessed One’s permission, take leave of all my venerable elders and fellow celibates, and then return here?"
“...may she attain final Nibbāna. And just as this thought occurred to the elder nun, so too did it occur to her five hundred followers of bhikkhunīs.
Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“Once, the Lamp of the World, in the Great Forest at Vesālī;”
The Charioteer of Men dwelt in the Gabled Hall at Kusinārā.
At that time, the Jina’s maternal aunt, the bhikkhunī Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī,
resided there in the delightful city within the nunnery quarters.
“Released from the bhikkhunīs, together with five hundred of them, she had gone into seclusion.
Then this thought arose in her mind:
‘The Parinibbāna of the Buddha, or that of the foremost pair of disciples—’”
“I shall not obtain the sight of those who delight in Rāhula and Nanda—
neither after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, nor that of the pair of foremost disciples,
nor that of Mahākassapa and Nanda, nor that of Ānanda and Rāhula.”
“Having first relinquished the formative forces of life,
may I go to Nibbāna with the permission of the Great Seer, the Lord of the World.
Likewise, such was the thought conceived by the five hundred bhikkhunīs.”
Khemā and the others also thought this very same thing:
“At that time there was an earthquake, and the divine drums resounded;
the deities dwelling in their abodes were oppressed by grief.”
Lamenting most piteously, they shed tears there;
those nun-friends approached Gotamī,
prostrated with their heads at her feet, and spoke these words:
There, having been sprinkled with drops of water, Māyā’s mother said in private:
“The earth has trembled and shaken, the celestial drums have resounded, and lamentations are heard; for what reason, surely, is Gotamī?”
Then she told them everything exactly as she had reflected upon it;
they all likewise spoke exactly as they had reflected upon it:
“If it pleases you, Noble Lady, that Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss;”
“We shall all attain Nibbāna together, O virtuous ones, with the Buddha’s permission.
Having gone forth together from both home and existence,
we shall go together to Nibbāna, the supreme state.”
“‘What shall I say to those who are departing for Nibbāna?’— saying this,
she then went forth from the nunnery together with them all.
‘May the deities who dwell in the monastery forgive me.’”
"This is my last sight of the bhikkhunīs' dwelling.
I shall go to that unconditioned state where there is neither old age nor death, no meeting with those who are unpleasant, and no separation from those who are dear."
“Having heard those words from the mouth of the Sugata, those who were not yet free from passion lamented, overwhelmed by grief: ‘Alas! How small is our merit!
The dwelling place of the nuns is empty; it has become desolate without them.’”
Like stars at dawn, the sons of the Conqueror are no longer seen.
"Gotamī goes to Nibbāna together with five hundred [disciples],
just as the Ganges with its five hundred tributaries flows into the ocean."
“Seeing them traveling along the road, faithful female lay devotees came out from their homes, prostrated at their feet, and said this:
‘Be gracious, O one of great wealth! You have left us behind, we who are without a protector.’”
Unable to attain Nibbāna through her [absence], they lamented out of their longing for her.
To dispel their sorrow, he spoke these sweet words:
"Enough with weeping, my children; today is a time for laughter."
“Suffering has been fully understood by me; the cause of suffering has been abandoned;
cessation has been realized by me, and the path has also been well-cultivated.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been accomplished.”
Heavy is the burden left behind; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home to the homeless life—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.
“As long as the Buddha and his True Dharma remain undiminished, it is time for me to attain Nibbāna;
do not grieve for me, my little daughter.
Koṇḍañña, Ānanda, Nanda, and the others remain, and Rāhula is a Victor.”
The Saṅgha is happy and united, while the heretics have been struck down.
The glory of the Okkāka lineage has risen high, crushing Māra.
Is this not now the time for me, my little son, to attain Nibbāna?
“From long ago, that which I have desired is fulfilled today;
this is the time for the drum of joy—why do you weep, my children?
If there is compassion for me, if there is gratitude;”
For the sake of the endurance of the true Dhamma, exert all firm energy.
“The Fully Awakened One granted the going-forth to Thīna when he was entreated by me;
therefore, just as I have rejoiced, so do you likewise follow that path.”
Having thus instructed them and being escorted by the bhikkhunīs, she approached the Buddha, paid homage, and spoke these words:
“O Sugata, I am your mother; and you, O Hero, are my father.”
“O Lord who grants the bliss of the true Dhamma, I was born from you, Gotama.
‘This physical body of yours, O Sugata, was nurtured by me;
but the blameless Dhamma-body has been nurtured by you.’”
“For a moment you were a monk for me, and milk was drunk by you from me;
but by you, I have been made to drink the milk of the Dhamma, which is peaceful and ultimate.
O Great Sage, you are free from debt to me regarding my protection from bondage.”
Women who desire sons obtain such a son through their prayer:
"O son, she who was the mother of Mandhātā and other noble kings was submerged in the ocean of existence;
by you, she has been delivered across the sea of becoming."
“‘The King’s mother, the chief queen’—such a name is easy for women to obtain;
but the name ‘Mother of the Buddha,’ that is exceedingly rare.
And yet, O Great Hero, you have obtained that very thing through my aspiration.”
Whether small or great, all that has been filled by me.
"I wish to attain final Nibbāna, leaving behind this physical body;
grant me your permission, O Hero, Leader who has made an end of suffering."
“Stretch out your feet, which are as soft as lotuses and covered with the wheel-marks, the ankusha-sign, the banner, and the calluses; I shall pay homage to you, O most excellent son.
Make your body, which resembles a heap of gold, visible.”
“Having well observed your body, O Leader, I go to peace.
The Conqueror showed his mother his body, endowed with the thirty-two marks, adorned with beautiful radiance, like the sun at dawn.
“Resembling a full-blown lotus, with the radiance of the rising sun,
and with soles marked by the wheel— thereupon she prostrated herself with her head.
‘I bow to the Sun among men, the banner of the Solar dynasty.’”
"At my final death, I shall not see you again.
O Foremost One in the World, women are considered the source of all faults.
If there is any fault in me, forgive me, O Compassionate One."
“I repeatedly entreated you for the going forth of women;
if there is any fault in that on my part, O Bull among Men, may you forgive it.
By your permission, O Hero, the bhikkhunīs have been instructed by me.”
“If there is anything ill-spoken therein, forgive it, O Lord of Forgiveness.
For what need is there for forgiveness toward one who is not capable of forgiving, even in one adorned with virtues?
What further can I say to you, who are departing for Nibbāna?”
“When my pure and complete community of monks was capable of escaping from this world,
the crescent moon of the Dhamma appeared at dawn, seeing those who had fallen into calamity.
Then the other bhikkhunīs followed the Supreme Victor, as stars follow the moon to Mount Sumeru.”
Having circumambulated him and bowed at his feet, she stood gazing intently into his face:
“Never before have I been satiated by the sight of you, nor has my ear been satiated by your speech.
My mind alone, having attained you, finds satisfaction through the flavor of the Dhamma.”
“O you who possess the skill of a musician, as you play amidst the assembly,
those who shall behold your face are truly fortunate, O bull among men. Your fingers are long,
your nails are copper-colored, and your beautiful heels are broad.”
“Those who shall bow at your feet, O bearer of virtues, they too are fortunate.
Those whose sweet, joyful, faultless,
and beneficial words are heard, they too are fortunate, O supreme among men.”
“Fortunate am I, O Great Hero, intent upon worshipping your feet,
having crossed the wilderness of saṃsāra through the well-spoken words of the Glorious One. Then,
having made this proclamation, she who was firm in her vows also addressed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having paid homage to Rāhula and Ānanda, he spoke these words:
"In this body, which is like the lair of a venomous serpent,
a dwelling place for disease, one should become disenchanted with this mass of suffering that has aging and death as its domain."
“In this world strewn with various stains of defilement, dependent on others, and devoid of agency, I desire to attain extinction through that [path]. Grant me your permission, my sons.
Nanda and the auspicious Rāhula shall be free from sorrow and free from taints.”
Firmly established in immovable stability, they reflected upon the nature of phenomena:
"Shame on the conditioned! It is fickle, pithless like a plantain tree, resembling an illusion or a mirage—fleeting and unstable."
“Since even this Gotamī, the maternal aunt of the Conqueror and the nurse of the Buddha,
must meet her end— how impermanent are all conditioned things!
And at that time Ānanda was still a learner, overcome with grief, yet dearly beloved by the Conqueror.”
Making his tears fall there, he lamented piteously: “Alas!
Gotamī goes to peace; surely the Buddha too will go to extinction.
He will depart before long, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.”
To Ānanda, who was thus lamenting, Gotamī said:
“O son, as deep as the ocean, you are devoted to attending upon the Buddha.
It is not fitting for you to grieve, my son, when this time for joy has arrived.”
“Nirvana, my son, has become my refuge through you.
“Father, it was at your request that we were permitted to go forth;
do not be despondent, my son, for your exertion has borne fruit.”
“That state which was not seen even by the ancient teachers of other sects has been realized by these delicate girls, seven years of age.
O protectors of the Buddha’s teaching, this is your final sight.”
“Go there, my son, where once gone one is no longer seen.
“Once, while teaching the Dhamma, the Leader of the World threw down [a handful of earth];
at that time, out of compassion, I spoke these words of aspiration:”
“Live long, O Great Hero; remain for an eon, O Great Sage!
For the welfare of the whole world, be one who is free from aging and death.
To me, who spoke thus, the Buddha said this:
“Buddhas are not to be venerated in the manner that you venerate them, Gotamī.
How indeed, O All-Knowing One, are the Tathāgatas to be venerated?
How are the Buddhas not to be venerated? Tell me this when I ask you.”
“Behold these disciples who are harmonious, diligent in energy, resolute, and always firm in their exertion— this is the homage paid to the Buddhas.
Then, having gone to my dwelling, I reflected all alone:”
The Protector, who has reached the end of the three worlds, silenced the assembled multitude:
“Come now, I shall attain final Nibbāna; let me not see misfortune.
Having thought thus, he beheld the Seventh Sage.
“I informed the Leader of the time for my final Nibbāna;
then he gave his consent, saying, ‘Know the time yourself, Gotamī.
My defilements have been burnt away; all states of existence have been uprooted.”
Like a snake that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
"How welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Buddha!
The three knowledges have been attained, and the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled."
“The four analytical knowledges and these eight liberations have been realized, along with the six direct knowledges; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Those fools who fell into doubt regarding the penetration of the Dhamma—”
To abandon their wrong views, Gotamī displayed her supernormal powers.
Then, having prostrated before the Sambuddha and leaping into the sky,
Gotamī, with the Buddha’s permission, displayed manifold miracles.
“Being one, she became many; likewise, being many, she became one.
She appeared and disappeared; she passed through walls and through mountains.
Moving without obstruction, she even sank into the earth.”
He walked upon the earth as if on water that does not wet;
then, like a bird in the sky, he moved through the air cross-legged.
He exercised mastery over his body as far as the abode of Brahmā.
“Making Mount Sineru his staff and the great earth his parasol,
he walked back and forth in the sky, having overturned it root and all.
At the time of six sunrises, he made the world smoky.”
Like the world at the end of an aeon, she filled it with a mass of flames.
Between the great Mucalinda mountain and the base of Mount Meru,
she seized everything with a single fist, as if it were a mustard seed.
“He covered the maker of light along with the maker of night with the tip of his finger;
he bore thousands of moons and suns like a garland.
He held the waters of the four oceans with a single hand.”
Having the appearance of a cloud at the end of an eon, you let fall a great rain.
She measured out a wheel-turning monarch together with his retinue upon the surface of the sky;
she displayed a garuḍa, an elephant, and a lion roaring aloud.
“Having manifested herself alone as an immeasurable host of bhikkhunīs,
and then making them vanish again, she spoke to the Sage alone:
‘O Great Hero, your maternal aunt is here, carrying out your teaching.’”
"Having attained her own goal, she bowed at the feet of the One with Vision.
Having displayed various miraculous powers and descended from the sky,
she paid homage to the Lamp of the World and sat down to one side."
“I am one hundred and twenty years of age, O Great Sage;
enough of this, O Hero, I shall attain Nibbāna, O Leader.
Then the entire assembly, utterly amazed, stood with palms joined in reverence.
“O Avocati, how was it? You possessed incomparable psychic power and prowess.
‘The Victor named Padumuttara, the eye-seer regarding all phenomena, arose as the Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.’”
“At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī into a family of ministers,
one endowed with every kind of assistance, prosperous, flourishing, and possessing great wealth. Once,
accompanied by my father and preceded by a retinue of female slaves...”
Accompanied by a great retinue, he approached that Bull among Men—
[who was] raining down the stainless cloud of Dhamma like Vāsava,
and blazing with a web of rays like the autumnal sun.
“Having seen him and gladdened his heart, and having heard his well-spoken words,
the Leader of Men placed his maternal aunt among the foremost of bhikkhunīs.
Having heard this and having given a great gift for seven days to that Tathāgata,”
"To the Bull among Men together with his Saṅgha, I offered many requisites.
Prostrating at the soles of his feet, I aspired for that very state.
Then, in the midst of the great assembly, the Seventh Sage spoke:"
“I shall proclaim the praise of her who fed the Leader of the World together with the Saṅgha for seven days; listen to me as I speak.
A hundred thousand aeons ago, one born of the Okkāka clan—”
One named Gotama by clan will become a teacher in the world.
Among his teachings, there will be a legitimate daughter, fashioned by the Dhamma,
a female disciple of the Teacher named Gotamī.
“This woman, the maternal aunt of that Buddha,
who has sustained his life, shall attain preeminence among the bhikkhunīs of long standing.
Having heard this and rejoiced, she then [served] the Conqueror for as long as she lived.
Having been sustained by these conditions, I then passed away.
Reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas,
where every desire is fulfilled, I excelled others in ten respects.
“By means of forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles;
by life-span, beauty, happiness, and fame;
and likewise by sovereignty, having attained these, I shine forth.”
There, I was the beloved chief queen of the Lord of the Immortals.
Wandering through saṃsāra, driven by the wind of karma,
I was born in the territory of King Kāsi, in the village of Dāsa.
“At that time, fifteen hundred minus one lived there;
I was the wife of the eldest among them all.
Five hundred Self-Awakened Ones entered the village for alms.”
Seeing them, I was delighted along with all the women.
"Having formed a group, we all attended upon him for four months;
having given him the three robes, we, together with our husbands, wandered through the cycle of existence."
“Having passed away from there, we all went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven;
and now, in our final existence, we have been born in the city of Devadaha.
My father is Añjana-Sakka, and my mother is Sulakkhaṇā.”
Then, having gone to Kapilavatthu, she entered the house of Suddhodana.
"The others, born in the Sakya clan, went to the houses of the Sakyans;
I alone was distinguished among them all, for I became the nurse of the Conqueror."
“My son went forth from home and became a Buddha, a leader;
later, having gone forth together with five hundred wise Sākiyan women, I too touched the bliss of peace.”
"In a previous birth, they were our masters.
Together with us, they performed meritorious deeds and established great assemblies;
favored by the Sugata, they attained arahantship."
Then the other bhikkhunīs ascended into the vault of the sky;
like a cluster of stars, those of great psychic power shone forth.
They displayed manifold miracles, just like a variety of ornaments worn upon the body.
Like a well-trained smith with gold that is workable,
having displayed many diverse miracles and having satisfied the eminent debater,
the Sage, together with his assembly, at that time—
Having ascended into the sky and paid homage to the Seventh Sage,
they were granted permission by the Leader of Men and sat down in their respective places.
“Gautamī has long been compassionate toward us all,” [said they].
“Vāsitā has reached the destruction of the taints through your merits.
‘Our defilements have been incinerated; all states of existence have been uprooted.
Like a nāga who has severed its bonds, we dwell free from taints.’”
“Welcome indeed to us in the presence of the Best of Buddhas!
The three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical insights and these eight liberations—”
The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
We are masters of the supernormal powers, of the divine ear-element, and we are masters of the knowledge of others’ minds, O Great Sage.
“We know our former abodes, and the divine eye is purified;
all taints are utterly exhausted, so there is now no further becoming.
In the meaning, the Dhamma, the phrasing, and the inspired eloquence, we possess clear knowledge.”
“Knowledge has arisen within us, O Great Hero, in your presence.
We have served you with hearts full of loving-kindness, O Leader;
grant permission for all of us to attain Nibbāna, O Great Sage.”
“‘We shall attain Nibbāna’—what more shall I say to you who speak thus?
‘Now is the time for you,’ so the Victor declared.
Then those bhikkhunīs, headed by Gotamī, [approached] the Victor.”
Having paid homage, they rose from their seats and departed.
Together with a great multitude of people, that hero, the Leader of the World,
traveled as far as Mātuccha-yāvakoṭṭhaka.
“Then Gotamī, together with all those women, fell at the feet of the Kinsman of the World, performing her final salutation.
‘This is my last sight of the Lord of the World,’ she thought.”
“Never again shall I behold your face, which has the form of the Deathless.
O Hero, my prostration at your most delicate feet, O Foremost One in the World, shall not touch them today; I am going to Nibbāna.”
“What is the use of this form of yours, which is exactly as it appears in the present life?
All this is merely conditioned, providing no consolation and being but temporary.
Having said this, she went together with them to her own nunnery.
Folding his legs in the half-lotus posture, he sat upon the supreme seat. Then,
the female lay devotees there, who were devoted to the Buddha’s teaching,
having heard news of him, approached to pay homage at his feet.
“Beating their breasts, like creepers whose roots have been severed,
they fell to the ground, wailing piteous cries, overcome by grief.
‘O Lord who grants refuge, do not depart for Nibbāna, leaving us behind!’”
Having prostrated themselves, they all entreated with their heads bowed:
“Among those women, there was a female lay disciple named Saddhāpaññā who was most diligent in her striving;
as she was wiping his head, she spoke these words.”
“Enough, my sons, with despondency, which follows the snares of Māra;
everything conditioned is impermanent, ends in separation, and is unstable.
Then, having dismissed them, she attained the first sublime jhāna.”
He entered the second and the third, and the fourth.
He entered the sphere of infinite space and likewise the sphere of infinite consciousness,
as well as the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, each in its proper order.
“Gotamī entered the meditative absorptions in reverse order,
from the first absorption down to the fourth.
Then, having emerged from them, she attained final Nibbāna, like a lamp going out, free from all taints.”
There was a great earthquake, and lightning flashed from the sky.
The drums resounded, and the deities lamented;
a rain of flowers fell from the heavens, showering down upon the earth.
“Even Meru, the king of mountains, trembled like an actor on the stage;
and the ocean, with its mournful roar, was exceedingly distressed by grief.
At that moment, the devas, nāgas, asuras, and Brahmās were all filled with agitation.”
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned things, for they have come to this dissolution.
Those who surrounded me, carrying out the Teacher’s instruction— even those three—
have attained final peace through non-clinging, like extinguished lamps.”
“Alas, unions end in separation! Alas, all that is conditioned is impermanent!
Alas, life ends in destruction!”—such was his lamentation.
Then the gods and Brahmā [realized] the conformity with the ways of the world.
Having approached the seventh of the Sages, they acted in accordance with the occasion.
Then the Teacher addressed Ānanda, that ocean of learning:
"Go, Ānanda, announce the passing away of the Bhikkhus' mother."
“Then Ānanda, joyless and with eyes full of tears,
spoke in a hoarse voice: ‘Let the bhikkhus assemble from the east,
the south, the west, and from the vicinity of the north.’”
“Listen to my words, O monks, disciples of the Sugata:
‘Gautamī, who with great effort nourished the body of the Sage until his final passing,
has gone to peace, like a star at the rising of the sun.’”
“Even the Mother of the Buddha, having established her conceptual designation,
has gone to that destination where even the Leader with his five eyes cannot see a path.
Whoever has faith in the Sugata, and whoever is dear to the Great Sage— ”
"Let the Well-Gone One’s disciple pay honor to the Mother of the Buddha.
Hearing this, even from afar, the bhikkhus came quickly—
some through the power of the Buddha, others being skilled in supernormal powers.
“In a most delightful and excellent gabled chamber, beautiful and made entirely of gold,
they placed a couch where Gotamī lay asleep.
The four World-Protectors supported her with their shoulders.”
The remaining deities, headed by Sakka, gathered together in the gabled halls.
All those gabled halls numbered five hundred;
they were the color of the autumnal sun and were indeed fashioned by Vissakamma.
“All those bhikkhunīs had been lying on couches;
having ascended the shoulders of the gods, they were led away one after another.
The surface of the sky was completely covered by a canopy.”
The moon and sun, marked with stars, were made of gold.
Many banners were raised aloft, spread with floral canopies;
lotuses reached up into the sky, while flowers sprouted from the earth.
“The moon and sun are visible, and the stars are blazing;
yet even when the sun has reached the meridian, it does not heat as much as the moon.
The gods [are adorned] with divine fragrances and with sweet-smelling garlands.”
They honored her with instrumental music, dances, and choral performances.
"The nāgas, asuras, and brahmas, according to their capacity and according to their strength,
paid homage to the Mother of the Buddha as she was being carried forth, now extinguished."
“All have been led forward, extinguished by the essence of the Sugata;
Gotamī is led behind, honored as the nourisher of the Buddha.
Before her go gods and humans, along with nāgas, asuras, and brahmās.”
Later, the Buddha, accompanied by his disciple, went to pay homage to his mother.
"The parinibbāna of the Buddha was not like this;
the parinibbāna of Gotamī was truly extraordinary."
“Monks, the Buddha did not lament for the Nibbāna of the Buddha;
likewise, Sāriputta and the others did not lament for the Nibbāna of Gotama the Buddha.
Having prepared funeral pyres made entirely of fragrant scents, they—”
They burned them there, scattering them with fragrant powders.
"The remaining portions were consumed by fire, and the bones alone remained entirely behind.
Then Ānanda spoke these words, which were capable of stirring deep spiritual urgency.
“Gotamī has met her end, and her body shall be cremated;
before long, the meeting with the Buddha’s nibbāna will take place.
Then, those relics of Gotamī that had been placed in her bowl—”
Urged by the Buddha, Ānanda offered them to the Protector.
Taking them up with his hand, the Seventh Sage said:
"Just as when a great, sturdy tree stands firm..."
“That great pillar which was destined to crumble through impermanence—
so too has Gotamī passed away, the leader of the community of bhikkhunīs. Oh,
what a marvel for me, that even my mother has attained final Nibbāna!”
When only the physical body remains, there is no sorrow or lamentation.
There is no need to grieve for others who have crossed the ocean of saṃsāra;
they have avoided all torment, become cooled, and attained perfect peace.
“You are wise and possessed of great wisdom, as well as broad wisdom;
you are one of long standing among the bhikkhunīs—thus should you be remembered, O bhikkhus.
You were a master of the supernormal powers and possessed of the divine ear-element.”
Gotamī had mastery over the knowledge of the minds of others.
She recollected her past lives and purified her divine eye;
all taints were utterly destroyed, and for her there is no further becoming.
“Regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the etymologies, and likewise regarding inspired eloquence—his knowledge was perfectly pure; therefore, she is not to be grieved for.
Like a blazing fire struck by an iron bar...”
Just as the destination of one who has gradually attained peace is not known,
so too for those who are rightly liberated, who have crossed over the flood of the bonds of sensual desire—
there is no way to describe their destination, for they have reached unshakable bliss.
“Therefore, be islands unto yourselves, with mindfulness as your domain;
having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, you shall make an end of suffering.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.
7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Gutta The verses beginning with “Gutta, for what purpose did you go forth? belong to the elder nun Gutta.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation in various states of existence, gradually gathered the requisites for emancipation.

Having offered [the sacrifice], those whose roots of merit were fully ripened continued to wander only among happy destinies until, in this present age of a Buddha, they were reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī;

her name was Gutta-Tissa. Having reached the age of discretion, impelled by the perfection of her spiritual predispositions (*upanissaya*), she felt revulsion for the household life and, having obtained permission from her parents, [approached] Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
She went forth. Having gone forth, as she applied herself to meditation by establishing insight, her mind—due to long-standing habituation—ran after external objects and failed to become one-pointed.

Seeing this, the Teacher, wishing to assist her, remained seated in his fragrant cell and, pervading it with radiance, manifested himself as if sitting in the air near her. Addressing her with this instruction:
“Son, for whatever purpose you have gone forth, having abandoned your son and even your beloved wealth—cultivate that very purpose;
do not fall under the sway of the mind.
Deceived by the mind, beings take delight in the realm of Māra.”
“Fools, lacking true knowledge, run on through the saṃsāra of many births.
Sensual desire, ill will, the view of a self-existent body,
adherence to rules and observances, and doubt as the fifth.”
“Having abandoned these fetters that lead to the lower realms, O bhikkhunī,
you shall not come back here again.
Having avoided passion, conceit, ignorance, and restlessness;”
“Having severed the fetters, you will make an end of suffering.
Having exhausted the cycle of birth and fully understood renewed existence,
you will wander, free from craving and at peace, in this very life.”— with these verses he spoke.
In this context, "cultivate that very thing" means for the sake of that goal—the parinibbāna of the defilements and the parinibbāna of the aggregates.

Having abandoned children, wealth, and those dear ones—the circle of relatives who are worthy of affection—as well as the mass of possessions, the going forth in my teaching and the living of the holy life (brahmacariya) are desired; you should cultivate and accomplish that very thing.
"Do not fall under the power of the mind" means: do not go under the sway of that deceptive mind which has long been nourished by objects such as forms and so forth.
For this mind is like an illusion; deceived by it, blind worldlings follow the power of Māra and do not transcend saṃsāra. Therefore it is said: "Deceived by the mind," and so forth.
"These are fetters" refers to those five things previously mentioned—namely, "sensual desire and ill will"—in the sense of being bonds.

“Having abandoned the fetters”: having completely severed them by means of the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). “Bhikkhunī” is an address to her. “Leading to the lower realm” (*oram-bhāgamanīya*):
they are beneficial and helpful for human life in the lower portion, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), below the form and formless realms, because they serve as conditions for rebirth there.
The letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*). [An alternative reading is] “leading to the lower region” (*oram-āgamanīya*).

The Pāli reads *pāḷi*, which has this meaning. "You shall not come back again" (*na idaṃ punar ehi*) means that, through the abandoning of the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*), you will not return to this state of sensual desire—that is, to existence in the sense-sphere realm (*kāma-bhava*)—by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The letter *r* serves as a phonetic euphonic junction (*padasandhikara*).
Alternatively, the Pāli reads *ittham*; the meaning is simply "this state of being" (*itthattaṃ*), namely, existence in the sense-sphere realm.
"Lust" refers to lust for the fine-material realm (*rūparāga*) and lust for the immaterial realm (*arūparāga*). "Pride" refers to the pride abandoned by the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
The same method applies here to "ignorance" (*avijjā*) and "restlessness" (*uddhacca*). "Having avoided" means having suppressed them through insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having severed the fetters" means having completely eradicated these five higher fetters, beginning with lust for the fine-material realm, by means of the path of Arahantship (*arahattamagga*).
"You shall make an end of suffering" means you will reach the limit, the conclusion, of all the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"Having exhausted the cycle of birth" means having brought to an end the occurrence of *saṃsāra* together with its root, which is birth. "Free from hunger" means free from craving (*taṇhā*). "Peaceful" means peaceful through the complete subsiding of all defilements (*kilesa*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
When the Teacher had spoken these verses, at the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Nun attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Having attained [this state], the Blessed One spoke these verses according to his own established custom of uttering inspired utterances (*udāna*). For that very reason, they became known as the verses of the Elder Nun.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Gutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Vijayā.
"Three times," etc., are verses by the Elder Nun Vijayā. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas;
accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, her roots of merit gradually matured.
Wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a certain noble family in Rājagaha.
Having reached the age of discretion, she became a childhood friend of the Elder Nun Khemā during their time as householders.
Upon hearing that she had gone forth, [the friend] thought, "If even the king’s chief queen has gone forth, how much more so should I?
Desiring to go forth herself, she approached the Elder Nun Khemā. Knowing her intention, the Elder taught her the Dhamma accordingly.
Just as her mind became agitated by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), she developed deep faith in the Teaching (*sāsana*).
Having heard that Dhamma, she was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and, having gained faith, requested ordination. The Elder Nun ordained her.

Having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, she established insight (*vipassanā*); and because of her perfection of causes, before long, together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), [she attained the fruits of the path].
Having attained arahantship and reflecting upon her own practice,
she uttered this inspired utterance: “Four times and five times I went forth from my dwelling,
Failing to find peace of mind, for I had no mastery over my heart.”
“Having approached a bhikkhunī, I questioned her respectfully;
she taught me the Dhamma, including the elements and the sense-bases.
[She taught] the four noble truths, the faculties, and the powers.”
The factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path for the attainment of the supreme goal.
Having heard his words and carrying out his instruction,
during the first watch of the night, I recollected my previous births.
“In the middle watch of the night, I purified the divine eye;
in the final watch of the night, I shattered the mass of darkness.
And at that time, having suffused my body with rapture and bliss, I dwelt therein.”
"On the seventh day I stretched out my foot, having shattered the mass of darkness"—
thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, "the bhikkhunī" refers to the Elder Nun Khemā.
"Bojjhaṅga-aṭṭhaṅgika-maggaṃ" means the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path. "Uttamatthassa pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining or reaching arahantship or Nibbāna itself.

"Pītisukhena" means by means of the joy and happiness included within the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti). "Kāyaṃ" refers to the mental body associated with that [state], and by extension, the physical body as well.
"Pharitvā" means having touched or pervaded. [This occurs] on the seventh step.
"I stretched out my feet" means that on the seventh day after I began the practice of insight (vipassanā), I broke my cross-legged posture and stretched out my feet.
How so? Having shattered the mass of darkness—that mass of delusion never before shattered—with the sword of the knowledge of the supreme path (aggamagga-ñāṇa).
The rest is exactly as described below.
The commentary on the *Vijayā Therīgāthā* is finished.
The commentary on the *Chakkanipāta* (The Section of Six) is finished.
7. The *Sattakanipāta* (The Section of Seven).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Uttarā: "Having taken up the pestles," etc., are the verses of the elder nun Uttarā.
She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome kamma conducive to liberation in various states of existence, gradually [progressed].

Having cultivated roots of merit, accumulated the requisites for liberation, and brought to maturity those qualities conducive to the ripening of deliverance, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in a certain noble family in Sāvatthī.
Having received the name Uttarā and gradually attained the age of discretion, she approached the presence of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā. The Elder Nun—
He preached the Dhamma to her. Having heard the Dhamma, she became deeply moved by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and, having gained great faith in the Teaching, she went forth.
Having gone forth and performed the preliminary duties, she established insight meditation in the presence of the elder nun Paṭācārā and devoted herself to its cultivation;
and because she was endowed with the necessary potential and her faculties had reached full maturity, before long—
Having made insight his primary pursuit, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having reached Arahantship, however, and reflecting upon his own course of practice, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):
“Taking up pestles, the young men pound the grain;”
“While supporting their wives and children, young men acquire wealth.
Strive in the teaching of the Buddha, doing that for which one does not later regret;
having quickly washed your feet, sit down to one side.”
“Having established the mind, one-pointed and well-concentrated,
examine conditioned phenomena as ‘other,’ and not as ‘self.
Having heard those words of hers, the instruction of Paṭācārā, I—
Having washed my feet, I sat down to one side.
During the first watch of the night, I recollected my past births;
during the middle watch of the night, I purified my divine eye.
“In the last watch of the night, I shattered the mass of darkness;
having attained the threefold knowledge, I have arisen—your instruction has been fulfilled.
Just as the gods of the Thirty-three [rejoice] over Sakka, who is undefeated in battle...”
“Placing them before me, I shall dwell, a possessor of the threefold knowledge, free from taints”—these verses he spoke.
Therein, “having established the mind” means having established the mind of meditation upon the subject of meditation. How? Single-pointedly.
"Examine it well-composed" means: examine the practice; contemplate the three characteristics—namely, that formations are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
This was spoken by way of exhortation and instruction for herself and for other elder nuns and so forth at the time of giving counsel.
"The instruction of the Elder Paṭācārā" refers to the Elder Paṭācārā.
The instruction. Alternatively, there is also the reading: “The teaching for Paṭācārā.
Then, “she rose up” means that after she had attained the state of one possessing the three knowledges (tevijjā), she rose from her seat.
This elder nun also, one day, having refined her meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) in the presence of the elder nun Paṭācārā, entered her own dwelling place and sat cross-legged.

Having folded his legs crosswise, he sat down. Having made the firm resolve, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging," he began the practice of contemplation.

Gradually bringing insight (vipassanā) to its peak, he attained Arahantship—accompanied by the super-knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—according to the sequence of the paths, and [reviewed it] with the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge.
Having uttered these verses in exultation, thinking, "Now my task is accomplished," as she was about to set out, she extended her feet at the time of dawn.
Then, when the night had properly brightened, she approached the Elder Nun and recited these verses in response.
Therefore it is said: "Your instruction has been carried out," and so forth. The rest is all according to the method explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Uttarā is finished. 2.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Cālā begins with the words "Having established mindfulness," etc. This nun also had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas.

Having accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) throughout various existences, she was reborn in this current era of a Buddha’s appearance in the village of Nālaka among the Magadhans, in the womb of the Brahmin woman Rūpasārī.
On the day her name was given, they named her Cālā; her younger sister was named Upacālā, and the youngest of them all was named Sīsūpacālā. These...
Tissa also had three younger sisters, and the sons of these three also had this same name.
It is with reference to them that it is said in the *Theragāthā*: “Cāla, Upacāla, and Sīsūpacāla.
Now, when these three sisters heard that “the Dhammasenāpati has gone forth,” they thought, “Surely he is not an ordinary man.”
"This is the Dhamma and Vinaya; this is no inferior going-forth where our noble lady has gone forth.
Having thus become inspired and filled with intense zeal, they abandoned their kinsmen and attendants who were weeping with tearful faces and went forth.
Having gone forth, by striving and exerting themselves, they attained arahantship before long. Having reached arahantship, they dwelt in the bliss of Nibbāna and the bliss of the fruit.

Among them, one day after her meal, having returned from her almsround, the nun Cālā entered the Blind Men’s Grove and sat down for her midday rest. Then Māra approached her and enticed her with sensual pleasures. It is with reference to this that it is said in the Sutta:
“Then the nun Cālā, having dressed in the morning and taken her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal, having returned from her almsround, she went to the Blind Men’s Grove...”
He approached for his midday rest. Having plunged deep into the Andhavana forest, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Cālā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Cālā.
While [the Buddha] was seated for his midday rest in the Andhavana forest, Māra approached him, desiring to interrupt his practice of the holy life, and asked, "For whom have you shaved your head?

and so forth. Then, having proclaimed the virtues of the Teacher and the liberating nature of the Dhamma, he announced the Teacher's transcendence of Māra’s domain by demonstrating that his own task was accomplished. Having heard this—
Māra, suffering and dejected, vanished right there. Then she, reciting as an inspired utterance (*udāna*) the verses spoken by herself and by Māra, said:
“Having established mindfulness, the bhikkhunī with developed faculties penetrated the peaceful state, the bliss of the subsiding of conditioned formations.”
“For whose sake have you shaved your head?
You appear like a female ascetic, yet you do not approve of other sects. Why do you wander about so bewildered?
Outside of this [teaching], there are other sects that rely upon dogmatic views.”
They do not understand the Dhamma; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.
"There is one born in the Sakyan clan, a Buddha, a peerless person;
he has taught me the Dhamma that transcends all views."
“Suffering, the origin of suffering, and the overcoming of suffering,
as well as the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering—
having heard his words, I dwelt delighted in his teaching.”
The threefold knowledge has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!
She spoke these verses.

Therein, "having established mindfulness" means having properly established mindfulness regarding the body and so forth by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), through the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.
"A bhikkhunī" refers to herself. "One whose faculties are developed" means...
Through the cultivation of the Noble Path, he possessed the five faculties beginning with faith that have been developed. He penetrated the peaceful state;

that is, through the penetration of direct realization, he realized the peaceful state of Nibbāna. It is the "subsiding of all formations" because it is the cause for the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena.
It is "bliss" because it is ultimate bliss.
The verse beginning with “Kaṃ nu uddissa” was spoken by Māra. Its summary meaning is as follows:

In this world there are many systems and many teachers who proclaim them—namely, the founders of various sects. With whom among these do you have in mind that you have shaven your head, that you are one whose hair is cut off?
Not only have you shaven your head, but you also appear like an ascetic (samaṇī) because of wearing the yellow robe (kāsāva).
"And you do not approve of the heretics": you do not approve of those various other systems among the heretics, who serve as mirrors for ascetics, wanderers, and the like.

"Why do you wander in confusion? means: what indeed is this, that having abandoned the straight path to Nibbāna established by the heretics, you now follow a wrong path that leads only to the present life; thus you wander and roam about, utterly deluded?
Having heard this, the Elder Nun, rebuking him by way of giving a reply, said: "Outside of this," and so forth.
In that context, "heretics outside of this" refers to those such as the Kuṭīsakas and Bahukāras who are outside of this teaching of the Fully Enlightened One.
For they are called "heretics" (pāsaṇḍā) because they cast and set snares—namely the snare of craving and the snare of views—for sentient beings. Therefore he said:
“Dependent upon views”: having approached and become dependent on the positions of eternalist views; the meaning is that they have adopted those positions of views.
And to the extent that they are dependent upon views, to that same extent they are dependent upon sectarian dogmas (*pāsaṇḍa*). “They do not understand the Dhamma”:
those sectarians who are dependent upon the positions of eternalist views [think], “This process proceeds in this way.”

They do not understand even the phenomenon of occurrence as it truly is. "They are not skilled in the Dhamma" means they are unskilled even in the phenomenon of cessation, [not knowing] "this is cessation;
it ceases in this way. For they are deluded even regarding the path of the phenomenon of occurrence, so how much more so regarding the phenomenon of cessation?

Having thus demonstrated the lack of deliverance in the doctrines of the various sects, he now spoke the words beginning with “There is one born in the Sakyan clan” in order to answer the question, “For whom, then, have you shaved your head?
Therein, “the surmounting of views” refers to the means for surmounting all views—the unraveling of the net of views. The rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Cālā is finished. 3.

Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Upacālā "Endowed with mindfulness," etc., are the verses of the Elder Nun Upacālā. The story of her life is exactly as that of the Elder Nun Cālā has been told. For she too, having gone forth like Cālā, established insight, and attained Arahantship, uttered this inspired utterance:
“Mindful and possessed of vision, the bhikkhunī with developed faculties has penetrated the state of peace, which is not frequented by base men.
Thus he spoke this verse.

In this context, "possessing mindfulness" means endowed with mindfulness; having been possessed of supreme mindfulness and circumspection in the preliminary stage, she subsequently becomes endowed with the highest mindfulness through the attainment of the fullness of mindfulness resulting from the cultivation of the Noble Path—this is the meaning.
"Possessing vision" means endowed with the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*), that is, with the noble wisdom that, from the outset, leads to arising and passing away.
Having become endowed with penetrative wisdom, it is said that she was possessed of the supreme eye of wisdom through the attainment of the fullness of insight (*paññā*).
"Practiced by men who are not base" means practiced by noble beings, the supreme persons, the Arahants, such as the Buddha and others.
The verse beginning, "Why do you not approve of birth? was spoken by Māra, who desired to lead the Elder Nun away toward sensual pleasures. "Why..."
When asked by Māra, “Do you not approve of this, Bhikkhunī? the Elder Nun replied, “Indeed, friend, I do not approve of birth.
Then Māra, showing her that because there is enjoyment of sensual pleasures for one who is born, therefore birth must also be desired and sensual pleasures must also be enjoyed, said:
“Why do you not approve of birth? One who is born experiences sensual pleasures.
Enjoy the delights of the senses; let there be no regret later,” she said, reciting this verse.
The meaning of this is as follows: What indeed could be that reason, Upacāla, by which you would not approve of birth, nor should you approve of it?

No such reason exists. Because one who is born experiences sensual pleasures; being born here, while partaking of forms and other objects associated with the strands of sense-pleasure, one enjoys the happiness of sensual desire.
For that does not exist for one who is unborn. Therefore, enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure.

Experience the pleasures of sensual desire. Do not be one who regrets later; do not be one who later feels remorse, thinking, "While youth existed and wealth was available, I did not experience the pleasure of sensual desires.
The intention is that in this world, the purpose of things (*dhamma*) is solely for the attainment of welfare, and welfare is for the sake of sensual pleasure—this meaning is evident.
Having heard this, the Elder Nun, clarifying for him how birth is the cause of suffering and how she herself had transcended its sphere, rebuked him:
“For one who is born there is death; there is the severing of hands and feet;
through the afflictions of execution and imprisonment, the born person encounters suffering.”
“There is one born in the Sakya clan, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, unconquered;
he taught me the Dhamma for the transcending of birth:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the overcoming of suffering.”
“The Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
Having heard his words, I dwelt delighting in the teaching;
the three knowledges were attained, and the Buddha’s instruction was fulfilled.
“Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!”—thus he spoke these verses.
Regarding that, "for one who is born there is death": because death occurs for a being who has been born, not for one who is unborn. It is not only death;
rather, all those disadvantages such as aging, sickness, and so forth, as many as they may be, belong to one who is born and have birth as their cause.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair [come to be]."
"...they come to be. For this very reason he said: "The cutting off of hands and feet"—the cutting off of hands and feet occurs only for one who is born, not for one who is unborn.
And it should be understood that by way of the example of the cutting off of hands and feet, all thirty-two forms of punishment are also shown here.
For this very reason he said: "Once born, one undergoes suffering consisting of execution, bondage, and affliction."
The affliction of slaughter— consisting of such things as being deprived of life or struck by the fist— and the affliction of bondage— consisting of such things as being bound with cords—
as well as whatever other suffering there may be, all that one who is born inevitably encounters,
but not one who is unborn; therefore, I do not delight in birth.
Now, demonstrating from the very root the state of having completely transcended both birth and sensual desires, he said:
