“There is one born in the Sakyan clan,” and so forth. In this context, “unconquered” means not defeated by anyone, such as the Māra of the defilements.
For the Teacher stands having utterly overcome the world together with its devas; therefore, he is unconquered.
The remainder is self-evident because it follows the method already stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Upacālā is finished.
The commentary on the Sattaka-nipāta (The Book of Sevens) is finished.
8. The Aṭṭhaka Nipāta. 1.
The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sīsūpacālā. In the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta, the verses beginning with “The bhikkhunī endowed with virtue” are those of the elder nun Sīsūpacālā. Of her too...
The story of the Elder Nun Cālā is exactly as told in her own account. For she too, having heard of the venerable Dhammasenāpati’s state of renunciation, was herself inspired with zeal;
she went forth, performed the preliminary duties, established insight meditation, and by striving and exerting herself, attained Arahantship before long.
Having reached Arahantship, through the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*),...
While dwelling there, one day, having reflected upon her own practice and feeling joyful that her task was accomplished,

she uttered this verse by way of an inspired utterance: “A bhikkhunī endowed with virtue, well-restrained in her sense faculties, shall attain the peaceful state, which is refreshing and full of vigor.”
In this context, "endowed with virtue" means being possessed of and complete in the pure moral discipline of a bhikkhunī.
"Well-restrained in the sense-faculties" means being thoroughly restrained in the six faculties, including the mind;

having abandoned lust for attractive objects such as forms, aversion toward unattractive ones, and delusion regarding indifference, she has well-closed her sense-doors. "Irresistible and full of vital essence"—

It is the Noble Path— or indeed Nibbāna itself— which is not poured out by anyone, is rich in nutritive essence, naturally sweet, and serves as a medicine for the subsiding of the disease of all defilements.
For it is fitting to call even the Noble Path "the peaceful state" (padaṃ santaṃ), because it is to be practiced by those seeking Nibbāna and because it is free from the fever of the defilements.
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods and the Yāma gods, and also the Tusita deities;
the Nimmānaratin gods and those gods who are Vasavattins—
set your heart upon that place where you formerly dwelt.”
This verse was spoken by Māra—who desired to cause the Elder Nun to fall from her meditative attainment—by way of inciting her toward attachment to the sensual heavens.
In that context, the place where thirty-three persons who performed meritorious deeds were reborn is called Tāvatiṃsa.
All the sons of the gods born there are also called Tāvatiṃsa. Some, however, maintain that "Tāvatiṃsa" is merely the name of those deities themselves.
They say: the Yāmas are so called because they have gone to, approached, and attained divine bliss that is superior to the two lower deva-worlds.

The Tusitas are so called because they are satisfied and delighted by divine prosperity. The Nimmānaratin are so called because, when they desire to enjoy more than the objects provided by nature, they create enjoyments according to their wish and take delight in them.
[The Paranimmitavasavattins are so called] because, having understood the mind's desire, they exercise mastery over the enjoyments created by others...
"Those who exercise mastery over enjoyments are called *vasavattino* (mastery-wielders). Regarding that, 'set your mind upon it' means:
place your mind upon that assembly of gods, such as the Tāvatiṃsa, and create a longing for rebirth there.

It is the Tāvatiṃsa and other such realms that are mentioned [here], with the intention that the enjoyments of the Cātumahārājika gods are inferior to those of the others. 'Where you formerly dwelt' refers to those [realms]."
"Among the hosts of devas, you have previously dwelt. It is said that formerly, when she was arising among the devas, she purified the five heavens of sensual pleasure starting from Tāvatiṃsa;
then, descending again from above, she remained in the Tusita heaven, and having passed away from there, she has now been reborn among humans.
Hearing this, the Elder Nun said: "Let be, Māra, the world of sensual pleasures spoken of by you. But the entire world, including all others, is [consumed] by the fires of passion and the like."
"Blazing and fiercely burning—there the minds of the wise do not delight. Having thus shown her mind to be turned away from both sensual desire and the world, she rebuked Māra:
"The Yāma gods, the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the Yāmas, and also the Tusita deities;”
The gods who delight in their own creations, and those gods who wield power over others’ creations—
again and again they pass from one existence to another, preoccupied with personal identity;
unable to transcend personal identity, they continue wandering through birth and death.
“The whole world is set ablaze; the whole world is aflame;
the whole world is burning; the whole world is trembling.
It is unshakable, incomparable, and not frequented by ordinary people.”
The Buddha taught the Dhamma, and my mind found delight therein.
Having heard his words, I dwelt rejoicing in the teaching;
the three knowledges were attained, and the Buddha’s instruction was fulfilled.
“Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!”—thus he spoke these verses.
In this context, "at the proper time" (*kālaṃ kālaṃ*) means at each respective occasion. "From existence to existence" (*bhavā bhavaṃ*) means from one state of becoming to another.
"In individuality" (*sakkāyasmiṃ*) refers to the five aggregates. "Honoring" (*purakkhatā*) means those who pay homage. This is what is meant:

O Māra, the gods of the Thirty-three and others, whom you have mentioned, as they pass from one existence to another, [enter] into individuality, which is crowded with many dangers such as impermanence.

They are established [in identity]; therefore, at the time of arising, at the middle period, and at the final period of that existence, they remain with self-identity (sakkāya) alone placed before them.

For that very reason, not having transcended it and not being oriented toward the escape from self-identity, they run hither and thither along the very shore of self-identity, wandering through birth and death, following after passion and the other defilements again and again.
"They recollect only birth and death; therefore, they are not liberated from them.

"The entire world is ablaze," Māra—meaning that it is not only the world of sense-desires (kāmāloka) mentioned by you, but the entire world designated as the three elements (dhātu) is also ablaze with the eleven fires, such as the fire of passion (rāgaggi).
Because it is set ablaze again and again by those very [fires], it is said to be "kindled" (padīpita).
It is ablaze because it has become a single, continuous mass of flame. It is trembling and shaking because it is agitated and shaken here and there by craving and by all the defilements.
Thus, because this world is set on fire, ablaze, and trembling, it cannot be moved or shaken by anyone at all.
It is unshakable; it is incomparable because it is impossible to weigh its qualities by saying "it is this much" and because there is no one equal to it.
It is not practiced by ordinary worldlings because it is frequented only by noble ones such as the Buddhas, having been reached through the cultivation of the objective sphere.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, [possesses] the ninefold supramundane dhamma, distinguished as the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna, by means of great compassion...
With his mind thus stirred, he taught, spoke, and proclaimed it to the world with its devas.
In that noble Dhamma, my mind was delighted and took pleasure; the meaning is that it did not turn back from it. The rest is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sīsūpacālā is finished.
The commentary on the Aṭṭhaka-nipāta is finished.
9. Navaka-nipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of Vaḍḍhamātā Therī.
In the *Navaka-nipāta*, there are the verses beginning with "O Vaḍḍha, may you not [be born] in the world," spoken by the elder nun Vaḍḍhamātā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, gradually gathered the requisites for liberation.
Then, during the arising of this present Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Bhārukacchaka.
Having reached marriageable age, she went to her husband’s family and gave birth to a son. His name was Vaḍḍha; from that time on, she was known as Vaḍḍhamātā (Mother Vaḍḍha).

Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhus, she gained faith, entrusted her son to her relatives, and went to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters to go forth. Hereafter, that which is to be said is as follows:

This is already included in the account of the Elder Vaḍḍha. For when his own son, wearing only his inner and upper garments and coming alone to the nuns' quarters to see him, the Elder Vaḍḍha rebuked him, saying, "Why have you come here all alone, clad only in your inner and upper garments? and then exhorted him:
“May you never, O Vaddha, have any forest-thicket of craving in this world;
may you not, my son, again and again become a partaker of suffering.
For the sages, O Vaddha, are happy—unshakable and with doubts severed.”
“Having become cool and attained self-mastery, they dwell free from taints.
‘O Vaḍḍha, cultivate that path practiced by the seers for the attainment of vision and for the making of an end to suffering.’”
He spoke these three verses.
Therein, "O Vaddha, may there never be for you in the world any entanglement (*vanatha*)"—the word *mā* is merely a particle.
"Vaddha, my son, in the entire world of beings and the world of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), may there never at any time be for you the entanglement of the defilements (*kilesa-vanatha*)."
“May I not have been; may I not come to be. Regarding this, she states the reason: “O little son, may you not, again and again, be a partaker of suffering.
Thus, while cutting down the thicket of craving, she says: “May you not be a partaker, time and again, of the suffering of birth and so forth, which has that [craving] as its cause.
Having thus shown the disadvantage in the non-eradication of the thicket, she now shows the benefit in its eradication:
He spoke the verse beginning with “For happiness, O Vaḍḍha. Its meaning is as follows: “O son, O Vaḍḍha, those who possess the dhamma of munificence are *munis*;
they are *anejas* (unshaken) due to the absence of craving, which is termed *ejā*;

they have severed their doubts through the very path of vision; they have become cooled by the absence of the fever of all defilements; and because they have attained the supreme state of self-control...”
Having attained self-mastery and being free from taints, those whose taints are exhausted dwell in happiness;
for them there is no mental suffering now, and in the future, all suffering will simply not come to be.
Since this is so, therefore one should cultivate that which was practiced by those seers... [as above] ...cultivate that which was practiced by those seers whose taints are exhausted.
"O Vaḍḍha, you should cultivate and increase this path of serenity and insight that has been entered upon for the attainment of knowledge and vision,
and for the bringing of an end to the entire suffering of the cycle of existence.
Having heard this, the Elder Vaḍḍha thought, "Surely my mother has established herself in Arahatship," and, making that matter known—
“You speak with such confidence that it produces this meaning within me.
I think, dear lady, that surely no undergrowth exists within you. Thus he spoke this verse.
Therein, “You speak with such confidence that it produces this meaning within me” means: “O you who have grown, may there be no undergrowth for you in the world.”
“‘Never have I spoken thus’—this is the meaning of this advice. ‘O mother, you speak to me having become free from timidity, unattached and unclinging anywhere.
Therefore, I think: ‘Surely, dear lady, no undergrowth exists in you.
‘Surely, dear lady, O mother, not even a mere undergrowth of worldly affection toward me exists in you,’ I think; the meaning is ‘not mine.’”
Having heard this, the Elder Nun said, "Not even the slightest defilement exists in me regarding any object whatsoever," and manifesting her own state of having accomplished what was to be done,
she declared: "Whatever conditioned phenomena there are, whether inferior, superior, or middling—
whether minute or even the most subtle— no undergrowth of craving exists within me."
“All my taints are exhausted for me as I meditate with diligence;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus he spoke these two verses.
In this context, "whatever" (*ye keci*) is an indefinite expression. "Formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhammā*). "Inferior" (*hīna*) means base or contemptible.

"Superior and middling" (*ukkaṭṭha-majjhima*) means both excellent and intermediate. Alternatively, among these, the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) is inferior, that which is conditioned by birth (*jāti-saṅkhata*) is superior, and those mixed with both are middling.
Or else, those produced by inferior desire and so forth are inferior, while those produced by middling [desire] are middling.
The sublime are superior. Unwholesome states are inferior; supramundane states are superior; others are middling.

"Even the minute, even the infinitesimal" means that not only in you, but in all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) whatsoever—whether distinguished as inferior and so forth—even a minute, an infinitesimal, or an exceedingly small forest-thicket of defilement does not exist in me.
Regarding this, he states the reason: “All my taints are exhausted for one who meditates with heedfulness.
Here, “for one who meditates with heedfulness” means for one who meditates heedfully; it is stated thus by way of a change in gender.
And herein, because the three true insights have been attained, the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished. Because she is heedful and meditative, therefore all [taints]...
"The taints (āsava) within me are exhausted; not even the slightest, atom-like trace of the undergrowth of craving (vanatha) exists in me"—this is the construction [of the verse].
Having taken the advice thus spoken as a goad, the Elder, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), went to the monastery and sat in his daytime resting place.
There, having developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship, he reflected upon his own practice and was filled with joy.
Having gone into his mother’s presence, he declared his attainment of enlightenment:
“Truly noble was the goad my mother uttered,
Verses containing the supreme goal, Just like one who is compassionate.”
“Having heard those words of my mother’s instruction,
I experienced a spiritual urgency for the sake of attaining the security from bondage.
With my mind intent on striving, untiring by day and night, I— ”
"Though urged by my mother, I attained supreme peace"—with these three verses she spoke.

Then the elder nun, taking her own words as a goad and her heart gladdened by her son’s attainment of *arahantship*, herself recited the verses spoken by him. Thus, they too became known as the elder nun’s verses (*therīgāthā*).

In this context, "exalted" (*uḷāra*) means vast and great. "The goad" (*patoda*) refers to the goad of exhortation. The construction is: "He let it rain down correctly" (*samavassari*), meaning he caused it to proceed rightly.
But what is that goad? He says: "Verses connected with the ultimate truth" (*paramatthasañhitā gāthā*).

He speaks with reference to those verses beginning, "O Vaḍḍha, may you not [be] in the world," and so forth. "Just as one who is compassionate" (*yathāpi anukampiko*)—just as others... [text continues].

"Encouraging": the meaning is that my mother thus urged me on with a sublime goad-stick known as the verses that reveal the occurrence and cessation [of phenomena], which inflames the speed of my wisdom.
"He attained a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega)": because it brought about the fear of knowledge, he experienced an exceedingly great and terrifying sense of urgency.

"Exerting oneself with diligence" means having one's mind directed toward the divine through the practice of the fourfold right exertion (*sammappadhāna*). "I have touched supreme peace" means that I have touched and attained the unsurpassed peace, which is Nibbāna.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Vaḍḍhamātā is finished.
The commentary on the Ninth Chapter (*Navaka-nipāta*) is finished.
10. The Section of Eleven (Ekādasaka-nipāta) 1.

Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Kisāgotamī In the Section of Eleven, the verses beginning with "Good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) belong to the elder nun Kisāgotamī. It is said that she [was born] during the time of Padumuttara...
In the time of the Blessed One, she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī.
Having reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher designate a certain bhikkhunī as the foremost among those who wear coarse robes.
Having performed an act of service, she aspired to that very position. For a hundred thousand aeons...
Wandering through births among gods and humans, she was reborn in this present age of a Buddha’s appearance in a poor family in Sāvatthī.
Her name was Gotamī, but because of her emaciated body, she was known as “Kisāgotamī.
When she went to her husband’s family, they treated her with contempt, saying, “She is the daughter of a poor family. She gave birth to a son; and because of the gain of a son, she received honor.
They did so. But her son, while playing, ran about and wandered here and there, and then passed away. Because of this, an intense surge of grief arose within her.
Thinking, "In the past I was treated with contempt, but from the time my son was born, I have received honor;
yet these people are even striving to cast my son outside," she took the corpse onto her lap out of that surge of grief.
“Give medicine for my son,” she said, as she wandered through the city, visiting house after house. People reviled her, asking, “Where is there any medicine?

She paid no heed to their words. Then a certain wise man thought to himself, “This woman has reached a state of mental distraction due to grief for her son; only the One of Ten Powers will know the medicine for her.”
“Mother, go to the Fully Enlightened One and ask for medicine for your son,” he said.
She went to the monastery at the time of the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching and said, “Venerable Blessed One, give medicine for my son.
Seeing her underlying potential (*upanissaya*), the Teacher said, “Go, enter the city, and find a house where no one has ever died before.”

"Then bring some mustard seeds," he said. She, delighted in heart, replied, "Very well, Bhante," and entering the city, she went to the very first house and said, "The Teacher has me bring mustard seeds for my son's medicine.
If no one in this house has ever died, give me some mustard seeds. "Who is there to count the dead here? [she was told].
"She is able. Thinking, "What need has she for these mustard seeds? she went to a second and a third house.
Through the power of the Buddha, her intoxication vanished and she returned to her natural state of mind. She thought, "This same rule will surely apply throughout the entire city;
this must have been seen by the Blessed One, who is compassionate for our welfare. Having thus attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), she departed from there.
Having gone out and abandoned his son in the raw charnel ground, he spoke this verse:
“The law of the village is not the law of the town, nor is it the law of a single family;
for the entire world, including the devas, this alone is the law: namely, impermanence.”
Having spoken thus, she went into the presence of the Teacher. Then the Teacher said to her, "Gotamī, have you obtained the white mustard seed?
She replied, "The task with the white mustard seed is finished, venerable sir, but please be my support. Then the Teacher spoke to her:
"A man who is intoxicated by children and cattle, whose mind is distracted..."
“Just as a great flood sweeps away a village, so does Death carry one away,” he said,
reciting this verse.
At the conclusion of the verse, while remaining exactly where he stood, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry and requested ordination from the Teacher.
The Teacher granted her permission to go forth. She circumambulated the Teacher three times, keeping him to her right, and after paying homage, she went to the nuns' quarters.
Having gone forth and received full ordination, she soon thereafter applied herself to her task with wise attention and increased her insight.
Then the Teacher said to her:
“Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the deathless state,
is a single day’s life for one who sees the deathless state.”—
Thus he spoke this illuminating verse.
At the conclusion of that verse, she attained *arahantship*. Becoming preeminent in the use of discarded requisites, she wandered about wearing a robe made of three coarse materials.

Then, while seated in Jeta’s Grove, the Teacher, as he was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective ranks, placed her at the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes. She [regarding] herself...

Having reflected upon his own practice, and thinking, "It is by relying on the Teacher that I have attained this distinction," he spoke these verses by way of praising the quality of having a virtuous friend:
"The Sage, pointing to the world, has praised the state of having a virtuous friend."
By associating with virtuous friends, even a fool may become wise.
“One should associate with true persons; for those who associate with them, wisdom thus increases.
By associating with true persons, one may be liberated from all sufferings.”
“One should understand suffering, and the origin and cessation of suffering;
and the Eightfold Path—these are the Four Noble Truths.
‘The female state is suffering,’ so it has been declared by the Charioteer of those to be tamed by men.”
For even the suffering caused by co-wives exists:
some women give birth only once, yet they have their throats cut, while others, being delicate, eat poison;
having fallen among those who kill people, both suffer calamities.
“Going along while in labor, I saw my husband dead on the road;
having given birth on the way, I had not yet reached my own home.
Two sons have died, and now my husband is dead on the road for me, a wretched woman.”
Mother, father, and brother—all burn upon a single funeral pyre.
"O you of ruined lineage, O wretched one, immeasurable suffering has been experienced by you;
tears have flowed from you through many thousands of births."
“Mastering myself in the midst of the charnel ground, I even ate the flesh of my own son;
though born of a low family and despised by all, with my husband dead, I attained the Deathless.
The Noble Eightfold Path, leading to the Deathless, has been cultivated by me.”
“Nibbāna has been realized; I have looked into the mirror of the Dhamma.
‘I am one whose arrows are pulled out, my burden laid down, and what was to be done has been done,’ thus spoke the elder nun Kisāgotamī, her mind liberated.”
In this context, "good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) means one who has a good, auspicious, and beautiful friend (*kalyāṇamitto*).

A person is a "good friend" if they are one who encourages another in virtues such as moral discipline, who destroys what is harmful, and who provides what is beneficial; thus, being a friend who assists in every way, that individual is a "good friend.
The state of being such is "good friendship," which is the quality of possessing a good friend. [The word] "by the Sage" (*muninā*)...
By the Teacher. "Praised with reference to the world" means that it should be followed regarding virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta) with reference to the world of beings:
"Ānanda, this entire holy life is just this: having virtuous friends, having virtuous companions, having virtuous associates.
"Meghiya, for a bhikkhu who has a virtuous friend, a virtuous companion, and virtuous associates, this is to be expected..."
"He will be virtuous and will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha"—thus has he been praised by such words as these.
"Associating with good friends," and so forth, is the demonstration of the benefits of having good friends.

In this context, "even a fool might become wise" means that a person associating with good friends, though previously a fool due to a lack of learning and so on, would become wise through hearing what was not heard before and so forth.

"Virtuous persons are to be honored": because they are the cause for even a fool to become wise, virtuous persons—such as the Buddhas and others—should be served from time to time by approaching them and so forth.

"Wisdom thus increases for those who honor them": for those honoring spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta), wisdom thus increases, expands, and reaches fulfillment. Just as anyone among them—whether a kshatriya or otherwise—[is honored].
The construction is: "By associating with true persons (sappurisa), one may be liberated from all sufferings such as birth and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to show the method of liberation by means of the method of relying on virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta), it is said: "One should understand suffering," and so on.
In that context, "the four noble truths" refers to suffering, the origin of suffering, cessation, and the eightfold [path].
The construction is: "One should know and penetrate these Four Noble Truths, including the Path.
The two verses beginning with "Femalehood is suffering" were spoken by a certain female *yakkhinī* who was censuring her own female state.
In that context, "femalehood is declared to be suffering" refers to fickleness, the bearing of a fetus, and [the burden] at all times...
"Life dependent on others"—through such dangers as these, the state of being female is suffering;
this was spoken by the Blessed One, the charioteer of men to be tamed. "Even having an enemy is suffering": dwelling with an enemy, living together with an enemy, is also suffering;
the intention is that this too is a disadvantage in the state of being female. "Some, having given birth once... refers to certain [women].
Women who have given birth only once, unable to endure the pain of childbirth in their first pregnancy, even cut their own necks.
"The delicate ones eat poison" means that those with delicate bodies, unable to bear the exhaustion due to their very delicacy, even consume poisons. "Having fallen among those who kill people."
"Janamāraka" refers to a miscarriage. It is the "slayer" (*māraka*) of the woman's people;
the meaning is that those who have reached the middle [of the womb] and those who have entered the belly are "slayers of people," namely, miscarriages.
"Both experience calamities" means that both the fetus and the pregnant woman reach death and death-like calamities. Others, however, say: "As for those called 'slayers of people'..."

"Defilements; having fallen into their midst and being caught within the continuity of those defilements, both husband and wife here incur calamities through the fever of defilement, and in the future, through the defilement of rebirth in the miserable states.
It is said that these two verses were spoken by that yakkhinī as she recollected the suffering she had experienced in her previous existence.
The Elder Nun, however, [spoke] for the purpose of elucidating the dangers inherent in the female state.
Repeating [the words], she spoke.
The two verses beginning with “Going along while near her time of birth” were spoken concerning the conduct of the elder nun Paṭācārā.
Therein, “going along while near her time of birth” means going along the road having reached the time of delivery; not yet having reached her own...
The construction is: "Having given birth on the road in a house, I saw my husband dead.

"Kapaṇikāya" means "by the wretched woman. It is said that these two verses were spoken by the Elder Nun (Therī) merely as an imitation of the manner in which Paṭācārā had then spoken when she was overcome by grief and madness, for the purpose of illustrating the dangers inherent in the female state.
Having brought both of these forward as examples, she now speaks the verse beginning with "In a family of the destitute" (*khīṇakuline*) in order to illustrate the suffering she herself experienced.
In this context, "one whose family is ruined" refers to one whose family has fallen into destitution through the loss of wealth and so forth.
"Miserable" refers to one who has reached the utmost state of contempt. Both of these are words of address directed to oneself.
"Immeasurable suffering has been experienced by you" means that in this present existence, or in existences prior to this, no small amount of suffering has been undergone by you. Now, that...
In order to show suffering by dividing it into its various parts, it was said: "And tears have flowed from you," and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows: while wandering through this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), many thousands of births have passed for you while overcome by sorrow;
and this has been stated without making any distinction, such that it would indeed be even more abundant than the water of the great ocean.
“Vasitā susānamajjhe” means she lived in the midst of the charnel ground, having become a dog, a jackal, and so forth, devouring human flesh.
“Khāditāni puttamaṃsāni” means that at times when she was a tiger, a leopard, a cat, and so on, she devoured the flesh of her own offspring.
“Hatakulikā” means one whose family lineage has perished. “Sabbagarahitā” means despised and fallen into reproach by all householders. “Matapatikā” means one whose husband has died.
“Widow. These three types, however, she mentions by referring to her own previous existences.
Even having become such, she attained the Deathless—reached Nibbāna—by means of serving spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta) which she obtained by chance.
Now, in order to demonstrate that very attainment of the Deathless more clearly, it is said: “Developed,” and so forth. Therein, “developed” means:
It has been analyzed, generated, increased, and penetrated by means of the clear realization through cultivation (*bhāvanābhisamaya*).
"I beheld the mirror of the Dhamma" means that I saw, I perceived, the mirror consisting of the Dhamma.
"I am one whose arrows have been pulled out" means that I am one whose arrows of craving, hatred, and so forth have been utterly eradicated by the Noble Path. "The burden has been laid down."
"Having laid down the burden of the aggregates of desire, the defilements, and volitional formations;
for what was to be done has been done"—that is, the sixteenfold duty consisting of the various types of full understanding (*pariññā*) and so forth, has been completed and brought to its conclusion.

"With a well-liberated mind, she spoke this"—the Elder Nun Kisāgotamī, whose mind is entirely liberated, spoke this matter in the form of a verse beginning with "Good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*), thus [describing] herself and others.
The Elder Nun speaks thus. Herein, this is the *apadāna* of this Elder Nun:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had reached the further shore of all phenomena, arose as the Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from now.”
“At that time, born into a certain family in Haṃsavatī,
I approached that best of men and went to him for refuge.
And I heard his Dhamma, which is comprised of the Four Noble Truths.”
Sweet, supremely delicious, and bringing the happiness of peace from the cycle of existence.
And then the Hero, the Supreme Person, praising a bhikkhunī who wore coarse robes, placed her at the foremost position.
“Having experienced no small measure of joy upon hearing of the virtues of the bhikkhunī,
and having performed service for the Buddha according to my ability and strength,
I prostrated before that best of sages and aspired for that very state.”
Then the Fully Awakened One, the Leader, expressed his approval for the attainment of that position:
"In a hundred thousand aeons hence, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, shall become a Teacher in the world."
“An heir to his teachings, a true-born daughter fashioned by the Dhamma,
you shall become a female disciple of the Teacher, known by the name Kisāgotamī.
Having heard this, she became joyful and [served] the Conqueror for as long as she lived.
With a mind of loving-kindness, I served the Guide with the necessary requisites.
By that well-performed deed, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having cast off this human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
“In this auspicious aeon, a man of great renown, a kinsman of Brahmā,
named Kassapa by clan, arose as the best among those who speak.
At that time, the lord of men was the attendant of the Great Seer.”
In the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king of Kāsi named Kikī.
I was his fifth daughter, renowned by the name Dhammā.
Having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror, I resolved to go forth into homelessness.
“Father did not grant us permission;
we then remained in the household for twenty thousand years, wandering about without weariness.
We, daughters of royalty raised in comfort, practiced the celibate life of a maiden.”
Delighting in waiting upon the Buddha, there were seven joyful daughters:
Samaṇī and Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī and Bhikkhudāyikā,
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and the seventh was Saṅghadāyikā.
“Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā and Kuṇḍalā;
myself and Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.
By those well-performed deeds and by our intentions and aspirations,”
Having cast off my human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Now, in this final existence, I was born into a family of wealthy merchants;
having come from a lineage that was destitute, poor, and ruined, I have gone to a family possessed of great wealth.
“Except for my husband, all the rest will show me contempt, thinking I am destitute”;
yet when I had given birth, I was beloved by them all.
When he was young, auspicious, delicate, and brought up in comfort;
“Like a beloved with his hand still in mine, so was I when I fell under the power of Yama.
With faces distorted by grief and distress, eyes streaming with tears, and mouths weeping,
I went along carrying the corpse of my dead son and lamenting.”
“Then, sent by one [person], I approached the supreme physician and said:
‘Sir, give me medicine that will bring my son back to life.
‘In whatever house there is no mustard seed from among the dead, from that [house] take it.’”
"Bring it," said the Victor, who is skilled in the means of discipline.
"At that time, having gone to Sāvatthī, I did not find such a house;
how then could I have obtained white mustard seeds? Therefore, I regained my mindfulness."
“Having cast aside the corpse, I approached the Leader of the World.
Seeing me from afar, he spoke with a sweet voice:
‘Though one should live for a hundred years without seeing rise and fall...’”
A single day of life is better for one who perceives arising and passing away.
It is not the custom of a village, nor the custom of a town, nor even the custom of a single family;
this alone is the law for the entire world, including the devas: namely, impermanence.
“Having heard these verses, I purified the eye of Dhamma;
then, having understood the true Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, I am devoted to the teaching of the Conqueror.”
In no long time at all, I attained arahantship.
I have mastery over the supernormal powers, possess the divine ear-element, and know the minds of others;
I am one who carries out the Teacher’s instruction.
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
Having exhausted all taints, I am pure and stainless.
The Teacher has been served by me; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.”
The heavy burden has been laid down; the fetter to existence has been eradicated.
That purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.
“Regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, and the linguistic definitions, and likewise regarding inspired eloquence—
my knowledge is stainless and pure through the power of the Best of Buddhas.
Having taken [bones] from heaps of refuse, from cemeteries, and even from roadsides...”
Then, having made it into a patched outer robe, I wore that coarse garment.
The Victor, pleased with that quality of wearing coarse robes,
the Guide placed me at the foremost rank among the assemblies.
“The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Kisāgotamī is finished.
The commentary on the Eleventh Chapter (Ekādasanipāta) is finished.
11. The Twelfth Chapter (Dvādasaka-nipāta) 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā In the Twelfth Chapter, the verses beginning with "Both mother and daughter" are the verses of the elder nun Uppalavaṇṇā. This [nun] also...

During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, having been reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī and having reached maturity, she went with a great multitude of people into the presence of the Teacher.

While listening to the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhunī to the position of being the foremost among those possessed of supernormal powers (*iddhimantānaṃ*). For seven days, [she made offerings] to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha...
Having given a great gift, she aspired for that state. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout her life, she passed through the cycle of existence among gods and humans;
during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the household of King Kiki of Bārāṇasī, became one of seven sisters, and practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years.
Having built a dwelling for the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*), she was reborn in the world of the gods.
Falling away from there, when she returned again to the human world, she was reborn in a certain village in a position where she had to earn her living by performing manual labor with her own hands.
One day, while going to a field hut, she saw in a lake along the way a lotus that had blossomed at dawn.
Having seen that lotus flower, she descended into the lake, took both the flower and a lotus leaf for the purpose of putting in the parched grain,
and having cut rice ears from a field, sat down in her hut, roasted the grain, and prepared five hundred parched grains, setting them aside. At that moment,
a certain Paccekabuddha emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana.

Having arrived, she stood in a place not far from him. Upon seeing the Paccekabuddha, she took a lotus flower along with some parched grain, descended from her hut, placed the parched grain into the Paccekabuddha’s bowl, covered the bowl with the lotus flower, and gave it to him.
Then, after the Paccekabuddha had gone a short distance, it occurred to her: "Those who have gone forth [do not accept] flowers..."
Thinking, "I do not need it; I shall take the flower and wear it," she went and took the flower from the hands of the Paccekabuddha.
Then she thought again, "If the noble one had no need for the flower, he would not have placed it on the rim of his bowl;
surely the noble one must have need of it. Thinking this, she went back and placed it on the rim of the bowl.
Having asked the Paccekabuddha for forgiveness, she made this aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the merit of these fried grains, may I have as many sons as there are grains;
and by the merit of this lotus flower, may a lotus flower spring up at every step in whatever place I am born.
While she was looking on, the Paccekabuddha departed through the air for Mount Gandhamādana.
She placed that lotus as a foot-wiping cloth near the steps used by the Paccekabuddhas at the Nandamūlaka cave.
By the result of that deed, she took rebirth in the world of the gods.
From the moment of her birth, a great lotus flower sprang up at every step she took. Having passed away from there, she was reborn at a lotus pond on the foothills of a mountain.
It was reborn within the calyx of a lotus. A certain ascetic lived depending on that [lake].
Early in the morning, having gone to the lake for the purpose of washing his face, he saw that flower and thought: "This flower is larger than the others;
while the others have blossomed, this one remains merely a bud. There must be a reason for this. Having descended into the water, he [reached] it...
He took a flower; as soon as it was taken by him, it blossomed. The ascetic saw the girl lying within the interior of the lotus.
From the moment he saw her, he felt a motherly affection for his daughter;
taking her along with the lotus, he led her to the leaf-hut and laid her down upon a couch. Then, through the power of her merit, milk flowed from her thumb. He...
When that flower had withered, she brought another fresh flower and laid her upon it.
From the time she became capable of playing by running hither and thither, a lotus flower would rise up at every step she took;
her body’s complexion became like a heap of saffron. She had not yet attained the splendor of a goddess, but she had transcended the appearance of a human being. She...
When her father had gone out for fruits, she remained behind in the leaf-hut.
Then one day, when she had reached maturity and her father had gone out for fruits, a forest-dweller saw her and thought:
"Such beauty as this does not belong to humans; I shall test her," [he said] to the ascetic.
He sat waiting for his arrival. When her father approached, she went out to meet him on the path and took the leather water-pot from his hand;
once he had returned and sat down, she performed the duties of hospitality for him.
At that time, the forest-dweller, recognizing him as a human being, paid homage to the ascetic and sat down. The ascetic [addressed] that forest-dweller...
Having invited him with forest roots, fruits, and water, he asked, "O man, will you stay in this very place, or will you go? "I shall go, venerable sir; what would I do staying here?
"Will you be able to tell what you have seen here after going from this place? "If the noble one does not wish it, for what reason [should I tell]?"
"I shall tell you," he said; then, having paid homage to the ascetic, he departed, making marks on branches and signs on trees so that he might recognize the path when he returned.
He went to Bārāṇasī and saw the king. The king asked, "Why have you come? "I have come, Your Majesty, for your sake."
Having seen a wondrous woman-jewel at the foot of the mountain, the forest-dweller has come here,” he related the entire account.
Having heard his words, [the king] went swiftly to the foot of the mountain, encamped his army in a place not far away,
and together with the forest-dweller and other men, performed the meal-offering for the ascetic.
Having gone there at the time when [the ascetic] was seated, he paid homage, exchanged friendly greetings, and sat down to one side.
The king placed the requisites for the ascetic’s renunciation at his feet and said, “Venerable sir, what shall we do here?
We shall depart. “Go, Great King,” he replied. “Yes, I am going, venerable sir; however, as for the noble one...”
“We have heard that there is a community of those of a different kind nearby; this woman is unsuitable for those who have gone forth.
Let her go with us, venerable sir. “The minds of men are indeed difficult to satisfy; how will she live in the midst of so many?
“From the moment she becomes our choice, we shall appoint her to the position of senior among the rest and look after her, venerable sir.”
Having heard the king’s words, he called his daughter by the name she had been given in her childhood: “Daughter, Padumavatī!
At that single utterance, she emerged from the leaf-hut, paid homage to her father, and stood before him.
Then her father said to her: “Daughter, you have reached marriageable age; ever since the time you were seen here by the king...”
"It is not fitting for you to live here; go with the king, mother. She accepted her father's words, saying, "Very well, father," and after paying him homage, she stood there weeping.

The king, thinking, "I shall win her father's heart," placed her right there upon a heap of kahāpaṇas and performed the consecration ceremony. Then, taking her with him, he brought her to his own city.
From the moment she arrived, he would not look at the other women but took his pleasure with her alone.
Those women, overcome by jealousy and wishing to create a rift between her and the king, spoke thus: "Great King, this woman is not of human birth.
Where indeed have you ever seen lotuses springing up in places frequented by humans? Surely..."
“This is a female *yakkha*; drive her out, Great King! When the king heard their words, he remained silent.
Later, at another time, the border region rose in rebellion. Thinking, “Padumavatī is heavily pregnant,” he left her behind in the city and departed for the border.
Then those women, having given a bribe to her nurse, [said], “Let us take this child from her...”
“Remove him as soon as he is born, smear a single wooden splinter with blood, and place it near him,” they said.
Not long after, Padumavatī also gave birth. Prince Mahāpaduma alone conceived rebirth in her womb;
the remaining four hundred and ninety-nine children [were conceived] from the womb of the Prince’s mother.
When she had gone out and was lying down, they were reborn as moisture-born beings.

Then, knowing that "she has not yet regained her mindfulness," her attendant smeared a wooden stick with blood, placed it near her, and gave a signal to those women. Those five hundred women each took a child.
Having sent messengers to the midwives, they had baskets brought;
they laid each of their own infants therein, sealed them on the outside, and set them aside.
Padumavatī, having regained consciousness, asked her nurse, "What have I given birth to, mother?"
Having intimidated her, she said, "Where will you get a child? and placed before her a piece of wood smeared with blood, saying, "This is the child born from your womb.
Upon seeing it, she became distressed and said, "Quickly split this apart and take it away;
if anyone should see it, it would be a cause for shame. She [the other woman] spoke these words to her...
Having heard this, as if desiring his welfare, they split the wooden doll and threw it onto the hearth.
The king, having arrived from the borderlands while awaiting the auspicious conjunction of the stars, sat down after pitching camp outside the city.
Then those five hundred women came out to meet the king and said: "O Great King, you..."
"You do not believe us; what we have said seems groundless to you. Summon the queen’s attendant and question her;
the queen has given birth to a wooden doll. Without investigating the matter, the king thought, "She must be of non-human origin," and expelled her from the palace.
At the very moment she departed from the royal residence, [the wooden doll vanished].
The lotus flowers vanished, and the complexion of her body also became discolored. She set out alone along the middle of the street.
Then, an elderly woman of mature age saw her, and feeling a motherly affection for her like that for a daughter, said, "Where are you going, my child?
"I am a newcomer; I am wandering about looking for a place to stay. "Come here," she said.
Saying, "Mother," she gave her a place to stay and prepared food for her.
As she lived there according to this very routine, those five hundred women became of one mind and said to the king:
"Great King, while you have gone to war, we have made a vow to the goddess of the Ganges: 'If our lord returns victorious from battle..."
“Once he has arrived, we shall perform the offering ceremony and then engage in water-sports”; this was their wish, and “O King, let us inform you of this matter.
Delighted by their words, the king went to the Ganges to engage in water-sports.
They too, each having concealed the casket she had taken, took it with her and went to the river; then, from those caskets—
Having put on [the robes] again and again for the sake of concealment, they fell into the water and released them into a basket.
All those baskets went along together and became caught in a spread-out net at a lower current.
Then, after playing in the water, when the king had emerged, those who were hauling up the net saw the baskets and brought them into the presence of the king.
The king, looking into the baskets, asked, "What is this, dear ones, in the baskets? "We do not know, Your Majesty," they replied.
He had the baskets opened for him to look; first, he had the basket of Prince Mahāpaduma opened.
However, on the very day they were placed within those baskets, by the power of their merit, from [his] thumb—
Milk was produced. To ensure the king was free from doubt, Sakka, the king of the gods, had letters inscribed inside the casket:
"These princes were born from the womb of Padumavatī, the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī;
then their co-wives, five hundred women, placed them in caskets and cast them into the water."

“Let the king know this reason. As soon as the basket was opened, the king read the letters and, seeing the children, lifted up Prince Mahāpaduma, quickly yoked him to the chariot, and said, “Harness the horses;
today, having entered the city, I shall do what is pleasing to certain women. Having spoken thus, he ascended the excellent palace.
Having placed a thousand coins upon the neck of an elephant, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
"Whoever sees Padumavatī, let that person take this thousand.
Hearing those words, Padumavatī gave a signal to her mother, saying: "Mother, take the thousand from the elephant's neck."
“I am not able to take such a thing,” she said. When he spoke thus a second and a third time, she replied, “What shall I say so that you will take it, mother?
“Tell him, ‘My daughter sees Queen Padumavatī,’ and then take it.
She thought, “Let it be this or that,” and having gone there, she took a chest with a thousand locks. Then people questioned her.
"Do you see Queen Padumavatī, mother? "I do not see her; my daughter, they say, sees her," she replied.
They asked, "But where is she, mother? and having spoken thus, they went with her, recognized Padumavatī, and fell at her feet.
At that time, she, knowing, "This is Queen Padumavatī," thought, "Alas, what a heavy burden for a woman!"
"What karma has been done! That she, being the chief queen of such a king, should dwell in such a place without protection," he said.
Those royal officers, having had Padumavatī’s residence surrounded with white canopies and stationed guards at the door, went and reported this to the king.
The king sent a golden palanquin, but she said, "I will not go in this manner."
"From my residence all the way to the royal palace, let fine cloth and painted carpets be spread along this entire path;
let a canopy of cloth variegated with golden stars be fastened above;
and when all the ornaments for my adornment have been provided, I shall go on foot. In this way, the city-dwellers will behold my splendor."
The King said, "Do as Padumavatī wishes. Then Padumavatī, having adorned herself with all her finery, set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go to the royal palace.
As she stepped forward, at every place where she trod, the fine cloth and painted carpets were pierced, and lotus flowers sprang up. She [showed] herself to the great multitude...
Having displayed his wealth and ascended the royal palace, he had all those silk and cotton cloths given as a maintenance allowance for that old woman.
The king, moreover, summoned those five hundred women and said, "O Queen, I give these to you as your female slaves."
He said, “Excellent, Great King! Have it made known throughout the entire city that these have been given by me.
The king caused a drum to be beaten in the city, proclaiming: “Five hundred women who were the mistresses of Padumāvatī have been given to her as her handmaidens.
When she learned that their status as handmaidens had been recognized by the entire city, she thought, “I shall make my handmaidens free.”
“I am able to do so, Your Majesty,” she said, and asked the king. “It is your wish, Queen,” he replied.

“That being the case,” she said, “summon that same drum-beater and have him beat the drum again, proclaiming: ‘The five hundred women who were given to Queen Padumavatī as her own slaves have all been made free. Once they had been made free, she—[counting] those who were one short...
Having entrusted five hundred sons into the hands of those very women for their upbringing, he himself took Prince Mahāpaduma alone.
Later, when those princes had reached the age for play, the king had various places for recreation constructed in the park.
When they were all about sixteen years old, they gathered together as one in the park at a place covered with lotuses.
While playing in the Maṅgala lotus pond, they saw newly blossomed lotuses and old lotuses falling from their stalks;
perceiving this as an object of meditation, they thought, "If such decay overtakes even these things that are not subject to grasping, how much more so for our own bodies?
For this body, too, will surely come to the same end. Thus, they all attained the knowledge of *paccekabodhi*.
Having been reborn, they rose up again and again and sat cross-legged upon lotus calyxes.
Then, the king’s men who had gone with them, realizing that much of the day had passed, said, "Noble sons, you should know it is time.
They remained silent. The men went and reported to the king: "Sire, the princes—"
“Sitting upon the pericarps of the lotuses, they do not utter a single word even while we are speaking. “Let them sit as they please,” he said.
Having been placed under guard throughout the entire night, they caused the dawn to break while remaining seated upon the pericarps of the lotuses in that very manner.
On the following day, the men approached and said, “O gods, you know the time.”
“We are not gods, O King; we are called Paccekabuddhas. “Noble ladies, you speak heavy words;
those called Paccekabuddhas are not like you. They wear hair and beard two finger-breadths long, and eight requisites are fastened upon their bodies.
They touched their heads with their right hands, and at that very moment, the marks of householders vanished.
Eight requisites were fastened to his body. Then, even as the great multitude looked on, they went through the air to the Nandamūlaka cave.
Queen Padumavatī, however, having fallen into heart-rending grief, thinking, "Having been one with many sons, I have become sonless," [fainted].
Having passed away from that very state of sorrow, she was reborn in the village of Dvāra near the city of Rājagaha, in a place where she lived by performing manual labor with her own hands.
Later, when she had gone to her father’s house, one day, while she was carrying rice-gruel to her husband’s field,
she saw eight Paccekabuddhas traveling through the air at the time of their alms-round among her own sons.
Seeing them, she went very quickly and informed her husband: "Look, noble sir, at these Paccekabuddhas; let us invite them and feed them. He said:
"These are merely 'ascetic-birds' who wander about in this manner elsewhere as well; they are not Paccekabuddhas.
Even as they were speaking, the birds alighted in a place not far away. That woman, on that day, [prepared] her own food, hard and soft...
Having given them [the food], she said, "May eight people also take my alms tomorrow. [The Paccekabuddhas replied: "Very well, laywoman;
let your hospitality be just this much, and let there be only eight seats. Having seen many other Paccekabuddhas as well, your heart will find even greater confidence.
On the following day, she prepared eight seats and arranged an offering of hospitality for the eight, and then sat down.
The Paccekabuddhas who had been invited gave notice to the rest: "Sirs, do not go elsewhere today;
all of you together should attend upon your mother. Having heard their words, they all came through the air together and appeared at the door of her house.
Because she had received the notice first, even though she saw many of them, she did not tremble.

She led them all into the house and had them sit upon seats. As they sat down in succession, the ninth [woman] prepared eight other seats for them and sat herself upon the seat at the head. As long as the seats increased, so too did the house expand.
Thus, when they were all seated, that woman [prepared food] for the eight Paccekabuddhas.

Having provided the five hundred with as much hospitality as they desired, he brought eight handfuls of blue lotuses (*nīluppala*), placed them at the feet of the invited *paccekabuddhas* alone, and made this aspiration:
"Venerable sirs, in whatever place I am reborn, may the color of my body be like the inner hue of these blue lotuses. The *paccekabuddhas*—
Having offered their approval to their mother, they went back to Gandhamādana itself.
She too, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as she lived, passed away from there and was reborn in the world of the gods.
In this present dispensation of the Buddha, she took conception in a merchant’s family in Sāvatthī. Because her complexion was like the interior of a blue lotus, she was known simply as Uppalavaṇṇā.

They gave her a name. Then, when she had reached maturity, the kings and merchants throughout the whole of Jambudīpa sent messengers to the merchant, saying, "Give us your daughter. There was no one who did not send such a message.
Thereupon the merchant thought: "I shall not be able to satisfy everyone's wishes; however, I will employ a certain stratagem."
Having summoned his daughter, he said, "Daughter, will you be able to go forth?
Because she was in her final existence, her father’s words were like hundred-fold refined oil poured upon her head. Therefore, she said to her father, "I shall go forth, father.
He honored her, led her to the nunnery, and ordained her. Not long after she had gone forth—

In this way, her turn to serve as the timekeeper in the Uposatha hall arrived. She lit a lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and while standing there having fixed her attention upon the flame of the lamp, she looked at it again and again.

Having thereby produced jhāna with the fire-kasiṇa as its object, and making that very attainment the basis, she reached Arahantship. Along with the fruit of Arahantship, she also attained the direct knowledges and the analytical insights (abhiññā-paṭisambhidā).
They succeeded. In particular, he had attained mastery in the transformation of psychic power (*iddhivikubbana*). Therefore, it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“The Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all phenomena, arose as a Leader one hundred thousand aeons ago from here.”
“At that time, I was born in Haṃsavatī in a family of wealthy merchants;
I was endowed with great happiness amidst the radiance of various jewels.
Having approached that Great Hero, I heard his teaching of the Dhamma.”
Then, having conceived faith, I went for refuge to the Victor:
“The Blessed One, the Leader, has praised me as the foremost among those possessed of psychic power—
a bhikkhunī who is modest, such-like, and skilled in concentration and meditation.”
“Then, with a joyful heart and longing for that state,
I invited the Ten-Powered One, the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha.
Having fed them for seven days and having given them the triple robe, I— ”
Taking a garland of seven lotuses, fragrant as celestial deities,
and placing them at the Teacher’s feet, I worshipped his wisdom.
Prostrating with my head at his feet, I spoke these words:
“O Hero, O Sage, such as you have described for the eighth [birth] from now, such shall I become, if it is to be accomplished, O Leader.
Then the Teacher said to me: “Be confident, girl.”
"In a future time, you shall obtain that heart’s desire:
'In a hundred thousand aeons, one born of the Okkāka clan,
named Gotama by lineage, will become a Teacher in the world.'"
“Her heirs in the Dhamma, her own children born of the Dhamma,
she who is renowned for her name ‘Uppalavaṇṇā’ and for her beauty;
having attained mastery in the higher knowledges, she is a fulfiller of the Teacher’s instruction.”
"With all taints completely destroyed, you shall become a female disciple of the Teacher.
Then, filled with joy, for as long as I lived, I served the Conqueror—
the Leader of the World— along with his Saṅgha, with a heart of loving-kindness.
“By that well-performed kamma, and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.
Passing away from there, I was reborn among humans as a self-enlightened one.”
I gave him almsfood covered with lotuses.
Ninety-one eons ago, a leader named Vipassī arose,
beautiful to behold and possessed of vision regarding all phenomena.
“Having been the daughter of a treasurer then, in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī,
she invited the Fully Awakened One, the Leader of the World, together with his Saṅgha.
Having given a great gift of lotuses to the Guide, she— ”
Having worshipped him with my mind, I prayed for the beauty of complexion:
"In this auspicious eon, a highly renowned kinsman of Brahmā named Kassapa by clan arose, the best among those who speak."
“At that time, the king of men, the ruler of Kāsi named Kikī, was the attendant of the Great Sage in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī.
I was his second daughter, known by the name Samaṇaguttā.”
Having heard the Dhamma from the Conqueror’s chief disciple, I resolved upon the going forth.
My father did not grant us permission, so we remained in the household life;
for twenty thousand years, we wandered about without weariness.
“Seven daughters, raised in happiness as princesses,
were devoted to the celibate life of a maiden (komāribrahmacariya) and delighted in attending upon the Buddha.
They were Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, and Bhikkhudāyikā;”
Dhammā and Sudhammā, and Saṅghadāyikā as the seventh.
“I am Khemā and Sappaññā, Paṭācārā and Kuṇḍalā;
Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.”
“By those well-performed deeds and by my intentions and aspirations,
having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Passing away from there, I was reborn among humans in a great family.”
I gave a fine, smooth, yellow cloth to an Arahant.
Having passed away from there, I was born in the city of Ariṭṭhapura into a brahmin family as the daughter of Tiriṭivaccha, named Ummādantī, captivating the mind.
“Then, having passed away from that country, I was born into a certain family that was not very prosperous.
At that time, I was guarding a field of rice.
Seeing a Paccekabuddha, I offered him five hundred parched grains of rice.”
Having given five hundred sons here covered with lotuses, I made a wish;
they too, having given honey to the Self-Existent One, made a wish.
Passing away from there, I was born here in a forest within the heart of a lotus.
“Having been the chief queen of the King of Kāsī,
honored and revered, I gave birth to no fewer than five hundred princes.
When they had reached youth and were playing at water-sports, ...”
Seeing the fallen lotuses, the individual leaders (paccekabuddhas) said:
“Deprived of those heroes of learning, I am sorrowful;
having passed away from the slopes of Isigili, I have been reborn in a village.”
“When the Buddha Sutamatī was away,
and while she was carrying rice-gruel for her husband and the eight individual leaders (paccekabuddhas),
I saw her going to the village for alms and remembered my sons.
A stream of milk flowed forth from me then out of love for my son.
Then, with my own hands, I gave them rice-gruel with a devout heart.
Passing away from there, I was reborn in the Nandana grove of the Thirty-three gods.
“Having experienced pleasure and pain, and having wandered through various states of existence,
O Great Hero, even my life was sacrificed for your sake.
You are my daughter, O Great Hero, possessed of wisdom and radiant with splendor.”
Much difficult work has been done by me, work that is exceedingly hard to perform.
Both Rāhula and I, throughout many hundreds of births,
were born into the same existence, with identical desires and minds.
“Birth occurs in one place, and birth also occurs in another;
when the final existence is reached, both arise in different places.
The meeting of those former Conquerors has been shown by you.”
“O Great Sage, I have had great authority for your sake.
O Sage, remember that wholesome deed which was performed by me;
O Great Hero, merit has been accumulated by me for your sake.”
“Having avoided what is unfitting, they restrain me from improper conduct;
for your sake, O Great Hero, much of my life has been sacrificed.
Thus have there been manifold sufferings and manifold prosperities.”
When his final existence had arrived, he was born in the city of Sāvatthī,
in a family of a very wealthy merchant— prosperous, well-adorned,
radiant with various jewels, and endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
“Honored and worshipped, likewise revered and esteemed;
having attained beauty and splendor, highly honored among noble families.
And I was exceedingly desired on account of my beauty, grace, and majesty.”
I was sought after by many hundreds of sons of merchants.
Having abandoned the household life, I went forth into homelessness;
before even half a month had passed, I attained the Four Noble Truths.
“Having fashioned a four-wheeled chariot by means of my psychic power,
I shall pay homage at the feet of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World.
I am a master of the various psychic powers and possess the divine ear-element.”
O Great Sage, I have attained mastery over the knowledge of the minds of others.
I know my past lives, and my divine eye has been purified.
All taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
“In the meanings, the phenomena, and the definitions, and likewise in inspired eloquence,
my knowledge is stainless and pure through the power of the Great Seer.
Robe, almsfood, requisites, and lodgings— ”
In an instant, thousands [of offerings] were presented from all sides.
"The Victor, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost rank;
the Leader, amidst the assemblies, declared me the foremost of those possessing psychic power."
“I have served the Teacher; the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled.
The heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
For the sake of which I went forth from the home to the homeless life—”
“Thus my goal has been attained: the destruction of all fetters.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [and so on]... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Now, this elder nun, when the Blessed One was at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, performing the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree...”
Having approached the Teacher, he paid homage and spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One permits it, I shall perform a miracle.

Thus he let out a lion’s roar. Taking this as the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), the Teacher, seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Great Monastery of Jetavana, [assigned] the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order.

Establishing this elder nun in the foremost position among those possessed of psychic power, she spent her time in the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), the bliss of the fruit [of the path], and the bliss of Nibbāna.

One day, while reflecting upon the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, she recited in response verses spoken by the daughter of the elder Gaṅgātīriya’s mother—who had become spiritually stirred by the thought of living with a co-wife:
[She recited: "Just as a lotus, though born in the water, does not get wet by the water, so too, though born in the world, I do not cling to the world. [And so forth.]
“Both mother and daughter were once my co-wives;
at that sight, a profound sense of spiritual urgency arose within me—extraordinary and hair-raising.
‘Fie on sensual pleasures! They are impure, foul-smelling, and full of thorns.’”
“Where mother and daughter were once wives to me,
having seen the peril in sensual pleasures and seeing renunciation as security,
she went forth from the home life into homelessness at Rājagaha.”
He spoke these three verses.
Therein, "Both mother and daughter—we were co-wives" means that both we, the mother and the daughter, were co-wives with one another.
It is said that at the time of dawn, a fetus was conceived in the womb of the wife of a certain merchant in Sāvatthī.
She remained there, but she did not recognize him. When the night had turned to dawn, the merchant loaded his goods onto the carts and set out toward Rājagaha.
As time passed for her, her pregnancy developed and reached maturity.
Then her mother-in-law said to her, "My son has been away for a long time, and you are pregnant; something wicked must have been done by you. She replied, "By you..."
"I know no man other than my son," she said. Although she heard this, the mother-in-law, lacking faith, drove her out of the house.
Searching for her husband, she eventually arrived at Rājagaha.
At that very moment, as the winds of her karma began to stir, she entered a certain *sāla* tree near the road and gave birth to a child. He was like a golden *bimba* fruit...
Having given birth to her son and laid him down in the hall for the destitute, she went outside for the purpose of performing water-rites.
Then a certain caravan leader who was childless, traveling along that path, thought, "This is a child of a woman without a master;
he shall be my son," and placed him in the hands of a nurse. Thereupon, his mother, having completed her water-rites and taking up water, returned.
Not seeing her son, overcome with grief, she lamented and, instead of entering Rājagaha, set out upon the road.
A certain chief of bandits saw her on the way, and his heart being bound by passion, he made her his wife.
While living in his house, she gave birth to a daughter. Then one day, she stood there holding her daughter.
Having quarreled with her husband, he threw his daughter onto a couch; he slightly injured the girl’s head.
Thereupon, out of fear of her husband, she returned to Rājagaha itself and lived there as a courtesan.
Her son, having reached the prime of youth, took her as his wife without knowing she was his mother. Later, that daughter of the chief thief—
Not realizing she was his sister, he married her and brought her to his own home.
Thus, having made his mother and sister his wives, he lived with them; consequently, both of them lived together as co-wives.
Then one day, the mother, having untied her daughter’s hair-braid and looking for lice, saw a wound on her head and thought, "Could this perhaps be my own daughter?"

Having questioned [her], she became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). She went to the nuns’ quarters in Rājagaha, received the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), and after performing the preliminary duties, lived in seclusion.
Reflecting upon her own former conduct, she recited the verses beginning with “Both mothers.
Furthermore, this [text] repeats those very verses spoken by her, illustrating the perception of the danger in sensual pleasures (*kāma*).
The Elder Nun said, “Both mother and daughter,” and so forth. Therefore it was said:
“Passing her time with the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of fruition, and the bliss of Nibbāna, she spoke these three verses.
Therein, “impure” (asuci) means impure because of the trickling of the impurity of defilements; “foul-smelling” (duggandhā) means having a putrid odor because of the wafting of a poison-like stench.
"Bahukaṇṭakā" means that, by way of piercing good conduct through the occurrence of internal strife (*visūyikappavatti*), they are the thorns of manifold defilements (*kilesakaṇṭaka*).
For it is said that those sensual pleasures (*kāma*) are like spears and spikes. "Yattha" means in which sensual pleasures that are to be enjoyed.
"Sabhariyā" means having a common wife; the meaning is "having rivals" (*sapattiyo*).
“I know my former births, the divine eye is purified;
the knowledge of penetrating others’ minds is attained, and the faculty of hearing is purified.
My supernormal powers have been realized, and the destruction of the taints has been reached.”
“The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
These two verses, beginning with “Past lives,” were spoken by the Elder Nun who had become filled with joy and gladness after reflecting upon the specific distinctions she had attained.
In this context, *cetopariccañāṇa* means the knowledge of encompassing the minds [of others] (*cetopariyañāṇa*); the connection is that these have been “realized” or “attained.”
“Having fashioned a four-wheeled chariot by means of psychic power,
I paid homage at the feet of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Lord of the World.”—
This verse was spoken when the Blessed One approached the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree to perform the Twin Miracle.

This elder nun, having fashioned such a chariot and gone with him into the presence of the Teacher, said, "Bhagavā, I shall perform a miracle to crush the pride of the heretics; please grant me permission," and she stood before the Teacher;
this was spoken out of faith. Therein, having manifested by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*), [she created] a four-wheeled chariot.
The intention is that she, having miraculously conjured a chariot yoked with four horses, paid homage at the feet of the Blessed Buddha and stood to one side.
“Having approached a tree with flowers in full bloom, you stand alone at the foot of a *sāla* tree;”
"And yet you have no companion at all; O foolish woman, do you not fear rogues?
In this context, *supupphitagga* means "with its tips in full bloom"; the meaning is that it is covered in blossoms from the very top down.
*Pādapa* means a tree; however, here the *sāla* tree is intended. *Ekā tuvaṃ* means "you alone."
"Here you stand. And yet you have no companion"—meaning there is no one at all to act as your friend or protector;
nor do you have anyone as a second to match your physical beauty. Possessing peerless form, you stand all alone in this secluded place.
"O foolish girl, you are not afraid of rogues"—O young woman, you [are not afraid] of rogue men.
"How is it that you do not fear?"—the intention is: "Are you a rogue who acts with worldly attachments?
It is said that one day Māra, seeing the Elder Nun sitting for her midday rest in a Sāla grove in full bloom, approached her.
Desiring to sever her from her seclusion and testing her, he spoke this verse. Then the Elder Nun, intimidating him by means of her own spiritual power, [replied]:
“Even if a hundred thousand such rogues were to assemble together, my hair would not quiver nor would it tremble; what can you do to me alone, Māra?
I shall either vanish from here or enter into your belly.”
“I stand between the eyebrows; you will not see me standing there.
“I have attained mastery over my mind; the bases of psychic power are well-developed.
The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.”
“Sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes, a violent hammering upon the aggregates.
That which you call the delight of sensual pleasure is now, for me, a source of aversion.
Delight has been destroyed everywhere; the mass of darkness has been shattered.”
"Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O End-maker!"—thus he spoke these verses.
Therein, "even hundreds of thousands of rogues might assemble like this" refers to those such as you.
"Even if there were to gather such scoundrels as these, numbering many hundreds of thousands—if they were to come together—my hair would not quiver, nor would it tremble;
not even a single hair would quiver or tremble. 'What will you do to me, Māra?'—O Māra, what will you alone be able to do to me?"
Now, demonstrating that Māra was utterly unable to do anything at all to her, she spoke this verse:
“I shall vanish right here. Its meaning is as follows: O Māra, while standing right before you, I shall vanish; I shall go out of sight.
Without even your knowing it, I shall either enter your belly or stand between your eyebrows. And while I am thus standing...
"You do not see me. Why is that?
Because I have attained mastery over my mind, the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) have been well-cultivated by me; I am Māra, and my mind has reached the state of mastery.
The four bases of psychic power have been thoroughly cultivated and frequently practiced by me; therefore, I..."
"I am capable" because of the aforementioned range of psychic power (*iddhivisayatā*). The rest is all clear, as it follows the method already explained below.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā is finished.
The commentary on the Twelfth Chapter is finished.
12. The Sixteenth Chapter (Soḷasanipāta) 1.

Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Puṇṇā In the Sixteenth Chapter, the verses beginning with "I was a water-carrier, cold... are the verses of the elder nun Puṇṇā. She, too, [attained enlightenment] under previous Buddhas...

Having performed their duties and accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, they were reborn into noble families during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī.
Upon reaching maturity, being endowed with the necessary causes, they became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having gone to the presence of the bhikkhunīs and heard the Dhamma, they gained faith, went forth, and maintained perfectly pure virtue while mastering the Three Piṭakas.
Having mastered it, she became one who was learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a preacher of the Dhamma.

And just as in the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī, so too in the dispensations of the Blessed Ones Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, she went forth, became endowed with virtue, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a preacher of the Dhamma. Because of her prideful nature...
However, she was unable to completely eradicate the defilements.

Because she had performed kamma based on the underlying tendency of conceit (māna), she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the womb of a house-servant of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika;
her name was Puṇṇātissā. Having become a stream-enterer upon hearing the teaching of the Sīhanāda Sutta, she later [encountered] the Brahmin Udakasuddhika...
Having been tamed by the merchant, she was honored by him and granted her freedom;
