having obtained his permission to go forth, she took ordination and, while practicing insight meditation (*vipassanā*), attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long.
Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī, of Sikhī, of Vessabhū,
of the Sage Kakusandha, of Koṇāgamana the Leader,
and of the Buddha Kassapa— ”
A bhikkhunī endowed with virtue, prudent, and with senses restrained;
one who is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, one who inquires about the meaning of the Dhamma;
one who has mastered the teachings, a listener, and an attendant.
“Descending here into the midst of people, I was in the teaching of the Conqueror;
because of that great learning, I looked down upon those who were well-behaved.
And now, in my final existence, in Sāvatthī, the supreme city...”
I was born in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika as the daughter of a water-carrier woman.
Once, while I had gone to fetch water, I saw a Sotthiya Brahmin standing in the midst of the water, shivering from the cold. Seeing him, I spoke these words:
“I am a water-carrier, Sītā; I always descend into the water, O Brahmin, terrified by the fear of my masters’ punishment and constrained by the fear of verbal abuse.
Of whom are you afraid, Brahmin, that you always descend into the water?”
With my limbs trembling, I feel a great cold.
"Surely you know me, lady Puṇṇikā," you say as you question me,
"one who performs wholesome deeds and restrains what has been done as evil."
“Whether one is old or young, whoever commits an evil deed—
by means of an ablution with water, even he is released from that evil deed.
As I was crossing over, I spoke this verse, which is endowed with the meaning of the Dhamma.
Having heard that, he was moved with spiritual urgency; having gone forth, he became an arahant.
"Since I was born into the family of a slave, completing the number of less than a hundred, they gave me the name 'Puṇṇā' and made me a free woman."
Having obtained the merchant’s permission, I went forth into the homeless life;
and in no long time at all, I attained arahantship.
I have mastery over the supernormal powers, and [mastery] over the divine ear-element.
“I am a master of the knowledge of the minds of others, O Great Sage.
I know my former births, and the divine eye has been purified.
All taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.”
“Regarding the meanings, the phenomena, the linguistic expressions, and likewise regarding inspired eloquence—my knowledge is stainless and pure, through the power of the Best of Buddhas.
Through meditation, I possess great wisdom; through learning, I am truly learned.”
“Even one born of a low family does not lose their karma through pride.

Having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he uttered this inspired exclamation: “The defilements have been burnt away by me... [the rest of the verse] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
(Dhp 153–154) Then, having attained arahantship and reviewing his own progress, he spoke as an inspired utterance:
“I am a water-carrier, Sītā; I always descend into the water out of fear of my masters’ punishment and because I am terrified of verbal abuse.
“Of what are you afraid, brahmin, that you always descend into the water?”
With your limbs trembling, you feel intense cold.
"Surely you know me, O lady Puṇṇikā," you say,
as you question me while I am performing wholesome deeds and obstructing one who has committed evil.
“Whether one is old or young, whoever commits an evil deed—
by means of an ablution with water, even that person is released from the evil deed.
“Who indeed told this to you— a non-knower to one who does not know?”
“By the ritual of water-consecration, one is indeed released from evil karma.
Surely all the frogs and turtles, the nāgas and crocodiles, and whatever other creatures move in the water, shall go to heaven.”
“Dog-catchers, pig-butchers, fishermen, deer-trappers;
thieves, executioners, and others who commit evil deeds—
even they are liberated from their evil karma by the sprinkling of water.”
“If these rivers did not carry away the great evil you committed in the past,
nor even your merit, then you would be excluded from them.
O Brahmin, it is because you are afraid of this that you always descend into the water.”
“O Brahmā, do not harm me; do not strike my skin with cold.
“You have brought me, who had entered a wrong path, onto the Noble Path.
Because of your sprinkling with water, O Lord, I give this robe to you.”
“Let this garment be yours; I do not desire the garment.
If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you, do not commit an evil deed, whether in public or in private.”
If you will do or have done an evil deed,
there is no escape from suffering for you, even if you flee after death.
If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you—
“Go for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha;
undertake the precepts, and that will be for your welfare.
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha.”
“I undertake the precepts; that shall be for my welfare.
“Formerly I was a kinsman of Brahmā, but today I am a true brahmin:
one who possesses the threefold knowledge, perfected in the Vedas, a learned scholar, and a cleansed one.”
He spoke these verses.

Therein, "a water-carrier" means one who carries water with a jar. "At that time I entered the water in the cold" means that even during the cold season, I entered the water day and night at all times;
whenever my grandmothers had need of water, at those times I would enter the water.
The intention is that, having entered the water, they bring the water [to the surface]. "Terrified by the fear of the masters' punishment" means terrified by the fear of punishment from their elders.
"Afflicted by the fear of verbal abuse and the fear of malice" means distressed and oppressed by both the fear of verbal punishment and the fear of ill-will;
the construction is that they enter the water even in the cold.
Then one day, a maidservant named Puṇṇā went to a water-crossing to fetch water in a jar. There she saw a certain brahmin performing a water-purification rite;

while a great cold was prevailing at the time of a snowfall, he had descended into the water early in the morning, submerged himself up to his head, recited mantras, and having emerged from the water, was shivering with his clothes and hair still wet.
He was playing a lute made of teeth. Seeing him, his mind stirred by compassion and wishing to detach him from that wrong view, she spoke this verse:
"Of whom, brahmin, are you afraid? Therein, "Of whom, brahmin, are you afraid? means:
of what cause for fear have you become afraid that you always descend into the water—that is, you descend into the water every evening and morning? Having descended...
With your limbs and bodily parts throbbing and trembling, you experience intense cold;
you undergo and experience the suffering of cold which is exceedingly difficult to bear.

"Truly, lady, you know me"—O lady Puṇṇikā, you truly question me while I am performing this descent into water, creating wholesome karma capable of obstructing and warding off that accumulated evil karma.
"Is it not true that this matter is well known in the world? Let us speak further to you," showing this, he spoke the verse beginning with "And whoever is old.

Its meaning is as follows: Whether one is old, young, or middle-aged, whoever commits evil deeds such as violence and performs them excessively—that person, being utterly devoted to evil deeds, [is freed] from them by the sprinkling of water, that is, by bathing.
"One is released from evil karma; one is utterly liberated.
Having heard this, Puṇṇikā, giving him her reply, said, "Who indeed has told you this? and so forth. Therein, "Who indeed has told you this? means:
to you who do not know, who are ignorant—that is, to you who are entirely ignorant of the ripening of kamma—[who has told this] regarding the ripening of kamma?
"Who indeed could have declared this matter—that an ignorant, unwise fool is liberated from evil karma by means of water-consecration?
His word is not to be trusted, nor is it logical; this is the intended meaning.
Now, demonstrating that very lack of logic, she says, "Surely they will go to heaven," and so forth. In that regard:
“Nāgas” refers to crocodiles. “Susumārās” refers to water-monsters (kumbhīlas).
And as for those others who move in the water—whether they be other aquatic creatures or fish, makaras, nandiyāvattas, and so forth—they too will surely go to heaven;
that is, they will be reborn in the world of the devas, for the meaning is that liberation from evil karma occurs through the sprinkling of water.

“Slaughterers of sheep” (orabbhikā) are those who kill sheep. “Slaughterers of pigs” (sūkarikā) are those who kill pigs. “Fishermen” (macchikā) are those who catch fish. “Trappers” (migabandhakā) are hunters.
“Executioners” (vajjhaghātā) are those appointed to the work of executing criminals. “May they not carry away even my merit”:

just as these rivers, such as the Aciravatī and others, might carry away much of the evil you previously committed by means of sprinkling water there, so too may these rivers carry away the merit performed by you.
[They] would wash it away. Because of that, you would be excluded; being so, by means of that meritorious deed you would be excluded and indeed deprived [of its fruit].

But this is not logical—this is the intended meaning. Or, just as there is no washing away of merit for one who enters the water by means of the water itself, likewise there is no washing away of evil either. Why? Because bathing is not the cause of the evils.
Because it lacks the nature of being an antidote. Whatever destroys something is its antidote; for example, light is the antidote to darkness, and knowledge is the antidote to ignorance.
Bathing is not like that in relation to evil. Therefore, one must reach the conclusion here:
"Liberation from evil does not come through the sprinkling of water. Thus the Blessed One said:
“One does not become pure by water; many people bathe here [in it].

He in whom there is truth and Dhamma—he is pure, and he is a brahmin. Now, in order to show that if you wish to wash away evil, you must not commit any evil at all, [the Blessed One said]: “For one who...”* *The following verse is supplied from the source text: “For one who has no anger toward beings, who has laid aside the stick toward all living things, who is restrained and dwells with a mind of harmlessness—him I call a brahmin. (Sn 621)*
He spoke this verse: “O Brāhmaṇa. Therein, “Do not commit that very thing, O Brāhmaṇa” means:
O Brāhmaṇa, do not commit that very evil from which you are afraid. Furthermore, bathing in water during such cold weather merely afflicts the body.
Therefore he said: “Let the cold not strike your skin,” meaning the cold produced by the sprinkling of water during such a cold season.
"Do not strike my body; do not harm me"—this is the meaning.

"To one who has entered upon a wrong path" means to me, who had entered upon this wrong path and false conviction that "purity comes through sprinkling with water," and who was standing there holding onto it.
"He brought me to the Noble Path" means [the path] defined as "the non-doing of all evil, the cultivation of the wholesome..."
"Upasampadā"—she brought her along this path traveled by the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddha, and led her correctly toward it;
therefore, "Sir," she said, "I give this garment to you as a gift of joy and as your teacher’s fee (*ācariyabhāga*)," the meaning being that he should accept it.
Having declined that, she preached the Dhamma and established her in the Refuges and the Precepts, saying: "The garment is yours alone."
Having said, "Let it be; I do not desire this cloth," he spoke the verse beginning with, "If you fear suffering," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
If you fear the various kinds of suffering—such as the lack of comfort and the state of wretchedness found both in all the states of misery (apāya) and in the happy realms (sugati);
if that [suffering] is unpleasant and undesirable to you; or if, openly—that is, by making it manifest to others—you do not conceal it...
Do not commit, nor cause to be committed, even the slightest evil or base deed— whether by way of bodily or verbal action such as taking life,
or by way of the mind-door through covetousness and so forth, or by concealing it in secret and out of sight. Furthermore,
whether you will perform that evil deed in the future or are performing it now, [know that] in the four [realms] beginning with hell...

Even if one approaches and intentionally flees with the intention, "The suffering that is the fruit of this [evil deed] will not pursue me as I flee here or there among the states of misery (apāya) or among humans," there is no liberation or release from that evil;

the meaning is that it certainly ripens when the convergence of other conditions such as the destiny (gati), time, and so forth occurs. Alternatively, the reading is "uppaccā," which means "having flown up. Thus, regarding evil...
Having shown the absence of suffering through non-action, he now says, "If you are afraid," and so forth, in order to show it even through the performance of merit.
Therein, *tādinam* refers to one who has attained the state of being "such" (*tādi*) regarding what is seen and so forth.

Or, because he is to be seen in the same manner as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Ones, he is "such" (*tādi*); the construction is: "Go for refuge to that Buddha. The same applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.
The same method applies here. The construction is: "They gather the Dhamma of those supreme Buddhas who are such (tādī), and the Saṅgha of the eight types of noble persons.
"That" refers to the going for refuge and the undertaking of the precepts. "He will be" means he will come to be.
That brahmin, having established himself in the refuges and the precepts, later on heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
Having gained faith and gone forth, by striving and exerting himself, he became a possessor of the three knowledges (*tevijja*) before long.
Reflecting upon his own practice and uttering a spontaneous exclamation (*udāna*), he spoke the verse beginning with "A kinsman of Brahmā" (*brahmabandhu*).
Its meaning is as follows: Previously, merely by virtue of being born into a brahmin family, I was known as a "kinsman of Brahmā. Likewise, [by mastering] the *Irubbeda* and so forth...
"Formerly, by means of mere recitation and so forth, I was called 'one possessing the three Vedas,' 'one perfected in the Veda,' 'a learned scholar,' and 'a purified one.
But now, because all evil has been entirely banished, I am a true Brahmin, a Brahmin in the ultimate sense; because of the attainment of the triple knowledge, I am 'one possessing the three Vedas';
because of being endowed with the 'Veda' known as the knowledge of the Path, I am 'perfected in the Veda'; and because of having washed away all evil, I am a 'purified one. Herein—
Since both the verses spoken by the brahmin and those spoken by herself were later uttered individually by the Elder Nun,
all of them became the verses of the Elder Nun alone.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Puṇṇā is finished.
The commentary on the *Soḷasanipāta* is finished.
13. The *Vīsatinipāta*. 1.
Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Ambapālī.
In the *Vīsatinipāta*, the verses beginning with “Black, resembling the color of bees,” etc., are those of the Elder Nun Ambapālī.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, went forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Sikhi.
Having received full ordination and dwelling while undertaking the training rules for bhikkhunīs, one day—
While she was walking ahead of an elder nun who had destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*), having paid homage to a shrine together with many bhikkhunīs and circumambulating it,
she suddenly spat a globule of saliva that fell onto the courtyard of the shrine.
When the elder nun who had destroyed the taints had gone on without noticing, this woman following behind saw that globule of saliva and thought, "What kind of courtesan is this?"

“…she spat a lump of spittle on the spot,” he reviled her. During her time as a bhikkhunī, she had maintained her virtue and, loathing the dwelling in a womb, had set her mind upon a spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).

Consequently, in her final existence, she was reborn spontaneously at the foot of an *amra* tree in the royal park at Vesālī. Seeing her, the park keeper led her into the city. At the foot of the *amra* tree...

Because she was thus born, she was known simply as Ambapālī. Then, seeing her—handsome, beautiful, pleasing, and endowed with distinguished qualities such as grace and charm—several princes, desiring to take her as their own possession, fell into mutual strife.
To settle their quarrel, [the King], impelled by her past karma, [sent for her].
The judges, saying, "Let her be for all," appointed her to the position of courtesan.
Having gained faith in the Teacher, she built a monastery in her own park and dedicated it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
Later, having heard the Dhamma from her own son, the Venerable Vimalakoṇḍañña, she went forth and applied herself to insight meditation.
Reflecting on the state of her own body’s decay and being moved by a sense of spiritual urgency, she discerned the impermanence of conditioned phenomena:
“Once my hair was black, resembling the color of bees, with tips curling upwards;
now, through old age, it resembles hemp-fiber—just so, for the word of the Truth-teller is not otherwise.”
“Like a fragrant casket scented with perfume, my head-born son is filled with flowers;
that he has become like a hairy, stinking carcass through old age—this word of the Speaker of Truth is not otherwise.
Like a well-tended grove, planted by the gods, adorned at its tips with various baskets and needles;”
That [hair], thinned here and there by old age, is exactly as the word of the Speaker of Truth is:
"Adorned with black tufts and gold, it shone when fashioned into beautiful braids;
now that head has been made to falter by old age—exactly as the word of the Speaker of Truth is."
“Those eyebrows of mine, formerly so beautiful, like lines well-drawn by an artist, now hang down, wrinkled with age;
the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
Those eyes of mine were once bright and radiant like jewels, long and deep-blue.”
Struck by old age, they no longer shine; the word of the speaker of truth is otherwise not so.
The nose, like a delicate peak, shone beautifully in the prime of youth;
now, as if crushed by old age, it is no longer so—the word of the speaker of truth is otherwise not so.
“Like a well-fashioned, well-finished bracelet, they once graced my ears;
now, hanging down with the folds of old age, the word of the Speaker of Truth is proven not otherwise.
My teeth, which formerly shone like the color of a ripe *līma* fruit, [have fallen away].”
They have been broken and turned gray by old age; the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
"Like a cuckoo wandering through the thickets of the forest, I used to warble sweetly;
now that voice falters here and there due to old age—the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise."
“My neck, once so beautiful, shone like a well-polished conch shell;
now, broken and bent by old age, it stands as the infallible word of the Speaker of Truth.
Both my arms, which formerly shone like rounded door-bolts, [have likewise withered].”

Just as they were once adorned with delicate rings and fine gold, my hands shone beautifully; now, through old age, they are like roots and rootless stumps—such is the word of the speaker of truth, which is never otherwise. Just as they were once firm and strong as the *pāṭali* tree, so too is the word of the speaker of truth, which is never otherwise. Just as they were once adorned with delicate rings and fine gold, my hands shone beautifully;
now, through old age, they are like roots and rootless stumps—such is the word of the speaker of truth, which is never otherwise.
“Both my breasts, full, rounded, and well-developed, used to adorn me in the past;
they hung down like golden water-pots, for the word of one who speaks truth is never otherwise.
My body, too, used to shine beautifully in the past, like a well-polished slab of gold.”
Thus, covered with fine wrinkles, the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise.
"Both my thighs formerly shone like the coils of a serpent;
now, through old age, they are like bamboo joints—so the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise."
“Adorned with delicate anklets and gold, my shanks once shone so brightly;
now, through old age, they are like sesame stalks—truly, the word of the Speaker of Truth is not otherwise.
My two feet, which once resembled the likeness of cotton-filled pillows, shone so beautifully.”
They are cracked with age and wrinkled; the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise:
"Such was this composite body, decaying and a repository of many sufferings;
it has fallen into the clutches of defilement, a house of old age—the word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise."
He spoke these verses.
In this context, "black" (*kāḷaka*) means black in color. "Resembling the color of a bee" means that although they are black, their color is like that of a bee;
the meaning is that they are glossy blue. "Curled at the tips" means having curled ends; they are curled from the root all the way to the tips.
"Vellitā" means "curled. "Muddhajā" refers to the hair of the head. "Jarāya" means by reason of old age; [the hair] has its beauty impaired by old age.
"Sāṇavākasadisā" means resembling hemp or resembling bark; it also means resembling *sāṇa*-grass, resembling *vāk*-grass, and likewise resembling *makaci*-grass.

"The word of the speaker of truth is not otherwise" means that the word of the Speaker of Truth, the Non-false Speaker, the Perfectly Enlightened One—such as "All form is impermanent, overcome by old age," and so forth—is not otherwise.
"Not otherwise" means exactly as it is; there is nothing false therein.
"Like a fragrant casket" means like a perfume box scented with flowers, perfumes, aromatic powders, and so forth—having been made to take on a fragrance, it is sweet-smelling.
"My head is filled with flowers" means it is filled with flowers such as the *campaka*, *sumana*, jasmine (*mallikā*), and others.

The meaning is that previously my mass of hair was stainless. "That" refers to what was born from the head. Then later, at present, it has become "saloma-gandhika," which means it has acquired the natural odor of wool.
Alternatively, "saloma-gandhika" means having an odor similar to that of ram’s wool;
they also say it is the "odor of sheep's wool."
"Like a well-planted grove" means like a garden that has been properly planted, arranged in a dense formation, rising straight up with upright, long branches.

"Adorned with a variegated crest of hairpins and needles" means it was previously beautified by having its tips variegated through the disentangling of matted locks using hairpins and golden needles; or else, by its density, it was like a mass of hairpins.
It was beautified by hair-ends variegated with needles for parting. "That" refers to what is produced from the head.
"Sparse here and there" means that the hair had been shorn sparsely in various places.
"Adorned with a black tuft and gold" refers to a mass of black hair decorated with gold, diamonds, and other gems. Those...
However, some read "adorned with soft thorns of gold" (*saṇhakaṇḍakasuvaṇṇamaṇḍita*);

for them, the meaning is that it was adorned by the entangling of matted locks with soft golden needles. "It shone beautifully, adorned with fine braids" means that it formerly gleamed, having been adorned with beautiful braids of hair resembling rows of royal trees.
"That head, once so radiant, has now been made bald by old age. Thus it was adorned.
Now my head is made bald by old age, broken here and there, with its hair shorn away.
It shines like a line well-drawn by a skilled painter with blue pigment—like a streak beautifully executed by an artisan.
"My eyebrows were beautiful before" means that my lovely eyebrows used to possess great beauty. "Hanging down with wrinkles" means...
They remained hanging down from the wrinkles that had appeared at the corners of their foreheads.
*Bhassarā* means radiant. *Surucirā* means exceedingly beautiful. *Yathā maṇī* means like a jeweled ring.
*Nettahesun* means they possessed beautiful eyes. *Abhinīlamāyatā* means being deep blue and long. *Te* refers to those eyes. *Jarāyabhihatā* means afflicted by old age.
"Smooth and high" means it is smooth, elevated, and proportionate to the other facial features.
"It shines" means my nose shines like a stalk of a green palmyra palm that has been set upright after being rounded off.

"She has reached the prime of youth" means that at that beautiful time of fresh youth, that nose has now become like a withered stalk or a dried creeper, its former luster having been suppressed by old age.
"Like a well-fashioned, well-finished bracelet" means it is like a gold bracelet that has been thoroughly polished;
he says this with reference to its circular shape. "Sobhare" means they shine. Alternatively, the reading is "sobhante. "Su" is merely an expletive particle.
"Kaṇṇapāḷiyo" means the earlobes. "Valibhippalambitā" means they hang down, having become wrinkled by the folds that have arisen here and there on the earlobe.
They hang down, swaying like heaps of cloth cast away. They are similar in color to the *pattalī* flower;

that is, their color and shape resemble the *kadalī* flower. "Fragmented" means they have been broken and fallen apart, having reached a state of being in pieces. "Discolored" means they have reached a state of discoloration through the fading of their original hue.
Moving through the forest thickets in the woods, they warble sweetly like cuckoos while foraging and wandering within the groves.
Like a cuckoo dwelling in the forest groves and inhabiting the woods, I warbled with sweet-sounding notes. That "warbling" refers to the vocal utterance.
"Stammering here and there" means that due to conditions such as broken teeth, it became faltering in various places.

"Like a well-polished smooth conch" means it was thoroughly cleansed like a smooth golden conch shell. "Broken and bent" means that through the wasting away of flesh, the network of veins became prominent, causing them to be broken and drooping.

"Resembling a round door-bolt" means they are exactly like a circular door-bar. "Those two" refers to both arms. "Tremulous like *pāṭali* branches" means, due to their decrepit state, they resemble the trembling branches of the *pāṭali* tree.
"Adorned with smooth rings of gold" means they are decorated with golden rings that are polished and radiant. "Like radishes" means they resemble the roots of radishes.
"Plump, rounded, joined, and elevated" means they are plump, rounded, joined together with one another, elevated, and turned upward. They shine.
"Su thanakā pure mamā" means both my breasts shone like golden jars, having become as described.
Here, this singular form is used for a plural sense, and the present tense is used for the past.
"Thevikīva lambanti nodakā" means those two breasts of mine, being "nodakā"—that is, without leaking water—hung down like water-pots placed upon bamboo poles with their contents of water spilled out.
"Like a well-polished golden plate": it shines like a golden plate that has been smeared with natural cinnabar and rubbed for a long time.
"It is overspread with fine wrinkles": this body of mine is now stretched here and there with fine wrinkles;
it has reached the state of having wrinkled skin.

"Resembling the coils of a nāga" means they were equal to the trunk of a noble elephant (*hatthināga*). For here, that by which one enjoys is called "coil" (*bhoga*). "Those" refers to the thighs. "Like bamboo joints" means they now became like the segments of a bamboo cane.
"Adorned with soft, polished golden anklets" means they were decorated with smooth, glossy golden anklets.
"Shanks" refers to the bone-shanks. "Those" refers to those shanks. "Like sesame stalks" means because of their emaciated state due to having little flesh and blood.
They became like stalks of sesame that have been harvested, remaining only as dry husks. The letter *ra* is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*).

"Resembling cotton-wool" means, by virtue of being soft and smooth, they were like sandals stuffed with *simbali*-tree cotton. "Those feet of mine are now cracked, fissured, and wrinkled, having become lined.
"Of such a kind" means of this very nature. "It was" means it became of the aforementioned sort. "This heap" refers to this body of mine. "Decayed" means...
* Sithilābandho: "With loose bonds. *Bahudukkhānamālayo*: "A dwelling place for many sufferings," meaning it has become the abode of the many sufferings caused by old age and so forth.

*Sopalepapatito*: "He has fallen from his coating. The meaning is that this physical aggregate (*samussaya*) has fallen away, having fallen toward ruin through the exhaustion of the coating of volitional formations (*abhisankhāra*).
Alternatively, the word-analysis is *sopalepa-patito*, which carries the same meaning. *Jarāgharo*: "The house of old age."

It is like an old house, or it has become a house for old age. Therefore, because he speaks the truth after having correctly understood the true nature of phenomena as they really are, the word of my Teacher, the Truly Self-Enlightened One who speaks without falsehood, is not otherwise.
Thus, by way of observing the impermanence in her own personal existence, this elder [perceived] all phenomena belonging to the three realms as well.

Having contemplated impermanence and, following that, having applied the characteristics of suffering and non-self therein, she intensified her insight and reached Arahantship through the successive stages of the Path. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
“The great sage named Phussa, whose hair was as radiant as a sunbeam...”
I was his sister, born into a family of kṣatriyas.
Having heard his Dhamma with a serene mind,
I gave a great gift and aspired for perfection of form.
“Thirty-one eons ago, Sikhī, the leader of the world, the lamp of the world,
the Victor and refuge of the three worlds, appeared. At that time,
in the delightful city of Aruṇa, he was born into a family of brahmins.”
In my anger, I uttered a curse against a bhikkhunī whose mind was liberated:
“You are an unchaste harlot, a defiler of the Conqueror’s teaching!
Having reviled her thus, by that evil deed—
“Having gone to a terrible hell, afflicted by great suffering,
I passed away from there and was reborn among humans as an ascetic woman.
For ten thousand births, I practiced the life of a courtesan.”
"I shall not be released from that evil, like one who has consumed potent poison.
I practiced the holy life under Kassapa in the teaching of the Victor;
by the ripening of that karma, I was reborn in the city of the Thirty-three."
“When my final existence was reached, I was born by spontaneous rebirth;
having been born within the branches of a mango tree, therefore I am called Ambapālī.
Surrounded by tens of millions of living beings, I went forth in the teaching of the Victor.”
“I have attained the immovable state, the breast-born daughter of the Buddha.
I am a master of the supernormal powers, and through the purification of the ear-element,
I am a master of the knowledge of others’ minds, O Great Sage.”
“I know my former births; the divine eye has been purified.
All taints are utterly destroyed; there is now no further becoming.
In the meanings, the phenomena, the definitions, and likewise in inspired eloquence—”
My knowledge is stainless and pure, through the power of the Best of Buddhas.
My defilements have been incinerated, all states of existence have been uprooted;
like a female elephant that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
“Welcome indeed has come to me in the presence of the Best of Buddhas;
the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical insights and these eight liberations—”
"The six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he recited those very verses as an inspired utterance (*udāna*).
Thus ends the commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Ambapālī.
2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Rohinī. The verses beginning with “O lady, did you sleep well? are the verses of the elder nun Rohinī.

She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various existences; thus, ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Vipassi Buddha...
Having been reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One and having reached maturity, she one day saw the Blessed One walking for alms in the city of Bandhumatī.
Taking his bowl and filling it with cakes, she gave them to the Blessed One;

filled with joy and gladness, she paid homage to him by prostrating herself at the five points. By virtue of that meritorious deed, as she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, she gradually—
Having accumulated the requisites for liberation, she was reborn in this current dispensation of a Buddha in the home of a very wealthy brahmin in Vesālī.
Having received the name Rohinī and attained maturity, she went to the monastery while the Teacher was residing in Vesālī;
having heard the Dhamma, she became a stream-enterer. After teaching the Dhamma to her parents, she [entered] the Dispensation...
Having inspired confidence and obtained their permission, she herself went forth and applied herself to the practice of insight (vipassanā);
before long, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore it is said:
“In the city of Bandhumatī, of Vipassi, the Great Seer...”
As I was wandering for alms, I gave you food at that time.
By that well-performed deed, by my intention and aspiration,
and having gladdened my mind therein, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
“I exercised the role of chief queen for thirty-six divine kings;
I exercised the role of chief queen for fifty wheel-turning monarchs.
Whatever I desired in my mind, all that was fulfilled for me.”
Having experienced prosperity among both gods and humans,
in my final birth I was born into a brahmin family;
my name was Rohinī, and I was beloved by my kinsmen.
“Having gone into the presence of the bhikkhus and heard the Dhamma as it truly is,
with a mind filled with spiritual urgency, I went forth into the homeless life.
By applying myself with systematic effort, I attained arahantship.”
“In the ninety-first aeon, the gift that I gave then— I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of my former giving.
‘The defilements are burnt away by me... [the rest as per the standard formula] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.’”

But having attained arahantship and reviewing her own practice, she spoke these verses as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), referring to the verses previously exchanged between her father and herself during the time when she was a stream-enterer:
“You sleep thinking, ‘I am a recluse,’ and you wake up thinking, ‘I am a recluse.
You praise only recluses; surely you will become a recluse yourself.”
“You bestow abundant food and drink upon the recluses;
Rohinī, I now ask you: for what reason are those recluses dear to you?
They have no desire for work, they are indolent, and they live dependent on what is given by others.”
“Those who are full of longing and desire for sweetness—why do you hold those ascetics dear?
“After a long time indeed, my dear, you have questioned me about the ascetics.
I shall describe to you their wisdom, virtue, and exertion.”
“Desiring work and free from laziness, they perform the highest task;
they abandon lust and hatred—for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
Those who act with purity shake off the three roots of evil.”
They have abandoned all evil; for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
Their bodily action is pure, and their verbal action is likewise;
their mental action is pure; for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
“Stainless like a conch shell or a pearl, pure within and without,
filled with bright qualities— for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
They are deeply learned, upholders of the Dhamma, noble ones who live according to the Dhamma.”
They teach the goal and the Dhamma; for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
“Learned, upholders of the Dhamma, noble ones who live by the Dhamma;
one-pointed in mind and mindful—for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.”
“Those who go far, who possess mindfulness, who speak with measured words, and who are not arrogant—they understand the end of suffering;
for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
From whatever village they depart, they do not look back at anything at all.”
“They go without longing; therefore, these ascetics are dear to me.
They do not store grain in granaries, nor in jars, nor in storehouses;
seeking only what is already prepared, therefore, these ascetics are dear to me.”
“They take no gold, nor silver, nor bullion;
they live by what is present. Therefore, these recluses are dear to me.
They have gone forth from various families and from various lands.”
“They cherish one another; for that reason, these ascetics are dear to me.
‘Truly it is for our welfare, O lady, that you were born into this family as Rohinī, possessing faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and having profound reverence for them.’”
“You understand this well: it is the unsurpassed field of merit.
These ascetics will accept our offering as well.
For here the sacrifice is established; it shall become vast for us.”
If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,
go for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha;
undertake the precepts, and that will be for your welfare.
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha, the Tādins;
I undertake the precepts, and that shall be for my welfare.
Formerly I was a kinsman of Brahmā, but now I am a true brahmin.”
“I am one who knows the Three Vedas, a learned scholar, a master of the Vedas, and a purified bath-graduate.
He recited these verses.
Among them, the first three verses were spoken by him because he did not wish to grant his daughter’s consent to the monks. Therein—
"O ascetic! means: you sleep even at the time of sleeping while praising "ascetic, ascetic," speaking only talk connected with ascetics.

"You wake up as 'ascetic! means: even when rising from sleep, you wake up having spoken thus, "ascetic," emerging from your slumber. "You praise only ascetics" means: at all times, [you praise] only ascetics, indeed only of ascetics.
Or, "you praise and extol his virtues": although you stand here in the form of a householder, I think that in your heart you will surely become a *samaṇī*.

Or alternatively, "you will surely become a *samaṇī*": although you now stand in the form of a householder, before long you will surely become a *samaṇī*, because your inclination and tendency are directed solely toward the *samaṇas*.
"Do you love them? he asked. "Now I ask you, Rohiṇī," said the brahmin, questioning his own daughter, "O mother Rohiṇī, I ask this of you now. "By what [means] are the ascetics dear to you?
he continued, "O mother Rohiṇī, whether sleeping or waking, at other times as well, you praise only the virtues of the ascetics; for what reason indeed [is this so]?"
The meaning is that ascetics have become dear to you.
Now, pointing out the faults in ascetics to his daughter, the brahmin spoke this verse beginning with “akammakāmā.
Therein, “akammakāmā” means not desiring action; they do not wish to perform any deed that brings benefit to themselves or others. “Alasā” means lazy.
"Those who live on what is given by others" means those whose habit is to subsist solely on what has been bestowed by others.
"Those who hope for it" means those who expect food, clothing, and so forth from that very source. "Those who desire the sweet" means those who long only for food that is delicious and sweet.
All of this refers to the faults imagined by the brahmin himself, as he remains ignorant of the true virtues of the ascetics.
Having heard this, Rohinī thought, “Now I have found the opportunity to speak of the virtues of the Noble Ones.
With a joyful heart and desiring to proclaim the virtues of the monks, she first expressed her gladness at their praise by reciting the verse, “At last, indeed, O father!
(cirassaṃ vata maṃ, tātā). In this, *cirassaṃ vata* means “at last indeed. *Tātā* is an address to her father.
"Of recluses" (*samaṇānam*) means: you ask about those who are dear to me, whether it be among recluses or of recluses. "Of them" (*tesam*) means: of the recluses.
"Wisdom, virtue, and exertion" (*paññāsīlaparakkama*) means: wisdom, virtue, and effort.
"I shall proclaim" (*kittayissāmi*) means: I shall speak of them. Having made this declaration, they proclaim them as "indolent and desiring no work"; therefore, it was said.
Having first resolved the fault, he spoke the words beginning with “desirous of work” (*kammakāmā*) in order to show the virtue that is its opposite.
Therein, they are "desirous of work" because they desire and wish for the work consisting of the major and minor duties (*vatta-paṭivatta*), which is the duty of a recluse, by way of fulfilling it.
Being properly engaged therein, they exert themselves by rising up again and again; thus, because they are not indolent, they are "not lazy" (*analasā*).
Furthermore, because they perform that very best and most excellent karma which leads to Nibbāna, they are "doers of the best karma.
And while performing it, because that practice is blameless, they abandon lust and hatred;
for in such a way that lust and hatred are abandoned, the recluses perform their work. Therefore, "I am dear to the recluses" means by virtue of that aforementioned right practice.
The meaning is: "The ascetics are dear to me.
"Three roots of evil" refers to the three unwholesome roots known as greed, hatred, and delusion.
"They shake off" means they eradicate; the meaning is that they abandon them. "Performers of purity" means those who perform blameless deeds. "All evil has been abandoned by them."
By the attainment of the supreme path, all their evil has been abandoned.
Having thus explained in detail the meaning briefly stated as “the ascetics are doers of pure deeds,” he spoke the verse beginning with “bodily action. That is indeed easy to understand.
“Stainless like conch shells and pearls” means they are free from impurity, like well-washed conch shells and like pearls, being devoid of the stains of passion and the like.
"Pure both internally and externally" (*suddhā santarabāhirā*): "Internally and externally" means internal and external;

thus, "pure both internally and externally" means pure in terms of intention and application (*suddhāsayapayoga*). "Full of bright qualities" (*puṇṇā sukkāna dhammānaṃ*): they are full of entirely bright, blameless qualities;
the meaning is that they are endowed with the aggregates of virtue, etc., of one beyond training (*asekha*).
They have heard much of the Suttas, Geyyas, and so forth; or, they are "learned" (bahussuta) because [the knowledge] has arisen through what was heard.

The meaning is that they are endowed with both the great learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and the great learning of realization (paṭivedha-bāhusacca). They "bear" (dhārenti) that very same twofold Dhamma, thus they are "bearers of the Dhamma" (dhammadhara).

They are "Noble Ones" (ariya) because they are restrained by the training rules (sikkhāpada) regarding the conduct and behavior of beings. By means of the Dhamma, that is, by the right method (ñāya)...
"Living" means those who live by the Dhamma. "Teaching the meaning and the Dhamma" means they speak of and clarify both the meaning of what was spoken and the Dhamma as the teaching.
Alternatively, they teach and declare that which does not deviate from the meaning and does not deviate from the Dhamma.
"With one-pointed minds" means with concentrated minds. "Mindful" means possessing established mindfulness.

"Dūraṅgamā" means gone to the forest; having left the vicinity of human habitation, they go far away, or by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), they go to a distant place as they wish—thus they are "far-going.
"Mantā" is said to mean wisdom (*paññā*); because of their habit of speaking with that [wisdom], they are "wise-speakers" (*mantabhāṇī*).
"Not agitated" (*anuddhatā*) means not excited, being free from restlessness (*uddhacca*) and possessing a tranquil mind. The end of suffering...
"Understanding" means they penetrate Nibbāna, which is the ultimate limit of the suffering of saṃsāra.

"They do not look back at anything" means that from whatever village they depart, they do not look back upon any being or any conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāra*) in that village with a sense of longing; rather, they go forth and depart without such longing.
"They do not open their storehouse" means those recluses do not open their own storehouse containing their personal property.
They do not leave food uncollected because they lack such a means of storage. “In a pot” (*kumbhi*) means in a cooking-pot.

“In a basket” (*khaḷopiya*) means in a wicker basket. “Seeking what is already prepared” (*pariniṭṭhitamesanā*) means seeking food that has already been cooked for the sake of others in other families.

“Gold” (*hirañña*) means a coin (*kahāpaṇa*). “Silver” (*rūpiya*) means silver. “Sustaining themselves with the present” (*paccuppannena yāpenti*) means they sustain their existence and maintain their physical being by not grieving over the past and not longing for the future, but by relying on the present.
“They cherish one another” means they cultivate friendship toward one another. The reading “they cherish” (*pihāyanti*) is also found; it has the same meaning.

Thus, having heard of the monks’ virtues from his daughter’s presence, that brahmin, with a mind full of serene confidence, spoke the words beginning with “For our benefit indeed,” while praising his daughter.
“Of us too” (*amhampi*) means “of ours as well. “The sacrificial gift” (*dakkhiṇa*) refers to the object to be given.
"Among these" means among these ascetics. "Sacrifice" refers to the practice of giving. "Abundant" means having abundant fruit. The rest is exactly as previously explained.

Thus, the brahmin, established in the refuges and the precepts, later became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), went forth into homelessness, and by increasing his insight (*vipassanā*) and establishing himself in *arahantship*, he reflected upon his own practice and uttered this inspired utterance (*udāna*).
She spoke the verse beginning with “brahmabandhu. Its meaning has already been explained above.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Rohinī is finished.
3. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Cāpā.
"Laṭṭhihattho pure āsī... and so forth are the verses of the Elder Nun Cāpā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various states of existence, gradually built up her roots of merit and gathered the requisites for liberation;
then, during the arising of this present Buddha, in a certain district of the Vaṅgahāra country...
She was reborn in Migaluddaka Village as the daughter of the chief hunter, and her name was Cāpā.
At that time, the Teacher, who was departing from the Seat of Enlightenment for Bārāṇasī to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, encountered Upaka the Ājīvaka and said:
"Friend, your faculties are serene; you are perfectly pure."
Having asked, "Your complexion is very bright and clear. Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher?
Or whose Dhamma do you approve? he replied:
"I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all; I am unsullied by any phenomena."
Having abandoned all, liberated through the destruction of craving, having realized this for myself through direct knowledge, whom should I point to as my teacher?
"I have no teacher, and no one equal to me is found;
in the world with its devas, there is no rival to me."
“I am indeed the Worthy One in the world; I am the unsurpassed Teacher.
I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One; I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
To set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, I shall go to the city of Kāsī.”
“In this world that has become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.
When the Teacher had thus proclaimed his own state as the Omniscient Buddha and the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, he, with a mind full of faith, said, “Indeed, friend, you are worthy;
you are a Conqueror of the Infinite,” and taking the wrong path, he departed for the country of Vaṅgahāra.
He arrived there and took up residence near a village of deer-hunters. There, the chief hunter attended upon him.

One day, while going out on a long hunt for deer, he commanded his daughter to look after the recluse, saying, "Do not neglect my Arahant," and departed with his sons and brothers-in-law. His daughter was beautiful and lovely to behold.
Then, at the time for alms-round, the Ājīvaka Upaka went to the hunter’s house;

seeing the bow that had been brought there to be served, he was overcome by lust and, unable even to eat, took the food with the vessel, went to his dwelling place, set the food aside in a corner, and thought: "If I get the bow, I shall live."

"If not, I shall die," she said, and lay down refusing food. On the seventh day, the deer-hunter returned and asked his daughter, "Why have you not attended upon my Arahant? She replied, "He came for only one day, and since then has not come again.
The hunter immediately went to the place where he was staying and asked, "Venerable sir, are you unwell? at his feet.
As he was rubbing [Upaka’s back], he asked him. Upaka merely turned over while yawning. He said, “Speak, venerable sir;
whatever I am able to do, I shall do it all. Upaka explained his own intention by way of a single method:
“But do you know any craft, venerable sir? “I know none,” he replied. “No, venerable sir.”
“How can one live as a householder without knowing any craft? He replied, “I do not know any craft;
however, I shall be your meat-provider and I will sell the meat.
The hunter said, “This is exactly what we also desire,” and having given him an upper garment, he had him stay for a few days in the house of his own friend.
On such a day, having brought her home, he gave his daughter [in marriage].
Then, as time passed, through their cohabitation, a son was born; they gave him the name Subhadda.
When he was crying, Cāpā would say, "Son of Upaka! Son of an Ājīvika! Son of a meat-eater! Do not..."
With the song of praise for his son beginning with "Do not weep, do not weep," he mocked Upaka.
He replied, "O Cāpā, do not think of me as 'helpless'; I have a companion named Anantajina, and I shall go into his presence.
Knowing that he was thus distressed, Cāpā spoke to him in that same manner again and again. One day, by her [doing so], he...

Having spoken thus, he became angry and began to depart. Although she tried to win him over by saying various things to him, he did not yield to her persuasion and set out toward the western direction.
At that time, the Blessed One, dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, addressed the monks: “Whoever...”
“Monks, today Anantajina has come here and asks, ‘Where is Anantajina? Send him to me.
Upaka, asking “Where does Anantajina dwell? from place to place, eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.
Entering the monastery and standing in the middle of it, he asked, “Where is Anantajina? The monks [said to him]:
They led him into the presence of the Blessed One. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he said, "Does the Blessed One know me? "Yes, I know you," [the Blessed One replied].
"But where have you been living for all this time? "In the country of Vaṅgahāra, Bhante.
"Upaka, now that you have grown old, will you be able to go forth? "I shall go forth, Bhante. The Teacher—
He commanded a certain bhikkhu: “Come, bhikkhu, ordain this man. He ordained him.
Having been ordained, he received a meditation subject from the Teacher and applied himself to its cultivation;
before long, having established himself in the fruit of non-returning, he passed away and was reborn in the Aviha heaven, attaining arahantship at the very moment of his rebirth.
He attained [it]. Among the seven beings who were reborn in the Aviha heaven and immediately upon rebirth attained Arahatship, he was one of them. For it is said:
“Seven bhikkhus, reborn in Aviha, were liberated;
With lust and hatred utterly destroyed, they have crossed over the attachment to the world.”
“Upaka, Upālagaṇḍa, and Pakkusāti—those three;
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Siṅgi:
having abandoned their human bodies, they have attained union with the divine.”
When Upaka had departed, Cāpā, her heart filled with world-weariness, entrusted the boy to her grandfather.
Following the path previously taken by Upaka, she went to Sāvatthī, where she received the going-forth in the presence of the bhikkhunīs.
Performing the work of insight (vipassanā), she established herself in Arahantship through the successive stages of the path. Reflecting upon her own spiritual progress, she—
Having brought together as a single collection the verses previously spoken by Upaka and himself, he uttered them in the form of an *udāna*:
“In former times he was one with a staff in hand; now he is a deer-hunter.
Through his craving, he has fallen into a terrible mire; he was unable to reach the further shore.”
“Thinking me to be well-composed, she even gratified her son;
yet having severed the bond of Cāpā, I shall go forth once again.
Do not be angry with me, O Great Hero; do not be angry with me, O Great Sage.”
For one overcome by anger, there is no purity; how then could there be austerity?
"I shall depart from the reed-thicket; anger does not enter the reed-thicket.
They bind with the form of a woman those ascetics who live according to the Dhamma."
“Come, Kāḷa, turn back; enjoy sensual pleasures as before.
Both I and those who are my kinsmen shall be under your control.
And from this lute, give me a fourth part, just as you have spoken to me.”
For a person who is thus impassioned, that would indeed be something sublime—
like a black *takkarī* tree in full bloom upon a mountain peak,
like a flowering *dālimalaṭṭhī*, or like a *pāṭalī* tree in the midst of an island.
“O you whose limbs are anointed with yellow sandalwood, who wear the finest cloth of Kāsī—
leaving me, who am beautiful and at peace, to whom do you go?
Like a fowler wishing to capture a bird, you seek to bind me.”
"With this unlovely form, you shall not trouble me.
And this fruit of a son, O Kāḷa, which was produced by you for me— leaving me,
who am peaceful and possessed of a son, where are you going?"
“Wise men abandon their sons, and then their kinsmen, and then their wealth;
the great heroes go forth, like an elephant that has severed its bonds.
Now, with either a staff or a knife, [strike] this son of yours.”
"I will crush you to the ground; you shall not escape the grief for your son.
Even if you fall into the path of jackals or dogs, O vile woman, you will never bring me back to the state of being a mother to a son."
“Come now, venerable sir, where will you go, Kāḷa?
To which village, market town, city, or royal capital?
“We were formerly leaders of a group, not ascetics though imagining ourselves to be ascetics.”
We wandered from village to village, through towns and royal capitals.
"For there is that Blessed One, the Buddha, by the Nerañjarā River;
for the abandoning of all suffering, he teaches the Dhamma to living beings."
"I shall go into his presence; he will be my teacher.
"Now you should offer salutation to me, the unsurpassed Lord of the World;
and having performed a circumambulation, you should dedicate the merit."
“Indeed, this is obtainable for us, just as you have spoken to me:
we shall now offer our salutation to the unsurpassed Lord of the World.
Having performed the circumambulation, I shall designate the offering.”
Then Kāḷa departed toward the Nerañjarā River;
there he saw the Fully Awakened One teaching the state of deathlessness:
“Suffering, the arising of suffering, and the overcoming of suffering.”
"The Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
Having bowed at his feet and circumambulated him,
and having informed Cāpā, I went forth into the homeless life.
"The threefold knowledge has been attained; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished"—these verses he spoke.
Therein, "staff-in-hand" means holding a staff. "In the past" refers to his former time as a wandering ascetic, [when he encountered] fierce oxen, dogs, and so forth.
For the sake of protection, he wandered about carrying a staff in his hand.
Now, being a deer-hunter—meaning he has now become a hunter, a follower of Māghava, through association and living together with deer-hunters—he fell into a snare. "Āsāya" means by craving (*taṇhā*).

There is also the reading "āsayā," which means "by reason of his underlying disposition" (*ajjhāsaya*). "Palipā" refers to the mire of sensual desire (*kāma-paṅka*) and the mire of wrong view (*diṭṭhi-paṅka*).
It is "terrible" (*ghorā*) because it brings about vast and unknown calamities and because it is dreadful.
"He was unable to reach the further shore" means that he was unable to go to, or reach, *nibbāna*, which is the further shore of that very mire;
Upaka speaks thus with reference to himself.
“Thinking me well-intoxicated” means perceiving me as being thoroughly intoxicated, having reached a state of pride, or as being attached and negligent due to the lure of sensual desires.

“Cāpā delighted her son” means that Cāpā, the daughter of a deer-hunter, delighted and played with her son by teasing him with such words as, “You are the son of an Ājīvaka,” and so forth. “Thinking me asleep” means...
And they recite: "Thinking 'He is well-satisfied' (supati) is the meaning.

"Having severed the bond upon the bow" means having cut the bond of defilements that had arisen within you regarding the bow. "I shall go forth once more" means that for a second time, I shall go forth.
Now she says, "I have no need of him"; hearing this, Cāpā asks for forgiveness, saying, "Do not be angry with me."
He spoke this verse. Regarding that: "Do not be angry with me" means: do not be angry with me merely because of my playful behavior. "O Great Hero, O Great Sage"—this he addresses to Upaka.
For she, considering that he had gone forth in the past and now desired to go forth once more, said "Great Sage," hoping for his forbearance.
Therefore he said: "For there is no purity for one overcome by anger; from where [could it come]?"
The intention [of Cāpā] was: "If you cannot endure even this much austerity (*tapas*), how will you tame the mind, or how will you practice austerity?
Then, having gone to Nāḷa, when he was told by Cāpā, "Do you wish to live?", he said: "I shall depart from Nāḷa; anger dwells in Nāḷa.
Who here would dwell in Nāḷa? I shall indeed depart from Nāḷa itself. For he...
His birthplace was there; having departed from there, he went forth into homelessness. This refers to the region near the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa) in the kingdom of Magadha.
"Binding with the form of a woman, O Cāpā, those recluses who live by the Dhamma":
you stand binding with your own female form—by means of feminine gestures and coquettish movements—those righteous renunciants who live according to the Dhamma.
The intention is: "Because of this [conduct], I have now become such as I am; therefore, I renounce it.
When this was said, Cāpā, wishing to turn him back, spoke the verse beginning with "Come, Kāḷā. Its meaning is:
O Kāḷa—so called because of your dark complexion—O Upaka, come, turn back; do not depart. Enjoy sensual pleasures as you did before, both I and those...
“I have kinsmen; they have all been brought under your control and made subject to you because of your desire for me to depart.
Having heard this, Upaka spoke the verse beginning with “O Cāpā. In that context, *cāpe* means “O Cāpā.
For she received the name Cāpā because her limbs were like a bow (*cāpa*), hence she is called “Cāpā. O Cāpā, as you speak now—
"Whatever you have said, you should practice such endearing conduct toward me as is one-fourth of that.

That might indeed be a great thing for a man who is attached to you and overcome by passion; however, I am now detached from sensual pleasures in your regard, and therefore I do not abide by Cāpā’s words.
This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, Cāpā, wishing to arouse his attachment toward herself, said, "O Kāḷaṅginī. In that context, "Kāḷa" is an address to her.
"Aṅginī" means one endowed with beautiful limbs. "Iva" is a particle used for comparison.
"Takkāriṃ pupphitaṃ girimuddhani" means like a well-flowered branch of the *dālima* (pomegranate) tree standing upon the summit of a mountain. "Ukkāgāriṃ" [is as follows:]
And some read [the text] as *aṅgatthilaṭṭhiṃ viya*, which means "like a stalk of *atthila*. The term *girimuddhani* is stated for the purpose of showing that its beauty is unimpaired by anything.
Some, having cited the reading *kāliṅginīṃ*, explain its meaning as being "like a *kumbhaṇḍa* creeper.
*Phullaṃ dālimalaṭṭhiṃ va* means "like a flowering *bījapūra* creeper. *Antodīpeva pāṭaliṃ* means "like a *pāṭali* tree within the island."
"Like a flowering pāṭali tree"—here, the mention of a lamp is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the miracle of her beauty.
"With limbs anointed with yellow sandalwood" means one whose entire body is smeared with red sandalwood. "Wearing the finest Kāsī cloth" means wearing garments of the most excellent Kāsī silk.

"Such as me" (taṃ maṃ) means such as myself. "Possessing beauty" (rūpavatiṃ) means being endowed with physical form. "Being" (santiṃ) means while I am present. "Leaving whom do you go? means abandoning whom do you depart?
"Of what being, for what cause, or by what reason do you go away, having abandoned, relinquished, and forsaken us?
Following this, there are only verses of question and answer, with three concluding verses at the end.
In that context, "like a fowler" means like one who hunts birds. "With an attractive form" refers to the grooming of the body, such as the decoration of the hair and so forth.
"And by means of clothing, ornaments, and so forth"—the meaning is: by means of conditioned form (*rūpa*), beauty, fame, and cleverness.
"You will not trouble me" means: as before, you will not now be able to trouble me.
"The fruit consisting of a son" means: the fruit known as a son, namely, the birth of a son.
“Wise” means possessing wisdom; the intention is that they are endowed with the wisdom that discerns the peril in saṃsāra.
For it is they who, having abandoned their circle of relatives—whether small or large—or their mass of wealth, go forth into homelessness. Thus he said:
“The great heroes go forth, like a noble elephant breaking its bonds,” as an elephant breaks its iron shackles.
The meaning is that they go forth with great energy, having severed the bonds of household life, and not with inferior energy.

"With a staff" means with whatever kind of staff. "With a razor" means with a blade. "Or I shall crush them on the ground" means I will afflict them by throwing them down upon the earth and striking or piercing them.
"You shall not go because of grief for your son" means you shall not go on account of the sorrow caused by your son.
“Padāhisī” means you will show. “Puttakatte” means for the sake of a son. “Jammī” is an address to her; it means “wretched one.
Now, having granted him permission to go, [the Buddha] spoke the verse beginning with “Handa kho” in order to know his destination. The other [the son] said:
“Previously I stood having taken up a teaching that does not lead to liberation, but now, in this teaching that leads to liberation, of the Conqueror of the Infinite...”
Desiring to remain within the Teaching, he said, "We were," and so forth, showing that he would go into his presence. Therein, *gaṇino* means leaders of a group (*gaṇadharā*).
*Assamaṇā* means those who have not pacified their evil. *Samaṇamānino* means those who perceive themselves as having pacified their evil.
*Vicarimhā* (we wandered) refers to him speaking while including himself among Pūraṇa and the others.

"Near the Nerañjarā" means in the vicinity of the river Nerañjarā, on its bank. "The Buddha" refers to one who has attained full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*); he speaks with the intention that after attaining full enlightenment, the Blessed One dwelt right there at all times while teaching the Dhamma.
"Now you should offer my salutation" means you should speak my salutation; the sense is that you should speak to the Supreme Lord of the World on my behalf.
"And having performed a circumambulation, you should designate the gift" refers to the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having circumambulated [the stupa] three times and paid homage at the four places, he then, while assigning the merit to me, should dedicate the circumambulation;
for, because he has previously heard of the Buddha’s qualities and is thus endowed with the necessary causes, he speaks thus:
“This indeed can be obtained by us”—meaning that this merit from performing the circumambulation can be given by us to you, and not otherwise.
The intention is that it is not possible for him to turn back or to enjoy sensual pleasures as he did before. "They shall blame" means: I shall declare the blame regarding your veneration.
"He" refers to Kāḷa; "he saw" means he perceived.

In this teaching by the Teacher, because the discourse on truth is the primary focus and nothing exists apart from it, the words beginning with "suffering" are spoken; the rest is exactly as previously explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Cāpā is finished. 4.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Sundarī begins with the words, "O lady, these children of yours are dead. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as the necessary condition for the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various births, she was reborn in a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhu, thirty-one aeons ago.
Having reached maturity, one day she saw the Teacher wandering for alms;
with a mind full of faith, she gave him alms and paid homage to him by prostrating herself at his five points. The Teacher [perceived] her mental clarity of faith...
Having understood this and offered her appreciation, she departed. By virtue of that meritorious deed, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas;
there, having remained for the full span of her lifespan and enjoyed celestial splendor, she passed away from that state.
Wandering on from one happy destination to another, her wisdom became fully matured, and during the present arising of a Buddha, she was born as the daughter of a brahmin named Sujāta in Bārāṇasī.
Having offered the sacrifice, she was reborn. Because of her perfection of form, she was named Sundarī. When she reached the age of maturity, her younger brother passed away.
Then her father, overcome with grief for his son, wandered here and there until he encountered the Elder Nun Vāsiṭṭhī;
questioning her about the means to dispel his sorrow, he spoke the verses beginning with, "O lady, my children have become spirits... and so forth.

She spoke two verses. Knowing that she was overcome by grief and wishing to dispel it, the Elder Nun spoke the two verses beginning with “Many hundreds of sons,” and explained her own state of being free from sorrow.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin asked, “Noble lady, how have you become so free from sorrow?
In response, the Elder Nun described the virtues of the Triple Gem.
Then the brahmin, having asked, "Where is the Teacher? and hearing that he was currently staying at Mithilā, immediately yoked his chariot and went to Mithilā by chariot.
Approaching the Teacher, he paid homage, engaged in polite conversation, and sat down to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. He [listened to] the Dhamma...

Having heard this, he gained faith, went forth into homelessness, and by applying himself with diligence and exertion, established insight meditation (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship* on the third day.
Then the charioteer, taking the chariot, went to Bārāṇasī and reported the news to the brahmin woman.
Upon hearing that her son had gone forth, Sundarī said, "Mother, I too shall go forth."
She asked her mother for permission. Her mother said, "Whatever wealth exists in this house, all of that is yours;
you are the heiress of this family, so take charge of it, enjoy all these riches, and do not go forth.
She replied, "I have no need for wealth, Mother; I shall indeed go forth," and having obtained her mother's consent, she [prepared] a great...
Having discarded her prosperity like a globule of spittle, she went forth into homelessness. Having gone forth, while still a *sikkhamānā*, she developed insight;

by striving and exerting herself, and because her knowledge had reached maturity through the perfection of its causes, she attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). Thus it is said in the *Apadāna*:
“As I was wandering for alms, I took up a ladleful of rice and gave it to Vessabhu, the Great Seer, the Best of Buddhas.
Having accepted it, the Perfectly Awakened One, Vessabhu, the Leader of the World— ”
The Teacher, standing on the street, gave me his blessing of appreciation:
“Having given this alms-food with a ladle, you shall go to Tāvatiṃsa;
there you shall exercise the sovereignty of the Great Lord over the thirty-six divine kings.”
“You shall exercise the great sovereignty of fifty wheel-turning monarchs;
you will obtain everything desired by your mind at all times.
Having experienced such prosperity, you will go forth into homelessness, free from worldly attachments.”
“Having fully understood all taints, one will extinguish them,
being free from taints. Having said this, the Fully Awakened One, Vessabhū, the Leader of the World, the Hero,
rose up into the sky like a king of swans in the air.
“An excellent gift was given by me; the perfection of my sacrifice was well-offered.
Having given a spoonful of alms-food, I attained the unshakable state.
Thirty-one eons ago, that gift which I then gave—”
“I do not know a state of woe; this is the fruit of giving alms to a bhikkhu.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me... [as before] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having attained arahantship, she dwelt in the bliss of the fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna. Later on, regarding the Teacher...”
Thinking, “I shall roar the lion’s roar in the presence [of the Teacher],” she took leave of her preceptor, departed from Bārāṇasī, and together with many bhikkhunīs, gradually reached Sāvatthī.

Having approached the Teacher and paid homage to him, she stood to one side; then, after being greeted by the Teacher, she was addressed by him through the manifestation of her status as his own biological daughter and so forth.
She declared her attainment of final knowledge (*aññā*). Then, beginning with her mother, her entire circle of kinsmen and attendants went forth into homelessness.
Later, reflecting upon her own practice, she uttered this inspired verse (*udāna*), beginning with the stanza spoken by her father:
“In former times, O lady, you were devouring your own children as if they were dead;”
“By day and by night, you are exceedingly tormented. Having now devoured them all,
that brahmin woman with her hundred sons— Vāseṭṭhī,
for what reason are you not tormented intensely?”
“Many hundreds of sons, and hundreds of kinsmen,
have been devoured in the past, both mine and yours, O brahmin.
Having understood the escape from birth and death, I— ”
“I do not grieve, nor do I weep, nor am I tormented by distress.
‘O Vāseṭṭhī, you speak such a wonderful word!
Having understood whose Dhamma do you speak such words?’”
“That Buddha, the Brahmin, has come toward the city of Mithilā;
for the abandoning of all suffering, he teaches the Dhamma to living beings.
Having heard the Dhamma of that Arahant, O Brahmā, which is free from acquisitions...”
There, having understood the true Dharma, I dispelled my grief for my son.
"I too shall go toward the city of Mithilā;
perhaps that Blessed One might liberate me from all suffering."
The brahmin saw the Buddha, utterly liberated and free from acquisitions;
the Sage, who had gone beyond suffering, taught him the Dhamma:
suffering, the origin of suffering, and the transcendence of suffering.
“The Noble Eightfold Path, which leads to the stilling of suffering.
There, having understood the True Dhamma, he chose the going-forth;
well-born after three nights, he attained the three knowledges.
“Come, charioteer, go and bring back the chariot;
inquire after the health of the brahmin lady. The brahmin has now gone forth;
well-born, in three nights he has attained the three knowledges.”
Then, taking the chariot and the charioteer along with the thousand [pieces of gold],
he said to the brahmin woman, “The brahmin has now gone forth;
Sujāta, in three nights, has attained the threefold knowledge.”
“Having heard of the brahmin who possesses the threefold knowledge, I give this horse-chariot and a thousand coins to you, O charioteer,
along with a bowl full of alms. Let the horse-chariot and the thousand coins be yours alone, O brahmin.”
“I too shall go forth into homelessness in the presence of the one of excellent wisdom.
Having abandoned elephants, cattle, gems, earrings, and this flourishing household wealth—your father has gone forth; enjoy these riches, Sundarī.”
"You are the heir in this family.
Having abandoned elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, earrings, and this delightful household wealth,
my father has gone forth, tormented by grief for his son."
“I too shall go forth, tormented by grief for my brother.
“May that intention of yours be fulfilled, O Sundarī, which you have desired:
alms-food gathered from what has been set aside, gleanings, and a robe made of discarded rags.”
Having attained these, they are free from taints in the world beyond:
“O Noble Lady, while training, my divine eye was purified;
I know my former dwellings, where I lived in the past.”
“Relying on you, O auspicious one, O Elder who brings splendor to the Saṅgha, the three knowledges have been attained and the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.
Grant me leave, Noble Lady; I wish to go to Sāvatthī.”
"I shall roar the lion’s roar in the presence of the Best of Buddhas:
'Behold, Sundarī, the Teacher— golden-hued with tawny skin,
the tamer of the untamed, the Perfectly Awakened One who is fearless from all sides.'"
“Behold Sundarī approaching— liberated, free from acquisitions,
devoid of lust, dissociated, having done what was to be done,
and undefiled. Having departed from Benares, she has come into your presence.”
“O Great Hero, your beautiful female disciple pays homage at your feet.
‘You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher; O Brahmin, I am your own daughter, born from your mouth, one who has accomplished her task and is free from taints.’”
“Welcome to you, O blessed lady; it was not a long journey for you from there.
For thus do those who are tamed come, to pay homage at the feet of the Teacher—those free from passion, detached, having done what was to be done, and free from taints.”
He recited these verses.
In them, *petāni* means "the dead. *Bhoti* is used as a form of address to her. *Puttāni* is stated with a change of gender;
the meaning is "the deceased sons. Only one son of hers was dead, yet the brahmin, due to his long-standing grief—
Having become distressed, she wandered about; thinking, "I suppose many sons of hers have died," she spoke using the plural form.
Likewise: "Having devoured them all today, she is one whose hundred sons [are gone]. The word *khādamānā* is a term of reproach used according to worldly convention.
For in the world, when the children of a woman die one after another as they are born, those who censure her call her "one who devours her sons" (*puttakhādinī*), and so forth.
They say: "Atīva" means exceedingly, excessively, or intensely. "Paritappasi" means you are tormented;
it is to be construed with "pure" (formerly). This is the summary of the meaning here:
O Vāseṭṭhī, formerly, having lost your children, you wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, grieving, lamenting, and utterly overwhelmed by sorrow.
“Sājjāti” means she who was then is she who is today; the meaning is, “she who you are now. Alternatively, the reading is “sajjā. “By what quality? means by what reason.

“They have been eaten”—the Elder Nun speaks using the very same phrasing as the brahmin had used. Or, she says this with reference to species such as tigers, leopards, and cats, [meaning] they have been eaten.
“In the past” means in the past section; the meaning is, “in past existences. “Of both me and you” means of both myself and yourself.
"Having known the escape from birth and death" means having penetrated with the knowledge of the path that which is the escape from birth, aging, and death—namely, *nibbāna*.
"And yet I did not despair" means I did not fall into distress; the sense is that I did not undergo despondency.
"It is wonderful indeed" means it is marvelous (*acchariya*). For that which was previously non-existent is called "wonderful."
"Uttering such words"—meaning speech that demonstrates the absence of sorrow and so forth, saying: "I do not grieve, I do not weep, nor am I tormented.

"Whose Dhamma have you understood?"—the Teacher asks this regarding both the Master and the teaching, implying: "Since such a state as this cannot be attained [by anyone else], whose Dhamma have you understood that you speak these words? Thus he questions him concerning the Teacher and the Dispensation.

"Without substrate" (*nirupadhi*) means free from suffering. "Having understood the true Dhamma" (*viññātasaddhamma*) means having penetrated the Dhamma of the Noble Truths. "He dispelled" (*byapānudi*) means he extracted and abandoned.

"Completely liberated" (*vippamutta*) means entirely freed, disconnected from all defilements and from all states of existence. "To him" (*svassa*) means to that brahmin, [the Blessed One] the Fully Enlightened One.
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that teaching of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
"Deliver the chariot"—this means "deliver this chariot to the brahmin woman.
"And also a thousand"—the construction is: "taking also a thousand kahāpaṇas intended for the expenses of the journey, deliver them.
