"A horse-chariot" means a chariot yoked with horses. "A full bowl" refers to a gift given out of satisfaction.
When the brahmin lady was thus giving the gift of satisfaction, the charioteer, refusing to accept it and saying,
"Let it be yours alone," recited the verse and went directly into the presence of the Teacher, where he went forth. Once the charioteer had gone forth,
the brahmin lady addressed her daughter Sundarī, urging her to take up the life of a householder, and spoke the verse beginning with "The elephant and the ox."
In this context: *hatthī* means elephants; *gavassa* means cows and horses; *maṇikuṇḍalañca* means gems and earrings;

*phītañcimaṃ gahavibhavaṃ pahāya* means having abandoned this abundant household wealth—consisting of the aforementioned varieties such as elephants, as well as the unmentioned varieties such as fields, lands, silver, gold, and so forth—and other household requisites.
“Having abandoned everything, including male and female slaves, your father has gone forth into homelessness. Enjoy the wealth, Sundarī!”—meaning, “O Sundarī, you should enjoy these riches.
“You are the heir in this family”—meaning, “For you indeed are worthy of the inheritance in this family.
Having heard this, Sundarī, manifesting her own inclination toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*), spoke the verse beginning with “Of elephants and cattle,” and so forth.
Then his mother, urging him toward renunciation itself, spoke one and a half stanzas beginning with “May that succeed for you.
Therein, “O Sundarī, that which you aspire to”—O Sundarī, that which you now aspire to and desire;
“may that intention of yours for the going forth, may that longing for the going forth, succeed; may it be accomplished without obstacle. “Alms from house to house” means... [from house to house].

“Alms” (*bhikkhā*) refers to the portion of alms-food obtained after having established oneself [in a practice]. “Gleaning” (*uñcha*) means wandering from house to house for that purpose and standing in designated spots.
“These” refers to the *uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa* (leftover alms) and so forth. “They overcome” means they overcome them by relying on the strength of their legs without being discouraged;
the sense is that they accomplish them.
Then Sundarī, having replied to her mother, “Very well, mother,” went out and proceeded to the nuns’ dwelling.
While still a trainee (sikkhamānā), she realized the threefold knowledge (tisso vijjā).
Thinking, “I shall go into the presence of the Teacher,” she informed her preceptor and went to Sāvatthī together with the nuns. Therefore it was said: “I am a trainee, noble ladies,” and so forth.
In this context, "by me, while being a trainee" means by me while still a *sikkhamānā*. "Noble lady" (*ayye*) is an address to her own preceptor (*upajjhāyā*).
"O auspicious one, it is through you that the Elder of the Saṅgha shines"—this refers to the Elder of the Bhikkhunī-Saṅgha;
she is called "auspicious" (*kalyāṇī*) because she possesses the qualities of virtue and so forth that cause the Elder of the Saṅgha to shine through her seniority and her steadfastness.
"Venerable lady, it was by relying on you as a spiritual friend that I attained the three knowledges and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching"—this is the construction [of the sentence].
"Icche" means "I wish. "Sāvatthi gantave" means "to go to Sāvatthī. "I shall roar the lion’s roar" is said with reference specifically to the declaration of final knowledge (*aññā-byākaraṇa*).
Then, Sundarī gradually reached Sāvatthī, entered the monastery, and [saw] the Teacher seated upon the Dharma-seat.
Seeing this, experiencing sublime joy and gladness, she addressed herself and said, "Behold, Sundarī!
"Gold-colored" means having the color of gold. "With golden skin" means having skin resembling refined gold. And here, the Blessed One is called "gold-colored" by virtue of his yellow complexion;
yet, it was as if he had been properly polished with natural vermilion.
Having said "golden-colored" (*hemavaṇṇa*) to show that she resembles a well-polished golden mirror after being anointed, he says "green-skinned" (*harittaca*).

"Behold me, Sundarī, as I approach"—by this, she addresses the Blessed One, saying "behold me," who bears the name Sundarī, as she comes. By the words beginning with "completely liberated" (*vippamutta*), she speaks while manifesting the expansion of rapture (*pīti*) as she explains her state of liberation.
Furthermore, in order to dispel the doubts of those who might wonder, "From where has she come? Where has she come from? And what is this Sundarī like? [she speaks].

Having spoken the verse beginning with “From Bārāṇasī,” he uttered the verse beginning with “You are the Buddha” in order to make clearer the meaning already stated there by the words “and the female disciple.
Its meaning is as follows: In this world with its devas, you alone are the omniscient Buddha;
because you instruct me appropriately according to the ultimate truths pertaining to both the present life and the future life, you are my Teacher, and I am—
The Blessed One said: "The Brahmin woman whose taints are destroyed is 'born from your breast' because she was born of the noble lineage produced by your exertion;
she is 'born from your mouth' because she was born through the Noble Path, which is the mouth of the Dispensation and through which the sound of the Dhamma proceeds from your mouth;
she is 'one who has done what was to be done' because she has completed the tasks such as full comprehension; and she is 'taintless' because all taints have been utterly exhausted."
Then the Teacher, welcoming her arrival, spoke this verse: "Welcome to you. Its meaning is as follows:
You who have understood, exactly as it is, the Dhamma realized by me—to you, O blessed and beautiful lady, your coming here into my presence is a welcome coming.
For that very reason, it is not a difficult coming; it is no ill-coming.
Why? Because they have come with their senses thus subdued, O beautiful one; for just as you are, so too have they been tamed by the supreme restraint of the Noble Path.

Therefore, being entirely free from passion, with all fetters utterly severed, liberated, having accomplished their task, and free from taints, they come as worshippers at the feet of the Teacher. Thus, the construction is: "Therefore, welcome to you; you have not come unwelcomed."
The commentary on the *Sundarītherīgāthā* is finished.
5. Commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Subhā Kammāradhītā:
The verses beginning with "Daharāham" (I am young) belong to the Elder Nun Subhā, the daughter of a smith. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas.

Accumulating wholesome kamma that serves as the necessary condition for turning away from existence in various states of being, she gradually cultivated the roots of merit and gathered the requisites for liberation.
Wandering only through happy destinies, her wisdom became fully matured.
In this present era of a Buddha’s appearance, she was reborn in Rājagaha as the daughter of a certain goldsmith; because of the splendor of her physical perfection, she was named Subhā.
That was her name. Having gradually reached the age of discretion, she conceived faith in the Teacher upon his entry into Rājagaha;
one day, approaching the Blessed One and paying homage to him, she sat down to one side.
Seeing that her faculties were mature, the Teacher taught her the Dhamma containing the Four Noble Truths in accordance with her disposition. At that very moment, she—
Adorned with the thousandfold method, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Later, seeing the faults in the household life, she went forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī;

established in the virtue of a bhikkhunī, she devoted herself to meditation for the sake of the higher paths. Her relatives approached her from time to time, inviting her with sensual pleasures and [offering] abundant wealth.
They entice her by showing off their wealth. One day, when those who had come to her presence presented themselves, she explained the danger inherent in household life and sensual pleasures;

having preached the Dhamma with twenty-four verses beginning with “I am young,” she rendered them dispassionate, sent them away, and applied herself to the work of insight, purifying her faculties and practicing meditation.
Having exerted herself with diligence, she attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Having reached arahantship, she said:
“In my youth, while dressed in white, I heard the Dhamma;
for me, being heedful, there was the realization of the Truth.”
“Then, I developed a profound distaste for all sensual pleasures;
seeing fear in personal existence (sakkāya), I longed only for renunciation.
Having abandoned my circle of kinsmen as well as my slaves and laborers,”
"The villages and fields are flourishing, delightful and full of joy.
Yet, having abandoned not a small amount of wealth,
I have gone forth out of faith in this well-proclaimed True Dhamma."
“It would not be fitting for him to long for nothingness, he who,
having discarded gold and silver, has come back again.
For neither silver nor gold leads to enlightenment, nor to peace.”
This is not worthy of a recluse; this is not the wealth of the Noble Ones.
It is intoxicating and exhilarating, deluding and increasing passion;
it is fraught with danger and much trouble, and herein there is no lasting stability.
“Attached to this world and heedless, men with defiled minds,
hostile toward one another, create widespread strife. Killing, bondage,
affliction, loss, sorrow, and lamentation— ”
For those who are deeply immersed in sensual pleasures, much ruin is seen.
"Therefore, my kinsmen, why do you entice me with sensual pleasures as if I were an enemy?
Know me to be one who has gone forth, seeing danger in sensual pleasures."
“By means of gold and silver, the taints are not exhausted;
sensual desires are enemies, murderers, adversaries, and bonds of arrows.
Therefore, my kinsmen, like enemies, why do you entice me with sensual pleasures?”
“Know me as one who has gone forth, shaven-headed and clad in the outer robe.
Alms gathered from house to house and gleanings, and a rag-robe for clothing—
this indeed is fitting for me, the support of one who is homeless.”
“Sensual pleasures, both those of the devas and those of humans, have been cast away by the Great Seers.
Having been liberated in the secure state, they have attained unshakable happiness.
May I not encounter sensual pleasures, in which no refuge is to be found.”
Sensual desires are enemies and murderers, like a mass of blazing fire—painful.
This is an obstacle, a danger, full of affliction and thorns;
it is a most treacherous greed, a great gateway to delusion.
“An affliction of terrifying form are sensual pleasures, like the heads of serpents;
yet fools, blinded and being worldlings, take delight in them.
For many beings in the world, lacking true knowledge, are mired in the mud of sensual pleasures.”
They do not know the limit of birth and death.
"Driven by the cause of sensual desire, people mostly tread upon the path that leads to miserable rebirths—
a path that brings disease upon themselves."
“Thus sensual desires produce enemies, they are tormenting and defiling;
they are worldly baits, binding, and the shackles of death.
Sensual desires are intoxicating, boastful, and the afflictors of the mind.”
It was swiftly cast by Māra for the defilement of beings:
"Sensual pleasures have infinite dangers, much suffering, and great poison;
they offer little gratification, provoke conflict, and wither the bright side [of virtue]."
“Having committed such a deed, this calamity caused by sensual desire,
I shall not return to that [world], always delighting in Nibbāna.
Having crossed over the strife of sensual desires, I long for the state of coolness.”
“I shall dwell with diligence for the destruction of all fetters.
I will follow that straight path, the noble eightfold way— sorrowless, stainless, and secure— by which the great seers have crossed over.”
“Behold this Subhā, daughter of a smith, established in the Dhamma;
having attained the imperturbable, she meditates at the foot of a tree.
Having gone forth today on the eighth day, she is faithful and adorned by the true Dhamma.”
Vinītuppalavaṇṇā, possessing the three knowledges,
a slayer of death: she is free, debtless, a bhikkhunī with developed faculties,
detached from all bonds, having done what was to be done, and free from taints.
“Sakka, together with the host of gods, approached by means of his psychic power and paid homage to Subhā, the daughter of the smith”—these verses he spoke.
Therein, “I was young, dressed in pure garments, when I formerly heard the Dhamma”: because in the past I was young...
While still young, dressed in pure garments, wearing clean clothes, and adorned with ornaments, I heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher.
For me, being heedful, there was the realization of Truth;
for as I reflected upon the Dhamma as I had heard it, I became heedful, established mindfulness, and resolved upon virtue while practicing meditation.
While I was devotedly practicing, there occurred the realization of the Four Noble Truths—the penetration [of them] beginning with "This is suffering" and so forth.

From that point on, I developed a profound distaste for all sensual pleasures. For that reason—namely, because of having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher and because of having realized the Truths—I felt a very intense and extreme [disgust] toward all sensual pleasures, whether among humans or those of the devas.

I experienced discontent and longing. Having seen with the eye of knowledge that there is fear—the state of being fearful—within *sakkāya*, the five aggregates of clinging, I yearn for, indeed long for, and aspire to renunciation alone, which is the going-forth and Nibbāna itself.
"And slaves and laborers" means both slaves and laborers; this is stated using a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). "Village lands" means...
"In the village" refers to fields where early and late crops grow, or fields included within the village boundaries. "Prosperous" means flourishing.
"Delightful" means agreeable. "In joy" means being joyful; this is to be connected with the phrase "having abandoned a mass of wealth.
"Property" means one's own wealth—the articles of possession such as gems, gold, silver, and so forth. "Not small" means extensive.
“Having abandoned” (*pahāya*) is the construction. Thus, “having gone forth through faith” means:

having abandoned a vast circle of kinsmen and a great mass of wealth in the manner described by the passage beginning with “I, having left my circle of relatives,” and having developed faith in the objects of faith—the actions, the fruits of action, and the Three Jewels—through faith, one goes forth from the home into the well-expounded True Dhamma by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
I have gone forth in this noble discipline so well proclaimed.
For one who has thus gone forth, it is not fitting to return to those sensual pleasures that were abandoned.
Indeed, "striving for nothingness," I desire only the state of having nothing and the state of being without possessions. As for gold and silver—
How could a person who, having discarded gold, silver,
or any other kind of wealth, would take it up again, hold his head high among the wise?
For neither silver nor gold leads to enlightenment, nor to peace, nor to knowledge of the path, nor to Nibbāna.
The meaning is as follows: "This is not befitting for a recluse" means that this object of possession—such as gold, silver, and so forth—or the act of possessing it, is not suitable for recluses.
For it has been said: "Gold and silver are not allowable for the recluses, the sons of the Sakyan," and so on.
"This is not the wealth of the Noble Ones" means that this aforementioned object of possession is not the wealth consisting of faith and the other [spiritual treasures].
Just as there is no wealth consisting of noble qualities (*ariyadhamma*), it does not bring about the state of a noble one (*ariyabhāva*). Therefore, he said: "Lobhana," and so forth.

Therein, *lobhana* means the production of greed; *madana* means bringing about intoxication; *mohana* means the generation of delusion; *rajavaḍḍhana* means the increase of the dust of passion and the like.
Because that by which something is possessed brings about apprehension, it exists together with apprehension (*saha āsaṅkāya*).

"Full of apprehension" means that for one by whom it has been grasped, there is apprehension arising from this or that source; such is the meaning. "Much toil" means much exertion by way of protecting the virtuous and so forth.
"There is no lasting stability here" means that in this wealth, neither a state of permanence nor a state of stability exists; the meaning is that it is merely flickering and unsettled.
"Attached and heedless to this"—attached to this wealth, having conceived passion for it;
heedless due to being separated from mindfulness regarding the ten wholesome states; with defiled minds, meaning their hearts are indeed defiled by the corruptions such as greed;
and consequently, hostile toward one another, they create widespread strife, even between mother and son.
Even a mother [quarrels] with her son; thus, being obstructed by one another, many beings create strife and quarrel.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Furthermore, monks, for the sake of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the basis...
[and so on] ...even a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother," and so forth.
"Killing" means death. "Bondage" means being bound with leather thongs and other such bonds. "Affliction" means falling into afflictions such as the severing of hands and so forth.
"Loss" means both the loss of wealth and the loss of one's retinue. "Sorrow and lamentation" means sorrow and wailing. "Of those who are obsessed" means of those who are attached.
"Many calamities are seen" refers to the aforementioned varieties of killing, bondage, and so forth, as well as those not mentioned.
In sensual pleasures, much and manifold ruin—such as grief, despair, and so forth—is seen both in this present life and in the future.

Therefore, why do you, my kinsmen, though being relatives, seek my harm like enemies and urge me toward sensual pleasures? Why, for what reason, do you entice me—who am thus detached from sensual pleasures—into them?
Just as enemies would do, why do you, despite being my kin, desire my misfortune? Why do you urge me toward sensual pleasures?
"Appoint me. "Know me as one who has gone forth, seeing danger in sensual pleasures"—know me as one who has gone forth, perceiving danger in sensual pleasures;
the intention is: "What is there that you do not already know?
"Not by means of gold and silver, are the taints exhausted"—the taints of sensual pleasure and so forth are never exhausted by means of gold and silver.
They do not go to destruction; rather, they increase all the more because of them. Therefore it was said:
"Sensual pleasures are enemies and murderers, they are foes and bonds of arrows. For sensual pleasures are "enemies" (*amitta*) due to their lack of friendship, as they bring about what is harmful;

they are "murderers" (*vadhaka*) because they are like assassins with raised swords, being the cause of death; and they are like "foes who pursue one" (*sapatta*) because they bring misfortune even after having followed one.
They have conquered the enemies, namely the thorns of passion and so forth, because they bind [the mind]; thus they are "conquerors of the thorn-bonds" (*sallabandhana*).
They are "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*) because their hair has been shorn. Having gathered rags here and there, they are "clad in the patched robe" (*saṅghāṭipāruta*) by wearing the *saṅghāṭi* robe.
"Alms from standing" (*uttiṭṭhapiṇḍa*) refers to alms obtained by standing at each house when the doors are open. "Gleaning" (*uñcha*) is for that purpose.

The practice of gleaning (*uñchācariyā*). "The support for those who are homeless" (*anagārūpanissaya*) refers to the requisites of life that serve as a necessary support because they must be relied upon by those who have gone forth and are homeless; for it is by depending on these that those who have gone forth live.

"Vomited" (*vanta*) means discarded. "By the great seers" (*mahesīhi*) means by the great seers such as the Buddhas. "In a place of safety" (*khemaṭṭhāne*) means in a place free from calamities such as the yoke of sensual desire.
"In Nibbāna. Thus did those great seers attain the bliss of Nibbāna, which is immovable bliss.
Therefore, the intention is that one who aspires for that [bliss] must renounce sensual desires.
"May I never encounter sensual desires"—may I never at any time come into contact with sensual desires. If one asks why, he said:
“*Yesu tāṇaṃ na vijjatī*,” etc.: when these sensual pleasures (*kāmā*) are examined, there is not even a single one that provides protection against harm.
They are like a mass of fire in the sense of being greatly burning. They are suffering in the sense of being painful.
This danger—that is, what are called sensual pleasures—is an obstacle because they bring about vast, unrecognized harm. They are accompanied by vexation because they cause mental distress.
It is "thorny" because it pierces. It is "a very uneven greed" because it is the cause of greed; it is very uneven and a great impediment.
It is "great" in the sense of being difficult to overcome. It is "the mouth of delusion" because it is the cause for falling into infatuation.

It is "a terrifying affliction" in the sense of having an extremely fearsome nature, bringing harm and suffering like a great calamity from a deity. Sensual pleasures are "like the head of a snake" in the sense that they are full of danger.
"Beings stuck in the mire of sensual pleasure" means that beings are mired in the mud known as sensual desire (*kāma*).

"The path leading to an evil destination" refers to the path leading to the states of misery such as hell and so forth. "Caused by sensual pleasure" means caused by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.

"Abundant" means manifold, consisting of various types such as killing living beings and so on. "They bring about disease" means [they bring about] that which is reckoned as disease in the sense of causing affliction (*rujjanattha*).
It brings about suffering, which is divided into that pertaining to the present life and so forth.
"In this way" means in the manner described by the passage beginning with "enemies and murderers. "Generators of enemies" means those that produce the state of being an enemy.
"Tormentors" means those that cause burning; the sense is "those that are to be tormented. "Defiling" means bringing about defilement. "Worldly baits" refers to [objects] in the world...
They have become like bait. "To be bound" means they are to be increased by fetters that constitute bondage; the sense is that they are conducive to fettering (*saṃyojanīya*).
"Death-fetters" refers to those which act as the cause for the occurrence [of rebirth] in states such as existence (*bhava*), and thus serve as the impediments to death.

"Causes of madness" refers to those which produce the madness of sorrow through the separation from things subject to change, or alternatively, those which bring about further intoxication through prosperity.
*Ullapanā* means causing one to prattle repeatedly, saying, "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!
There is also a reading *ullolanā*, which means luring beings upward and upward for the sake of bait, like a dog wagging its tail for the sake of a morsel of food;

the meaning is that they cause one to fall into ruin by leading one away from what is beneficial. *Cittappamāthino* means those who, by producing feverish distress and so forth, [afflict] both the present and the future.
"Those whose nature is to crush the mind. Alternatively, the reading is "cittappamaddino," which has the same meaning.
However, for those who say "cittappamādino," the meaning is "those who bring negligence to the mind. "For the sake of defilement" means for the purpose of affliction or torment.
"Quickly cast by Māra" means that these sensual pleasures should be understood as a net cast by Māra, because they bring harm to sentient beings.

"Of boundless disadvantage" means that they have limitless faults and many defects, according to the method explained in the *Dukkha-khandha Sutta* and other discourses, such as: "Lust is intoxication," and "In this world, one is preceded by cold, preceded by heat," and so forth.
"Abounding in suffering" means they are followed by various kinds of suffering, such as that of the woeful states (*āpāyika*).

"Great poisons" means they are like the great poisons such as *halāhala*, because their fruit is bitter and disagreeable. "Little gratification" means [they are like] a drop of honey on the edge of a sword-blade.
They are like those who have little taste. They are "causers of strife" because they increase passion and the like.
They are "driers up of the white side" because they destroy the blameless portion of beings.
"Sāhaṃ" means "I am she," having acquired faith after hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher in the manner described above.
The meaning is: "having abandoned sensual desires and gone forth, one remains. "Such as this" means of this kind, of the sort described.

"Having done so" means *iti katvā* (having thus considered), that is, by the reason already stated. "I shall not return to that" means I shall not again consume those sensual desires which were vomited up by me previously.
"Always delighting in Nibbāna" means from the time of going forth onwards, at all times.
"Delighting in Nibbāna, therefore I shall not return to that"—this is the construction.

"Having crossed over the conflict of sensual desires" means having crossed over the conflict (*raṇa*) of sensual desires (*kāmā*); and that must be done by me through the striking blow of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
"Longing for the state of coolness" means [longing] for that which is designated as the state of coolness (*sītibhāva*) through the subsiding of the distress and fever of all defilements (*kilesa*).
"Longing for arahantship": [this means] they delight in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

"By whom the Great Seers have crossed over": by whichever Noble Path the Great Seers, such as the Buddhas, have crossed over the great flood of *saṃsāra*, I too follow that path traveled by them; the meaning is that I shall reach it through the practice of virtue and so forth.
"Established in the Dhamma": established in the Dhamma of the Noble Fruits. "Unshakable": having attained the name "unshakable" because of the subsiding of all agitation (*ejatā*).
The supreme fruit. "Having attained" means having fulfilled [the path] and having reached it through the realization of the supreme path.
"He meditates" means he contemplates that very fruition-jhāna (*phalajjhāna*).
"Today is the eighth day since going forth" means that having gone forth, today is the eighth day from the time of his going forth; from this...

The meaning is that she went forth on the eighth day of the past [fortnight]. "Faithful" means endowed with faith. "Resplendent in the True Dhamma" means resplendent through the attainment of the True Dhamma.
"Freed" means freed by the abandoning of the defilements which are like the state of a slave. "Debtless" means free from the debt of sensual desire and so forth.
It is said that these three verses were spoken after she had gone forth and attained *arahantship* on the eighth day, while sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
The Blessed One, having shown the Elder Nun sitting after she had attained the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and having praised her,
spoke thus. Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, seeing this occurrence with his divine eye, thought,
"Since this Elder Nun is being praised by the Teacher in this way, she ought to be attended upon by the devas," and immediately, together with the Tāvatiṃsa devas, [he arrived].
Having approached, paid homage, and stood with palms joined in reverential salutation, he remained there. With reference to him, the compilers of the collection said:
"Sakka, the lord of beings, together with the host of gods, having approached by means of his psychic power, pays homage to Subhā, the daughter of the smith."
In this context, Sakka, the king of the gods— who has obtained the name "Lord of Beings" (Bhūtapati) because he is the master over all beings within the three realms of sensual existence—
approached that beautiful smith’s daughter together with his host of gods by means of his divine power and paid homage;
the meaning is that he worshipped her by performing the fivefold prostration.
The commentary on the Therīgāthā of Subhā Kammāradhītā is finished.
The commentary on the Vīsatinipāta (The Book of the Twenty) is finished.
14. Tiṃsanipāta (The Book of the Thirty).
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Subhā Jīvakambavanikā. The verses beginning with "The Jīvakambavana grove is delightful" belong to the elder nun Subhā Jīvakambavanikā.
She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated wholesome karma conducive to liberation throughout various successive existences.
Having possessed well-developed roots of merit and having gradually cultivated the requisites for liberation, she reached full maturity of wisdom.
In this current dispensation of a Buddha, she was reborn in the city of Rājagaha into a prominent brahmin family of great wealth;
her name was Subhā. Indeed, because the various parts of her body were endowed with a beautiful complexion, the name Subhā was truly appropriate to her.
She was born [into that family]. Having gained faith upon the Teacher’s entry into Rājagaha, she became a lay follower (*upāsikā*).
Later, having become spiritually stirred regarding *saṃsāra* and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, perceiving renunciation as security, she went forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
Performing the work of insight (*vipassanā*), she established herself in the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) within just a few days.
Then one day, a certain profligate man living in Rājagaha—youthful and in the prime of his vigor—saw her going to Jīvaka’s mango grove for her midday rest.

His heart became bound with passion, and blocking her path, he invited her to sensual pleasures. She [explained] to him in various ways the danger of sensual desires and her own inclination toward renunciation.
Pavedantī preached the Dhamma. Although he heard the discourse on the Dhamma, he did not desist; he merely persisted.

Seeing that he would not abide by her word and was infatuated with her eye, the Elder Nun thought, "Well now, here is the eye you have so highly esteemed," and having plucked out one of her own eyes, she offered it to him.
Thereupon, that man was struck with terror and a sense of spiritual urgency arose within him.
There, having become free from passion, he apologized to the elder nun and departed. The elder nun went into the presence of the Teacher.
At the mere sight of the Teacher, her eye was restored to its natural state. Thereupon, she stood there, continuously suffused with joy directed toward the Buddha.
The Teacher, knowing the disposition of her mind, taught the Dhamma for the sake of attaining the highest path.

He explained the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to her. She suppressed her rapture (*pīti*), immediately intensified her insight (*vipassanā*), and attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).

Having attained *arahantship*, dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of *nibbāna*, she reflected upon her own practice and, as an inspired utterance (*udāna*), recited the verses spoken by that rogue: [The verses follow.]
“Jīvaka’s Grove is delightful; as the beautiful Bhikkhunī was going there, a rogue blocked her path. To him, Subhā spoke:
‘What offense have I committed against you, that you stand blocking my way?’”
"Friend, it is not fitting for one who has gone forth to engage in physical contact with a man.
'In the heavy teaching of my Teacher, the training taught by the Sugata is pure in its basis and free from blemish; why do you stand obstructing me? "
“With a turbid mind you stand obstructing me, who am unturbid, full of dust though I am dustless, free from blemish, and whose mind is liberated in every respect.
You are young and innocent; what will this going forth do for you?”
“Set aside your saffron robe; come, let us enjoy ourselves in this forest in full bloom.
The trees on all sides waft a sweet fragrance, stirred up by the pollen of their flowers;
the season of the first rains is pleasant—come, let us enjoy ourselves in this forest in full bloom.”
“The trees with their flowering crests, stirred by the wind, seem as if they are roaring.
What pleasure will there be for you if you enter the forest alone?
It is frequented by herds of wild beasts and agitated by rutting elephants and their females.”
“Without a companion, you wish to go to the great forest, which is desolate and terrifying.
‘O lady with thighs like refined gold, you wander like a celestial nymph upon a grove of mind-trees;
clad in beautiful garments of fine Kāsī silk, you shine, O peerless one.’”
“I would become a follower of your will if we were to dwell within the forest;
for there is no living being dearer to me than you, O Kinnarī with the beautiful eyes.
If you will do as I say, come and live happily at home.”
“Dwelling in a cool, pleasant palace, let women perform service for you.
Wear garments of fine Kāsī cloth and put on garlands and cosmetics;
I shall provide you with much gold, gems, and pearls, and various kinds of ornaments.”
“Ascend this beautiful, costly bed, newly spread with a well-washed royal coverlet, cushioned with woolen rugs and stuffed with cotton,
fragrant with the essence of sandalwood and adorned with jewels.
Like a blue lotus risen from the water, it is untouched by any non-human beings.”
"Thus you, O celibate woman, will grow old with your own limbs.
What do you consider to be the essence here in this body that increases the cemetery, filled with putrefaction,
and subject to dissolution— that which, having seen, you look on with a troubled mind?"
“Your eyes are like those of a peacock hen, or like those of a kinnarī in the mountain recesses;
having beheld them of yours, my delight in sensual pleasure increases all the more.
Your eyes are like the tips of blue lotuses upon your face, which is stainless and resembles refined gold.”
“Beholding your eyes, my sensual desire increases all the more.
Even though you have gone far away, O Kinnarī with long-lashed, pure-sighted eyes, we still remember them;
for there is nothing dearer to us than those eyes of yours, O lady with the gaze of a mandala.”
“You wish to escape through indifference; you seek a toy for a lion.
You wish to leap over Mount Meru, you who pursue a son of the Buddha.
Indeed, in this world with its devas, there is no passion by which I might now be bound.”
“I do not know what he was like before, but now he has been destroyed by the path, root and all.
He is like a heap of embers cast away, or like a poisonous leaf scorched by fire;
I do not see what he was like before, but now he has been destroyed by the path, root and all.”
“If there were one who has not reflected, or one who has not attended upon the Teacher—you might seduce such a person; but you will only distress her, for she knows this.
For regarding both abuse and praise, as well as pleasure and pain, I remain established in mindfulness.”
“Knowing that all conditioned things are unattractive, my mind does not cling to anything at all.
As a disciple of the Sugata, traveling by means of the vehicle of the Eightfold Path,
with the arrow extracted and free from taints, I delight in dwelling in empty huts.”
“I have indeed seen well-fashioned wooden puppets, beautiful to behold,
bound together with strings and pegs, performing various dances.
When those strings and pegs are removed, they are cast aside, broken, and scattered.”
When it is cut into pieces, one would not find [anything]; where, then, could one fix the mind?
"The bodies are just like that: they do not exist without those phenomena (dhammas).
Since they do not exist without phenomena, where, then, could one fix the mind?"
"Just as one might see a painting made on a wall smeared with yellow orpiment, so too is your distorted perception of that; human consciousness there is useless.
It is like a magical illusion created before one's eyes, or like a golden tree seen in a dream."
You approach the blind and hollow, like a puppet in the midst of a crowd.
Like a ball placed inside a hollow, with bubbles in the middle and accompanied by tears,
pustules and boils arise here, along with various kinds of eye-diseases clustered together.
“Having gouged out her beautiful eyes, she did not yield, for her mind was free from attachment.
‘Come now, take your eye,’ he said; and she gave it to that man immediately.
And at that very moment his passion ceased, and he asked her for forgiveness.”
"May it be well with you, O practitioner of the holy life; may such a thing never happen again.
Having assailed a person such as this—like embracing a blazing fire, like seizing a venomous serpent—will there indeed be safety? Please forgive us."
“Then that nun Muttā went into the presence of the Excellent Buddha;
upon seeing his excellent marks of merit, her sight became as it was before.”—
Thus she recited these verses.
In that context, *Jīvakambavana* means the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca. *Rammaṃ* means delightful.
It is said to be exceedingly charming and pleasing to the mind due to the excellence of its location, the abundance of shade and water, and the manner in which the trees were planted.
*Gacchantiṃ* means having gone toward the mango grove, approaching it for her midday rest.
“Subhā” is her name. “A rogue” means a womanizer.
It is said that there was a certain young man, handsome and a womanizer, the son of a very wealthy goldsmith living in Rājagaha, who was wandering about intoxicated.
Seeing her on the opposite path, his heart became bound to her, and he blocked the road and stood there. Therefore it is said: “The rogue stopped her.”
The meaning is: "You have forbidden my departure. *Tamenaṃ abravī subhā*: after she had restrained him, the nun Subhā spoke to that rogue who stood there.
And here, in the phrases "Subhā [spoke] to the nun Subhā as she was going" and "Subhā [spoke]," the Elder Nun speaks of herself as if she were another.
This is by way of showing the connection between the verses spoken by the Elder Nun.
The compilers of the collection spoke this verse.
Having said, "Subhā spoke," he then said, "What wrong have you done to me? and so forth, in order to show the manner in which she spoke.
Therein, "What wrong have you done to me" means: "Friend, what has been done wrongly by me to you? [referring to] having obstructed me...
“‘You stand’—the intention is: ‘That offense for which you stand here, having blocked me as I was going and prevented my departure, does not exist.
Then, showing that even if you act thus on the mere perception that she is a woman, it is still not appropriate, she said:
‘For a man, friend, physical contact is not permissible for one who has gone forth,’ friend Suvaṇṇakāraputta.”
Even by means of worldly conduct, it is not permissible for a man to have physical contact with those who have gone forth;

nor, for one who has gone forth, is it permissible to have physical contact even with a man who is an animal. Let alone contact with a human male—even contact with a man who is himself subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya) is not permissible for her who is herself subject to forfeiture, on account of lust.
Therefore he said, “In the heavy teaching of my Teacher,” and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
In the heavy teaching of my Teacher—which is to be held dear like a stone parasol—there are the trainings taught and prescribed for the bhikkhunīs by the Sugata, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By means of those [trainings], one’s state is completely pure, a portion of wholesome purity entirely free from the stains of passion and the like.

"Because of my absence [of defilements], I am free from blemish (*anaṅgaṇa*); for what reason do you stand obstructing me as I go forth in such a state? "You are one whose mind is turbid (*āvilacitta*)," [he replied].
"By way of sensual thoughts (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth, which cause the mind to become turbid, your mind is turbid;

but because of their absence, I am not turbid. You are full of dust (*saraja*) by way of the dust of passion (*rāgaraja*) and so forth, and possessed of blemish (*sāṅgaṇa*); but because of their absence, I am free from dust."
"Why do you stand obstructing me, who am free from blemish and whose mind is liberated through the liberation of total eradication regarding the entire pentad of aggregates?
When the elder nun had spoken thus, the rogue, explaining his own intention, said: "And she is young," and so forth, [reciting] the ten [verses].
She spoke this verse. In it, "daharā" means young, standing in the first stage of youth. "Apāpikā ca si" means you are not deficient in beauty;
the intention is that you possess the most excellent form. "Kiṃ te pabbajjā karissati" means:
what will renunciation do for you who stand thus in the first stage of life and are endowed with such beauty? [It is only for] one who is old and of hideous appearance.
Or he speaks with the intention that one should go forth. *Nikkhipa* means "discard. Alternatively, the reading is *ukkhipa*, which means "remove.
*Madhuraṃ* means "beautiful," in the sense of being fragrant. *Pavanti* means "blow. *Sabbaso* means "on all sides.

Regarding the phrase "the trees raised by the pollen of flowers": these trees, by means of the mass of flower-pollen arising from them through a gentle breeze, [are covered] by their own flower-pollen.
As if rising up of their own accord, they waft fragrant scents in every direction.
"The first spring is pleasant as a season" means that this first month of spring possesses a pleasant touch and its seasonal conditions prevail.
"With crests in full bloom" means with tips beautifully flowered. "As if roaring, stirred by the breeze" means that, shaken by the wind, they seem to roar.
They stand as if threatening. "If you alone shall enter the forest"—if you, being alone, shall plunge into the forest, what kind of pleasure will there be for you there?
He speaks thus because he himself is delighted by the pleasure of his own bonds.
"Haunted by herds of wild beasts" means frequented here and there by multitudes of wild animals such as lions, tigers, and so forth. "Agitated by rutting elephants and female elephants."
A place agitated by rutting male elephants and female elephants through their distressing of the minds of wild animals, and by the breaking of branches of trees, shrubs, and the like.
Although such a thing did not exist in that forest at that time, he spoke thus because he wished to terrify him by saying that a forest is of such a nature.
"Desolate" (*rahita*) means devoid of people, lonely. "Terrifying" (*bhiṃsanaka*) means producing fear.

"Like a polished golden plate," means like a plate of refined gold that has been burnished smooth. "Like a golden image fashioned by a highly skilled master mechanic through the application of mechanical skill," means you move about like a golden statue crafted by a master artisan using mechanical techniques; indeed, at this very moment, you are moving here and there.
"Like celestial nymphs in the Cittalatā Grove" means like the divine nymphs in the pleasure garden named Cittalatā. "With fine Kāsī cloth" refers to [the cloth] from the kingdom of Kāsī.
"With those that have arisen, exceedingly subtle. "Charming" (*vaggubhi*) means smooth and lustrous.
"You shine with beautiful garments"—this refers to the incomparable, peerless clothes used for undergarments and upper robes.
He speaks thus, making the future state appear as if it were currently occurring through the power of his own impending intention: "Now, you shine as one following my will."
"May I be one who follows your will"—this means that I too shall become a follower of your will, one who promises to carry out whatever you command.
"If we two should dwell within the forest"—this means that if both of us live together in the midst of the woods, we shall find delight.
"For there is none dearer to me than you"—this states the reason for being a follower of your will. *Pāṇo* means a living being; no other living being whatsoever [is dearer] than you.
"There is indeed nothing dearer to me"—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "life" refers to his own life;
the meaning is: "There is indeed no life of mine dearer than you. "O you with eyes like those of a kinnarī" means:
O you whose large, wide eyes are like those of a kinnarī.
“If you will do as I say, come and live happily at home.
If you will do my bidding, abandon the hardship of the holy life—its single seat and single bed—and come, living happily amidst the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, dwell in the household life.
Some read this as, “Come and dwell happily at home”; for them, the meaning is that she will become happy.
The meaning is: "dwelling in a house. "Dwelling in windless palaces" means residing in palaces that are free from drafts.
There is also the reading "dwelling in palaces and celestial mansions" (*pāsādavimānavāsinī*); the meaning is: dwelling in palaces that resemble celestial mansions.
"Service" (*parikamma*) means attendance. "Wear" (*dhāraya*) means put on; provide both an undergarment and an upper garment. "Adorn" (*abhiropehi*) means by way of decoration and embellishment.
"Or place it upon the body"—the meaning is "adorn it. "Mālavaṇṇaka" means both garlands and fragrant ointments.
"Kañcanamaṇimuttaka" means joined with gold, gems, and pearls; the meaning is "inlaid with golden gems and pearls.
"Bahu" means manifold, distinguished by various types such as hand-fans and so forth. "Vividha" means of various kinds through the diversity of their craftsmanship.
“With a well-washed royal coverlet” means with an upper coverlet from which the dust has been washed away by being thoroughly cleansed. “Beautiful” means lovely.
“Spread with a long-haired black woolen rug and cotton-down pillows” means spread with both a black woolen rug of long hair and a pillow filled with swan’s down and the like.
“New” means quite fresh. “Costly” means of great value. “Scented with the essence of sandalwood ornaments” [is the meaning].
"Perfumed with fragrance" means being adorned with heartwood sandalwood such as *gosisaka* and the like;
"ascend such a couch," the meaning of which is: having ascended it, lie down and sit as you please.
In the phrase "the blue lotus risen from the water," the particle *ca* is merely a filler (*nipātamatta*); it means risen, emerged, having gone up high from the water.
"A well-blossomed blue lotus standing there, frequented by non-human beings"— this means that because it was born in a pond possessed by a *rakkhasa*,
it would be frequented by those who are not human and remain entirely untouched by anyone else. "In this way, you are a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārinī*)"—
just as that blue lotus is well-blossomed, so too are you a practitioner of the holy life, [untouched] by your own limbs.
"You will reach old age while even some parts of your own body remain unused; you will become worn out by old age for naught.
When the rogue had thus revealed his intention, the Elder Nun, cutting him off there by demonstrating the true nature of the body, spoke the verse beginning with "What is it to you here?
Its meaning is as follows: "Friend, son of a goldsmith, in this [body] filled with the filth of hair and so forth..."
"In this impure carcass known as the body, which is destined solely for dissolution and increases the cemetery—
what indeed is considered by you to be its essential core? Tell me that, seeing which you have become despondent and lost your mental resolve regarding some object,
or seeing which you remain undesponded and look on with joy."

Having heard that, although the rogue saw her beauty adorned with gracefulness, from the very first sight he had become bound by his heart to that particular glance of hers; thus, referring to that very glance, he spoke the verse beginning, "Your eyes are like those of a *tūriya* bird," and so forth. Granted, this elder nun was one whose faculties were well-restrained and tranquil; yet, in those steady, clear, gentle, and continuous glances of her eyes— [The rest of the verse follows: "Your eyes are like those of a *tūriya* bird, Your face is like the moon, O lady of lovely form; But your smile, O fair-limbed one, is like the jasmine flower. [The commentary continues: In these words, he expressed his longing for her, saying, "I am not able to endure separation from you. He spoke thus because, while she was indeed self-controlled, her senses were tranquil, and her glances were firm, clear, gentle, and continuous; therefore, he spoke of her as being "like a *tūriya* bird" and so on. By this he meant that her eyes were like those of a *tūriya* bird, which is a kind of partridge (*cakora*) that feeds on moonbeams and is said to be intoxicated by the sight of the moon. Just as that bird, when it sees the moon, becomes intoxicated and its eyes roll about, so too did her eyes appear to him. Furthermore, the word *tūriya* here refers to the *tūriya* bird, not to the musical instrument of that name. As for the phrase "your face is like the moon": the moon is beautiful, cool, and pleasant to behold; so too is her face. "O lady of lovely form" means one possessing a beautiful body. "But your smile, O fair-limbed one, is like the jasmine flower": the jasmine flower is white, sweet-smelling, and delightful; so too is her smile. "Fair-limbed one" means one with beautiful limbs. "I am not able to endure separation from you": he said this because he could not bear being apart from her. Furthermore, the word *tūriya* here refers to the *tūriya* bird, not to the musical instrument of that name. As for the phrase "your face is like the moon": the moon is beautiful, cool, and pleasant to behold; so too is her face. "O lady of lovely form" means one possessing a beautiful body. "But your smile, O fair-limbed one, is like the jasmine flower": the jasmine flower is white, sweet-smelling, and delightful; so too is her smile. "Fair-limbed one" means one with beautiful limbs. "I am not able to endure separation from you": he said this because he could not bear being apart from her. He spoke thus because, while she was indeed self-controlled, her senses were tranquil, and her glances were firm, clear, gentle, and continuous; therefore, he spoke of her as being "like a *tūriya* bird" and so on. By this he meant that her eyes were like those of a *tūriya* bird, which is a kind of partridge (*cakora*) that feeds on moonbeams and is said to be intoxicated by the sight of the moon. Just as that bird, when it sees the moon, becomes intoxicated and its eyes roll about, so too did her eyes appear to him. Furthermore, the word *tūriya* here refers to the *tūriya* bird, not to the musical instrument of that name. As for the phrase "your face is like the moon": the moon is beautiful, cool, and pleasant to behold; so too is her face. "O lady of lovely form" means one possessing a beautiful body. "But your smile, O fair-limbed one, is like the jasmine flower": the jasmine flower is white, sweet-smelling, and delightful; so too is her smile. "Fair-limbed one" means one with beautiful limbs. "I am not able to endure separation from you": he said this because he could not bear being apart from her. He spoke thus because, while she was indeed self-controlled, her senses were tranquil, and her glances were firm, clear, gentle, and continuous; therefore, he spoke of her as being "like a *tūriya* bird" and so on. By this he meant that her eyes were like those of a *tūriya* bird, which is a kind of partridge (*cakora*) that feeds on moonbeams and is said to be intoxicated by the sight of the moon. Just as that bird, when it sees the moon, becomes intoxicated and its eyes roll about, so too did her eyes appear to him. Furthermore, the word *tūriya* here refers to the *tūriya* bird, not to the musical instrument of that name. As for the phrase "your face is

When his eyes—produced by the power of karma, adorned with the five clear faculties, and possessing a remarkable excellence of luster—fell upon him, that rogue, having been deceived by his own imagined displays of conduct, gestures, and coquetry, felt an especially intense passion for the sight of him.
In this context, the phrase "the eyes and the musical instruments" is used; here, *tūri* refers to...
*Migī*: the word *ca* is merely a particle; the meaning is, "Your eyes are like those of a doe.
Alternatively, the reading is *kōriyārivā*, which means "like a hen of the *kuñcaka* bird.
And "like a *kinnarī* in the mountain cleft" means that your eyes are like those of a female *kinnara* moving within the interior of a mountain. [May] your eyes be seen by me.
Having seen the specific qualities of your eyes as described, my delight in sensual pleasures increases further and further.

Your eyelashes (*pamha*) are like the tips of blue lotuses (*uppala-sikhara*), resembling the petals of a red lotus; they are *vimala*, meaning stainless. Regarding your face, which resembles a golden image, the construction is:
"I behold your eyes. Even if they have gone to a distant place (*api dūragatā*), I must hasten (*saramhasa*) toward your eyes without thinking of anything else.
Thus I recollect: "Āyatapamhe" means having long eyelashes; "visuddhadassane" means having pure vision (clear eyes). Regarding "na hi matthi tayā piyattaro nayane":
there is no one dearer to me than your eyes; that is, there is no one else more beloved to me than your eyes.
In the phrase "tayā," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*).

Thus, as that man—like one crazed by the excellence of her beauty—was prattling on about this and that, the Elder Nun, turning his mind toward its own desires, spoke these twelve verses beginning with "By a pathless way. Therein, "You wish to travel by a pathless way":
friend, son of a goldsmith, while other women exist, you—who are [a follower] of the Buddha, the Blessed One’s son...

You seek and long for me, my own breast-born daughter; yet you wish to travel and intend to set out upon a path that is not the true way—a crooked, thorn-covered, dangerous, and wrong road—when there exists a safe, secure, and straight path.
You seek the moon as a plaything, desiring to turn the lunar orb into a toy ball; you wish to leap over Mount Meru, which rises eighty-four thousand yojanas high.
The construction is as follows: "If you wish to stand on the other side after leaping over Sineru, the king of mountains, yet you seek me, the son of the Buddha"—this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show that he is beyond his reach and that such a longing brings only frustration, the words beginning with "natthi" (there is not) are spoken.
Therein, "rāgo yatthapi dāni me siyā" means: "wherever my passion might now arise for me," that [place].
There is simply no such object in the world with its devas. Nor do I know what it is like; I do not even know what that lust is like.
Then, regarding the phrase "destroyed by the Path, root and all": *atha* is merely a particle.
Lust, together with its root—namely, the root known as improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*)—has been destroyed and eradicated by the Noble Path.
*Ingālakuyā* means by a pit of embers. *Ujjhito* means like something cast away by the wind;
the sense is that it is like fuel for a fire. *Visapattoriva* means like a vessel containing poison. *Aggito kato* means made removed from the fire—that is, removed from the embers;
the sense is that it has been taken away and destroyed so that not even a trace of the poison remains.
"For whom there might be 'unexamined'" means for whichever woman this fivefold aggregate (khandha-pañcaka) might be uninvestigated and not fully understood by means of knowledge.
"Or she might be one who has not been instructed" means for whichever woman, due to the failure to see the body of Dhamma, she might be uninstructed.
"You entice such a one as that," friend, [means] you entice such a person whose mental formations (saṅkhāra) have not been thoroughly scrutinized.
"Come, tempt her with sensual pleasures while she is not yet reviewing supramundane states. "Knowing this, you shall be frustrated":
by approaching this nun Subhā—who knows the course of existence and its cessation as they truly are, and who has penetrated the Truths—you will be frustrated;
that is, you will fall into distress and suffering both now and in the future.
Now, demonstrating the reason for his falling into distress, she says, "For me," and so forth.
Therein, *hi* is a particle used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). *Akuṭṭhavandite* means in the face of abuse and in the face of praise.

*Sukhadukkhe* means in pleasure and in pain, or in the encounter with desirable and undesirable objects. *Satī upaṭṭhitā* means mindfulness established as being joined with reflective awareness (*paccavekkhaṇa*).

"Always established. "One should know the conditioned as foul": having understood that whatever pertains to the conditioned within the three planes is foul due to the oozing of the impurities of the defilements.
"In every respect": in all three realms of existence, my mind is not smeared by the taints of craving and so forth.

"Traversing the vehicle of the Eightfold Path": she has gone to, or reached, the city of Nibbāna by means of the Noble Vehicle known as the Eightfold Path. "With the thorns extracted": with the thorns of lust and the other defilements completely uprooted from her own continuum.
"Well-patterned" (*sucittita*) means well-designed or fashioned in the form of hands, feet, faces, and so forth. "Sombha" means *sumbhaka* (carved figures).
"Wooden figurines" (*dārukapillakāni*) refers to forms constructed from wooden rods and the like. "By strings" (*tantīhi*) means by cords made of sinews.
"By pegs" (*khīlakehi*) refers to the rods placed for the purpose of supporting the hands, feet, back, ears, and so on. "Bound together" (*vinibaddhā*) means bound in various ways.
"Various dances" (*vividhaṃ panaccakā*) means: the dances established by the weaving, selling, and so forth of yarns, threads, and the like;
the construction is to be understood as "they are seen as if they were dancing.

Regarding the phrase "the pegs in the thread removed from that": it receives the designation "form" (*rūpaka*) by virtue of being endowed with a specific arrangement distinguished by its configuration.
When the strings and pegs in that painting have been removed from their positions, it is "loosened" (*vissaṭṭha*); when they are separated from one another, it is "dismembered" (*vikala*);
when they are scattered here and there, it is "scattered" (*parikīrṇa*) or "dispersed" (*vikīrṇa*).

"One would not find it made into pieces" means that when the parts of the painted cloth figure have been broken into fragments, one would not find the painted cloth figure; one would not perceive it. This being so...
In what among those parts of the painted cloth-form should one fix the mind?

In what—whether in the wooden pegs, or in the strings, or in the lump of clay and so forth—should one fix the mind, that is, apply the mental perception? The meaning is that such a perception would never arise regarding the constituent parts, which are devoid of intrinsic nature (*visaṅkhāra*).
"Tathūpamā" means similar to that, resembling that painted cloth-form. If one asks how so, he says: "The bodies," and so forth. Therein:
"Body-parts" (*dehakāni*) refers to the members of the body, such as the hands, feet, face, and so forth. "They appear to me as connected" means they present themselves [to consciousness].
"By those phenomena" (*tehi dhammehi*) means by those phenomena consisting of earth and so forth, as well as the eye and so forth.

"They do not exist without them" means that there are no such things called "bodies" apart from the phenomena of earth and so forth arranged in such and such a way. "It does not exist without phenomena" means it does not function without these phenomena.
The body does not exist, nor is it found, apart from its parts and the properties of those parts. This being so, where should one fix the mind?
Where—should one fix the mental perception (*manasaññā*) upon what is called "the body," or rather upon the hands, feet, and so forth, within the earth element or the other elements?
Because this designation refers merely to the properties of the primary elements, such as earth and the rest; that is to say:
Whether it be called "body," or "hands and feet and so forth," or "being," or "woman," or "man"— therefore, for one who knows this,
there is no adherence whatsoever to anything therein.
Just as one might see a painting on a wall smeared with yellow orpiment, [done] by a skilled painter.
One might see a painted figure of a woman— a wall-surface smeared with yellow orpiment, plastered,
and made into a painting by applying that coating. In that regard, the notion that "this wall, having been supported and propped up by some action,
stands here leaning against something human" is useless, for the purpose designated as "human nature" is absent.
In that regard, because of its non-existence, the notion "it is human" is merely a perverted view on his part;

there is no apprehension of things as they truly are. The intention is that this should be understood as being exactly like the apprehension of "woman," "man," and so forth, which occurs toward what is merely a collection of phenomena (*dhammapuñja*).
"Made to appear before one like an illusion" means it was presented by a magician as something resembling an illusion. "Only in a dream" means...
"A row of golden trees, even in a dream"—just as one might see a tree made of gold appearing there.

"You approach, O blind one, this empty thing"—O blind fool, you approach and cling to this empty, hollow, and pithless personal existence (*attabhāva*), thinking "this is mine," as if it were substantial. "Like a puppet in the midst of people."
Like a form made by a magician shown in the midst of a great crowd, appearing as if it had solidity though it has none—this is the meaning.
Like a ball of lac is "like a rolling ball. "Placed in a hollow" means placed within the cavity of a tree trunk.
"Bubbles in the middle" means like water bubbles situated in the middle of an eyeball. "With tears" means accompanied by the fluid of tears. "A pimple" (pīḷakoḷikā).
The eye-dung. "It is born here" means it is produced within this circle of the eye, emitting a foul odor from both ends.

"Pīḷakoḷikā" refers to the pustules that arise on the eyelids. "Various" means manifold, by way of the white and black circles as well as the seven layers (paṭala) such as red, yellow, and so forth. "Eye-constituents" refers to the parts of the eye.
Or rather, it is because of its assistance to the eye, owing to its existence as many constituent parts (*kalāpa*). "Aggregated" means combined.
Thus, for one who is attached to the eye, he makes manifest the impurity and the impermanence of the eye through its lack of stability.
Having made these manifest, it is just as if someone, having taken a desirable commodity and set out upon a robber-infested wilderness—

Just as one who is obstructed by a core [of treasure] goes away after giving that alluring object, even so the Elder Nun, being obstructed by that man who was passionately attached to her eye, plucked out her own eye and gave it to him. Therefore it is said:
“Having plucked out [her eye], she of lovely appearance,” and so forth. Therein, *uppāṭiya* means having plucked out, having extracted from the socket of the eye.
“Of lovely appearance” means of pleasing appearance, of heart-stealing appearance. “And did not fall into [desire]” means she did not fall into attachment toward that eye.
“With a mind free from attachment” means with a mind unattached to any object whatsoever. “Here, take this eye” means:
since it was given by me precisely because it was desired by you, take this impure lump known as an eye; having taken it, carry it away.
"Lead me to a desired place suitable for inspiring confidence.
And as for the phrase "his passion ceased at that very moment," it means that at the very instant the rogue's eye was plucked out, his lust vanished.
"Therein" means in the eye, or in that elder nun. Alternatively, "therein" means in that very [moment].
"In this matter. "She asked for forgiveness" means she caused [him] to forgive. "May there be well-being for you, O lady of holy conduct" means:

O most excellent practitioner, O queen, may there be health for you alone. "There shall be no more of such a thing" means: henceforth, there shall be no engaging in such improper conduct; the sense is that "I shall not do it again."
"Having touched" means having struck. "Such as this" means one who is everywhere free from passion (*vītarāga*). "Embracing like a blazing fire" means as if embracing a flaming fire.
"Therefore" means for that reason, by those wicked men. "That bhikkhunī" refers to that Subhā bhikkhunī.
"She went into the presence of the excellent Buddha" means she approached and drew near to the Fully Enlightened One (*Sammāsambuddha*). "Beholding the marks of supreme merit."
Having seen the mark of a Great Man produced by the supreme accumulations of merit,
his eye became restored to its natural state, as it was before— just as it was prior to being plucked out, as if it were ancient.
Whatever has not been stated here and there is easily understood because it follows the method already explained.
The commentary on the verses of the Bhikkhunī Subhājīvakambavanikā is finished.
The commentary on the Tiṃsanipāta is finished.
15. The Cattālīsanipāta.
1. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Isidāsī: The verses beginning with "In the city named Kusuma," found in the *Cattālīsanipāta*, belong to the elder nun Isidāsī.

She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas; having existed in various states as a male being, she accumulated wholesome kamma conducive to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*).
In his seventh existence from the final one, having committed the act of adultery through association with the unwholesome, he was reborn in hell after the breakup of the body.
After being cooked in hell for many hundreds of years, passing away from there, he was reborn in the animal realm for three births.
Passing away from there, he was born as a neuter person in the womb of a female slave.
She was reborn there. Then, passing away from that state, she was reborn as the daughter of a certain poor cartwright.
When she reached maturity, Giridāsa—the son of a certain caravan leader—took her as his wife and brought her home.
That husband already had a wife who was virtuous and of noble character; overcome by jealousy toward her, he [treated the new wife]...

She performed an act of denunciation. Having remained there for the rest of her life, at the dissolution of the body, she was reborn during this current appearance of a Buddha in Ujjeni as the daughter of a wealthy merchant who was highly esteemed for his noble lineage, character, conduct, and other virtues; her name was Isidāsī.
When she reached marriageable age, her parents gave her to a certain merchant’s son who was her equal in family, appearance, age, wealth, and other such qualities.
She lived for about a month in his house as a devoted wife.
Then, through the power of her past karma, her husband became disenchanted with her and cast her out from the home. All of this is understood from the canonical text itself. Of those various...
However, because her husband was unworthy of her affection, she became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having obtained her father’s permission and gone forth under the elder nun Jinadattā, she applied herself to the practice of insight (*vipassanā*).

Before long, having attained *arahantship* together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), she spent her time in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of *nibbāna*. One day, while wandering for alms in the city of Pāṭaliputta...
Having completed her almsround and returned from her meal, she sat down on a sandy bank of the Mahāgaṅgā River and,
being asked by her companion nun named Bodhi Thera about the former conduct of her companion nun, she answered that matter by means of verses beginning with,
“In the excellent city of Ujjenī. Now, in order to show the connection between those questions and answers—
“In the city named Kusuma, Pāṭaliputta, the ornament of the earth,
there were two virtuous bhikkhunīs born of the noble Śākya clan.
One among them was Isidāsī, and the second was Bodhī, both endowed with moral discipline.”
“Delighting in meditation and reflection, learned,
and having shaken off the defilements— having walked for alms and finished their meal,
they washed their bowls and sat down comfortably in a secluded place; then these women uttered these words.”
These three verses were placed by the compilers of the collection:
“Noble lady, you are serene; your youth has not declined.
Having seen what, O Byālikā, have you now become devoted to renunciation?”
“Being thus questioned by him, she who was skilled in teaching the Dharma in private, the seer’s daughter, spoke these words: ‘Listen, O Bodhi, as to how I went forth.
Hereafter follow the verses of response.
“In the excellent city of Ujjenī, my father was a merchant restrained by virtue.
I was his only daughter, beloved, pleasing, and dear to him.
Then, suitors from Sāketa of the most noble lineage came to me.”
My father, a merchant possessed of abundant wealth,
gave me to him. Every evening and every morning, approaching my mother-in-law and father-in-law,
I bow my head to their feet and pay homage to them, just as I have been instructed.
“Whether they were my husband’s sisters, my brother’s, or his attendants—
seeing even a single one of them, I would give them a seat in agitation.
And with food, drink, and hard food, whatever was gathered there, [I served them].”
I cover her, I lead her forward, and I give whatever is appropriate for her.
Having attended to her at the proper time, I approach the threshold of the house;
washing my hands and feet, I approach my husband with palms joined in reverence.
“Taking a seat-cloth, a mirror, a collyrium box,
and a looking-glass, like a female attendant, I myself adorned my husband.
I myself prepared the rice, and I myself washed the dishes.”
Just as a mother protects her only son, so do I serve my husband.
“Though I am thus devoted, affectionate, diligent, humble,
industrious, untiring, and virtuous, my husband treats me with contempt.”
“Thus he spoke to his mother and father: ‘I shall go after taking my leave;
I will not wish to dwell together with Isidāsī under one roof.
‘Do not speak thus, my son,’ they said, ‘for Isidāsī is wise and discerning.’”
“Rising early and untiring, my son, what is it about you that does not please her?
“She harms me for nothing, nor do I have any intimacy with the seer’s daughter, Vacchā.
She is enough for me as a wife; I shall depart without asking her permission.”
“Having heard her words, my mother-in-law and father-in-law asked me:
‘What wrong have you committed? Speak freely and truthfully.
‘I have not committed any wrong here; I have neither harmed anyone nor spoken harsh words.’”
"What can be done by you, since my husband will see me?
"They led me back to my father's house, dejected and overcome by grief;
protecting our son, we were defeated like a beautiful Lakṣmī."
“Then my father gave me away into the home of a wealthy second-ranking noble;
thereafter, for half the bride-price, the merchant took me as his wife.
I lived for a month in his house as well, and then he too sent me back.”
"To her who serves like a slave-girl—faultless and perfected in virtue;
to him who wanders for alms, a tamer who is himself tamed—my father says:
'You shall be my son-in-law; lay down the millstone and the pestle.'"
“Having stayed there for a fortnight, he then said to his father: ‘Give me my bowl;
give me a water-pot and a begging-bowl, and I shall go out again to wander for alms.
Then his father said to him: ‘Mother and the entire circle of my kinsmen—’”
“What is it that you do not have here? Speak quickly, and we shall provide it for you.
Being addressed thus, he replied: “If my own self were capable, that would be enough for me;
I would not wish to dwell under one roof with Isidāsī.”
“He has been sent away and gone; I too am left all alone and reflect:
‘Having taken my leave, I shall go—either to die or to enter the homeless life.
Then the noble Jinadattā arrived, wandering for alms.”
“Father, she was one who upheld the discipline, learned, and endowed with virtue.
Having seen her, we rose from our seats and prepared a seat for her;
and when she was seated, having bowed at her feet, I gave her food.”
“Having satisfied them with food and drink, with solid foods, and whatever else was stored there, I said:
‘Noble ladies, I wish to go forth. Then my father said to me:
‘My son, practice the Dhamma right here;’”
“Satisfy the recluses and the twice-born with food and drink.
Then, weeping and extending my joined palms in reverence, I said to my father:
“Indeed, evil karma was committed by me; I shall exhaust that deed.”
“Then my father said to me: ‘Attain enlightenment and the supreme Dhamma;
may you obtain Nibbāna, that which the Best of Bipeds has realized.
Pay homage to your mother and father, and having honored the entire assembly of your kinsmen,’” he said.
Having gone forth for seven days, I realized the threefold knowledge.
“I know my own seven births, the fruit and ripening of which this is;
I shall declare that to you—listen with a single-minded focus.”
“In the city of Erakaccha, I was a goldsmith with great wealth;
intoxicated by the pride of youth, I consorted with another’s wife.
Having passed away from there, I suffered for a long time in the blazing hell.”
Having emerged from there, I entered the womb of a female monkey.
"When I was only seven days old, the great monkey, the leader of the troop, stripped me of my fur;
this is the fruit of that deed, just as it is for one who goes to another's wife."
“Having passed away from there and died,
I was reborn in the Sindhava forest in the womb of a female goat that was both blind and lame.
For twelve years, having been shorn bald, I carried the kids about.”
“Kimināvaṭṭa was unfit, just like one who has gone to another’s wife.
Having passed away from there, I was born as a calf in the cow of a cattle-dealer;
I was a calf reddish-brown with lac, shorn of hair for twelve months.”
“Having carried the plow and drawn the cart,
I was like one who, being blind, crippled, and lame, has gone to another’s wife.
Having passed away from there, I was born in the house of a slave girl on the street.”
Neither woman nor man [is truly such], just as one who has gone to another's wife [is defined by that act].
Having died at thirty years of age, he was reborn as a girl in a family of carters—
a family that was poor, of little means, and frequently visited by creditor-men.
“Then the caravan leader, having cut me off from my family home,
dragged me away while I was lamenting, despite my abundant and vast prosperity.
Then, in my sixteenth year, he saw that I, a maiden, had reached the bloom of youth.”
The son of Oruṇḍhattha was named Giridāsa by name.
He too had another wife who was virtuous, endowed with good qualities, and renowned;
she was devoted to her husband, yet I caused her to be reviled.
“This is the fruit of that karma: that they go about scattering me with abuse;
even as I serve like a slave-girl, I have set a limit to that as well.
Therein, in the city named Kusuma, that is, in the city whose name is taken by the word “Kusuma,” known as “Kusumapura.”
Now he shows that city by its actual name: "from Pāṭaliputta. "Adorning the earth" means adorning the entire earth, as it were, with a jewel.
"Born of the Sakyan clan" means daughters of noble families in the Sakyan clan; this is said because she had gone forth in the teaching of the Blessed One, the son of the Sakyans.
*Therein*: among those two bhikkhunīs. *Bodhi*: the elder (therī) named Bodhi. *Delighting in the cultivation of jhāna*:
she was devoted to the practice of mundane and supramundane jhāna. *Learned*: she was learned by virtue of her great mastery of the scriptures (*pariyatti*).
*One whose defilements were shaken off*: her defilements had been entirely eradicated by the supreme path (*aggamagga*). *For the sake of food*: for the purpose of obtaining almsfood.
Having finished his meal duties. "In a secluded place" means in a solitary location, devoid of people.
"Sitting at ease" means sitting comfortably with the happiness of renunciation and the happiness of seclusion. "These words" refers to the pleasant inquiries now being spoken.
"They spoke" means they spoke by way of answering questions.
The verse beginning with “Pāsādikāsī” was spoken by way of a question from the Elder Nun Bodhi. The verse beginning with “Evamanuyuñjiyamānā” was spoken by the compilers of the Saṅgīti themselves.
Indeed, all the verses beginning with “Ujjeniyā” were spoken by the Noble Lady Isidāsī herself.
In that context, “Pāsādikāsī” means you were one who brought forth confidence in those who saw you due to your perfection of form. “Vayopi te aparihīno” means even your youth has not declined.
"Declined" means you were established in the first stage of life. "Having seen what, O deceitful one?
means having seen what kind of deceit, fault, or danger in the household life. "Then you were devoted to renunciation"—here, *atha* is a mere particle;
it means you were devoted to renunciation, that is, to the going forth (*pabbajjā*).

"Being questioned" means being asked; she was Isidāsī—this is how it is to be construed. "In a secluded place" means in a solitary spot. "Listen, Bodhi, to how I went forth"—the Elder Nun Bodhi said: "Listen, listen to that ancient account of how I went forth. "In the preeminent city of Ujjenī" means in the supreme city named Ujjenī in the kingdom of Avantī.

"Dear" means worthy of being loved because she was her only daughter. "Pleasing" means those who increase the mind's delight through their virtue, conduct, and qualities. "Beloved" means worthy of being cherished.
"Then later," means when I had reached the age of maturity. "My suitors from Sāketa" means that suitors from the city of Sāketa came to prevent me [from going].
"Of the most noble family" means those who were of the foremost lineage in that city; the merchant by whom they were sent was one who possessed abundant wealth.
"My father gave me as a daughter-in-law to him" means he gave me to be the daughter-in-law of that merchant of Sāketa.
My father gave me to him after making me his son’s wife.
"In the evening and in the morning" means in the evening and in the forenoon.
