"Approaching with a prostration, I shall do so with my head" means that having approached the presence of my mother-in-law and father-in-law, I perform a prostration with my head; I bow at their feet. "Just as I have been instructed."
I act exactly as I have been instructed by them; I do not overstep their instruction.
*Tamekavarakampī* means even one who is a sole favorite. *Ubbiggā* means trembling with fear. *Āsanaṃ demī* means that for whichever person whatever is appropriate, I give that to him.
*Tattha* means in the place of serving food. *Sannihitaṃ* means being present, having been prepared. *Chādemī* means I cover over.
"Having covered [them], I bring them forward; having brought them forward, I give them"—the meaning is that even as she gives, she gives whatever is appropriate for each person.
"At the gate" means at the doorway. "Washing hands and feet" is to be construed as: "I was one who washed her hands and feet," and "having washed them, I approached the house.
"A comb" (koccha) refers to a comb for grooming the beard and hair. "Pastes" (pasāda) refers to fragrant powders and the like used as facial ointments.
“Pasādhana” is also a reading, meaning articles for adornment. “Añjani” means an ointment tube.
“Like a servant girl” means like a maidservant who attends upon the husband, even if she belongs to the highest family and is endowed with great wealth.
“I prepare” means I cook. The construction is: “Washing the vessel, I attend. (The vessel refers to a metal vessel.)
*Bhattikataṃ* means one who has performed services for his master. *Anurattaṃ* means one who possesses devotion. *Kārikaṃ* means one who performs whatever specific task is to be done.
*Nihatamānaṃ* means one whose pride has been removed. *Uṭṭhāyikaṃ* means one endowed with initiative and energy. *Analasaṃ* means for that very reason, one who is not indolent.
*Sīlavantaṃ* means one endowed with virtuous conduct. *Dussati* means he feels ill-will; having become angry, he speaks [harshly].
He said, "I shall go after taking leave. [The husband replied,] "Having taken leave of you, I shall go wherever I please.
He, my husband, spoke thus to his own mother and father. If one asks what he said, it is: "I will not dwell with Isidāsī;
I shall live together with her in the same house. In this context, *vacchaṃ* means "I will dwell."

*Desā* means those who are unloved. *Alaṃ me* means "she is sufficient for me"; the sense is that she is my purpose as a woman. *Apucchāhaṃ gamissāmi* means: "If you desire cohabitation with her, I shall depart for another land without asking your permission.
*Tassa* means "of my husband. *Kissa* means "what [wrong] has been done by you against his lord? *Aparaddhaṃ* means "an offense committed" or "an injury done.
*Napihaṃ aparajjhamīti* means "nor do I offend him," or "nor have I done anything wrong to him. Or rather, this is the reading: *napi hiṃsami*, meaning "nor do I harm him."
Nor do I cause harm. "Harsh speech" means ill-spoken words. "What can I possibly do, noble lady?

means what can I possibly do for you, noble lady? "Since my husband will despise me" means that, without any reason, my husband will despise me—that is, he will harbor a mind of resentment and anger toward me.
"Vimanāti" means dejected. "Puttamanurakkhamānā" means protecting their own sons by protecting my husband, their master, with their minds.
"Jitāmhase rūpiniṃ lakkhiṃ" means we have been conquered; indeed, we have been conquered by the beautiful Lakṣmī.
The meaning is: "We have been deprived of the goddess of fortune (Siri) who moves about in human guise."
"In the house of a wealthy second nobleman" means: he gave me to the house of a wealthy young man who was the second [in rank] relative to the first husband;
and in giving me, he gave me for half the price from that which the first [husband] had paid.
"By which price the merchant obtained me" is to be construed as: by half the price from that price by which the merchant first obtained or acquired me.

"He too" refers to the second husband. "He rejected me" means he drove me out; he cast me out from the house. "While she was serving him" means while she was attending upon him like a slave-girl, performing her duties.
"Innocent" means one who does not commit an offense. "Tamer" means one who tames the minds of others through the establishment of compassion.
It refers to one who wanders about for alms given by others, having made her own body and speech subdued and tranquil so that others might give something.
"Son-in-law" means the husband of one's daughter. "Throw away the cloth and the bowl" means: discard both the piece of rags you were wearing and the alms-bowl.
"He too, having stayed, departed"—that mendicant man also, after staying with me for about half a month, departed.
Then he says to him, "Father": my father, mother, and my entire circle of kinsmen, all together, say this to that mendicant.
How so? "What is not done for you here? What indeed is there that is not accomplished or achieved for you?
Speak quickly! That shall be done for you"—that will be performed for you.
"If my self is capable" means: if my self is independent and free, then there is no need for me for that female ascetic;
therefore, "I shall not dwell with her"—the construction is: "I shall not live together with her in the same house."
"He has been dismissed and gone": that mendicant, having been dismissed by his father, went according to his own wish.

"All alone" means being solitary. "Having taken leave, she goes": "I shall go after having dismissed my father. "In order to die" means for the purpose of dying. "Vā" is a particle used in the sense of an alternative.
"For alms" means for the sake of begging; the construction is: "She came to the father's family for alms."
"Her" refers to that Therī Jinadattā. "Having risen, I prepared a seat for her" means that having stood up, I arranged a seat for that Therī.
"Right here" means staying right in this very house. "O daughter"—he addresses his daughter with the conventional term "daughter," expressing compassion for her.
"Practice the Dhamma"—you, having gone forth, practice the Dhamma such as the holy life (brahmacariya) which ought to be practiced. "Twice-born" (dvijātī) means one of Brahmin birth.
"I shall wear out" means I shall cause to decay and eliminate.
"Enlightenment" (bodhi) refers to the perfect awakening to the Truths; the meaning is the knowledge of the Path.

"The supreme state" (aggadhamma) refers to the state of fruition, namely Arahatship. "Which the Best of Bipeds realized" refers to that supramundane state known as the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, which [the Best of Bipeds] realized.
The construction is: "May you obtain that which the Supreme Fully Enlightened One has realized.
"Having gone forth for seven days" means having become a renunciant for a period of seven days. "I touched" means I contacted or realized it.
"Of which this is the fruit and result" refers to that evil karma, of which this is the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*) consisting of the unpleasantness experienced by its owner.
The result. They will explain that to you; I shall tell you of that deed. "That" refers to the deed being explained, or else to my own words.
"Single-minded" means one-pointed mind (*ekaggamanā*). Or rather, this is the reading itself.
"In the city of Erakaccha" means in the city named Erakaccha. "He consorted with another's wife" means I, he, consorted with another's wife.

"Long cooked" means he was burned by the fires of hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. "And having emerged from there" means having departed and passed away from that hell. "He entered the womb of a female monkey" means he took rebirth in the belly of a female vanara.
"The troop-leader" means the leader of the troop. "He stripped him bare" means he stripped away and removed the seeds that are the characteristics of the male state.
"This is the fruit of that karma" means this is the result of the karma performed by me in the past. Just as...
"Having gone to another's wife" means having approached that other's wife.
"From there" means from the womb of a monkey. "In the forest of Sindhava" means in a forest region in the kingdom of Sindhava. "A she-goat" means a female goat.

"Carrying the child about" means having mounted her back and carried the young boy. "Crawling with worms" means being covered all over with worms at the place of birth, thus crawling and distressed. "Sick" means ill; "was" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
“Of the cow-dealer”: of one who lives by selling cows. “Lākhātamba” means possessed of hair that is tawny like the red juice of lac.
“Voḍhūna” means having carried. “Naṅgala” means a plow; the meaning is, “I carry even a cart. “Andhavaṭṭo” means being blind, he was oppressed (or distressed). “Vīthiyā” means in the city street.

“Born in the house of a slave-girl” means born from the womb of a domestic slave-girl; some also say “of a beauty-slave-girl” (*vaṇṇadāsī*). “Neither woman nor man” means I am neither female nor male; the meaning is, I am a person of indeterminate sex (*jātinapuṃsaka*).
“Died at thirty” means he died having become a eunuch at the age of thirty. “In a family of carters” means in a family of those who give birth [to such].
“Abounding in the arrival of creditor-men” means full of the frequent arrival of men who are creditors, being overwhelmed by many creditors.
“Accumulated” means built up. “Vast” means great. “Interest” means interest on debt. “Dragged down” means pulled down. “From my family home” means from the house of the family into which I was born.
"Avarundhatassa putto" means the son of that caravan leader; Giridāsa by name, with his heart bound to me, "avarundhati"—he keeps her as his own possession within his household.

"Anurattā bhattāraṃ" means she who follows after her husband. "Tassāhaṃ viddesanam akāsin" means I performed the act of causing aversion toward that husband for his co-wife; I behaved in such a way that he would become angry with her.
"Yaṃ maṃ apakīritūna gacchantī" means when they were about to depart, casting me aside like a slave-girl whom I had served there with great care.
There, having cast it away, discarded it, and become indifferent, they depart.
This is the ripening fruit of that deed of adultery I committed then, and of the act of reviling.
"I too have reached the end"—thus, the conclusion of that same cruel and evil deed of attachment has now been reached by me.
This was composed for one who has attained the supreme path; beyond this, there is no further suffering.
As for whatever has not been analyzed here in between, its meaning is self-evident because it follows the method already stated.
The commentary on the verses of the Therī Isidāsī is finished.
The commentary on the Cattālīsanipāta is finished.
16. Mahānipāta 1.
Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Sumedhā.
The verses beginning with "In the city of Mantāvati" in the Mahānipāta are the stanzas of the Therī Sumedhā.

She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, and diligently gathering the requisites for liberation, was reborn into a noble family during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana. Having reached maturity, she—her own...
Having become of one mind with her female friends and daughters of noble family, she had a great monastery built and dedicated it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
By that meritorious deed, upon the dissolution of her body, she went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
Having experienced divine glory there for the full span of her life, she passed away from there and was reborn among the Yāma devas. Passing away from there, she...
Having been reborn successively in the Tusita heaven, then passing away from there in the Nimmānarati heaven, and then passing away from there in the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven—
thus having arisen in the five celestial realms of sensual bliss and serving as the chief queen to the divine kings in each of those places—

she passed away from there to become the daughter of a very wealthy merchant during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Having gradually reached the age of discretion, she [entered] the Dispensation...
Having become full of serene confidence, she performed a sublime meritorious deed dedicated to the Triple Gem.

There, for as long as she lived, she lived according to the Dhamma and delighted in wholesome qualities; then, passing away from there, she was reborn among the Tāvatiṃsa devas and continued to wander through successive happy realms.
Now, during this current dispensation of a Buddha, in the city of Mantāvatī, [she was born] to Koñca...
She was reborn as the daughter of a king. Her parents gave her the name Sumedhā.
When she had gradually reached the age of maturity, her parents deliberated, saying, "We shall give her to the king named Anikaratta in the city of Vāraṇavatī.
From her childhood, however, she [had been surrounded] by princesses of her own age.

Having gone to the nuns' quarters together with her female servants and heard the Dhamma from the nuns, she—due to the service she had performed since long ago—became filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding *saṃsāra* and developed deep faith in the Teaching.
When she reached maturity, her mind turned away from sensual pleasures. Consequently, she sought the consent of her parents and kinsmen.
Having heard this, she said, "I have no need for the life of a householder;
I shall go forth. Although her parents tried to entice her back into the household life by entreating her in many ways, they were unable to persuade her.

Thinking, "In this way I shall be permitted to go forth," she took a sword and cut off her own hair; then, focusing on that very hair, she practiced the contemplation of repulsiveness (*paṭikkūla-manasikāra*).
There, because she had previously performed the necessary duties and had heard the instructions on mental attention from the bhikkhunīs,
she produced the sign of the foul and attained the first jhāna. Having attained the first jhāna,
she [dismissed] her entire circle of kinsmen and attendants, beginning with her parents who had come to urge her to leave the life of a householder.
Having caused the royal court to become deeply devoted to the Teaching, she departed from her home, went to the nunnery, and went forth.
Having gone forth, she established insight meditation;

and through the excellence of those qualities that ripen for liberation, once her knowledge had fully matured, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) before long. Thus it is said in the Apadāna:
“Under the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, in the newly built monastery within the Saṅghārāma,
we three female friends gave a gift of a dwelling.
Ten times, a hundred times, ten hundred times, and hundreds of hundreds of times;”
We were reborn among the devas, so what need is there to mention humans?
Among the devas we possessed great supernormal powers, so what need is there to mention the human realm?
I was the queen of the possessor of the seven treasures; I was the woman-treasure.
“Here we three— Dhanañjānī, Khemā, and I— were born into a family that had accumulated merit and was most prosperous.
Having constructed a well-made monastery, adorned with every detail,”
Having offered [this] to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, she was filled with joy:
“By the power of that deed, wherever I am reborn,
I have attained preeminence among the gods and likewise among human beings.”
“In this very eon, a highly renowned kinsman of Brahmā named Kassapa by clan arose, the best among those who speak.
At that time, the lord of men was the attendant of that Great Sage.”
In the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king of Kāsi named Kikī.
He had seven daughters, princesses raised in luxury,
who delighted in attending upon the Buddha and lived the holy life.
“Having been their companion, well-composed in the precepts,
I gave gifts with due care and practiced the holy life even while at home.
By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations,”
Having abandoned the human body, I went to the realm of the Thirty-three.
Passing away from there, I went to the world of Yama, and from there I went to Tusita;
and from there I went to Nimmānarati and the city of Vasavatti.
“Wherever I was reborn, impelled by my meritorious deeds,
there indeed I obtained the great sovereignty of chief queen among kings.
Having passed away from there, in the human state, [I became the chief queen] of universal monarchs.”
I served as the chief queen to kings who ruled over mandalas.
Having experienced prosperity among both gods and humans,
I wandered through many births, being happy in every place.
“Such is the cause, such is the source; that very patience within the Teaching is its root.
That is the first convergence; that is the Nirvana for one who delights in the Dhamma.
‘The defilements have been burnt away by me; all states of existence have been uprooted.’”
Like a serpent that has severed its bonds, I dwell free from taints.
"How welcome indeed was my arrival in the presence of the Best of Buddhas!
The three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled."
“The four analytical knowledges, these eight liberations, and the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Having thus attained arahantship and reflected upon his own practice, he uttered this inspired utterance:
“In the city of Mantāvati, I was the daughter of King Koñca’s chief queen;
I was Sumedhā, one who had gained confidence through those who act for the sake of the Teaching.
I was virtuous, eloquent, learned in the Buddha’s Dispensation, and well-disciplined.”
Approaching his mother and father, he said: "Listen, both of you!
I delight in Nibbāna, even more so than in the impermanent states of existence, even those of the devas.
How much more so, then, these empty sensual pleasures, which offer little gratification and much affliction?"
“Sensual pleasures are bitter, like poison, in which fools are infatuated;
they are delivered to hell for a long time, where they are slain and tormented.
Those of evil deeds, ever increasing in wickedness, grieve in the states of ruin.”
“Fools are unrestrained in body, speech, and mind.
Those fools are of poor wisdom; being mindless, they have not risen above the origin of suffering.
Not knowing even as they teach, they do not awaken to the Noble Truths.”
“O Mother, those excellent Buddhas have taught the Truths;
yet there are many who, not knowing them, rejoice in existence and long for rebirth among the gods.
Even rebirth among the gods is impermanent within existence, which itself is unstable and subject to decay.”
Fools do not find peace, for they must be born again and again.
"The four states of ruin and two destinies are somehow attained;
yet for those who have fallen into ruin, there is no going forth in the hells."
“Grant me permission, both of you, to go forth in the teaching of the One of Ten Powers;
free from anxiety, I shall strive for the abandoning of birth and death.
Why delight in the cycle of existence with this worthless, defiled body?”
With the cessation of craving for existence, grant me permission: I shall go forth.
The arising of Buddhas is rare; this opportune moment has been found.
May I not violate the precepts and the holy life for as long as I live.
“Sumedhā spoke thus to her parents: ‘I will not take food for as long as I remain a householder;
I shall surely fall under the power of death.
Her mother wept in distress, and so did her father.”
She was struck down completely;
they strove to revive her, who had fallen from the palace floor to the ground:
"Arise, my son! Why do you grieve? You were given by him in Vāraṇavatī."
“King Anīkaratta is handsome, and you have been given to him.
You shall become the chief queen, the consort of King Anīkaratta.
Virtue, the holy life, and renunciation—these are difficult to practice, my son.”
“In the kingdom there is authority, wealth, and sovereignty; enjoyments are pleasant while you are still young.
Enjoy sensual pleasures, my son; let there be a marriage for you.
Then Sumedhā said to them: “Do not speak such things, which are the worthless essence of existence.”
"Either renunciation shall come to pass, or death shall not hold me back.
"What indeed would I enter—this putrid body, impure, smelling of raw flesh, terrifying, a mere corpse;
this bellows that never rests, leaking and full of filth?"
“Why indeed, knowing it thus— revolting, smeared with flesh and blood,
a dwelling place for worms and food for birds— why is this carcass given away?
Soon the body, devoid of consciousness, is carried away to the charnel ground.
Abandoned like a piece of wood by relatives who loathe him:
"Having abandoned him in the charnel ground, his own mother and father—even they—bathe after the funeral meal, loathing him;
how much more so the common folk?"
“Attached to this worthless body— a mere collection of bones and sinews,
filled with spittle, excrement, and urine, a putrid mass—
Whoever could dissect it and turn its interior into its exterior;”
Unable to bear its odor, even one’s own mother would feel disgust for it.
Contemplating with wisdom that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are conditioned,
rooted in birth, and suffering— why would I desire marriage?
“If three hundred and ninety new arrows were to fall upon the body day after day,
even for a hundred years, death would be better, for thus there is the destruction of suffering.
One who understands the Teacher’s word should accept such death.”
Long is their saṃsāra, being slain again and again.
Among gods and humans, in the womb of animals, in the host of asuras,
among pretas and in the hells, immeasurable killings are seen.
“There are many slayers in the hells for one who has fallen into the states of misery and is being tormented;
even among the gods there is no refuge. There is nothing superior to the bliss of Nibbāna.
Those who are devoted to the teaching of the One Possessing Ten Powers have attained Nibbāna.”
Free from anxiety, they strive for the abandoning of birth and death:
"This very day, father, I shall go forth; what is the use of worthless riches?
I am weary of sensual pleasures, which are like vomit and like a palm tree that has been cut down."
“She spoke thus to her father, Anīkaratta, and to him to whom she had been given:
‘I shall go to Vāraṇavata when the time for my marriage has arrived.
Then Sumedhā, having cut her long, thick, and soft hair with a sword—”
Having closed the palace, she attained the first jhāna.
While she was thus absorbed there, Anīkaratta arrived at the city;
meanwhile, in the palace, Sumedhā thoroughly cultivated the perception of impermanence.
She gave him her attention, and the youth Ārūhī quickly climbed up;
with his limbs adorned with jewels and gold, he joined his palms and entreated Sumedhā:
“In kingship there is command, wealth, and sovereignty; there are enjoyments and pleasures—you are still young.”
“Enjoy the pleasures of the senses; sensual happiness is difficult to find in this world.
‘Your kingdom has been relinquished to you; enjoy its wealth and give gifts.
Do not be despondent; your mother and father are suffering.’”
“Sumedhā spoke thus to each of them: ‘I have no need for sensual pleasures, being free from delusion;
do not rejoice in sensual pleasures—see the danger in sensual pleasures!
Even King Mandhātā, who ruled over the four continents, was merely a path for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.’”
“Dissatisfied, he has passed away, and his desire was not fulfilled:
‘May the rain-god pour down the seven treasures, showering them upon all ten directions;
yet there is no satiety with sensual pleasures—men die still unsatiated.’”
“Sensual pleasures are like a razor’s edge; sensual pleasures are like the crest of a serpent.
Like a torch [carried against the wind], they burn; they are like a skeleton.
Sensual pleasures are impermanent and unstable; they bring much suffering and are a great poison.”
Like a red-hot iron ball, they are rooted in evil and bear fruit as suffering.
Sensual pleasures are like the fruit of a tree, painful like a lump of flesh,
deceptive like a dream, and comparable to borrowed goods.
“Sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes, a disease, a tumor, a calamity, and a plague;
they are like pits of glowing embers, the root of misfortune, fear, and slaughter.
Thus have sensual pleasures been declared to be full of suffering and obstacles.”
“Go away! I have no confidence in my own future existence.
What can another do for me when my own head is burning?
While old age and death pursue me, I must strive to destroy them.”
“Having opened the door and seen my mother, father,
and Anīkaratta sitting on the ground weeping, I said this:
‘Long is the cycle of existence for fools who weep again and again.’”
In this beginningless cycle of existence, consider the tears you have shed, the milk, and the blood, upon the death of a father, the slaughter of a brother, and your own killing.
As beings wander through *saṃsāra*, remember the accumulation of bones.
“O Sāriputta, the tears, breast-milk, and blood shed [in this life] would equal the four oceans;
the heap of bones accumulated over a single aeon would be vast as the earth.
As one wanders through the beginningless cycle of existence, the soil of Jambudīpa brought together [as footprints] would be equal to the great earth.”
Pills the size of jujube fruits would not suffice even for one's mothers alone.
"Recall the grass, wood, branches, and foliage brought from the beginningless cycle of existence:
even four-finger-width measures of earth would not suffice even for one's fathers alone."
“Remember the blind turtle in the eastern ocean, and from the west, the hole of a yoke;
that its head should happen to enter it—this is the simile for obtaining human birth.
Remember form as being like a lump of foam, this wretched body, which is without essence.”
Behold the aggregates as impermanent; remember the hells with their many afflictions.
"Remember how you have increased the funeral pyre again and again in those various births;
remember the terrors of the crocodiles, and remember the Four Truths."
“While the Deathless exists, what is the use of drinking the Five Bitters for you?
For all delights of sensual pleasure are more bitter than the Five Bitters.
While the Deathless exists, what is the use of sensual pleasures that are but burning fevers?”
For all delights of sensual pleasure are burning, boiling, quaking, and searing.
"While you are without enemies, what use have you for sensual pleasures which have many enemies?
Sensual pleasures are shared with kings, fire, thieves, water, and those who are dear; they have many enemies."
“Since liberation exists, what use have you for sensual pleasures, in which there is killing and bondage?
For those who are unwilling in regard to sensual pleasures experience the sufferings of killing and bondage.
A grass torch set ablaze burns not only the one who grasps it, but also the one who lets go.”
For sensual pleasures are like a flame; they burn those who do not let them go.
Do not, for the sake of a trifling sensual pleasure, abandon abundant happiness.
Do not, like a cat swallowing a hook, suffer later on.
“Surely you should subdue sensual desires, like a dog bound by a chain;
for sensual desires will surely torment you, as outcasts torment a hungry dog.
There is immeasurable suffering and many mental distresses.”
"You will experience [suffering] when bound by sensual desires; therefore, renounce these transient pleasures.
While the ageless state exists, what use have you for those desires in which aging resides?
All births everywhere are seized by death and disease."
“This is ageless, this is deathless, this is the ageless and deathless state, free from sorrow;
without enemies, without confinement, unshakable, fearless, and free from distress.
This has been attained by many, and even today it can still be obtained.”
"Whoever applies themselves with systematic attention, it cannot be accomplished by one who does not strive.
Thus spoke Sumedhā, finding no delight in the realm of conditioned formations;
dissuading him from his attachment, Sumedhā threw her hair onto the ground.
“Rising up, tireless and with palms joined, he entreated his father:
‘Release Sumedha, O wise one, that she may go forth and see the truth of liberation.
Released by her mother and father, she went forth, terrified by sorrow and fear.”
The six direct knowledges were realized as she trained for the supreme fruit.
"It was wonderful and marvelous, that Nibbāna which occurred for the royal maiden;
how she declared her past lives at the final hour."
“Under the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, at the newly established monastery in the Saṅghārāma,
we three female friends gave a gift of a dwelling.
Ten times, a hundred times, ten hundred times, and hundreds of hundreds of times;”
"We were reborn among the gods, so what need is there to mention humans?
Among the gods we possessed great supernormal power, so what need is there to mention the human realm?
I was the queen of the possessor of the seven treasures, the Woman-Jewel."
“Thus it is the cause, thus it is the source, that very patience in the Teaching is the root.
That is the first attainment; that is the Nibbāna for one who delights in the Dhamma.
Thus act those who have faith in the word of him of matchless wisdom.”
“They become disenchanted with the course of existence; having become disenchanted, they become dispassionate.”—He spoke these verses.
Therein, “in the city of Mantavati” means in the city named Mantavati. “Of King Koñca” means of Koñca.
I was born as a daughter in the womb of the king’s chief queen; my name was Sumedhā, meaning "the Wise One.

She was "inspired by those who carry out the Teacher’s instruction," meaning she was inspired in the dispensation by the Noble Ones (ariya) who carry out the Teacher’s instruction through their preaching of the Dhamma, having developed faith in the Three Jewels.

"Virtuous" means endowed with conduct and moral discipline (*sīla*). "A speaker on the mind" means a speaker on the Dhamma concerning the mind. "Highly learned" refers to [the qualities of] the bhikkhunīs.
"Endowed with the hearing of the Dhamma of the scriptures in their presence;

disciplined in the Buddha’s teaching"—thus they are "disciplined in the Buddha’s teaching" because, through wise attention following the Suttas, thinking "this is virtue, this is concentration, this is wisdom," the defilements have been turned away from them by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*); thus they are those whose body, speech, and mind are restrained. "Both of you, listen attentively. You...
"Both of you listen to my words," connects with "having approached, mother and father, she says.
Even if they shine—that is, even the celestial realms included within the world of the gods, known as the "state of existence"—all of it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
How much more so, then, empty sensual pleasures? That is to say, how much more so human sensual pleasures?
All of these are empty and void because they lack any core essence; like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword, they offer little gratification;
and they are fraught with many afflictions due to extensive suffering both now and in the future.

"Bitter" means undesirable. In the sense of being dangerous, they are comparable to venomous snakes. "In which sensual pleasures": "infatuated" means deeply attached. "Completely absorbed": entirely cast down and thrown by their own karma; the meaning is that they have been reborn [therein]. "Are slain" means they are oppressed.
They cause one to fall into the states of misery (*apāya*).
"Lacking intention" means lacking the intention for their own welfare. "Obstructed by the origin of suffering" means being confined within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) caused by craving.
"While the Teaching is being expounded" means while the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths is being taught. "Not knowing" means not understanding the meaning. They do not awaken.
"The Noble Truths" refers to the Noble Truths beginning with suffering; they do not awaken to them.
"O mother!"—he addresses her, making his mother the foremost. "Those who know less"—this is the construction:
those who rejoice in existence, who long for rebirth among the devas, and who do not know the Truths taught by the Excellent Buddha, are indeed the majority in this world.
"In all existence being impermanent": since all existence is impermanent, rebirth among the devas is not eternal;
even though this is so, fools do not become afraid, they do not tremble, and they do not experience a sense of spiritual urgency.
"Of one who must be born again and again" means of one who is being reborn repeatedly.
The four states of ruin (*vinipāta*) are: hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the realm of asuras; these four are destinies of ruin because they fall away from a happy existence.
However, only two destinies—rebirth among humans and among devas—are obtained with some difficulty and hardship, because meritorious action is difficult to perform.
"In hells" means in the states of misery devoid of happiness.

"Free from anxiety" means being without concern for other duties. The construction is: "I shall strive, I shall exert effort, I shall devote myself to meditation; what is the use of delighting in the worthless, hollow existence within the cycle of becoming?
"For the cessation of craving for becoming" means for the sake of the cessation, that is, the cause of the cessation, of craving directed toward existence.
"The arising of Buddhas has been obtained; the eight kinds of inopportune moments, such as rebirth in hell and so forth, have been avoided; the ninth moment [is at hand]."

"The moment has been gained" is the construction. "Virtues" refers to the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*).
"I shall not defile it" means "I shall not corrupt it.
"As long as I am a householder, I will not take food"—this means: "I shall not take food while remaining a householder."
"If I do not obtain the going-forth, I shall surely meet my death"—thus Sumedhā spoke to her parents; such is the construction of the sentence.
*Assā* means "of Sumedhā. *Sabbaso samabhihato* means "his face was completely overwhelmed by tears.
*Ghaṭenti saññāpetum* means that both mother and father strive to persuade Sumedhā, who had fallen to the ground on the terrace of the palace, to remain in the state of a householder.
They strive. There is also a reading, “ghaṭenti vāyamanti,” which has the same meaning.
“What is the use of grieving? means: what is the use of grieving that “I shall not obtain the going-forth”?

“You were given at Vāraṇavatī” means: you were given in the city of Vāraṇavatī. Having said “dinnāsi” (you were given), the further statement “tvaṃ dinnā” (you were given) is for the sake of making it firm.
For the purpose of showing that [the gift] has been bestowed.
"In the kingdom, your command prevails" means that in the kingdom, your command as the ruler proceeds.
"Wealth and sovereignty" refers to the wealth and sovereignty in this family and the husband's family; "possessions, pleasures, exceedingly desirable things"—all these possessions are yours.
“Presented” means it has come into his hands. “You are young” means you are a maiden; therefore, enjoy sensual pleasures.
For that reason, let there be a marriage for you to have sons—this is the construction of the sentence.

“No,” say the parents. “May there not be such things as these” means may such commands and so forth regarding the kingdom not exist. Why? He says: “Because the Blessed One is without essence,” and so forth.
"Like a worm" means like a worm. "A putrid body" refers to this foul carcass. "Foul-smelling" means emitting a rank, offensive odor.
"Terrifying" means bringing fear to those who have not yet abandoned passion (*avītarāga*).
"I would enter a skin-sack filled with a corpse" means a leather bag filled with a corpse, leaking and dripping, full of impurity—being full of various kinds of filth.
How could one, knowing it to be thus, form the misconception, "This is mine," toward that which is constantly oozing and flowing,
which is exceedingly repulsive— smeared with impure lumps of flesh and blood,
an abode for many swarms of worms, and food for birds? It is also called "the food of birds and the haunt of worm-swarms."
The meaning is: "It is the food for the worms and the remaining birds. Knowing that this was my own corpse, I stood there.
He shows why, by way of being given away, it is now being offered to me: "For what reason indeed (*kissa*)—by what cause (*kena nāma kāraṇena*)—is it being given?
The construction is: "What is that gift like (*tañca dānaṃ kimiva*)? It is like what (*kiṃ viya*)? [End of passage]
"Carried to the charnel ground before long, the body with consciousness departed"—this body, having very soon lost its consciousness, is carried and brought to the charnel ground.
"Cast off" means abandoned. "Like a log" means like a useless piece of wood.
"By relatives who feel disgust" means by the circle of kinsmen who also feel revulsion.
"Having abandoned it in the charnel ground" means having discarded that corpse in the charnel ground. "Food for others" means having become the food of others, such as dogs, jackals, and so forth.

"They bathe in disgust" means that even those who merely think, "We have come after this [corpse]," bathe while submerging themselves up to their heads out of disgust, let alone those who have actually touched it. "One's own mother and father" refers to one's own biological parents.
"But what need is there to say that the common multitude is disgusted?"—for the other [the wise] are likewise disgusted by the mass.
"Attached" means firmly adhered to by way of craving. "Insubstantial" means devoid of any essence such as permanence or substance.
"Having analyzed" means having performed an analysis of consciousness. "Unable to endure the odor" means [unable to endure] the odor of this body.
Unable to endure it—even her own mother would feel disgust, because by dissecting the constituent parts, the repulsiveness of the body becomes even more clearly manifest.
"Aggregates, elements, and bases" refers to these five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form; these eighteen elements, beginning with the eye element; and...

"The eye-base and so forth—these are the twelve bases. Thus, all this collection of material and immaterial phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and bases—is "conditioned" because it is produced by causes coming together and combining;
and this, as it occurs within that existence, is suffering, rooted in birth because birth is its condition. Thus one investigates with wise means.
Reflecting upon her marriage and wedding, she thought, "For what reason and for what purpose would I desire [this]?
In order to give a reply to her parents—who had said, "Virtues, the holy life, and renunciation are difficult to practice"—she spoke the words beginning with "Day after day.
In that context, it is said that three thousand seven hundred new [lotuses] might fall every single day.
"Upon the body": every day, three hundred spears—freshly sharpened by being alternately heated and tempered—should fall upon the body.
"Even for a hundred years, death is better": even if they were falling continuously for a hundred years, the aforementioned slaughter by spears would be better.
"And thus the exhaustion of suffering": if, in this way, there were a complete destruction of the suffering of saṃsāra.
The intention is that one should exert effort for the attainment of Nibbāna by enduring even such great suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Ajjhupagacche" means one should accept. "Evaṃ" means in the manner stated. This is what is meant:
the person who, having understood the Teacher’s word which demonstrates the beginningless *saṃsāra* and the immeasurable suffering of the cycle of existence...
Standing firm, one would endure the suffering of being struck by the aforementioned sword; through that very endurance, there might be an end to the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
Therefore he said: "Long is their saṃsāra, and they are struck again and again"—the meaning is that they are afflicted repeatedly by birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth.
"Among the *asura*-hosts" means among the classes of *preta* and *asura*, such as the *Kālakañjika*. "Slayings" (*ghāta*) refers to the injuries and killings of body and mind.
"Many" (*bahu*) means numerous slayings occurring by way of various punishments, such as the fivefold fetters and other forms of legal penalty.

"For one who has gone to the states of ruin" (*vinipātagatassa*) means even for one who has entered the states of ruin known as the remaining lower realms (*apāya*). "Being oppressed" (*pīḷiyamānassa*) refers to [suffering] through blows and so forth within the individual existence (*attabhāva*) of animals and the like.

"Of one who is being afflicted": even among the gods there is no refuge (*attaṇa*); that is, even in the state of existence as a god, there is no protection because of the presence of suffering and distress through the fever of passion and so forth.

"There is no happiness higher than the bliss of Nibbāna": other than the bliss of Nibbāna, there is no other supreme happiness; this is because worldly happiness has the nature of the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned formations. Therefore he said:
The Blessed One said: "Nirvana is the supreme happiness.

Those who have attained it are indeed called "those who have attained Nirvana. Alternatively, they alone have attained Nirvana. "Those who are devoted to the teaching of the One of Ten Powers" means those who are devoted and engaged in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Disgusted" means dispassionate. "By me" means by me. "Like vomit" means like the vomit of a dog. "Rendered like the stump of a palm tree" means made like the base of a palm tree.
Then, afterwards—having announced his own intention to his mother and father, and having heard that Anikaratta had arrived—he [said]:
"With a sword, he should cut the hair which is black, thickly matted, soft, and like the color of a sapphire;
which is dense in its mass, and soft with a touch like that of *simbali*-cotton. Thus, with a very sharp sword, he [should cut] his own hair.
"Having cut with a sword. "Having closed the palace" means having shut the bedchamber in her own residence;
the meaning is that she bolted its door. "She attained the first jhāna":
having placed her own hair in front after it was cut by the sword, she applied attention to the repulsive aspect therein, and thus attained the first [jhāna] that arose in the sign as it appeared.
Having attained mastery over jhāna, she entered into it.
And the intention is that Sumedhā, having entered that jhāna in the palace, cultivated the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).
This means that, having emerged from jhāna and made that jhāna the basis (*pādaka*), she established insight (*vipassanā*) by means of the formula beginning with, "Whatever form... and so forth.

He thoroughly develops the contemplation of impermanence; it should be understood that by the inclusion of the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering and the others are also included therein.
"With limbs adorned with jewels and gold" means his body was embellished with golden garlands and ornaments variegated with gems.

“Command over the kingdom” and so forth is an illustration of the manner in which she was entreated. Therein, “command” (*āṇāti*) means sovereignty. “Power” (*issariya*) means fame and the attainment of wealth. “Enjoyments and pleasures” (*bhogā sukhā*) refers to desirable and agreeable objects of sensual enjoyment. “You are young” means that you are currently youthful and tender.
“The kingdom has been relinquished to you” means that my entire three-league kingdom has been surrendered to you;
having taken possession of it, enjoy the riches. Do not be dejected, thinking, “This one is inviting me only with sensual pleasures.”
"Give gifts" means: let great gifts be bestowed according to your inclination upon ascetics and brahmins;
your parents are suffering and have fallen into grief upon hearing of your intention to go forth, therefore enjoy sensual pleasures.
While you are serving them, release their hearts from suffering—thus should the construction of the words here be understood.

"Do not delight in sensual pleasures" means: do not take pleasure in sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) or in the defilements of sensuality (*kilesakāma*). Rather, by following my word, see the danger and fault in those sensual pleasures; survey them with the eye of knowledge.
"Lord of the four continents" refers to the ruler of the four great continents, such as Jambudīpa.
"Mandhātā" was a king of that name, who was the foremost and preeminent among those who enjoy sensual pleasures. Therefore the Blessed One said: "Rāhu among embodied beings, Mandhātā..."

"Of those who enjoy sensual pleasures. "Dying unsatisfied": even after spending eighty-four thousand years in princely play, eighty-four thousand years as a viceroy, and eighty-four thousand years as a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) enjoying wealth like that of the gods;
and even after experiencing the splendors of heaven for the full lifespan of thirty-six Sakka-devas in the Tāvatiṃsa realm—yet he died unsatisfied.
He passed away while still unsated with sensual pleasures. His desire was not fulfilled; King Mandhātu’s longing for sense-pleasures remained unfulfilled.
"May the seven treasures rain down"—that is, may even the seven treasures fall as rain, the raining cloud spreading through the ten directions on every side.
Even if it were to rain everywhere according to a man’s desire—just as it did for the Great King Mandhātu—even so there is no satiety with sensual pleasures;
men die still unsatiated. Therefore the Blessed One said: “There is no satiety found in sensual pleasures, even by a rain of kahāpaṇa coins.”

Sensual pleasures are like meat-hooks in the sense that they cut deeply; they are like a snake’s fang in the sense that they are terrifying; they are like a firebrand or a grass-fire in the sense that they burn. Therefore, he said, “they burn. They resemble a skeleton in the sense that they offer little gratification. They are like great poisons such as *halāhala* and the like.
They are the root of misfortune (*aghamūla*), meaning they are the cause of suffering (*agha*). Therefore, he said, “they have suffering as their fruit.
They are like the fruit of a tree in the sense that they crush the limbs and members of the body. They are like a piece of meat in the sense that they are common property to many.

They are like a dream in the sense that they present themselves only for a brief moment; they are like an illusion because they are alluring. Therefore he said, "deceptive," meaning they are deceivers.
They are like borrowed goods in the sense that they are merely temporary. They are like a spear or a stake in the sense that they pierce through.
They are a disease in the sense of being afflicted, due to the ease with which suffering arises. They are a boil because of the trickling out of the filth of the defilements.
It is "aghā" (misery) in the sense of producing suffering; it is "nighā" (destruction) because it brings about death; it is like a pit of glowing embers in the sense of being a great torment.
It is called "bhayaṃ vadho" (fearful slaughter) because it is a cause of fear and because of the abundance of executioners—this is how it should be construed with "kāme" (sensual pleasures).

They are "declared to be obstacles" (*antarāyikā akkhātā*) means they were spoken of by the Buddha and others who have become like eyes as "obstructing the attainment of the path to heaven and the path leading to Nibbāna. "Go! he says, dismissing them along with their retinue so that they may not remain.

"What will another do for me?"—what indeed can another person do for my welfare when my own head, the supreme limb, is being consumed by eleven fires? Therefore he said, "While old age and death pursue.
For the sake of the destruction, the eradication, of that burning of the head which is old age and death, one must strive and exert oneself.
“They lament on the ground. I spoke these words—“Long is the saṃsāra of fools,” and so forth—which lead to a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

“Long is the saṃsāra of fools”: for blind fools who have not fully understood the basis [of existence], the saṃsāra—defined as the continuous succession of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, which consist of the rounds of defilements, karma, and results—is long; it cannot be delimited even by the Buddha’s knowledge.

For just as the prior limit of the continuity of existence is not discerned precisely because ignorance and craving are uninterrupted and thus unbounded, so too is the subsequent limit. And "weeping again and again" refers to those who weep repeatedly on account of sorrow;
by this, he likewise makes manifest the very fact that their ignorance and craving are uninterrupted.
"Tears, milk, and blood": this refers to the tears shed by those afflicted by the loss of kinsmen and other such misfortunes;
the milk drunk from the mother's breast during childhood; and the blood shed when slain by enemies.

Because the beginningless limit of *saṃsāra*—that is, because one cannot find its starting point through knowledge despite following it back even to its "endless" (i.e., unknown) limit—one has, through this long [journey], [experienced]...
Now, remember the wandering of beings as they transmigrate from one state to another;
remember and recollect how vast that wandering is—meaning, remember and keep in mind the accumulation of bones.
Now, in order to show by way of a simile the great extent of this disadvantage, he spoke the verse beginning, "Remember the four oceans. Therein:
"Remember the four oceans brought forth in comparison to the tears, breast-milk, and blood [of these beings]. Remember this:

for each and every one of these beings wandering through the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), the four oceans—the four great seas—have been brought forward by the Buddhas as a metaphorical measure for their tears, breast-milk, and blood. "The bones [of those who have lived] in a single aeon..."
One should remember that the accumulation of the bones of a single person over the course of one eon would equal the size of Mount Vepulla.
As it has been said: "The accumulation of the bones of a single person over the course of one eon..."
“There might be a heap equal to a mountain,” so it was said by the Great Seer:
“Indeed, this Vepulla, the great mountain,
lies to the north of Gijjhakūṭa among the mountains of Magadha.”
"Even if the great earth of Jambudīpa were brought [there]. Regarding the phrase "the pills the size of a jujube stone":

even if one were to reduce the great earth known as Jambudīpa into pills the size of a *kolaṭṭhi*—that is, the size of a jujube stone—and were to distribute them one by one, saying, "This is my mother;
this is my mother’s mother," those pills would not suffice for all the mothers. The mother... [would not be exhausted].
Even while one’s mothers have not yet passed away, those pills would reach exhaustion and termination;
but for a being wandering through the beginningless cycle of existence, there is no end to the number of times they have been one’s mother or grandmother.
Thus, attend to Jambudvīpa as a simile for the long duration of *saṃsāra*.
"Grass, sticks, branches, and foliage" means grass, wood, and twigs and leaves. "Brought forward" means brought forward by way of a simile.
"Of a beginningless end" means because of the state of having no discernible beginning for *saṃsāra*. "Four-fingerbreadth pieces" means fragments measuring four finger-breadths.
"Even for the fathers' fathers they would not suffice" means that those pieces would not even suffice for the paternal grandfathers. This...
This is what is meant: if all the grass, wood, branches, and foliage in this world were cut into four-finger-length pieces and each piece were assigned there—
one saying, "This was for my father," another, "This was for my grandfather"—
those sticks would reach exhaustion and total depletion, yet not even the end of the beginningless wandering in *saṃsāra* for a being would be reached.
"Father, grandfather," and so on. Thus, one should reflect upon how grass, wood, and branches and foliage have been brought through the long duration of *saṃsāra*.
At this point, however, it is said:
"Monks, this *saṃsāra* is without discoverable beginning; a first point is not discerned for beings hindered by ignorance."
“Of those wandering and transmigrating with the fetter of craving—what do you think, monks, which is more:

the tears that have flowed and streamed forth from you while weeping and crying out in lamentation during this long course of wandering and transmigration due to association with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant; or the water in the four great oceans?”
The passage beginning with “water,” etc., the *Anamatagga-pāḷi* (Discourse on the Beginningless) should be cited.
“Recall the blind turtle”: recall a turtle that is blind in both eyes. “A yoke-hole in the eastern ocean and in the west”:
[imagine] a yoke-hole in the eastern ocean and in the west—that is, in the western, northern, and southern oceans—driven by the force of the wind.
"Of a yoke revolving with a single hole," "and his head being placed therein"— this refers to the head of a blind tortoise,
and the insertion of that head into the hole of the yoke as it raises its neck at the end of every hundred years.
"The acquisition of human birth is the simile"— all of this [is said] in reference to the arising of a Buddha and the teaching of the Dhamma.

Having made a simile for the attainment of human status as if it were [the finding of] a yoke with a single hole in the great ocean, one should remember it with wisdom, because its nature is exceedingly difficult to obtain and because the state of being seized by fear is likewise exceedingly swift. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean," and so forth.

"Remember that form is like a lump of foam": remember that the form belonging to this turbid body—designated as "body"—which resembles a lump of foam because it cannot withstand being crushed, because it is a convergence of manifold misfortunes, and because it is devoid of any core such as permanence, is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
"See the aggregates as impermanent": see even these five aggregates of clinging as impermanent in the sense of their non-existence.

Behold with the eye of knowledge. Remember that the hells are full of affliction: recollect the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells, which are full of affliction, full of suffering, and full of great suffering.
Remember that they increase the funeral pyre: by being born again and again in various successive births.
Recall sentient beings as they increase the cemetery, the charnel ground, and the very heap of refuse.

Or, the reading is "vaḍḍhanto"; the construction is: "you, who are increasing. "The fears of crocodiles" refers to the fears of gluttony resulting from performing improper actions for the sake of nourishing the belly.
For it is said: "The 'fear of crocodiles,' monks, is a designation for gluttony. Remember this.

"Regarding the four truths": "This is the noble truth of suffering... [and so on] ...this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—thus, recollect and examine the four noble truths as they truly are.
Having thus revealed the danger in sensual pleasures and in saṃsāra by means of this multiform recollection, the princess—
Now, in order to demonstrate that same point through the method of contrast (*vyatireka*), he said, "While the Deathless exists," and so forth.
Therein, "while the Deathless exists" means while the Deathless of the True Dharma (*saddhamma*) brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One out of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is available.
"What to you with the five-fold bitter [poison] you have drunk? refers to the fivefold [misuse of requisites]: seeking, grasping, guarding, using, and the result [of such use].

Because it is accompanied by more intense suffering in various situations, because it is distressing, and because it is fraught with anxiety, what is the use to you of drinking the fivefold pungent taste of the five strands of sensual pleasure?
Now, making the point just stated even more evident, she said:
"For all delights of sensual pleasure are far more bitter than the fivefold pungent taste," meaning they are exceedingly more bitter.

"Those that are burning" means those sensual pleasures which are currently burning with the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*) and will be burning in the future with the fever of their ripening result (*vipāka-pariḷāha*);
they are great obstacles. Being "blazing, boiling, trembling, and scorched," they are set ablaze by eleven fires and, having become boiling, cause trembling and scorching for those who possess them.
“Free from enemies” means in renunciation (nekkhamma), which is devoid of adversaries. “While it exists” means while it is present.
Having stated, “It has many enemies,” the words beginning with “kings and fire” were spoken to show those by whom it has many enemies.
Kings, fire, thieves, water, and unloved ones such as heirs—because these are common to both [the worldly life and renunciation]—the similes were stated specifically for them.
"Killing and binding" means that in regard to those sensual pleasures there occurs the defilement of death, slaughter, and so forth, as well as the binding with fetters, shackles, and the like;
this is the meaning. "In sensual pleasures," etc., is a clarification of the very meaning already stated. Therein, *hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
Because, for the sake of sensual pleasures and on account of sensual pleasures, these beings experience and undergo the sufferings of killing and binding.
Therefore he says: “Asakāmā” means that these desires are non-existent, base, and contemptible. Alternatively, there is the reading “ahakāmā,” which has the same meaning;
for *aha* is a term for what is base, as in expressions such as “women called *ahaloka*.

“Ādīpitā” means set ablaze. “Tiṇukkā” means a fire made of grass. “Dahanti ye te muñcanti” means those beings who do not release these desires, but rather grasp them, they indeed burn—tormenting them both now and in the future.
"Do not, for the sake of the small"—that is, for the sake of limited sensual pleasure which is like the taste of a flower—"abandon or discard the vast, sublime, and refined supramundane happiness.
Do not be like the "broad-finned" fish, who, having swallowed a hook out of greed for bait, meets with disaster; such is the name given to that fish.
Without having abandoned sensual desires, do not be distressed later; do not fall into subsequent affliction.
Like a dog bound by a chain—just as a dog tied with a leash to a post, unable to go elsewhere, merely wanders about right there—so too are you [bound] by the craving for sensual pleasures.
"Bound! Now, even if you desire it, restrain yourself among sensual pleasures; subdue your senses!
For indeed, those sensual pleasures will treat you just as a hungry dog treats a Caṇḍāla"—the word "khu" is merely a particle.
The meaning is that those sensual pleasures will bring about your ruin and disaster, just as dogs with parched throats and hunger, upon catching a dog-cooker, lead him to his destruction.
“Immeasurable suffering” means the physical suffering in the hells and other realms, which is boundless and impossible to delimit by saying, “it is this much.
“And many mental distresses” means the numerous and manifold mental sufferings, the afflictions of the mind, that are experienced within the consciousness.
“You shall experience” means you will undergo them. “Addicted to sensual pleasures” means being joined with sensual desires, not relinquishing them.
"Relinquish desires that are unstable": the meaning is, abandon and turn away from desires that are unstable and impermanent.

"All births everywhere are seized by old age, death, and disease": because all births—distinguished by the divisions of inferior and so forth—in all states of existence and the like, are seized by old age, death, and disease, and are not liberated from them; therefore, [one should seek] in the undecaying Nibbāna.
The construction is: "What purpose do you have with sensual pleasures that exist [only] while one is not yet liberated from old age and the like?

Having thus revealed the danger in sensual pleasures and in states of existence by way of showing the qualities of Nibbāna, she now spoke two verses beginning with "This is ageless," etc., in order to reveal the very qualities of Nibbāna already produced. Therein, "this is ageless" means:
This alone is "ageless" (*ajara*) because of the absence of aging within it, and because it is the cause for the attainment of the absence of aging.
The same principle applies here to the term "deathless" (*amara*). He speaks of this as "ageless and deathless" (*ajarāmara*) by combining both qualities together for the sake of praise.

It is a "footprint" (*pada*) because it is that which should be departed toward and practiced by those desiring liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra; [it is so called] because of the causes of sorrow...
It is "without sorrow" (*asoka*) because of the absence [of suffering] and the absence of grief. It is "without enemy" (*asapatta*) because of the absence of states that produce enemies.

It is "unconfined" (*asambādha*) because of the absence of the confinement of the defilements (*kilesa*). It is "unerring" (*akhalita*) by virtue of the absence of misconduct, which is reckoned as stumbling.

It is "fearless" (*abhaya*) due to the total absence of fears such as self-reproach and so forth, as well as the fear of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭa*). It is "without torment" (*nirupatāpa*) because of the absence of both the torment of suffering and the defilements.

All of this is said with reference to the great Nibbāna, which is deathless. For she, appearing to them as it were through a mode established by tradition and so forth, spoke "this" as if pointing it out directly to their eyes.
"This deathless is not departed from by many"—this means that this deathless Nibbāna has not been abandoned by many, such as the infinite and immeasurable Buddhas and others.
It was attained by the Noble Ones, known by them, and made manifest to themselves. He does not speak with reference only to what was attained by them;
rather, it is also obtainable even today, and it is possible to attain it now as well. To the question "By whom is it obtainable? he says:
"by one who applies himself thoroughly," meaning that person who, through thorough means, [applies himself] to the instruction given by the Teacher.
"Standing firm, he applies himself and practices right effort; therefore, it is obtainable"—this is the construction. "And it cannot be achieved by one who does not strive":

however, for one who does not apply himself with wise attention (*yoniso*), by such a non-striver it cannot be achieved; the meaning is that it simply cannot be attained at any time. "Thus spoke Sumedhā":
in the manner thus described, the princess Sumedhā spoke this [verse] as an expression of her own spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding *saṃsāra*.
She delivered a discourse on the Dhamma conducive to penetration regarding sensual pleasures.

"Finding no delight in conditioned phenomena" means not finding even the slightest pleasure in the occurrence of conditioned things. "Persuading King Anikaratta" means making King Anikaratta understand.
"And she threw her hair upon the ground" means she cut off her own hair with her sword and threw it, cast it away, upon the earth.
Thus he entreated his father, the king of cranes, for the sake of Sumedhā, who was not fickle-minded.
When asked what he entreated, he said: "Release Sumedhā, that she may go forth as one who sees the truth of liberation.
The meaning is: "Release the princess Sumedhā so that she may go forth; and having gone forth, let her be one who sees the truth of liberation—that is, one who perceives Nibbāna without error."
"Frightened by fear and dread" means terrified by every kind of fear within saṃsāra, such as separation from kinsmen and so forth;

she was made to tremble by means of supreme knowledge. "While she was a trainee" means that while she was still a trainee (sikkhamānā), she realized the six direct knowledges (abhiññā), and for that very reason, she realized the highest fruit, which is Arahantship.
"Wondrous and marvelous was that Nibbāna for the princess"— the complete Nibbāna from defilements of Sumedhā,
the royal daughter, was indeed wondrous and marvelous. If it is asked how she attained the sixfold direct knowledge (*chaḷabhiññā*),
it is because she later, at the time of her final Nibbāna of the aggregates, recounted her own past conduct included within her previous existences (*pubbenivāsa*).
"One should understand it exactly as she explained it.
However, in order to show how she explained her previous births (*pubbenivāsa*), the passage beginning with "During the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana" was stated.
Therein, "during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana" means when the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) Koṇāgamana had appeared in the world. In the monastery (*saṅghārāma*)...
"In a new settlement" means in a monastery newly established for the sake of the Saṅgha.
"We three friends," namely Dhanañjānī, Khemā, and myself—"gave a gift of a monastery"—means that we three friends gave a monastery as a gift to the Saṅgha.
"Ten times, a hundred times"—by the power of that gift of a monastery, we were reborn among the devas ten times.
Then, having been reborn among humans, we were reborn among the devas a hundred times;
from there, having been reborn among humans, we were reborn among the devas a thousand times—ten hundred times—a thousandfold;
from there, having been reborn among humans, we were reborn among the devas ten thousand times—a hundred times a hundred—a ten-thousandfold. But who indeed...
"What need is there to speak of among humans? means that when one has arisen among humans, there is not even talk [of such power]; the sense is: "We have been reborn many thousands of times.
"Among the gods we were of great psychic power" means that at the time of being reborn among the gods, in each respective divine class, we were of great psychic power and great majesty.
"But what need is there to speak of in the human state? means that regarding the attainment of the human condition, there is no talk of possessing great psychic power.
There is none. Now, demonstrating that very excellence and great power within the human state, she said:
"I was the queen of the possessor of the seven jewels, the jewel among women.

In this context, one who possesses the seven jewels, such as the wheel-jewel and the rest, is called *sattaratano*, namely a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavattī*); [she was] the queen of such a possessor of the seven jewels. She was free from the six defects and possessed the five excellences.
"By being endowed with such qualities as having transcended human beauty and attained divine beauty, I became a jewel among women.
"That cause" refers to the gift of a monastery made to the Saṅgha during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana;
that is the cause for the aforementioned divine prosperity. "That source," "that root"—these are synonyms for the same thing. That very [root] is in the Dispensation...
"Patience" (khanti) here refers to the patience of reflective contemplation regarding the Dhamma within this Teacher’s dispensation.
"The first convergence with that" means that very first convergence or first meeting with the Dhamma of the Teacher’s dispensation.

By using the term "Nibbāna" at the end for one who delights in the Dhamma of the Teacher’s dispensation, he speaks of the cause by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit. Now, these four verses:
Because it proceeds by way of elucidating the *apadāna* of the Elder Nun, it has also been included within the *Apadāna-pāḷi*.
In the concluding verse, "those who act thus" means that just as I have acted and practiced in previous existences and now, so too do others act and practice.
To the question "Who acts thus?", he says: "those who have faith in the word."

Regarding the phrase "of one with peerless wisdom": those individuals who have faith in the words of the Perfectly Enlightened One—who possesses perfected wisdom due to his knowledge that has reached the very limit of all that can be known—and who resolve, "This is so," they act and practice accordingly.
Now, in order to demonstrate that through such a consummate practice, [the text says]: "They become disenchanted with the course of existence; having become disenchanted, they become dispassionate."

Thus it was said. Its meaning is as follows: those who believe the word of the Blessed One according to reality, practicing the path to purification, become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena belonging to the three planes within the entire range of existence by means of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*).
Having become disenchanted, they become entirely free from passion through the Noble Path and are liberated from the entire range of existence.
The meaning is as follows: when the Noble Path of dispassion (*virāga*) is attained, they indeed become liberated.
Thus, these elder nuns (*therikā*), beginning with Sumedhā and ending with her, have been collected here together under the category of verses;
they number seventy-three. However, according to the recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), there are approximately six hundred and two elder nuns and their verses. These—
Just as all [these nuns] are of one kind by virtue of being disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One, so too they are of one kind by virtue of their state of being beyond training (*asekha*):

through having lifted the crossbar, through having filled in the moat, through having pulled out the pillar, through being without bars, through having laid down the burden, through being detached, and through having completed the residence in the ten abodes of the noble ones;
for indeed, they have abandoned five factors and are endowed with six factors.

It is of one kind by way of such descriptions as: "guarded by a single protection, with a fourfold defense, having dispelled individual truths, having abandoned search for the uniform, with untroubled intention, with tranquil bodily formations, with well-liberated mind, and with well-liberated wisdom.
It is of two kinds through the distinction between being face-to-face and behind one's back; for those who were born into the noble birth at the time when the Teacher was still living...

Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and others are called "face-to-face female disciples" (*sammukhāsāvikā*). However, those who attained distinction after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One's aggregates are called "not face-to-face female disciples" (*parammukhāsāvikā*), because although the Teacher’s Dharma-body was directly present to them, his physical body was not.
Likewise, this classification applies according to whether one is liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutti*) or liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*).

However, those included here in the text are exclusively those liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Likewise, they are distinguished by whether they have a *apadāna* (biographical account) or not.

For those who possess an *apadāna*—defined as the performance of meritorious deeds under previous Fully Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*), Private Buddhas (*paccekabuddha*), or Disciple-Buddhas (*sāvakabuddha*)—they are "with *apadāna*" (*sāpadāna*).
Those who do not possess this are "without *apadāna*" (*nāpadāna*). Similarly, there are those who have received full ordination (*upasampadā*) from a Teacher.

"Ordination received from the Saṅgha" is twofold. Ordination received during the acceptance of the *garudhammas*—in the case of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī—is called "ordination received from the Teacher," because she received it in the very presence of the Teacher. All others are "ordination received from the Saṅgha.
These, too, are twofold: those ordained on one side (*ekatoupasampannā*) and those ordained on both sides (*ubhatoupasampannā*). Among these, as for those...
The five hundred Sakyan women who set out together with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī were "fully ordained on one side" (*ekatoupasampannā*),
because they received their full ordination from the Saṅgha of monks alone, excluding Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī herself. The others were "fully ordained on both sides" (*ubhatoupasampannā*),
because they received their full ordination from both Saṅghas.

The *ehibhikkhu* formula and the *ehibhikkhunī* formula are not found here. Why? Because there was no such way for the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of bhikkhunīs. If this is so, how do we account for what was said by Subhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā in the *Therīgāthā*:
“Having knelt down and paid homage, she placed her joined palms before me;
‘Come, Bhaddā,’ he said to me—that was my full ordination”?
Likewise, in the Apadāna:
“Then the Leader said to me when requested, ‘Come, blessed one!
At that moment I was ordained, and I saw a small amount of water.”

How is that so? This was not said with reference to the full admission (*upasampadā*) by way of the "Come, Bhikkhunī" formula. Rather, it was said because the Teacher’s command was the cause for her full admission:

"The Teacher’s command was my full admission. For it is stated thus in the Commentary: "He said to me, 'Come, Bhaddā, go to the bhikkhunīs' residence and receive the going-forth and the full admission in the presence of the bhikkhunīs'; he commanded me. That command of the Teacher was my full admission."
"Because it was the cause, it became the full ordination (*upasampadā*). By this very [statement], it should be understood that the meaning has also been explained in the verses of the *Apadāna*.
Furthermore, how is it that the phrase "Come, O Bhikkhunī" appears in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*?

It is a statement indicating the non-existence of the full ordination for bhikkhunīs by way of the "Come, O Bhikkhunī" formula; likewise, because there is no such full ordination for bhikkhunīs. If...
Thus, how is the exposition in the Vibhaṅga regarding "Come, bhikkhunī" formulated? It is by virtue of falling within the stream of the method of teaching.
For this so-called "falling within the stream" means that even when something is obtainable in a certain context, it is not explicitly mentioned there;

as for example, although the jhāna-factor is obtainable in the exposition of the mind-element (manodhātu) in the Abhidhamma, it is not mentioned because it falls within the stream of the fivefold sense-consciousness (pañcaviññāṇa).

It is not extracted [from the list] anywhere because it is impossible for it to occur in the teaching. Just as in that very same section on the description of bases (*vatthuniddesa*), the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is included even though it is not found anywhere else;
likewise in the description of those who abide for an eon (*ṭhitakappiniddesa*). As it is said:
"And what kind of person is one who abides for an eon? This person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry..."
“Even if the time for the conflagration of the aeon were to arrive, that aeon would not be consumed by fire until this person has realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Thus, it should be understood here as well in terms of the non-occurrence of such a possibility; for this is a hypothetical statement, [implying] "if the Blessed One..."
If he were to say to some woman who was fit for the state of a bhikkhunī, "Come, bhikkhunī," then in this way too the state of a bhikkhunī would come to be.
But why did the Blessed One not speak thus? Because there was an absence of those who had performed such service [in previous lives].
As for those who state the reason as being "due to the absence of proximity or presence," they say: "For it is the bhikkhus alone who are the Teacher’s constant attendants..."
They say, "Because they are present, those [men] deserve to be addressed as 'Come, monk,' but not the nuns";
that is merely their opinion. For the proximity or distance from the Teacher does not establish whether one is capable or incapable [of ordination]. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, even if a monk were to follow closely behind another, grasping the corner of his outer robe..."

If, while placing one foot after another, he is covetous for sensual pleasures, with intense passion, a mind of ill will, corrupt intentions, muddled mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, and unguarded in his faculties—then he is far indeed from me, and I am far from him.
Why is that? Because, monks, that bhikkhu does not see the Dhamma.
"One who does not see the Dhamma does not see me.
Even if a bhikkhu were to dwell a hundred yojanas away, bhikkhus, yet if he is free from covetousness for sensual pleasures,
without intense passion, with a mind devoid of ill will, with intentions that are not corrupt, established in mindfulness, clearly comprehending, and concentrated..."
“One whose mind is one-pointed and whose faculties are restrained is indeed close to me, and I am close to him.
For what reason? Because that bhikkhu, monks, sees the Dhamma; seeing the Dhamma, he sees me.

Therefore, proximity or distance from the Teacher in terms of location is not the cause. However, because they have not performed the necessary service, bhikkhunīs lack the fitness for that [ordination]. Hence it was said: “The ‘Come, bhikkhunī’ formula is not applicable here. Thus, [the ordination] is of two kinds.

There are three kinds of female disciples (sāvikā): the chief female disciple (aggasāvikā), the great female disciple (mahāsāvikā), and the ordinary female disciple (pakatisāvikā). Among these, the two elder nuns Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā are called the chief female disciples.

Granted, all elder nuns who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsavā) accomplish purity of virtue and so forth, maintain their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and develop the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as they really are according to the sequence of the path.
Having exhausted the defilements without remainder, they are established in the highest fruit (*aggaphala*). Nevertheless,

just as there is a desired distinction between one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*) compared to one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*), and between one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) compared to one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*)— a distinction established by the excellence of their prior-stage cultivation (*pubbhāgabhāvanā*)— so too,
