within a mental continuum that possesses an extraordinary excellence of qualities due to the greatness of its aspiration (*abhinīhāra*) and the greatness of its prior practice (*pubbayoga*), [there exists a further distinction].

They are "great female disciples" (*mahāsāvikā*) because they are great female disciples due to having perfected qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). Furthermore, they are so called because of their thorough,

uninterrupted, and long-standing practice— which served as the cause for generating the extraordinary power and function of right view and right concentration, which are the preeminent and primary factors among those very *bodhipakkhiya* (requisites of enlightenment)— and because of their corresponding application of effort (*tajjābhinīhāratā*).
Because they have attained the highest perfection in wisdom and concentration respectively, and because they stand pre-eminent among all qualities,

these two are called the "foremost female disciples" (aggasāvikā). However, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the others are called "great female disciples" (mahāsāvikā) on account of the greatness of their initial resolve,
the greatness of their prior application, and the excellence of the special qualities they have acquired.
The other elder nuns, such as Tissā, Vīrā, Dhīrā, and so forth, are called "ordinary *sāvika*s" because they lack the greatness of their initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*) and other such qualities.
They, however, are not limited in number like the Chief *Sāvika*s or the Great *Sāvika*s; rather, they should be understood to number many hundreds and many thousands.
Thus, they are threefold according to the division of Chief *Sāvika*s and so on. Likewise, they are threefold according to the division of the emptiness liberation (*suññatavimokkha*) and so on.

It is fourfold by way of the classification of the practice (*paṭipadā*) and so forth; fivefold by way of the classification of the predominance of the faculties (*indriya*); likewise fivefold by way of the classification of the mode of progress (*paṭipatti*) and so forth;

sixfold by way of the signless (*animitta*), the liberation (*vimutta*), and so on; sevenfold by way of the distinction of inclinations (*adhimutti*); eightfold by way of the classification of the burden-bearing practice (*dhura-paṭipadā*) and so forth;

and ninefold and tenfold by way of the classification of liberation (*vimutti*). Furthermore, these [types of persons] are [further categorized] according to the aforementioned distinction of burdens (*dhura*).

When analyzed, they become twenty; when analyzed by way of the analysis of the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*), they become forty. Furthermore, when analyzed by way of the divisions of the modes of practice and the divisions of the burdens (*dhura*), they become eighty.
Alternatively, when analyzed by way of the divisions of emptiness (*suññatā*), liberation (*vimutta*), and so forth, they become two hundred and forty.
Again, when analyzed by way of the further divisions of the faculties (*indriya*), they become one thousand two hundred and two.
Thus it is. In this way, the manifold diversity of these elder nuns (therīs) according to their own respective virtues should be understood.
This is the summary here; however, the detailed account should be taken according to the method already stated in the commentary on the *Theragāthā*.
The commentary on the verses of the Elder Nun Sumedhā is concluded.
The commentary on the Mahānipāta is finished.
The concluding verses:
To this extent—
“Those who are endowed with the perfected True Dhamma, the heart-born sons born from the mouth of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma— their heirs, fashioned by the Dhamma;
endowed with virtues such as moral discipline, having accomplished their task, and free from taints.”
The elders beginning with Subhūti, and the elder nuns beginning with Therikā—
having brought together all the verses spoken by them, such as those concerning the declaration of final knowledge (*aññabyākaraṇa*), they were compiled as the *Theragāthā*.
“The Great Elders compiled the *Therīgāthā* of the Tathāgata;
and in order to clarify their meaning,
I have undertaken this commentary on the meaning based upon the method of the ancient commentaries.”
Therein, the elucidation of the ultimate meanings, as appropriate in each respective place—
this work titled *Paramatthadīpanī* (The Elucidation of Ultimate Meanings)—
has reached its completion through unconfused analysis.
It consists of ninety-two units according to the recitation sections of the text.
"Thus, by compiling that which has been attained by me,
through the power of that merit, [may there be success] for the teaching of the Lord of the World."
“May all embodied beings, having plunged into the practice of virtue and the other perfections that lead to purity, partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world.”
“May all living beings always be full of reverence for him.
May the Lord of the World, the deity, also rain down in due season;
may he, devoted to the True Dhamma, rule the world by means of the Dhamma alone.”
The commentary on the meaning of the *Therīgāthā* composed by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla,
a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery, is completed.
The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nuns is finished.
